abstract: Information retrieval in a neural network is viewed as a procedure in which the network computes a "most probable" or MAP estimate of the unk(cid:173) nown information. This viewpoint allows the class of probability distributions, P, the neural network can acquire to be explicitly specified. Learning algorithms for the neural network which search for the "most probable" member of P can then be designed. Statistical tests which decide if the "true" or environmental probability distribution is in P can also be developed. Example applications of the theory to the highly nonlinear back-propagation learning algorithm, and the networks of Hopfield and Anderson are discussed.

paragraphs: The paper interprets neural-network information retrieval as maximum a posteriori estimation: the network computes the most probable value of unknown information. This places retrieval within a probabilistic framework and makes it possible to state explicitly which family of probability distributions a network can acquire.

Once that family is specified, learning can be described as a search for its most probable member. The same formulation also supports statistical tests of whether the environmental distribution belongs to the family. These are complementary questions: which available distribution best accounts for the information, and whether the network's available distributions include the one generating it.

The authors discuss applications to backpropagation and to Hopfield and Anderson networks. The framework therefore provides a shared language for analyzing different neural models. Its significance is that retrieval, learning, and representational suitability become connected statistical problems. A network's behavior can be assessed through both the estimate it computes and the range of distributions its model permits it to learn.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic framework links neural retrieval, learning, and tests of whether a network can represent its environment's distribution.

title: Probabilistic Characterization of Neural Model Computations

paragraphs: The paper evaluates bidirectional associative memories using successful recall in a synchronous discrete model. It examines 100 random memories of size 64 by 64 while varying the number of stored vectors. Their observed capacity falls well below the cited upper bound based on the smaller of the two layer dimensions.

On average, these memories achieve about 68% of the capacity of a Hopfield memory with the same number of neurons. Orthonormal coding increases effective storage capacity by only 25%. The authors attribute the restriction to spurious stable states: the network can settle into states that interfere with the intended recall.

The proposed remedy replaces thresholding in the back layer with a nonlinear process called Dominant Label Selection. This can avoid spurious stable states. Its simplest form, a winner-take-all network, is sensitive to faults, so the authors discuss orthogonal or unitary transformations to improve fault tolerance. A Fourier transform implemented by a lens supplies an optical example. The work connects a measured recall limitation with a change to the memory’s update mechanism.
summary.tldr: Bidirectional memories show limited recall capacity, motivating Dominant Label Selection to avoid spurious stable states.

paragraphs: The paper examines how the echolocating bat Eptesicus fuscus combines different echo features into a coherent perception of a target. Echo arrival delay provides information about overall distance, while the echo spectrum provides information about shape. The central issue is how these differently represented signals become an image organized along a common dimension of range.

In the account presented, the bat reconstructs timing differences between echoes from target parts at different distances using spectral information. It combines those reconstructed separations with the absolute delay obtained from echo arrival time. This places both the target's distance and its internal depth structure into a shared time-based representation.

The resulting image corresponds to an echo crosscorrelation function. It illustrates how physiologically distinct representations within one sensory modality can be combined into a unified percept. The abstract also reports echo-delay hyperacuity of 10 nanoseconds, relating unusually fine timing perception to the structure of the range image. The emphasis is on the computation that brings distance and shape information together.
summary.tldr: Bats combine echo arrival timing with spectral information to construct a unified image of target distance and depth.

title: Acoustic-Imaging Computations by Echolocating Bats: Unification of Diversely-Represented Stimulus Features into Whole Images

abstract: We consider feed-forward neural networks with one non-linear hidden layer and linear output units. The transfer function in the hidden layer are ei(cid:173) ther bell-shaped or sigmoid. In the bell-shaped case, we show how Bern(cid:173) stein polynomials on one hand and the theory of the heat equation on the other are relevant for understanding the properties of the corresponding networks. In particular, these techniques yield simple proofs of universal approximation properties, i.e. of the fact that any reasonable function can be approximated to any degree of precision by a linear combination of bell(cid:173) shaped functions. In addition, in this framework the problem of learning is equivalent to the problem of reversing the time course of a diffusion pro(cid:173) cess. The results obtained in the bell-shaped case can then be applied to the case of sigmoid transfer functions in the hidden layer, yielding similar universality results. A conjecture related to the problem of generalization is briefly examined.

paragraphs: This paper studies feedforward networks with one nonlinear hidden layer and linear output units. Its central question is what functions such networks can represent when the hidden units use either bell-shaped or sigmoid responses. Because the output is linear, the network constructs its answer by combining the responses of its hidden units.

For bell-shaped units, the authors connect network behavior to Bernstein polynomials and the heat equation. These mathematical tools yield simple proofs of universal approximation: linear combinations of bell-shaped functions can approximate any reasonable target function to arbitrary precision. Within the same framework, learning becomes equivalent to reversing the evolution of a diffusion process.

The authors then transfer results from bell-shaped functions to sigmoid functions, obtaining similar universality conclusions. This gives the two kinds of hidden units a shared mathematical treatment despite their different response shapes. The paper also briefly examines a conjecture about generalization. Its main contribution concerns representational capability and a mathematical interpretation of learning, with the diffusion connection offering another way to understand the function-fitting problem.
summary.tldr: Connections to polynomial approximation and diffusion establish universal approximation results for networks with bell-shaped or sigmoid hidden units.

title: Computing with Arrays of Bell-Shaped and Sigmoid Functions

abstract: Five experiments were performed using several neural network architectures to identify the location of a wave in the time ordered graphical results from a medical test. Baseline results from the first experiment found correct identification of the target wave in 85% of cases (n=20). Other experiments investigated the effect of different architectures and preprocessing the raw data on the results. The methods used seem most appropriate for time oriented graphical data which has a clear starting point such as electrophoresis Or spectrometry rather than continuous teSts such as ECGs and EEGs.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether neural networks can locate a particular wave in graphical results from a medical test. The input is ordered in time, and the task is to identify the target wave's location. This focuses the recognition problem on a feature within a trace, rather than on assigning a label to the entire test.

The researchers perform five experiments using several network architectures. The first establishes a baseline of correct target identification in 85% of 20 cases. Other experiments examine how the network architecture and preprocessing of the raw data affect the results, treating both representation and model design as parts of the recognition problem.

The authors conclude that the methods appear best suited to time-oriented graphs with a clear starting point, such as electrophoresis or spectrometry. They distinguish these from continuous recordings such as ECGs and EEGs. This stated scope matters because a defined beginning gives the graphical sequence a shared temporal reference. The findings therefore support a particular kind of wave-location application rather than unrestricted analysis of medical traces.
summary.tldr: Five experiments explore neural wave localization in medical graphs, with an initial 85% success rate and strongest suitability for traces with clear starting points.

title: Computer Recognition of Wave Location in Graphical Data by a Neural Network

abstract: Spotting tasks require detection of target patterns from a background of richly varied non-target inputs. The performance measure of interest for these tasks, called the figure of merit (FOM), is the detection rate for target patterns when the false alarm rate is in an acceptable range. A new approach to training spotters is presented which computes the FOM gradient for each input pattern and then directly maximizes the FOM using b ackpropagati on. This eliminates the need for thresholds during training. It also uses network resources to model Bayesian a posteriori probability functions accurately only for patterns which have a significant effect on the detection accuracy over the false alarm rate of interest. FOM training increased detection accuracy by 5 percentage points for a hybrid radial basis function (RBF) - hidden Markov model (HMM) wordspotter on the credit-card speech corpus.

paragraphs: Spotting systems must detect target patterns amid many kinds of irrelevant input. Their useful performance depends on detecting targets while keeping false alarms within an acceptable range. This paper trains a network directly for that tradeoff through a figure of merit, defined by detection performance over the false-alarm range of interest.

The method computes each input pattern’s contribution to the figure-of-merit gradient and uses backpropagation to maximize the objective. This removes the need for thresholds during training. It also concentrates accurate posterior-probability modeling on patterns that materially affect detection in the relevant false-alarm range, directing network resources toward the decisions that influence the evaluation measure.

Applied to a wordspotter combining a radial basis function network with a hidden Markov model, the method increased detection accuracy by five percentage points on the credit-card speech corpus. The finding supports aligning the training objective with the operational detection criterion. Here, that alignment concerns a particular range of acceptable false alarms, rather than detection accuracy considered in isolation.
summary.tldr: Directly optimizing detection over an acceptable false-alarm range improved a hybrid wordspotter’s accuracy by five percentage points.

title: Figure of Merit Training for Detection and Spotting

abstract: We study model feed forward networks as time series predictors in the stationary limit. The focus is on complex, yet non-chaotic, behavior. The main question we address is whether the asymptotic behavior is governed by the architecture, regardless the details of the weights . We find hierarchies among classes of architectures with respect to the attract or dimension of the long term sequence they are capable of generating; larger number of hidden units can generate higher dimensional attractors. In the case of a perceptron, we develop the stationary solution for general weights, and show that the flow is typically one dimensional. The relaxation time from an arbitrary initial condition to the stationary solution is found to scale linearly with the size of the network. In multilayer networks, the number of hidden units gives bounds on the number and dimension of the possible attractors. We conclude that long term prediction (in the non-chaotic regime) with such models is governed by attractor dynamics related to the architecture. paragraphs: This paper studies what feedforward neural networks can generate when used as time-series predictors over long periods. It focuses on stationary, non-chaotic behavior and asks how strongly network architecture constrains the eventual sequence, beyond the particular choices of weights. The key object is the attractor: the long-term behavior toward which the generated sequence settles.

For a perceptron, the authors derive a stationary solution for general weights and find that its flow is typically one-dimensional. They also find that the time needed to approach the stationary solution grows linearly with network size. These results connect a simple architecture to both its eventual dynamics and the duration of its transient behavior.

For multilayer networks, the number of hidden units bounds the number and dimensions of possible attractors. More hidden units can support higher-dimensional long-term behavior. The central implication is specific to the studied non-chaotic regime: architecture helps determine the dynamical possibilities available to a predictor, so long-term prediction cannot be understood solely through its fitted weights.
summary.tldr: In non-chaotic time-series prediction, network architecture constrains the attractors and long-term dynamics a model can generate.

title: Analytical Study of the Interplay between Architecture and Predictability

abstract: A fundamental problem with the modeling of chaotic time series data is that minimizing short-term prediction errors does not guarantee a match between the reconstructed attractors of model and experiments. We introduce a modeling paradigm that simultaneously learns to short-tenn predict and to locate the outlines of the attractor by a new way of nonlinear principal component analysis. Closed-loop predictions are constrained to stay within these outlines, to prevent divergence from the attractor. Learning is exceptionally fast: parameter estimation for the 1000 sample laser data from the 1991 Santa Fe time series competition took less than a minute on a 166 MHz Pentium PC.

paragraphs: A model of a chaotic time series can predict the next few observations well yet reproduce the wrong attractor. The attractor describes the structure within which the system's dynamics evolve. This paper addresses the gap between minimizing short-term prediction errors and reproducing that larger dynamical structure.

The proposed approach learns short-term prediction and the outlines of the attractor simultaneously. It identifies those outlines using a new form of nonlinear principal component analysis. Closed-loop predictions are constrained to remain within the learned outlines, with the aim of preventing the predicted dynamics from diverging away from the attractor.

The authors report fast parameter estimation on a 1,000-sample laser dataset from the Santa Fe time-series competition: less than one minute on a 166 MHz Pentium PC. This is a concrete timing result for that example. The broader methodological contribution is to incorporate attractor structure directly into learning and prediction, addressing a property that short-term prediction accuracy alone does not guarantee.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning short-term predictions and attractor outlines constrains closed-loop chaotic forecasts to remain within the learned dynamical region.

title: Robust Learning of Chaotic Attractors

abstract: Many researchers have explored methods for hierarchical reinforce(cid:173) ment learning (RL) with temporal abstractions, in which abstract actions are defined that can perform many primitive actions before terminating. However, little is known about learning with state ab(cid:173) stractions, in which aspects of the state space are ignored. In previ(cid:173) ous work, we developed the MAXQ method for hierarchical RL. In this paper, we define five conditions under which state abstraction can be combined with the MAXQ value function decomposition. We prove that the MAXQ-Q learning algorithm converges under these conditions and show experimentally that state abstraction is important for the successful application of MAXQ-Q learning.

paragraphs: The paper studies how hierarchical reinforcement learning can ignore selected aspects of the state while still learning reliably. It distinguishes state abstraction from temporal abstraction, where a higher-level action may execute many primitive actions before ending. State abstraction instead simplifies what the learner represents about its situation.

The authors work within MAXQ, a framework that decomposes the value function for a hierarchy of tasks. They define five conditions under which state abstraction can be combined with this decomposition. These conditions provide a formal basis for deciding when aspects of the state can be omitted while preserving the stated learning guarantee.

They prove that MAXQ-Q learning converges under those conditions and present experiments showing that state abstraction is important for successful application of the algorithm. The theoretical result is conditional on the specified requirements. Together, the proof and experiments connect representational simplification with both convergence and practical learning, explaining how a hierarchy can benefit from simplifying the states used within it.
summary.tldr: Five conditions allow state abstraction in MAXQ with a convergence proof, while experiments show its practical importance.

title: State Abstraction in MAXQ Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning

paragraphs: The paper develops a unified approach to adaptive transform coding for compression. Transform coders are often assembled by choosing a transform and then separately arranging bit allocation and quantization. The authors instead begin with a probabilistic model so that the coding procedure can be derived from a common foundation rather than assembled from loosely connected choices.

Their starting model is a mixture of constrained Gaussian mixtures with latent variables. From it, they derive a coding algorithm that is a constrained form of the generalized Lloyd algorithm for vector quantizer design. The derivation also produces a new transform basis explicitly optimized for coding. This makes the choice of representation part of the compression objective itself.

Image compression experiments report signal-to-noise ratio improvements of up to 3 dB over global transform coding and 0.5 to 2 dB over other adaptive transform coders. These are reported experimental gains, with the largest global-transform improvement expressed as an upper observed gain. The results support coordinating transform design and coding decisions within the proposed probabilistic framework.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic mixture model yields a coding-optimized transform algorithm that improves image compression signal-to-noise ratio in experiments.

title: From Mixtures of Mixtures to Adaptive Transform Coding

abstract: We present three ways of combining linear programming with the kernel trick to find value function approximations for reinforcement learning. One formulation is based on SVM regression; the second is based on the Bellman equation; and the third seeks only to ensure that good moves have an advantage over bad moves. All formu(cid:173) lations attempt to minimize the number of support vectors while fitting the data. Experiments in a difficult, synthetic maze problem show that all three formulations give excellent performance, but the advantage formulation is much easier to train. Unlike policy gradi(cid:173) ent methods, the kernel methods described here can easily 'adjust the complexity of the function approximator to fit the complexity of the value function.

paragraphs: The paper presents three methods for approximating value functions in reinforcement learning using linear programming and kernels. A value function supplies evaluations that help an agent choose actions. The shared aim is to fit the available data while keeping the number of support vectors small, linking the quality of the approximation to the size of its representation.

The three formulations impose different demands on learning. One follows support vector regression, another uses the Bellman equation, and a third asks only that good moves receive an advantage over bad moves. The last formulation focuses on the distinction needed for choosing between actions, rather than requiring the same kind of value fit as the other approaches.

All three perform excellently on a difficult synthetic maze problem, but the advantage formulation is much easier to train. The authors also emphasize that these kernel methods can readily adjust approximator complexity to value-function complexity. The reported results make the training objective an important practical choice even among methods with strong task performance.
summary.tldr: Three kernel-based value approximators perform strongly on a synthetic maze, with an action-advantage formulation proving much easier to train.

title: Batch Value Function Approximation via Support Vectors

abstract: Experimental data has shown that synaptic strength modification in some types of biological neurons depends upon precise spike tim(cid:173) ing differences between presynaptic and postsynaptic spikes. Sev(cid:173) eral temporally-asymmetric Hebbian learning rules motivated by this data have been proposed. We argue that such learning rules are suitable to analog VLSI implementation. We describe an eas(cid:173) ily tunable circuit to modify the weight of a silicon spiking neuron according to those learning rules. Test results from the fabrication of the circuit using a O.6J.lm CMOS process are given.

paragraphs: Some biological neurons change their connection strengths according to the precise timing difference between incoming and outgoing spikes. This observation motivates learning rules in which the temporal relationship between spikes matters. The paper investigates how such temporally asymmetric Hebbian rules can be implemented in analog silicon circuitry.

The authors argue that these rules are suitable for analog VLSI and describe a circuit that changes the weight of a silicon spiking neuron accordingly. A central design feature is that the circuit is easily tunable. This makes the work a concrete hardware treatment of timing-dependent learning, connecting a proposed rule for synaptic modification with a circuit that can implement it.

The circuit was fabricated using a 0.6-micrometer CMOS process, and the paper presents test results from that fabrication. Its contribution therefore extends beyond proposing a learning rule or outlining an implementation. It supplies a built circuit and experimental tests, supporting investigation of how biologically motivated changes in connection strength can be realized in silicon.
summary.tldr: The paper presents and tests a tunable analog circuit that implements spike-timing-dependent changes to a silicon neuron's weight.

title: Citcuits for VLSI Implementation of Temporally Asymmetric Hebbian Learning

abstract: We consider a problem of blind source separation from a set of instan(cid:173) taneous linear mixtures, where the mixing matrix is unknown. It was discovered recently, that exploiting the sparsity of sources in an appro(cid:173) priate representation according to some signal dictionary, dramatically improves the quality of separation. In this work we use the property of multi scale transforms, such as wavelet or wavelet packets, to decompose signals into sets of local features with various degrees of sparsity. We use this intrinsic property for selecting the best (most sparse) subsets of features for further separation. The performance of the algorithm is ver(cid:173) ified on noise-free and noisy data. Experiments with simulated signals, musical sounds and images demonstrate significant improvement of sep(cid:173) aration quality over previously reported results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover separate sources from observed signals that are instantaneous linear mixtures. The mixing matrix is unknown, so the method must work without being told how the sources were combined. Its starting point is that separation can improve when sources have sparse representations in an appropriate collection of signal features.

The authors use multiscale transforms, including wavelets and wavelet packets, to break signals into local features. Different subsets of those features have different degrees of sparsity. The algorithm exploits this variation by choosing the sparsest subsets for subsequent separation. Feature selection is therefore tied to where the transformed signals offer the strongest sparse structure.

The approach is evaluated on both noisy and noise-free data, with experiments covering simulated signals, musical sounds, and images. The authors report substantial improvements in separation quality over previously reported results. These findings support selecting informative parts of a multiscale representation for the tested separation problems, while the stated problem formulation remains unknown instantaneous linear mixing.
summary.tldr: Selecting the sparsest subsets of multiscale signal features improves blind source separation in experiments with signals, music, and images.

title: Blind Source Separation via Multinode Sparse Representation

abstract: We propose a new approach to reinforcement learning which combines least squares function approximation with policy iteration. Our method is model-free and completely off policy. We are motivated by the least squares temporal difference learning algorithm (LSTD), which is known for its efﬁcient use of sample experiences compared to pure temporal difference algorithms. LSTD is ideal for prediction problems, however it heretofore has not had a straightforward application to control problems. Moreover, approximations learned by LSTD are strongly inﬂuenced by the visitation distribution over states. Our new algorithm, Least Squares Policy Iteration (LSPI) addresses these issues. The result is an off-policy method which can use (or reuse) data collected from any source. We have tested LSPI on several problems, including a bicycle simulator in which it learns to guide the bicycle to a goal efﬁciently by merely observing a relatively small number of completely random trials.

paragraphs: Least Squares Policy Iteration combines least-squares function approximation with policy iteration for reinforcement learning. Its motivation comes from least-squares temporal-difference learning, which uses experience efficiently for prediction. The paper seeks to carry that benefit into control, where the learner must improve its action choices rather than only evaluate behavior.

The authors identify two challenges: the lack of a straightforward control application for the earlier method and the strong influence of state-visitation frequencies on its approximations. LSPI addresses these issues through a model-free, fully off-policy approach. It can use or reuse experience gathered from any source, allowing learning to draw on observations collected outside the policy currently being improved.

The method is tested on several problems, including a bicycle simulator. In that example, it learns to guide the bicycle to a goal efficiently after observing a relatively small number of entirely random trials. The result illustrates the practical value of combining reusable experience with least-squares estimation in a procedure that improves a control policy.
summary.tldr: LSPI combines least-squares estimation and policy iteration to learn control policies from reusable off-policy experience.

title: Model-Free Least-Squares Policy Iteration

abstract: In this work, we study an information ﬁltering model where the relevance labels associated to a sequence of feature vectors are realizations of an unknown probabilistic linear function. Building on the analysis of a re- stricted version of our model, we derive a general ﬁltering rule based on the margin of a ridge regression estimator. While our rule may observe the label of a vector only by classfying the vector as relevant, experiments on a real-world document ﬁltering problem show that the performance of our rule is close to that of the on-line classiﬁer which is allowed to observe all labels. These empirical results are complemented by a theo- retical analysis where we consider a randomized variant of our rule and prove that its expected number of mistakes is never much larger than that of the optimal ﬁltering rule which knows the hidden linear model.

paragraphs: An information filter must decide which arriving items are relevant, but its decisions can also determine what feedback it receives. This paper studies a setting where an item's label becomes visible only when the filter marks it relevant. Relevance labels are assumed to arise from an unknown probabilistic linear function of the feature vectors.

Starting with an analysis of a restricted version of this model, the authors derive a more general filtering rule based on the margin of a ridge regression estimator. The margin informs the relevance decision, linking prediction to selective feedback. In a real document-filtering experiment, the rule performs close to an online classifier that can observe every label.

The theoretical analysis concerns a randomized variant of the rule. Its expected mistake count is shown to stay within a controlled excess over that of an optimal filter that knows the hidden linear model. The empirical comparison and theoretical guarantee therefore address distinct versions or aspects of the approach, both under the stated information-filtering setup.
summary.tldr: A ridge-regression margin rule learns with selectively revealed labels, with encouraging document-filtering results and a mistake guarantee for a randomized variant.

title: Margin-Based Algorithms for Information Filtering

abstract: We introduce a novel learning algorithm for binary classi(cid:12)cation with hyperplane discriminants based on pairs of training points from opposite classes (dyadic hypercuts). This algorithm is further extended to nonlinear discriminants using kernel functions satisfy- ing Mercer’s conditions. An ensemble of simple dyadic hypercuts is learned incrementally by means of a con(cid:12)dence-rated version of Ad- aBoost, which provides a sound strategy for searching through the (cid:12)nite set of hypercut hypotheses. In experiments with real-world datasets from the UCI repository, the generalization performance of the hypercut classi(cid:12)ers was found to be comparable to that of SVMs and k-NN classi(cid:12)ers. Furthermore, the computational cost of classi(cid:12)cation (at run time) was found to be similar to, or bet- ter than, that of SVM. Similarly to SVMs, boosted dyadic kernel discriminants tend to maximize the margin (via AdaBoost). In contrast to SVMs, however, we o(cid:11)er an on-line and incremental learning machine for building kernel discriminants whose complex- ity (number of kernel evaluations) can be directly controlled (traded o(cid:11) for accuracy).

paragraphs: The paper builds a binary classifier from simple decision boundaries defined by pairs of training examples from opposite classes. Each pair supplies a candidate hyperplane, called a dyadic hypercut. Kernel functions satisfying Mercer's conditions extend these simple boundaries to nonlinear classification, allowing the same construction to represent more complex separations.

A confidence-rated version of AdaBoost adds hypercuts incrementally to form an ensemble. Boosting provides a strategy for searching the finite collection of candidate boundaries, and the resulting classifier tends to increase the classification margin. The incremental construction also gives direct control over the number of kernel evaluations, allowing prediction cost to be traded against accuracy.

On the reported UCI datasets, generalization was comparable to support vector machines and nearest-neighbor classifiers. Prediction cost was similar to or better than that of support vector machines. These findings support the method as an online, incremental alternative with an adjustable computational budget; they do not establish that it is uniformly more accurate or faster.
summary.tldr: Boosting simple boundaries defined by opposite-class example pairs produces incremental kernel classifiers with controllable prediction cost.

title: Boosted Dyadic Kernel Discriminants

abstract: This paper addresses the issue of numerical computation in machine learning domains based on similarity metrics, such as kernel methods, spectral techniques and Gaussian processes. It presents a general solution strategy based on Krylov subspace iteration and fast N-body learning methods. The experiments show significant gains in computation and storage on datasets arising in image segmentation, object detection and dimensionality reduction. The paper also presents theoretical bounds on the stability of these methods.

It presents a general solution strategy based on Krylov subspace iteration and fast N-body learning methods. The experiments show significant gains in computation and storage on datasets arising in image segmentation, object detection and dimensionality reduction. The paper also presents theoretical bounds on the stability of these methods.

paragraphs: Many learning methods organize their computations around similarities between data points. This paper addresses numerical computation shared by kernel methods, spectral techniques, and Gaussian processes. Its focus is on the computational machinery underlying these approaches, offering a strategy that can apply across several learning domains.

The proposed strategy combines Krylov subspace iteration with fast N-body learning methods. These are brought together as a general solution approach for the numerical problems arising in similarity-based learning. The scope matters: the paper treats computational efficiency as a common challenge across methods, rather than tying its contribution to one prediction task or one type of dataset.

Experiments on datasets used for image segmentation, object detection, and dimensionality reduction show significant improvements in computation and storage. The paper also supplies theoretical bounds on numerical stability. Together, these contributions address resource use and the reliability of the numerical procedures. The experimental gains establish benefits in the tested settings, while the stability analysis provides a separate theoretical basis for assessing the methods.
summary.tldr: Combining Krylov iteration with fast N-body methods yields reported computation and storage gains for similarity-based learning, alongside theoretical stability bounds.

title: Fast Krylov Methods for N-Body Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of learning accurate models from multiple sources of "nearby" data. Given distinct samples from multiple data sources and estimates of the dissimilarities between these sources, we provide a general theory of which samples should be used to learn models for each source. This theory is applicable in a broad decision-theoretic learning framework, and yields results for classification and regression generally, and for density estimation within the exponential family. A key component of our approach is the development of approximate triangle inequalities for expected loss, which may be of independent interest.

Given distinct samples from multiple data sources and estimates of the dissimilarities between these sources, we provide a general theory of which samples should be used to learn models for each source. This theory is applicable in a broad decision-theoretic learning framework, and yields results for classification and regression generally, and for density estimation within the exponential family. A key component of our approach is the development of approximate triangle inequalities for expected loss, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: When several related data sources are available, learning a model for one source raises a selection question: which samples from the other sources should contribute? This paper studies that question for sources that are nearby but distinct. Its inputs include separate samples from each source and estimates of how dissimilar the sources are.

The authors develop a general theory for selecting samples to learn a model for each source. The formulation uses a broad decision-theoretic learning framework, with results covering classification and regression, as well as density estimation within the exponential family. Source relationships therefore inform the choice of training information across several kinds of prediction problems.

A central technical contribution is a collection of approximate triangle inequalities for expected loss. These provide relationships among losses that support the sample-selection theory and may also be useful independently. The paper's significance is its principled treatment of when information from related sources should enter a source-specific model, using dissimilarity estimates as explicit inputs to that reasoning.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a theory for choosing training samples across related data sources using estimates of their dissimilarity.

title: Learning from Multiple Sources

abstract: We investigate a new, convex relaxation of an expectation-maximization (EM) variant that approximates a standard objective while eliminating local minima. First, a cautionary result is presented, showing that any convex relaxation of EM over hidden variables must give trivial results if any dependence on the missing values is retained. Although this appears to be a strong negative outcome, we then demonstrate how the problem can be bypassed by using equivalence relations instead of value assignments over hidden variables. In particular, we develop new algorithms for estimating exponential conditional models that only require equivalence relation information over the variable values. This reformulation leads to an exact expression for EM variants in a wide range of problems. We then develop a semidefinite relaxation that yields global training by eliminating local minima.

In particular, we develop new algorithms for estimating exponential conditional models that only require equivalence relation information over the variable values. paragraphs: Training models with hidden variables often involves objectives with local minima. This paper investigates a convex relaxation of an expectation-maximization variant, aiming to approximate a standard objective while removing those local minima. It begins by identifying a fundamental obstacle: convex relaxations over hidden variables yield trivial results if dependence on the missing values is retained.

The authors bypass this obstacle by changing how hidden information is represented. They use equivalence relations instead of assigning particular values to hidden variables. This supports new algorithms for estimating exponential conditional models that need information about equivalence among variable values, shifting the formulation away from the assignments that cause the negative result.

The reformulation gives an exact expression for EM variants across a wide range of problems. The authors then develop a semidefinite relaxation that permits global training without local minima. The distinction between these steps matters: the equivalence-based expression is exact, while the convex training method is a relaxation. The paper's central contribution is a representation change that makes this globally optimizable formulation possible.
summary.tldr: Representing hidden information through equivalence relations enables a semidefinite relaxation of EM-style training that eliminates local minima.

title: Convex Relaxations of Latent Variable Training

abstract: We introduce a functional representation of time series which allows forecasts to be performed over an unspeciﬁed horizon with progressively-revealed informa- tion sets. By virtue of using Gaussian processes, a complete covariance matrix between forecasts at several time-steps is available. This information is put to use in an application to actively trade price spreads between commodity futures con- tracts. The approach delivers impressive out-of-sample risk-adjusted returns after transaction costs on a portfolio of 30 spreads.
originalAbstract: We introduce a functional representation of time series which allows forecasts to be performed over an unspeciﬁed horizon with progressively-revealed informa- tion sets. By virtue of using Gaussian processes, a complete covariance matrix between forecasts at several time-steps is available. This information is put to use in an application to actively trade price spreads between commodity futures con- tracts. The approach delivers impressive out-of-sample risk-adjusted returns after transaction costs on a portfolio of 30 spreads.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a way to represent time series as functions so that forecasts can extend over a horizon that is not specified in advance. The representation also accommodates information becoming available progressively. These features address forecasting situations in which both the future interval of interest and the evidence available for prediction can evolve.

The method uses Gaussian processes, which provide a complete covariance matrix for forecasts at multiple future times. That matrix describes how uncertainty at one forecast time relates to uncertainty at another. Consequently, the forecasting output includes relationships among future predictions, giving the application access to more than separate estimates for individual time steps.

The authors use this information to actively trade price differences between commodity futures contracts. On a portfolio of 30 spreads, they report impressive out-of-sample returns relative to risk after accounting for transaction costs. The stated result demonstrates the approach in that trading application, where the dependence among forecasts is put to practical use.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process representation supports flexible-horizon forecasts with joint uncertainty and delivers strong reported trading results on 30 commodity spreads.

title: Augmented Functional Time Series Representation and Forecasting with Gaussian Processes

abstract: We describe a new algorithm, Relaxed Survey Propagation (RSP), for ﬁnding MAP conﬁgurations in Markov random ﬁelds. We compare its performance with state-of-the-art algorithms including the max-product belief propagation, its se- quential tree-reweighted variant, residual (sum-product) belief propagation, and tree-structured expectation propagation. We show that it outperforms all ap- proaches for Ising models with mixed couplings, as well as on a web person disambiguation task formulated as a supervised clustering problem.
originalAbstract: We describe a new algorithm, Relaxed Survey Propagation (RSP), for ﬁnding MAP conﬁgurations in Markov random ﬁelds. We compare its performance with state-of-the-art algorithms including the max-product belief propagation, its se- quential tree-reweighted variant, residual (sum-product) belief propagation, and tree-structured expectation propagation. We show that it outperforms all ap- proaches for Ising models with mixed couplings, as well as on a web person disambiguation task formulated as a supervised clustering problem.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Relaxed Survey Propagation, or RSP, for finding MAP configurations in Markov random fields. A MAP configuration is a joint assignment of variables with the highest probability under the model. The task requires choosing variables together, because relationships among them affect which complete assignment is most plausible.

The authors assess RSP against several established inference methods: max-product belief propagation, sequential tree-reweighted max-product, residual sum-product belief propagation, and tree-structured expectation propagation. This comparison places the proposed algorithm alongside different approaches to inference in related graphical models. The central evidence is comparative performance on the problems studied.

RSP outperforms all of these compared approaches on Ising models with mixed couplings and on a web person disambiguation task. The latter is formulated as supervised clustering, connecting the inference method to a problem of separating references to people on the web. These results establish favorable empirical performance in both the stated model setting and an applied clustering task, rather than a universal guarantee across Markov random fields.
summary.tldr: Relaxed Survey Propagation outperforms the compared inference methods on mixed-coupling Ising models and a web person disambiguation task.

title: Cooled and Relaxed Survey Propagation for MRFs

abstract: Estimation of three-dimensional articulated human pose and motion from images is a central problem in computer vision. Much of the previous work has been limited by the use of crude generative models of humans represented as articu- lated collections of simple parts such as cylinders. Automatic initialization of such models has proved difﬁcult and most approaches assume that the size and shape of the body parts are known a priori. In this paper we propose a method for automatically recovering a detailed parametric model of non-rigid body shape and pose from monocular imagery. Speciﬁcally, we represent the body using a param- eterized triangulated mesh model that is learned from a database of human range scans. We demonstrate a discriminative method to directly recover the model pa- rameters from monocular images using a conditional mixture of kernel regressors. This predicted pose and shape are used to initialize a generative model for more detailed pose and shape estimation. The resulting approach allows fully automatic pose and shape recovery from monocular and multi-camera imagery. Experimen- tal results show that our method is capable of robustly recovering articulated pose, shape and biometric measurements (e.g. height, weight, etc.) in both calibrated and uncalibrated camera environments.

paragraphs: Recovering a person's three-dimensional pose and body shape from images requires both a useful body representation and a way to fit it automatically. Earlier approaches often used simple articulated parts, struggled with initialization, and assumed known body dimensions. This paper combines direct image-based prediction with subsequent generative refinement to address those difficulties.

The body is represented by a parameterized triangular mesh learned from human range scans. A discriminative model, specifically a conditional mixture of kernel regressors, predicts the mesh's pose and shape parameters from a single image. These predictions then initialize a generative model that performs more detailed estimation. The first stage supplies a starting configuration for the second.

The resulting system supports fully automatic recovery from monocular and multiple-camera imagery. Reported experiments show robust estimation of articulated pose, body shape, and biometric measurements such as height and weight in calibrated and uncalibrated camera environments. The contribution is an integrated route from an image to a detailed body model, with automatic initialization built into the estimation process.
summary.tldr: Direct image-based prediction initializes a detailed generative body model for automatic recovery of human pose, shape, and biometric measurements.

title: Combined discriminative and generative articulated pose and non-rigid shape estimation

abstract: We describe an application of probabilistic modeling and inference technology to the problem of analyzing sensor data in the setting of an intensive care unit (ICU). In particular, we consider the arterial-line blood pressure sensor, which is subject to frequent data artifacts that cause false alarms in the ICU and make the raw data almost useless for automated decision making. The problem is complicated by the fact that the sensor data are acquired at fixed intervals whereas the events causing data artifacts may occur at any time and have durations that may be significantly shorter than the data collection interval. We show that careful modeling of the sensor, combined with a general technique for detecting sub-interval events and estimating their duration, enables effective detection of artifacts and accurate estimation of the underlying blood pressure values.

In particular, we consider the arterial-line blood pressure sensor, which is subject to frequent data artifacts that cause false alarms in the ICU and make the raw data almost useless for automated decision making. The problem is complicated by the fact that the sensor data are acquired at fixed intervals whereas the events causing data artifacts may occur at any time and have durations that may be significantly shorter than the data collection interval. We show that careful modeling of the sensor, combined with a general technique for detecting sub-interval events and estimating their duration, enables effective detection of artifacts and accurate estimation of the underlying blood pressure values.

paragraphs: Arterial-line blood pressure measurements in intensive care can contain frequent artifacts that trigger false alarms and hinder automated interpretation. This paper applies probabilistic modeling to distinguish those disturbances from the blood pressure values of interest. The challenge involves both understanding the sensor and reasoning about events that occur between its recorded observations.

Measurements arrive at fixed intervals, but the events causing artifacts can begin at any time and may last much less than one interval. A model therefore needs to accommodate a finer event timescale than the observation schedule. The authors combine careful sensor modeling with a general technique that detects these sub-interval events and estimates their duration.

The reported approach effectively identifies artifacts and accurately estimates underlying blood pressure values. Those two results are linked: explaining a brief disturbance helps interpret the measurement it affected. The contribution shows how explicit modeling of short event timing can support useful inference from regularly sampled sensor data, even when the events themselves are shorter than the gaps between observations.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic sensor modeling detects artifacts shorter than sampling intervals and supports accurate underlying blood pressure estimation.

title: Probabilistic detection of short events, with application to critical care monitoring

abstract: Hypergraph clustering refers to the process of extracting maximally coherent groups from a set of objects using high-order (rather than pairwise) similarities. Traditional approaches to this problem are based on the idea of partitioning the input data into a user-defined number of classes, thereby obtaining the clusters as a by-product of the partitioning process. In this paper, we provide a radically different perspective to the problem. In contrast to the classical approach, we attempt to provide a meaningful formalization of the very notion of a cluster and we show that game theory offers an attractive and unexplored perspective that serves well our purpose. Specifically, we show that the hypergraph clustering problem can be naturally cast into a non-cooperative multi-player ``clustering game, whereby the notion of a cluster is equivalent to a classical game-theoretic equilibrium concept. From the computational viewpoint, we show that the problem of finding the equilibria of our clustering game is equivalent to locally optimizing a polynomial function over the standard simplex, and we provide a discrete-time dynamics to perform this optimization. Experiments are presented which show the superiority of our approach over state-of-the-art hypergraph clustering techniques.

paragraphs: Hypergraph clustering groups objects using similarities involving more than two objects at a time. The paper questions the usual starting point of dividing all the data into a predetermined number of groups. Instead, it asks what makes a collection of objects a coherent cluster in its own right.

The authors formulate a non-cooperative game with multiple players and connect clusters to a classical equilibrium concept. This gives the proposed notion of a cluster a mathematical definition grounded in the game's behavior. The contribution is therefore both a different interpretation of clustering and a route to computing the groups that satisfy that interpretation.

Computationally, finding these equilibria is equivalent to locally optimizing a polynomial over the standard simplex, a space of nonnegative weights summing to one. The authors provide a discrete-time update process for this optimization. Their experiments report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art hypergraph methods. The local nature of the optimization is significant: the stated equivalence concerns local optimization, rather than a promise to find a global optimum.
summary.tldr: The paper defines hypergraph clusters through game-theoretic equilibria and computes them through local polynomial optimization.

title: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Hypergraph Clustering

abstract: Sparse methods for supervised learning aim at finding good linear predictors from as few variables as possible, i.e., with small cardinality of their supports. This combinatorial selection problem is often turned into a convex optimization problem by replacing the cardinality function by its convex envelope (tightest convex lower bound), in this case the L1-norm. In this paper, we investigate more general set-functions than the cardinality, that may incorporate prior knowledge or structural constraints which are common in many applications: namely, we show that for nondecreasing submodular set-functions, the corresponding convex envelope can be obtained from its Lovasz extension, a common tool in submodular analysis. This defines a family of polyhedral norms, for which we provide generic algorithmic tools (subgradients and proximal operators) and theoretical results (conditions for support recovery or high-dimensional inference). By selecting specific submodular functions, we can give a new interpretation to known norms, such as those based on rank-statistics or grouped norms with potentially overlapping groups; we also define new norms, in particular ones that can be used as non-factorial priors for supervised learning.

This combinatorial selection problem is often turned into a convex optimization problem by replacing the cardinality function by its convex envelope (tightest convex lower bound), in this case the L1-norm. In this paper, we investigate more general set-functions than the cardinality, that may incorporate prior knowledge or structural constraints which are common in many applications: namely, we show that for nondecreasing submodular set-functions, the corresponding convex envelope can be obtained from its Lovasz extension, a common tool in submodular analysis. paragraphs: Sparse supervised learning seeks useful linear predictors that rely on few variables. The usual selection cost counts the chosen variables, and its convex relaxation leads to the L1 norm. This paper generalizes that idea by allowing the cost of a selected set to express prior knowledge or structural preferences.

For nondecreasing submodular set functions, the authors show how to obtain the corresponding convex envelope through the Lovász extension. This produces a family of polyhedral norms. They provide computational tools, including subgradients and proximal operators, along with theoretical conditions for recovering the selected-variable support and for inference in high-dimensional settings.

Choosing different submodular functions gives new interpretations of known penalties, including rank-based norms and group norms with overlapping groups. The framework also yields new norms that can encode priors involving dependencies among variables. Its significance is a systematic connection between a structured preference over variable sets and a convex penalty that can be optimized, with guarantees stated through the conditions developed in the paper.
summary.tldr: Submodular set functions yield structured sparsity norms through convex envelopes, unifying existing penalties and enabling new ones.

title: Structured sparsity-inducing norms through submodular functions

abstract: A number of recent scientific and engineering problems require signals to be decomposed into a product of a slowly varying positive envelope and a quickly varying carrier whose instantaneous frequency also varies slowly over time. Although signal processing provides algorithms for so-called amplitude- and frequency-demodulation (AFD), there are well known problems with all of the existing methods. Motivated by the fact that AFD is ill-posed, we approach the problem using probabilistic inference. The new approach, called probabilistic amplitude and frequency demodulation (PAFD), models instantaneous frequency using an auto-regressive generalization of the von Mises distribution, and the envelopes using Gaussian auto-regressive dynamics with a positivity constraint. A novel form of expectation propagation is used for inference. We demonstrate that although PAFD is computationally demanding, it outperforms previous approaches on synthetic and real signals in clean, noisy and missing data settings.
originalAbstract: A number of recent scientific and engineering problems require signals to be decomposed into a product of a slowly varying positive envelope and a quickly varying carrier whose instantaneous frequency also varies slowly over time. Although signal processing provides algorithms for so-called amplitude- and frequency-demodulation (AFD), there are well known problems with all of the existing methods. Motivated by the fact that AFD is ill-posed, we approach the problem using probabilistic inference. The new approach, called probabilistic amplitude and frequency demodulation (PAFD), models instantaneous frequency using an auto-regressive generalization of the von Mises distribution, and the envelopes using Gaussian auto-regressive dynamics with a positivity constraint. A novel form of expectation propagation is used for inference. We demonstrate that although PAFD is computationally demanding, it outperforms previous approaches on synthetic and real signals in clean, noisy and missing data settings.

paragraphs: Some signals need to be separated into a slowly changing positive amplitude envelope and a rapidly oscillating carrier whose instantaneous frequency changes slowly. This decomposition is ill-posed: the observed signal alone does not uniquely determine the desired components. The paper addresses that ambiguity by treating demodulation as probabilistic inference.

The proposed model assigns explicit temporal dynamics to both components. Instantaneous frequency follows an autoregressive extension of the von Mises distribution, while the envelope follows Gaussian autoregressive dynamics subject to positivity. These modeling choices express how the components are expected to evolve over time. A new form of expectation propagation performs inference.

Experiments on synthetic and real signals show that probabilistic amplitude and frequency demodulation outperforms earlier approaches in clean, noisy, and missing-data settings. The stated trade-off is computational demand: the method is expensive despite its demonstrated performance benefits. Its contribution is to make temporal expectations and amplitude constraints explicit parts of the decomposition, giving probabilistic structure to an otherwise ambiguous task.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model separates signal amplitude and frequency effectively across tested data conditions, at substantial computational cost.

title: Probabilistic amplitude and frequency demodulation

abstract: In this paper, we argue for representing networks as a bag of {\it triangular motifs}, particularly for important network problems that current model-based approaches handle poorly due to computational bottlenecks incurred by using edge representations. Such approaches require both 1-edges and 0-edges (missing edges) to be provided as input, and as a consequence, approximate inference algorithms for these models usually require $\Omega(N^2)$ time per iteration, precluding their application to larger real-world networks. In contrast, triangular modeling requires less computation, while providing equivalent or better inference quality. A triangular motif is a vertex triple containing 2 or 3 edges, and the number of such motifs is $\Theta(\sum_{i}D_{i}^{2})$ (where $D_i$ is the degree of vertex $i$), which is much smaller than $N^2$ for low-maximum-degree networks. Using this representation, we develop a novel mixed-membership network model and approximate inference algorithm suitable for large networks with low max-degree. For networks with high maximum degree, the triangular motifs can be naturally subsampled in a {\it node-centric} fashion, allowing for much faster inference at a small cost in accuracy. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach, when compared to that of an edge-based model, has faster runtime and improved accuracy for mixed-membership community detection. We conclude with a large-scale demonstration on an $N\approx 280,000$-node network, which is infeasible for network models with $\Omega(N^2)$ inference cost.

For high-maximum-degree networks, they propose node-centered motif subsampling, trading a small reported accuracy cost for faster inference.

The paper also demonstrates the approach on a network of approximately 280,000 nodes. The benefit depends on degree structure or subsampling: changing the representation reduces the computational burden in the stated settings while retaining useful information for community inference.
summary.tldr: Representing networks with two- and three-edge triangular motifs enables faster mixed-membership inference, particularly for networks with low maximum degree.

title: On Triangular versus Edge Representations --- Towards Scalable Modeling of Networks

abstract: We address the problem of comparing the risks of two given predictive models - for instance, a baseline model and a challenger - as confidently as possible on a fixed labeling budget. This problem occurs whenever models cannot be compared on held-out training data, possibly because the training data are unavailable or do not reflect the desired test distribution. In this case, new test instances have to be drawn and labeled at a cost. We devise an active comparison method that selects instances according to an instrumental sampling distribution. We derive the sampling distribution that maximizes the power of a statistical test applied to the observed empirical risks, and thereby minimizes the likelihood of choosing the inferior model. Empirically, we investigate model selection problems on several classification and regression tasks and study the accuracy of the resulting p-values.

paragraphs: Choosing between two predictive models can require collecting fresh labeled test data. Existing training data may be unavailable, or they may represent a different distribution from the one that matters at deployment. With a fixed labeling budget, the question becomes which test instances will provide the most useful evidence for comparing the models' risks.

The paper proposes an active comparison method that selects instances using an instrumental sampling distribution. It derives the distribution that maximizes the power of a statistical test based on the observed empirical risks. The goal is to direct labeling effort toward a more decisive comparison and thereby reduce the probability of choosing the inferior model.

The authors investigate this approach on classification and regression model-selection tasks and examine the accuracy of the resulting p-values. Assessing those values matters because the procedure should support meaningful confidence statements as well as model choices. The contribution treats test-data collection itself as an optimization problem, with the comparison between two given models determining how the labeling budget is used.
summary.tldr: The paper optimizes which test instances to label to make a statistically powerful comparison between two models under a fixed budget.

title: Active Comparison of Prediction Models

abstract: Applications of Bayesian nonparametric methods require learning and inference algorithms which efficiently explore models of unbounded complexity. We develop new Markov chain Monte Carlo methods for the beta process hidden Markov model (BP-HMM), enabling discovery of shared activity patterns in large video and motion capture databases. By introducing split-merge moves based on sequential allocation, we allow large global changes in the shared feature structure. We also develop data-driven reversible jump moves which more reliably discover rare or unique behaviors. Our proposals apply to any choice of conjugate likelihood for observed data, and we show success with multinomial, Gaussian, and autoregressive emission models. Together, these innovations allow tractable analysis of hundreds of time series, where previous inference required clever initialization and at least ten thousand burn-in iterations for just six sequences.

This paper develops Markov chain Monte Carlo methods for the beta process hidden Markov model. The application is discovering patterns shared across video and motion capture sequences, including behaviors that appear only rarely.

The stated improvement is therefore about making the flexible model practical at a much larger collection size.
summary.tldr: New split-merge and reversible jump proposals make inference in beta process hidden Markov models practical for hundreds of time series.

title: Effective Split-Merge Monte Carlo Methods for Nonparametric Models of Sequential Data

abstract: In the matrix completion problem the aim is to recover an unknown real matrix from a subset of its entries. This problem comes up in many application areas, and has received a great deal of attention in the context of the netflix prize. A central approach to this problem is to output a matrix of lowest possible complexity (e.g. rank or trace norm) that agrees with the partially specified matrix. The performance of this approach under the assumption that the revealed entries are sampled randomly has received considerable attention. In practice, often the set of revealed entries is not chosen at random and these results do not apply. We are therefore left with no guarantees on the performance of the algorithm we are using. We present a means to obtain performance guarantees with respect to any set of initial observations. The first step remains the same: find a matrix of lowest possible complexity that agrees with the partially specified matrix. We give a new way to interpret the output of this algorithm by next finding a probability distribution over the non-revealed entries with respect to which a bound on the generalization error can be proven. The more complex the set of revealed entries according to a certain measure, the better the bound on the generalization error.

paragraphs: Matrix completion attempts to reconstruct a matrix from only some of its entries. A standard strategy chooses the lowest-complexity matrix consistent with the observations, measuring complexity through rank or trace norm. Many guarantees for this strategy assume that observed entries were sampled randomly, an assumption that often does not hold in practice.

The paper retains that reconstruction step but changes how its output is assessed. After finding a consistent low-complexity matrix, the method finds a probability distribution over unobserved entries. It then proves a generalization-error bound with respect to that distribution, allowing guarantees to be obtained for any initial observation set.

The distribution is essential to interpreting the result: the guarantee concerns error under the constructed weighting of missing entries, rather than automatically providing uniform accuracy everywhere. The bound improves as the observed set becomes more complex according to the paper's specified measure. This offers a way to extract meaningful performance guarantees when random-observation analyses do not apply.
summary.tldr: Matrix-completion guarantees for arbitrary observation sets become possible by constructing a distribution over missing entries for evaluating error.

title: Matrix Completion From any Given Set of Observations

abstract: Hypergraphs allow to encode higher-order relationships in data and are thus a very flexible modeling tool. Current learning methods are either based on approximations of the hypergraphs via graphs or on tensor methods which are only applicable under special conditions. In this paper we present a new learning framework on hypergraphs which fully uses the hypergraph structure. The key element is a family of regularization functionals based on the total variation on hypergraphs.

The key element is a family of regularization functionals based on the total variation on hypergraphs.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent higher-order relationships in data, allowing a relationship to involve a group rather than only a pair of objects. This gives them flexibility as learning models. The paper addresses how to build learning methods that use that richer structure directly, rather than relying on a representation that reduces the relationships to ordinary graph connections.

The authors identify two existing approaches: approximating a hypergraph with a graph, and using tensor methods that apply only under special conditions. They propose a new learning framework whose central ingredients are regularization functionals based on total variation on hypergraphs. These functionals bring the hypergraph structure into the formulation of learning itself.

The stated contribution is this direct framework and its family of regularizers. Its significance is that higher-order relationships remain part of the learning formulation, instead of entering only through a graph approximation. The abstract presents a methodological foundation for learning on hypergraphs, with total variation providing the common organizing principle for the proposed regularization functions.
summary.tldr: A family of hypergraph total-variation regularizers enables learning that directly uses higher-order relationships.

title: The Total Variation on Hypergraphs - Learning on Hypergraphs Revisited

abstract: In this paper, we study the following new variant of prototype learning, called {\em $k$-prototype learning problem for 3D rigid structures}: Given a set of 3D rigid structures, find a set of $k$ rigid structures so that each of them is a prototype for a cluster of the given rigid structures and the total cost (or dissimilarity) is minimized. Prototype learning is a core problem in machine learning and has a wide range of applications in many areas. Existing results on this problem have mainly focused on the graph domain. In this paper, we present the first algorithm for learning multiple prototypes from 3D rigid structures. Our result is based on a number of new insights to rigid structures alignment, clustering, and prototype reconstruction, and is practically efficient with quality guarantee. We validate our approach using two type of data sets, random data and biological data of chromosome territories. Experiments suggest that our approach can effectively learn prototypes in both types of data.

paragraphs: A prototype summarizes a group of objects with a representative structure. This paper studies how to learn several such representatives for a collection of three-dimensional rigid structures. The objective is to find K prototypes, each representing a cluster, while minimizing the total dissimilarity associated with those groupings and their representatives.

The authors present what they describe as the first algorithm for learning multiple prototypes in this setting. Their approach draws on new insights into aligning rigid structures, forming clusters, and reconstructing prototypes. These are interconnected parts of the problem: comparing structures and building a representative both depend on how their geometric relationships are handled.

The algorithm is described as practically efficient and comes with a quality guarantee. The authors evaluate it on random data and biological data describing chromosome territories. Those experiments suggest that it can learn useful prototypes in both settings. The contribution broadens prototype learning beyond the graph-focused work highlighted in the abstract, giving a method tailored to collections of rigid three-dimensional structures.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces an efficient algorithm with a quality guarantee for learning K representative prototypes of clustered three-dimensional rigid structures.

title: k-Prototype Learning for 3D Rigid Structures

abstract: We study agnostic active learning, where the goal is to learn a classifier in a pre-specified hypothesis class interactively with as few label queries as possible, while making no assumptions on the true function generating the labels. The main algorithms for this problem are {\em{disagreement-based active learning}}, which has a high label requirement, and {\em{margin-based active learning}}, which only applies to fairly restricted settings. A major challenge is to find an algorithm which achieves better label complexity, is consistent in an agnostic setting, and applies to general classification problems. In this paper, we provide such an algorithm. Our solution is based on two novel contributions -- a reduction from consistent active learning to confidence-rated prediction with guaranteed error, and a novel confidence-rated predictor.

paragraphs: Active learning lets a classifier choose which examples to have labeled, aiming to learn with fewer label requests. This paper studies the agnostic setting: the learner works within a specified class of classifiers without assuming that the true label-generating function follows a particular form. Saving labels must therefore remain compatible with that lack of assumptions.

The authors identify a gap between two existing approaches. Disagreement-based methods require many labels, while margin-based methods apply only in relatively restricted settings. Their proposed algorithm addresses the combination of goals that this gap leaves open: improved label complexity, consistency in the agnostic setting, and applicability to general classification problems.

The approach connects active learning to confidence-rated prediction with a guaranteed error level. One contribution is a reduction showing how such prediction can support consistent active learning; the other is a new confidence-rated predictor. Together, these contributions provide a different route to deciding where labeling effort is needed. The result expands the available algorithmic approach while retaining the agnostic learning requirement.
summary.tldr: A new confidence-rated prediction approach improves label efficiency for general agnostic active learning while preserving consistency.

title: Beyond Disagreement-Based Agnostic Active Learning

abstract: Syntactic constituency parsing is a fundamental problem in naturallanguage processing which has been the subject of intensive researchand engineering for decades. As a result, the most accurate parsersare domain specific, complex, and inefficient. In this paper we showthat the domain agnostic attention-enhanced sequence-to-sequence modelachieves state-of-the-art results on the most widely used syntacticconstituency parsing dataset, when trained on a large synthetic corpusthat was annotated using existing parsers. It also matches theperformance of standard parsers when trained on a smallhuman-annotated dataset, which shows that this model is highlydata-efficient, in contrast to sequence-to-sequence models without theattention mechanism. Our parser is also fast, processing over ahundred sentences per second with an unoptimized CPU implementation.

paragraphs: Constituency parsing identifies the grammatical grouping of a sentence. The paper approaches this task with an attention-enhanced sequence-to-sequence model, using a general modeling architecture for a problem traditionally handled by specialized parsers. Its central finding is that this domain-agnostic architecture can achieve strong parsing results under two different training conditions.

When trained on a large synthetic corpus annotated by existing parsers, the model achieves state-of-the-art performance on the most widely used constituency parsing dataset. With a small human-annotated training set, it matches standard parsers. These are distinct findings: the strongest reported benchmark result uses large-scale parser-generated supervision, while the smaller-data result establishes competitive performance with human annotations.

The authors interpret the small-data performance as evidence of high data efficiency, contrasting it with sequence-to-sequence models without attention. The parser also processes more than one hundred sentences per second in an unoptimized CPU implementation. Together, the findings show that a general sequence architecture can combine parsing accuracy, effective use of limited annotations, and fast processing in the reported setting.
summary.tldr: An attention-based sequence-to-sequence parser achieves strong accuracy with both large synthetic and small human-annotated training sets.

title: Grammar as a Foreign Language

abstract: We consider the \emph{Threshold Bandit} setting, a variant of the classical multi-armed bandit problem in which the reward on each round depends on a piece of side information known as a \emph{threshold value}. The learner selects one of $K$ actions (arms), this action generates a random sample from a fixed distribution, and the action then receives a unit payoff in the event that this sample exceeds the threshold value. We consider two versions of this problem, the \emph{uncensored} and \emph{censored} case, that determine whether the sample is always observed or only when the threshold is not met. Using new tools to understand the popular UCB algorithm, we show that the uncensored case is essentially no more difficult than the classical multi-armed bandit setting. Finally we show that the censored case exhibits more challenges, but we give guarantees in the event that the sequence of threshold values is generated optimistically.
