paragraphs: The threshold-bandit problem changes how an action earns a reward. On each round, the learner selects one of K actions, which draws a random sample from a fixed distribution. The learner earns a unit reward only if that sample exceeds a threshold supplied as side information.

The paper distinguishes two feedback settings. In the uncensored version, the learner always sees the sample. In the censored version, the sample is visible only when it fails to meet the threshold. These observation rules matter because the learner must use past feedback to decide which actions are likely to succeed at subsequent thresholds.

Using new analytical tools for the UCB algorithm, the authors show that the uncensored setting is essentially no harder than the classical multi-armed bandit problem. Censoring introduces additional challenges, and the paper supplies guarantees when threshold values are generated optimistically. Thus, the positive result for censored feedback depends on the stated threshold-generation condition, while the uncensored analysis establishes a closer connection to standard bandit learning.
summary.tldr: Threshold bandits remain essentially as tractable as classical bandits with full sample feedback, while censored-feedback guarantees require optimistic threshold generation.

title: Threshold Bandits, With and Without Censored Feedback

abstract: We propose a novel method to {\it directly} learn a stochastic transition operator whose repeated application provides generated samples. Traditional undirected graphical models approach this problem indirectly by learning a Markov chain model whose stationary distribution obeys detailed balance with respect to a parameterized energy function. The energy function is then modified so the model and data distributions match, with no guarantee on the number of steps required for the Markov chain to converge. Moreover, the detailed balance condition is highly restrictive: energy based models corresponding to neural networks must have symmetric weights, unlike biological neural circuits. In contrast, we develop a method for directly learning arbitrarily parameterized transition operators capable of expressing non-equilibrium stationary distributions that violate detailed balance, thereby enabling us to learn more biologically plausible asymmetric neural networks and more general non-energy based dynamical systems. The proposed training objective, which we derive via principled variational methods, encourages the transition operator to "walk back" (prefer to revert its steps) in multi-step trajectories that start at data-points, as quickly as possible back to the original data points. We present a series of experimental results illustrating the soundness of the proposed approach, Variational Walkback (VW), on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN and CelebA datasets, demonstrating superior samples compared to earlier attempts to learn a transition operator. We also show that although each rapid training trajectory is limited to a finite but variable number of steps, our transition operator continues to generate good samples well past the length of such trajectories, thereby demonstrating the match of its non-equilibrium stationary distribution to the data distribution. The paper instead directly trains the transition rule, allowing more general dynamics, including stationary distributions that do not satisfy detailed balance.

summary.tldr: Variational Walkback directly learns stochastic transitions that generate good samples without requiring detailed balance.

title: Variational Walkback: Learning a Transition Operator as a Stochastic Recurrent Net

abstract: Federated learning poses new statistical and systems challenges in training machine learning models over distributed networks of devices. In this work, we show that multi-task learning is naturally suited to handle the statistical challenges of this setting, and propose a novel systems-aware optimization method, MOCHA, that is robust to practical systems issues. Our method and theory for the first time consider issues of high communication cost, stragglers, and fault tolerance for distributed multi-task learning. The resulting method achieves significant speedups compared to alternatives in the federated setting, as we demonstrate through simulations on real-world federated datasets.
originalAbstract: Federated learning poses new statistical and systems challenges in training machine learning models over distributed networks of devices. In this work, we show that multi-task learning is naturally suited to handle the statistical challenges of this setting, and propose a novel systems-aware optimization method, MOCHA, that is robust to practical systems issues. Our method and theory for the first time consider issues of high communication cost, stragglers, and fault tolerance for distributed multi-task learning. The resulting method achieves significant speedups compared to alternatives in the federated setting, as we demonstrate through simulations on real-world federated datasets.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains models across a network of devices, creating statistical and computational challenges at the same time. This paper argues that multi-task learning is naturally suited to the statistical side of that setting. Treating learning as a collection of related tasks provides a framework for addressing distributed modeling needs while considering relationships among the tasks.

The authors introduce MOCHA, an optimization method designed around the systems issues that arise in distributed multi-task learning. Its method and theory account for expensive communication, slow participants known as stragglers, and fault tolerance. These issues matter because the progress of a distributed learning procedure depends on how computation and communication proceed across its participants.

Simulations using real-world federated datasets show significant speedups over the alternatives considered. The evidence therefore supports MOCHA's efficiency in the simulated federated settings studied. The broader contribution is to combine a statistical formulation appropriate for federated learning with an optimizer that explicitly considers practical systems behavior, bringing those two parts of the problem into the same treatment.
summary.tldr: MOCHA combines federated multi-task learning with optimization that accounts for communication costs, stragglers, and fault tolerance.

title: Federated Multi-Task Learning

abstract: A powerful approach for understanding neural population dynamics is to extract low-dimensional trajectories from population recordings using dimensionality reduction methods. Current approaches for dimensionality reduction on neural data are limited to single population recordings, and can not identify dynamics embedded across multiple measurements. We propose an approach for extracting low-dimensional dynamics from multiple, sequential recordings. Our algorithm scales to data comprising millions of observed dimensions, making it possible to access dynamics distributed across large populations or multiple brain areas. Building on subspace-identification approaches for dynamical systems, we perform parameter estimation by minimizing a moment-matching objective using a scalable stochastic gradient descent algorithm: The model is optimized to predict temporal covariations across neurons and across time. We show how this approach naturally handles missing data and multiple partial recordings, and can identify dynamics and predict correlations even in the presence of severe subsampling and small overlap between recordings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach both on simulated data and a whole-brain larval zebrafish imaging dataset.

The motivation is that methods restricted to a single recording cannot identify dynamics distributed across separate measurements of a larger neural population.

The method builds on subspace identification for dynamical systems. It estimates parameters by matching moments, training the model to predict how neural activity covaries across neurons and over time. A scalable stochastic gradient descent procedure minimizes this objective. This approach connects separate observations through their temporal statistical relationships.

The authors show that it can identify dynamics and predict correlations despite severe subsampling and little overlap between recordings. Demonstrations use simulated data and whole-brain imaging of larval zebrafish. The contribution expands the range of recordings that can be combined to study shared low-dimensional neural dynamics.
summary.tldr: Matching temporal correlations allows scalable recovery of low-dimensional neural dynamics across multiple incomplete recordings.

title: Extracting low-dimensional dynamics from multiple large-scale neural population recordings by learning to predict correlations

abstract: The wide adoption of DNNs has given birth to unrelenting computing requirements, forcing datacenter operators to adopt domain-specific accelerators to train them. These accelerators typically employ densely packed full-precision floating-point arithmetic to maximize performance per area. Ongoing research efforts seek to further increase that performance density by replacing floating-point with fixed-point arithmetic. However, a significant roadblock for these attempts has been fixed point's narrow dynamic range, which is insufficient for DNN training convergence. We identify block floating point (BFP) as a promising alternative representation since it exhibits wide dynamic range and enables the majority of DNN operations to be performed with fixed-point logic. Unfortunately, BFP alone introduces several limitations that preclude its direct applicability. In this work, we introduce HBFP, a hybrid BFP-FP approach, which performs all dot products in BFP and other operations in floating point. HBFP delivers the best of both worlds: the high accuracy of floating point at the superior hardware density of fixed point. For a wide variety of models, we show that HBFP matches floating point's accuracy while enabling hardware implementations that deliver up to 8.5x higher throughput.

summary.tldr: HBFP combines block-floating-point dot products with floating-point operations to match reported training accuracy while enabling up to 8.5 times higher hardware throughput.

title: Training DNNs with Hybrid Block Floating Point

abstract: We interpret meta-reinforcement learning as the problem of learning how to quickly find a good sampling distribution in a new environment. This interpretation leads to the development of two new meta-reinforcement learning algorithms: E-MAML and E-$\text{RL}^2$. Results are presented on a new environment we call `Krazy World': a difficult high-dimensional gridworld which is designed to highlight the importance of correctly differentiating through sampling distributions in meta-reinforcement learning. Further results are presented on a set of maze environments. We show E-MAML and E-$\text{RL}^2$ deliver better performance than baseline algorithms on both tasks.

paragraphs: This paper interprets meta-reinforcement learning as learning how to quickly obtain a useful sampling distribution in a new environment. Under this view, adaptation involves learning how to gather experience that supports effective behavior. The distribution of sampled experience becomes a central part of the learning problem rather than merely the source of training observations.

That interpretation leads to two algorithms, E-MAML and E-RL². The paper emphasizes correctly differentiating through sampling distributions in meta-reinforcement learning. This matters to the proposed perspective because learning how to adapt must account for how the learner’s behavior determines the experience it collects in a new environment.

The authors introduce Krazy World, a difficult high-dimensional gridworld designed to expose the importance of that sampling treatment. They also evaluate the algorithms on maze environments. Both E-MAML and E-RL² perform better than the baseline algorithms on the two tasks. The findings support the paper’s sampling-centered account of adaptation in these evaluations and motivate explicitly considering experience collection when designing meta-reinforcement learning methods.
summary.tldr: Treating adaptation as learning a useful sampling distribution produces two meta-RL algorithms that improve performance on gridworld and maze tasks.

title: The Importance of Sampling inMeta-Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the Kronecker product regression problem, in which the design matrix is a Kronecker product of two or more matrices. Formally, given $A_i \in \R^{n_i \times d_i}$ for $i=1,2,\dots,q$ where $n_i \gg d_i$ for each $i$, and $b \in \R^{n_1 n_2 \cdots n_q}$, let $\mathcal{A} = A_i \otimes A_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes A_q$. Then for $p \in [1,2]$, the goal is to find $x \in \R^{d_1 \cdots d_q}$ that approximately minimizes $\|\mathcal{A}x - b\|_p$. Recently, Diao, Song, Sun, and Woodruff (AISTATS, 2018) gave an algorithm which is faster than forming the Kronecker product $\mathcal{A} \in \R^{n_1 \cdots n_q \times d_1 \cdots d_q}$. Specifically, for $p=2$ they achieve a running time of $O(\sum_{i=1}^q \texttt{nnz}(A_i) + \texttt{nnz}(b))$, where $ \texttt{nnz}(A_i)$ is the number of non-zero entries in $A_i$. Note that $\texttt{nnz}(b)$ can be as large as $\Theta(n_1 \cdots n_q)$. For $p=1,$ $q=2$ and $n_1 = n_2$, they achieve a worse bound of $O(n_1^{3/2} \text{poly}(d_1d_2) + \texttt{nnz}(b))$. In this work, we provide significantly faster algorithms. For $p=2$, our running time is $O(\sum_{i=1}^q \texttt{nnz}(A_i) )$, which has no dependence on $\texttt{nnz}(b)$. For $p<2$, our running time is $O(\sum_{i=1}^q \texttt{nnz}(A_i) + \texttt{nnz}(b))$, which matches the prior best running time for $p=2$. We also consider the related all-pairs regression problem, where given $A \in \R^{n \times d}, b \in \R^n$, we want to solve $\min_{x \in \R^d} \|\bar{A}x - \bar{b}\|_p$, where $\bar{A} \in \R^{n^2 \times d}, \bar{b} \in \R^{n^2}$ consist of all pairwise differences of the rows of $A,b$. We give an $O(\texttt{nnz}(A))$ time algorithm for $p \in[1,2]$, improving the $\Omega(n^2)$ time required to form $\bar{A}$. Finally, we initiate the study of Kronecker product low rank and and low-trank approximation. For input $\mathcal{A}$ as above, we give $O(\sum_{i=1}^q \texttt{nnz}(A_i))$ time algorithms, which is much faster than computing $\mathcal{A}$.

paragraphs: A regression design matrix formed as a Kronecker product can be enormous even when its component matrices are manageable. This paper develops faster algorithms for approximating regression solutions without explicitly forming that expanded matrix. It considers residual norms with p between one and two, including ordinary least-squares regression.

For p equal to two, the stated running time depends on the total number of nonzero entries in the factor matrices, with no dependence on the number of nonzero entries in the response vector. For p below two, the running time also includes the response vector's nonzero entries. These improve the corresponding earlier bounds described in the abstract.

The authors also study regression over all pairwise differences of input rows, giving an algorithm whose stated running time depends on the original matrix's nonzero entries and avoids constructing the quadratic-size expansion. Related Kronecker low-rank approximation algorithms likewise work at the scale of the factors. The common contribution is computation that exploits structured inputs without paying to materialize their much larger expansions.
summary.tldr: New algorithms accelerate Kronecker-product regression and related approximation problems by avoiding explicit construction of expanded matrices.

title: Optimal Sketching for Kronecker Product Regression and Low Rank Approximation

abstract: Conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) have gained a considerable attention in recent years due to its class-wise controllability and superior quality for complex generation tasks. We introduce a simple yet effective approach to improving cGANs by measuring the discrepancy between the data distribution and the model distribution on given samples. The proposed measure, coined the gap of log-densities (GOLD), provides an effective self-diagnosis for cGANs while being efficiently, computed from the discriminator. We propose three applications of the GOLD: example re-weighting, rejection sampling, and active learning, which improve the training, inference, and data selection of cGANs, respectively. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods outperform corresponding baselines for all three applications on different image datasets.

paragraphs: Conditional GANs generate examples associated with specified classes, but their generated distribution may still differ from the data distribution. This paper introduces the gap of log-densities, or GOLD, as a way to assess that mismatch on particular samples using information efficiently computed from the discriminator.

The authors use this diagnostic in three places. Example reweighting changes the influence of training examples, rejection sampling changes which generated outputs are retained, and active learning changes which data are selected. These applications respectively target training, inference, and data acquisition.

Across different image datasets, all three applications outperform their corresponding baselines. The abstract does not report the size of the gains or specify the exact estimation conditions behind the density-gap measure. The main contribution is a shared discriminator-based diagnostic that can guide several distinct stages of a conditional generation pipeline, rather than a wholly new generator architecture.
summary.tldr: A discriminator-derived density gap improves conditional-GAN training, sampling, and data selection.

title: Mining GOLD Samples for Conditional GANs

abstract: We consider the problem of online forecasting of sequences of length $n$ with total-variation at most $C_n$ using observations contaminated by independent $\sigma$-subgaussian noise. We design an $O(n\log n)$-time algorithm that achieves a cumulative square error of $\tilde{O}(n^{1/3}C_n^{2/3}\sigma^{4/3} + C_n^2)$ with high probability. We also prove a lower bound that matches the upper bound in all parameters (up to a $\log(n)$ factor). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first **polynomial-time** algorithm that achieves the optimal $O(n^{1/3})$ rate in forecasting total variation bounded sequences and the first algorithm that **adapts to unknown** $C_n$.Our proof techniques leverage the special localized structure of Haar wavelet basis and the adaptivity to unknown smoothness parameters in the classical wavelet smoothing [Donoho et al., 1998]. We also compare our model to the rich literature of dynamic regret minimization and nonstationary stochastic optimization, where our problem can be treated as a special case. We show that the workhorse in those settings --- online gradient descent and its variants with a fixed restarting schedule --- are instances of a class of **linear forecasters** that require a suboptimal regret of $\tilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{n})$. This implies that the use of more adaptive algorithms is necessary to obtain the optimal rate.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential forecasting when the underlying sequence has bounded total variation, meaning its accumulated changes are limited. Observations contain independent subgaussian noise. The challenge is to predict as data arrive while adapting to how much the sequence changes, even when that variation budget is unknown.

The proposed algorithm runs in O(n log n) time. These methods require a worse square-root dependence on sequence length in the stated regret comparison. This explains why more adaptive forecasting is necessary to attain the optimal rate in this setting.
summary.tldr: A fast wavelet-based forecaster adapts to unknown total variation and achieves an error bound matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

title: Online Forecasting of Total-Variation-bounded Sequences

abstract: Text-to-image generation, i.e. generating an image given a text description, is a very challenging task due to the significant semantic gap between the two domains. Humans, however, tackle this problem intelligently. We learn from diverse objects to form a solid prior about semantics, textures, colors, shapes, and layouts. Given a text description, we immediately imagine an overall visual impression using this prior and, based on this, we draw a picture by progressively adding more and more details. In this paper, and inspired by this process, we propose a novel text-to-image method called LeicaGAN to combine the above three phases in a unified framework. First, we formulate the multiple priors learning phase as a textual-visual co-embedding (TVE) comprising a text-image encoder for learning semantic, texture, and color priors and a text-mask encoder for learning shape and layout priors. Then, we formulate the imagination phase as multiple priors aggregation (MPA) by combining these complementary priors and adding noise for diversity. Lastly, we formulate the creation phase by using a cascaded attentive generator (CAG) to progressively draw a picture from coarse to fine. We leverage adversarial learning for LeicaGAN to enforce semantic consistency and visual realism. Thorough experiments on two public benchmark datasets demonstrate LeicaGAN's superiority over the baseline method. Code has been made available at https://github.com/qiaott/LeicaGAN.

paragraphs: Generating an image from text requires translating a description into appearance, shape, and spatial arrangement. LeicaGAN organizes this task into three phases inspired by learning visual knowledge, imagining an overall picture, and progressively drawing its details. The phases form a single text-to-image generation framework.

First, a text-image encoder learns priors about semantics, texture, and color, while a text-mask encoder learns priors about shape and layout. Next, the model combines these complementary sources of information into an overall representation. Noise is added at this aggregation stage to support diverse generated images. This separates the acquisition of different kinds of visual knowledge from their combination for a particular description.

A cascaded attentive generator then creates an image from coarse structure toward finer detail. Adversarial learning encourages both visual realism and consistency with the description. Experiments on two public benchmark datasets show that LeicaGAN outperforms the baseline method. The reported findings support coordinating multiple learned priors with progressive generation to address the gap between textual meaning and visual content.
summary.tldr: LeicaGAN combines learned appearance and layout priors with progressive image generation to improve text-to-image results over its evaluated baseline.

title: Learn, Imagine and Create: Text-to-Image Generation from Prior Knowledge

abstract: Diffusion distance is a spectral method for measuring distance among nodes on graph considering global data structure. In this work, we propose a spec-diff-net for computing diffusion distance on graph based on approximate spectral decomposition. The network is a differentiable deep architecture consisting of feature extraction and diffusion distance modules for computing diffusion distance on image by end-to-end training. We design low resolution kernel matching loss and high resolution segment matching loss to enforce the network's output to be consistent with human-labeled image segments. To compute high-resolution diffusion distance or segmentation mask, we design an up-sampling strategy by feature-attentional interpolation which can be learned when training spec-diff-net. With the learned diffusion distance, we propose a hierarchical image segmentation method outperforming previous segmentation methods. Moreover, a weakly supervised semantic segmentation network is designed using diffusion distance and achieved promising results on PASCAL VOC 2012 segmentation dataset.

paragraphs: Diffusion distance measures relationships between graph nodes while accounting for the graph's global structure. This paper brings that idea into image segmentation through spec-diff-net, a differentiable network that learns image features and diffusion distances together. Its distance computation uses an approximate spectral decomposition, connecting a graph-based measure to end-to-end learning.

The training design aligns the learned output with human-labeled image segments at two resolutions. A low-resolution kernel matching loss guides the learned relationships, while a high-resolution segment matching loss guides agreement with segments. A learned feature-attentional interpolation strategy then supports upsampling, allowing the system to produce high-resolution diffusion distances or segmentation masks.

The authors use the resulting distances in a hierarchical segmentation method that outperforms previous segmentation methods in their evaluation. They also build a weakly supervised semantic segmentation network using diffusion distance and report promising results on PASCAL VOC 2012. The approach matters because it makes a global structural distance trainable for the segmentation task, while explicitly addressing the need to recover detailed outputs from lower-resolution computations.
summary.tldr: Spec-diff-net learns graph-based diffusion distances end to end and uses them for hierarchical and weakly supervised image segmentation.

title: Neural Diffusion Distance for Image Segmentation

abstract: Effectively leveraging large, previously collected datasets in reinforcement learn- ing (RL) is a key challenge for large-scale real-world applications. Offline RL algorithms promise to learn effective policies from previously-collected, static datasets without further interaction. However, in practice, offline RL presents a major challenge, and standard off-policy RL methods can fail due to overestimation of values induced by the distributional shift between the dataset and the learned policy, especially when training on complex and multi-modal data distributions. In this paper, we propose conservative Q-learning (CQL), which aims to address these limitations by learning a conservative Q-function such that the expected value of a policy under this Q-function lower-bounds its true value. We theoretically show that CQL produces a lower bound on the value of the current policy and that it can be incorporated into a policy learning procedure with theoretical improvement guarantees. In practice, CQL augments the standard Bellman error objective with a simple Q-value regularizer which is straightforward to implement on top of existing deep Q-learning and actor-critic implementations. On both discrete and continuous control domains, we show that CQL substantially outperforms existing offline RL methods, often learning policies that attain 2-5 times higher final return, especially when learning from complex and multi-modal data distributions.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning tries to learn a decision policy from a fixed dataset without collecting more experience. A central difficulty is that the learned policy can behave differently from the policies represented in that data. This distribution shift can make standard methods overestimate the value of their decisions, particularly with complex or multimodal datasets.

Conservative Q-learning, or CQL, addresses the problem by learning deliberately conservative value estimates. The theoretical target is that a policy's expected value under the learned Q-function lower-bounds its true value. The authors establish such a bound for the current policy and show how to incorporate CQL into policy learning with improvement guarantees. The bound concerns policy value, rather than asserting that every individual Q-value is a lower bound.

In implementation, CQL adds a Q-value regularizer to the usual Bellman error objective, making it straightforward to integrate with deep Q-learning and actor-critic methods. Experiments cover discrete and continuous control. CQL substantially outperforms the compared offline methods, often achieving two to five times higher final return, with especially strong results on complex and multimodal data distributions.
summary.tldr: CQL adds conservative value regularization to offline reinforcement learning, yielding theoretical policy-value bounds and substantial empirical gains.

title: Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many real-world sequential decision problems involve multiple action variables whose control frequencies are different, such that actions take their effects at different periods. While these problems can be formulated with the notion of multiple action persistences in factored-action MDP (FA-MDP), it is non-trivial to solve them efficiently since an action-persistent policy constructed from a stationary policy can be arbitrarily suboptimal, rendering solution methods for the standard FA-MDPs hardly applicable. In this paper, we formalize the problem of multiple control frequencies in RL and provide its efficient solution method. Our proposed method, Action-Persistent Policy Iteration (AP-PI), provides a theoretical guarantee on the convergence to an optimal solution while incurring only a factor of $|A|$ increase in time complexity during policy improvement step, compared to the standard policy iteration for FA-MDPs. Extending this result, we present Action-Persistent Actor-Critic (AP-AC), a scalable RL algorithm for high-dimensional control tasks. In the experiments, we demonstrate that AP-AC significantly outperforms the baselines on several continuous control tasks and a traffic control simulation, which highlights the effectiveness of our method that directly optimizes the periodic non-stationary policy for tasks with multiple control frequencies.

While these problems can be formulated with the notion of multiple action persistences in factored-action MDP (FA-MDP), it is non-trivial to solve them efficiently since an action-persistent policy constructed from a stationary policy can be arbitrarily suboptimal, rendering solution methods for the standard FA-MDPs hardly applicable. In this paper, we formalize the problem of multiple control frequencies in RL and provide its efficient solution method. Our proposed method, Action-Persistent Policy Iteration (AP-PI), provides a theoretical guarantee on the convergence to an optimal solution while incurring only a factor of $|A|$ increase in time complexity during policy improvement step, compared to the standard policy iteration for FA-MDPs. Extending this result, we present Action-Persistent Actor-Critic (AP-AC), a scalable RL algorithm for high-dimensional control tasks. In the experiments, we demonstrate that AP-AC significantly outperforms the baselines on several continuous control tasks and a traffic control simulation, which highlights the effectiveness of our method that directly optimizes the periodic non-stationary policy for tasks with multiple control frequencies.

paragraphs: Some control problems have several action variables that are updated at different frequencies, so their effects persist for different periods. The paper formalizes this setting through multiple action persistences in factored-action Markov decision processes. Simply constructing a persistent policy from a stationary one can be arbitrarily suboptimal, making standard solution methods difficult to apply effectively.

The authors introduce Action-Persistent Policy Iteration, or AP-PI. It has a theoretical guarantee of convergence to an optimal solution, while its policy-improvement step costs only an additional factor of |A| compared with standard policy iteration for factored-action problems. The method directly accounts for the timing structure rather than treating persistence as an adjustment made after choosing a stationary policy.

They extend this result into Action-Persistent Actor-Critic, or AP-AC, for high-dimensional control. Experiments show substantial improvements over baselines on several continuous-control tasks and a traffic-control simulation. These findings support directly optimizing a periodic, non-stationary policy when different action components operate on different schedules, while the optimality guarantee belongs to the policy-iteration method.
summary.tldr: Action-persistent policy iteration and actor-critic methods explicitly handle different control frequencies, combining a policy-iteration optimality guarantee with strong empirical control results.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Control with Multiple Frequencies

abstract: Autonomous part assembly is a challenging yet crucial task in 3D computer vision and robotics. Analogous to buying an IKEA furniture, given a set of 3D parts that can assemble a single shape, an intelligent agent needs to perceive the 3D part geometry, reason to propose pose estimations for the input parts, and finally call robotic planning and control routines for actuation. In this paper, we focus on the pose estimation subproblem from the vision side involving geometric and relational reasoning over the input part geometry. Essentially, the task of generative 3D part assembly is to predict a 6-DoF part pose, including a rigid rotation and translation, for each input part that assembles a single 3D shape as the final output. To tackle this problem, we propose an assembly-oriented dynamic graph learning framework that leverages an iterative graph neural network as a backbone. It explicitly conducts sequential part assembly refinements in a coarse-to-fine manner, exploits a pair of part relation reasoning module and part aggregation module for dynamically adjusting both part features and their relations in the part graph. We conduct extensive experiments and quantitative comparisons to three strong baseline methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Given a collection of three-dimensional parts that form one object, an assembly system must determine where each part belongs and how it should be oriented. This paper addresses that visual pose estimation problem. For every input part, it predicts a rigid rotation and translation, together forming a six-degree-of-freedom pose that places the parts into a single shape.

The proposed method represents the parts and their relationships in a dynamic graph. An iterative graph neural network refines the assembly from coarse estimates toward finer arrangements. A relation reasoning module and an aggregation module update both the part features and the relationships between parts, allowing the graph representation to change as the proposed assembly develops.

This approach makes geometric reasoning and relationships among parts part of the same refinement process. The authors report extensive experiments and quantitative comparisons against three strong baseline methods that demonstrate its effectiveness. The scope is the visual prediction of assembled poses; robotic planning and control are identified as subsequent parts of an autonomous assembly system.
summary.tldr: A dynamic graph neural network iteratively predicts the rotations and positions needed to assemble 3D parts into one shape.

title: Generative 3D Part Assembly via Dynamic Graph Learning

abstract: We consider a general adversarial multi-armed blocking bandit setting where each played arm can be blocked (unavailable) for some time periods and the reward per arm is given at each time period adversarially without obeying any distribution. The setting models scenarios of allocating scarce limited supplies (e.g., arms) where the supplies replenish and can be reused only after certain time periods. We first show that, in the optimization setting, when the blocking durations and rewards are known in advance, finding an optimal policy (e.g., determining which arm per round) that maximises the cumulative reward is strongly NP-hard, eliminating the possibility of a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) for the problem unless P = NP. To complement our result, we show that a greedy algorithm that plays the best available arm at each round provides an approximation guarantee that depends on the blocking durations and the path variance of the rewards. In the bandit setting, when the blocking durations and rewards are not known, we design two algorithms, RGA and RGA-META, for the case of bounded duration an path variation. In particular, when the variation budget B_T is known in advance, RGA can achieve O(\sqrt{T(2\tilde{D}+K)B_{T}}) dynamic approximate regret. On the other hand, when B_T is not known, we show that the dynamic approximate regret of RGA-META is at most O((K+\tilde{D})^{1/4}\tilde{B}^{1/2}T^{3/4}) where \tilde{B} is the maximal path variation budget within each batch of RGA-META (which is provably in order of o(\sqrt{T}). We also prove that if either the variation budget or the maximal blocking duration is unbounded, the approximate regret will be at least Theta(T). We also show that the regret upper bound of RGA is tight if the blocking durations are bounded above by an order of O(1).

Their dynamic approximate regret guarantees require bounded blocking durations and bounded reward variation. If either is unbounded, the authors prove a linear lower bound on approximate regret. They also establish tightness of RGA's upper bound when blocking durations are bounded by a constant.
summary.tldr: The paper develops algorithms and performance limits for adversarial bandits whose chosen resources become temporarily unavailable.

title: Adversarial Blocking Bandits

abstract: Combinatorial dimensions play an important role in the theory of machine learning. For example, VC dimension characterizes PAC learning, SQ dimension characterizes weak learning with statistical queries, and Littlestone dimension characterizes online learning. In this paper we aim to develop combinatorial dimensions that characterize bounded memory learning. We propose a candidate solution for the case of realizable strong learning under a known distribution, based on the SQ dimension of neighboring distributions. We prove both upper and lower bounds for our candidate solution, that match in some regime of parameters. This is the first characterization of strong learning under space constraints in any regime. In this parameter regime there is an equivalence between bounded memory and SQ learning. We conjecture that our characterization holds in a much wider regime of parameters.

paragraphs: Learning theory often uses combinatorial dimensions to describe which problems can be learned under particular rules. This paper seeks an analogous characterization when a learner has limited memory. The setting is realizable strong learning under a known distribution, so the proposed characterization addresses a specific statistical and computational framework.

The authors construct a candidate measure using the statistical-query dimension of neighboring distributions. They prove upper and lower bounds based on this candidate, connecting sufficient resources for learning with resources that are unavoidable. In some parameter regimes, the bounds match, yielding a characterization of strong learning under memory constraints.

Within the regime where the bounds coincide, bounded-memory learning and statistical-query learning are equivalent. This connects two ways of restricting a learner: limiting its storage and restricting how it obtains statistical information. The authors identify this as the first characterization of strong learning under space constraints in any regime. They conjecture that the result extends to a substantially wider range of parameters, but that broader claim remains a conjecture.
summary.tldr: A statistical-query-based combinatorial measure characterizes bounded-memory strong learning in a particular parameter regime, with a broader characterization conjectured.

title: Towards a Combinatorial Characterization of Bounded-Memory Learning

abstract: As in standard linear regression, in truncated linear regression, we are given access to observations (A_i, y_i)_i whose dependent variable equals y_i= A_i^{\rm T} \cdot x^* + \eta_i, where x^* is some fixed unknown vector of interest and \eta_i is independent noise; except we are only given an observation if its dependent variable y_i lies in some "truncation set" S \subset \mathbb{R}. The goal is to recover x^* under some favorable conditions on the A_i's and the noise distribution. We prove that there exists a computationally and statistically efficient method for recovering k-sparse n-dimensional vectors x^* from m truncated samples, which attains an optimal \ell_2 reconstruction error of O(\sqrt{(k \log n)/m}). As a corollary, our guarantees imply a computationally efficient and information-theoretically optimal algorithm for compressed sensing with truncation, such as that which may arise from measurement saturation effects. Our result follows from a statistical and computational analysis of the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithm for solving a natural adaption of the LASSO optimization problem that accommodates truncation. This generalizes the works of both: (1) [Daskalakis et al. 2018], where no regularization is needed due to the low dimensionality of the data, and (2) [Wainright 2009], where the objective function is simple due to the absence of truncation. In order to deal with both truncation and high-dimensionality at the same time, we develop new techniques that not only generalize the existing ones but we believe are of independent interest.

paragraphs: Truncated linear regression observes a sample only when its response falls within a specified set. The response still follows a linear relationship plus independent noise, but some outcomes never enter the dataset. This paper studies recovering a high-dimensional coefficient vector when only a small number of its entries are nonzero, combining truncation with sparsity.

The authors analyze stochastic gradient descent for a version of the LASSO objective adapted to truncation. Under favorable conditions on the inputs and noise, the method is computationally and statistically efficient. For an n-dimensional vector with k nonzero entries and m retained samples, it attains optimal Euclidean reconstruction error of order square root of k log n divided by m.

As a consequence, the guarantees yield an efficient, information-theoretically optimal algorithm for compressed sensing with truncation, including truncation that can arise from measurement saturation. The theoretical work handles two challenges together: regularization is needed for high dimensionality, while the objective must account for selective observation. Its analysis extends results that previously handled either low-dimensional truncation or untruncated sparse regression.
summary.tldr: A truncation-aware LASSO method efficiently recovers sparse high-dimensional linear models at an optimal error rate under favorable input and noise conditions.

title: Truncated Linear Regression in High Dimensions

abstract: Recently, Transformer-based language models have demonstrated remarkable performance across many NLP domains. However, the unsupervised pre-training step of these models suffers from unbearable overall computational expenses. Current methods for accelerating the pre-training either rely on massive parallelism with advanced hardware or are not applicable to language models. In this work, we propose a method based on progressive layer dropping that speeds the training of Transformer-based language models, not at the cost of excessive hardware resources but from model architecture change and training technique boosted efficiency. Extensive experiments on BERT show that the proposed method achieves a 25% reduction of computation cost in FLOPS and a 24% reduction in the end-to-end wall-clock training time. Furthermore, we show that our pre-trained models are equipped with strong knowledge transferability, achieving similar or even higher accuracy in downstream tasks to baseline models.

paragraphs: Transformer language models can perform well across language tasks, but their initial unsupervised training requires substantial computation. This paper targets that training stage with progressive layer dropping. The central idea is to change how the network's layers participate in training so that learning requires less work, using architectural and training choices to improve efficiency.

The approach matters because accelerating training through additional hardware can make large models difficult to access. Here, the reported savings come from the training method itself. Experiments with BERT show a 25% reduction in floating-point computation and a 24% reduction in total training time. Reporting both measures establishes that the computational reduction also translates into elapsed-time savings in those experiments.

The authors also evaluate whether the resulting pretrained models remain useful for subsequent tasks. Their models achieve similar or sometimes higher downstream accuracy than the baseline models. These findings indicate that the tested reduction in pretraining cost can coexist with strong transfer to other tasks, rather than merely producing a cheaper model whose learned knowledge is less useful.
summary.tldr: Progressive layer dropping reduces BERT pretraining computation and elapsed time while preserving or improving accuracy on the downstream tasks tested.

title: Accelerating Training of Transformer-Based Language Models with Progressive Layer Dropping

abstract: We introduce a new problem setting for continuous control called the LQR with Rich Observations, or RichLQR. In our setting, the environment is summarized by a low-dimensional continuous latent state with linear dynamics and quadratic costs, but the agent operates on high-dimensional, nonlinear observations such as images from a camera. To enable sample-efficient learning, we assume that the learner has access to a class of decoder functions (e.g., neural networks) that is flexible enough to capture the mapping from observations to latent states. We introduce a new algorithm, RichID, which learns a near-optimal policy for the RichLQR with sample complexity scaling only with the dimension of the latent state space and the capacity of the decoder function class. RichID is oracle-efficient and accesses the decoder class only through calls to a least-squares regression oracle. To our knowledge, our results constitute the first provable sample complexity guarantee for continuous control with an unknown nonlinearity in the system model.

To enable sample-efficient learning, we assume that the learner has access to a class of decoder functions (e.g., neural networks) that is flexible enough to capture the mapping from observations to latent states. paragraphs: RichLQR describes a control problem with a simple hidden structure and complicated observations. The underlying state is low-dimensional, evolves linearly, and incurs quadratic costs. The agent, however, receives high-dimensional nonlinear observations, such as camera images. Learning must therefore connect those observations to the hidden state needed for effective control.

The paper assumes access to a decoder function class flexible enough to represent the mapping from observations to latent states. Under this setup, the proposed RichID algorithm learns a near-optimal policy with sample complexity scaling only with latent-state dimension and decoder-class capacity. This ties the data requirement to the hidden control structure and the difficulty of decoding it.

RichID accesses the decoder class through a least-squares regression oracle and is oracle-efficient. Its computational statement is therefore expressed in terms of access to that regression capability. The authors describe the result as, to their knowledge, the first provable sample-complexity guarantee for continuous control with an unknown nonlinearity in the system model. The decoder assumption is central to making that guarantee possible.
summary.tldr: RichID provably learns near-optimal control from nonlinear observations when a sufficiently expressive decoder class can recover the low-dimensional latent state.

title: Learning the Linear Quadratic Regulator from Nonlinear Observations

abstract: $k$-means++ \cite{arthur2007k} is a widely used clustering algorithm that is easy to implement, has nice theoretical guarantees and strong empirical performance. Despite its wide adoption, $k$-means++ sometimes suffers from being slow on large data-sets so a natural question has been to obtain more efficient algorithms with similar guarantees. In this paper, we present such a near linear time algorithm for $k$-means++ seeding. Interestingly our algorithm obtains the same theoretical guarantees as $k$-means++ and significantly improves earlier results on fast $k$-means++ seeding. Moreover, we show empirically that our algorithm is significantly faster than $k$-means++ and obtains solutions of equivalent quality.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the cost of choosing initial centers for k-means clustering. The widely used k-means++ approach combines ease of implementation, theoretical guarantees, and strong practical results, but its seeding procedure can be slow on large datasets. The research question is whether that initialization can be accelerated while preserving its quality guarantees.

The authors introduce a seeding algorithm based on rejection sampling with near-linear running time. They establish that it retains the same theoretical guarantees as k-means++ and improves earlier results on fast seeding. Thus, the claimed speed improvement comes with a formal connection to the quality assurances that make the original method attractive.

The empirical evaluation reports substantially faster execution than k-means++ and solutions of equivalent quality. The theoretical and experimental findings address complementary concerns: the analysis preserves the guarantee, while the experiments check whether speed and quality align in practice. The contribution makes a well-established clustering initialization more efficient without a reported sacrifice in solution quality.
summary.tldr: A near-linear-time seeding algorithm preserves k-means++ guarantees and empirically achieves comparable quality with much faster execution.

title: Fast and Accurate $k$-means++ via Rejection Sampling

abstract: Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning (RL) have led to considerable progress in many 2-player zero-sum games, such as Go, Poker and Starcraft. The purely adversarial nature of such games allows for conceptually simple and principled application of RL methods. However real-world settings are many-agent, and agent interactions are complex mixtures of common-interest and competitive aspects. We consider Diplomacy, a 7-player board game designed to accentuate dilemmas resulting from many-agent interactions. It also features a large combinatorial action space and simultaneous moves, which are challenging for RL algorithms. We propose a simple yet effective approximate best response operator, designed to handle large combinatorial action spaces and simultaneous moves. We also introduce a family of policy iteration methods that approximate fictitious play. With these methods, we successfully apply RL to Diplomacy: we show that our agents convincingly outperform the previous state-of-the-art, and game theoretic equilibrium analysis shows that the new process yields consistent improvements.

paragraphs: Diplomacy presents reinforcement learning with a combination of challenges: seven players, simultaneous moves, and a large combinatorial action space. Its interactions mix common interests with competition, making the setting more complex than a purely adversarial two-player game. This paper develops methods for learning to play the no-press version through approximate best responses and policy iteration.

The authors introduce an approximate best-response operator designed specifically to handle simultaneous decisions and large combinations of actions. They also develop a family of policy-iteration methods that approximate fictitious play. Together, these components provide a way to improve policies while accounting for the strategic interactions among multiple players.

The resulting agents convincingly outperform the previous state of the art in the reported evaluation. A game-theoretic equilibrium analysis also finds consistent improvements from the new training process. These findings support the use of approximate response computation and iterative policy updates in a setting where action complexity and mixed interests make direct application of simpler reinforcement learning approaches difficult.
summary.tldr: Approximate best responses and policy iteration produce stronger no-press Diplomacy agents, with consistent improvements supported by equilibrium analysis.

title: Learning to Play No-Press Diplomacy with Best Response Policy Iteration

abstract: Autoencoders (AE) aim to reproduce the output from the input. They may hence tend to overfit towards learning the identity-function between the input and output, i.e., they may predict each feature in the output from itself in the input. This is not useful, however, when AEs are used for prediction tasks in the presence of noise in the data. It may seem intuitively evident that this kind of overfitting is prevented by training a denoising AE, as the dropped-out features have to be predicted from the other features. In this paper, we consider linear autoencoders, as they facilitate analytic solutions, and first show that denoising / dropout actually prevents the overfitting towards the identity-function only to the degree that it is penalized by the induced L2-norm regularization. In the main theorem of this paper, we show that the emphasized denoising AE is indeed capable of completely eliminating the overfitting towards the identity-function. Our derivations reveal several new insights, including the closed-form solution of the full-rank model, as well as a new (near-)orthogonality constraint in the low-rank model. While this constraint is conceptually very different from the regularizers recently proposed, their resulting effects on the learned embeddings are empirically similar. Our experiments on three well-known data-sets corroborate the various theoretical insights derived in this paper.

paragraphs: An autoencoder learns to reconstruct its input, which creates an easy but potentially unhelpful solution: copying each feature directly to its output. For prediction with noisy data, that behavior can undermine the purpose of learning relationships between features. The paper examines whether denoising training actually prevents this form of overfitting.

The authors study linear autoencoders because these allow analytic solutions. They show that ordinary denoising or dropout limits copying only through the L2 regularization it induces. The intuition that removing some inputs must eliminate identity-like behavior therefore overstates what ordinary denoising achieves. Their main theorem shows that an emphasized denoising autoencoder can completely eliminate this particular problem in the analyzed setting.

The derivations also produce a closed-form solution for the full-rank model and a new near-orthogonality constraint for the low-rank model. Although this constraint differs conceptually from recently proposed regularizers, its effects on learned embeddings are empirically similar. Experiments on three datasets support the theoretical insights. The central contribution is a precise account of identity overfitting and how to remove it in linear autoencoders.
summary.tldr: For linear autoencoders, ordinary denoising only regularizes identity copying, while emphasized denoising can eliminate that form of overfitting.

title: Autoencoders that don't overfit towards the Identity

abstract: Trajectory prediction for scenes with multiple agents and entities is a challenging problem in numerous domains such as traffic prediction, pedestrian tracking and path planning. We present a general architecture to address this challenge which models the crucial inductive biases of motion, namely, inertia, relative motion, intents and interactions. Specifically, we propose a relational model to flexibly model interactions between agents in diverse environments. Since it is well-known that human decision making is fuzzy by nature, at the core of our model lies a novel attention mechanism which models interactions by making continuous-valued (fuzzy) decisions and learning the corresponding responses. Our architecture demonstrates significant performance gains over existing state-of-the-art predictive models in diverse domains such as human crowd trajectories, US freeway traffic, NBA sports data and physics datasets. We also present ablations and augmentations to understand the decision-making process and the source of gains in our model.

paragraphs: Predicting motion in a scene with multiple agents requires accounting for how those agents affect one another. A pedestrian, vehicle, or player does not move independently of surrounding entities. This paper develops a general trajectory-prediction architecture organized around inertia, relative motion, intent, and interaction, giving these motion-related patterns an explicit role in the model.

A relational component represents interactions between agents across different environments. At its center is Fuzzy Query Attention, an attention mechanism that makes continuous-valued decisions and learns corresponding responses. The use of graded decisions is motivated by the fuzzy nature of human decision making. It gives the architecture a way to model interactions without treating every decision as an all-or-nothing choice.

The authors report significant gains over existing state-of-the-art predictive models on human crowds, US freeway traffic, NBA sports data, and physics datasets. They also use ablations and augmentations to investigate how the model makes decisions and where its gains originate. The range of tested domains supports the usefulness of combining interaction modeling with motion-specific structure, beyond a single type of trajectory data.
summary.tldr: Fuzzy Query Attention models graded interactions between agents and improves trajectory prediction across several tested motion domains.

title: Multi-agent Trajectory Prediction with Fuzzy Query Attention

abstract: Areas under ROC (AUROC) and precision-recall curves (AUPRC) are common metrics for evaluating classification performance for imbalanced problems. Compared with AUROC, AUPRC is a more appropriate metric for highly imbalanced datasets. While stochastic optimization of AUROC has been studied extensively, principled stochastic optimization of AUPRC has been rarely explored. In this work, we propose a principled technical method to optimize AUPRC for deep learning. Our approach is based on maximizing the averaged precision (AP), which is an unbiased point estimator of AUPRC. We cast the objective into a sum of dependent compositional functions with inner functions dependent on random variables of the outer level. We propose efficient adaptive and non-adaptive stochastic algorithms named SOAP with provable convergence guarantee under mild conditions by leveraging recent advances in stochastic compositional optimization. Extensive experimental results on image and graph datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms prior methods on imbalanced problems in terms of AUPRC. To the best of our knowledge, our work represents the first attempt to optimize AUPRC with provable convergence. The SOAP has been implemented in the libAUC library at https://libauc.org/.

Experiments on image and graph datasets show better AUPRC than prior methods on the evaluated imbalanced problems. The contribution combines a training objective aligned with the chosen metric, algorithms that handle its nested dependencies, and conditional convergence guarantees, with an implementation made available in the libAUC library.
summary.tldr: SOAP optimizes average precision with stochastic algorithms that have conditional convergence guarantees and improve reported AUPRC on imbalanced image and graph tasks.

title: Stochastic Optimization of Areas Under Precision-Recall Curves with Provable Convergence

abstract: Bayesian neural networks are theoretically well-understood only in the infinite-width limit, where Gaussian priors over network weights yield Gaussian priors over network outputs. Recent work has suggested that finite Bayesian networks may outperform their infinite counterparts, but their non-Gaussian output priors have been characterized only though perturbative approaches. Here, we derive exact solutions for the function space priors for individual input examples of a class of finite fully-connected feedforward Bayesian neural networks. For deep linear networks, the prior has a simple expression in terms of the Meijer $G$-function. The prior of a finite ReLU network is a mixture of the priors of linear networks of smaller widths, corresponding to different numbers of active units in each layer. Our results unify previous descriptions of finite network priors in terms of their tail decay and large-width behavior.

paragraphs: A Bayesian neural network places a probability distribution over its weights, which induces a distribution over its outputs before observing training data. Infinite-width networks have a well-understood Gaussian description under Gaussian weight priors. Finite networks can have non-Gaussian output distributions, and this paper derives exact expressions for a class of those distributions.

The results concern individual input examples in finite, fully connected feedforward networks. For deep linear networks, the output prior can be written using the Meijer G-function. For ReLU networks, it becomes a mixture of linear-network priors with smaller widths, reflecting the different possible numbers of active units in each layer.

This mixture description connects the activation pattern of a finite network to its output uncertainty. The exact formulas also unify earlier descriptions based on tail decay and large-width behaviour. Their scope is marginal priors at individual inputs: the contribution is an exact account of this aspect of finite networks, rather than a new empirical claim that finite networks always outperform infinite ones.
summary.tldr: The paper derives exact single-input output priors for a class of finite linear and ReLU Bayesian networks.

title: Exact marginal prior distributions of finite Bayesian neural networks

abstract: Neural volume rendering became increasingly popular recently due to its success in synthesizing novel views of a scene from a sparse set of input images. So far, the geometry learned by neural volume rendering techniques was modeled using a generic density function. Furthermore, the geometry itself was extracted using an arbitrary level set of the density function leading to a noisy, often low fidelity reconstruction.The goal of this paper is to improve geometry representation and reconstruction in neural volume rendering. We achieve that by modeling the volume density as a function of the geometry. This is in contrast to previous work modeling the geometry as a function of the volume density. In more detail, we define the volume density function as Laplace's cumulative distribution function (CDF) applied to a signed distance function (SDF) representation. This simple density representation has three benefits: (i) it provides a useful inductive bias to the geometry learned in the neural volume rendering process; (ii) it facilitates a bound on the opacity approximation error, leading to an accurate sampling of the viewing ray. Accurate sampling is important to provide a precise coupling of geometry and radiance; and (iii) it allows efficient unsupervised disentanglement of shape and appearance in volume rendering.Applying this new density representation to challenging scene multiview datasets produced high quality geometry reconstructions, outperforming relevant baselines. Furthermore, switching shape and appearance between scenes is possible due to the disentanglement of the two.

paragraphs: Neural volume rendering can synthesize new views from a sparse collection of images, but recovering clean geometry from a generic density field can be difficult. This paper makes geometry the basis of the density representation. It uses a signed distance function to represent the surface and applies the Laplace cumulative distribution function to obtain volume density.

The authors identify three benefits of this construction. It gives learning a useful geometric bias, supports a bound on opacity approximation error, and enables efficient unsupervised separation of shape and appearance. The error bound guides accurate sampling along viewing rays, helping couple the recovered geometry with the radiance used to render images.

On challenging multiview scene datasets, the method produces high-quality geometric reconstructions and outperforms relevant baselines. The separation of shape and appearance also allows them to be exchanged between scenes. These results show how explicitly structuring the density around a surface representation can support both reconstruction quality and control over rendered scene attributes.
summary.tldr: Defining volume density from a signed distance function improves surface reconstruction and enables separation of shape and appearance.

title: Volume Rendering of Neural Implicit Surfaces

abstract: This paper presents a topological learning-theoretic perspective on causal inference by introducing a series of topologies defined on general spaces of structural causal models (SCMs). As an illustration of the framework we prove a topological causal hierarchy theorem, showing that substantive assumption-free causal inference is possible only in a meager set of SCMs. Thanks to a known correspondence between open sets in the weak topology and statistically verifiable hypotheses, our results show that inductive assumptions sufficient to license valid causal inferences are statistically unverifiable in principle. Similar to no-free-lunch theorems for statistical inference, the present results clarify the inevitability of substantial assumptions for causal inference. An additional benefit of our topological approach is that it easily accommodates SCMs with infinitely many variables. We finally suggest that our framework may be helpful for the positive project of exploring and assessing alternative causal-inductive assumptions.

paragraphs: Causal inference asks questions that require more than identifying patterns in observed data. This paper investigates how far such inference can go without substantive assumptions. It introduces topologies on spaces of structural causal models, giving a mathematical framework for studying which causal conclusions can be learned and what assumptions make them possible.

The central result is a topological causal hierarchy theorem: substantive causal inference without assumptions is possible only within a meager set of models. Here, meager describes smallness in a topological sense; it is not a numerical probability assigned to those models. The authors also connect their framework to an established relationship between open sets in the weak topology and statistically verifiable hypotheses.

Through that connection, the paper shows that inductive assumptions sufficient for valid causal inference are statistically unverifiable in principle. The result clarifies why assumptions are unavoidable, rather than making causal inference pointless. The framework also accommodates infinitely many variables, and the authors suggest it could help researchers compare alternative causal assumptions.
summary.tldr: A topological analysis shows why substantive causal inference generally requires assumptions that cannot themselves be statistically verified.

title: A Topological Perspective on Causal Inference

abstract: We propose a canonical point autoencoder (CPAE) that predicts dense correspondences between 3D shapes of the same category. The autoencoder performs two key functions: (a) encoding an arbitrarily ordered point cloud to a canonical primitive, e.g., a sphere, and (b) decoding the primitive back to the original input instance shape. As being placed in the bottleneck, this primitive plays a key role to map all the unordered point clouds on the canonical surface, and to be reconstructed in an ordered fashion. Once trained, points from different shape instances that are mapped to the same locations on the primitive surface are determined to be a pair of correspondence. Our method does not require any form of annotation or self-supervised part segmentation network and can handle unaligned input point clouds within a certain rotation range. Experimental results on 3D semantic keypoint transfer and part segmentation transfer show that our model performs favorably against state-of-the-art correspondence learning methods.

paragraphs: Matching points across different 3D shapes is difficult because point clouds have no inherent ordering. This paper introduces a canonical point autoencoder that learns dense correspondences between shapes belonging to the same category. Its central idea is to give different shapes a shared reference surface through which their points can be compared.

The encoder maps an unordered point cloud onto a canonical primitive, such as a sphere, and the decoder reconstructs the original shape from that primitive. Placing the shared surface at the autoencoder’s bottleneck encourages an ordered reconstruction. After training, points from different instances are treated as corresponding when they map to the same location on the canonical surface.

The method needs neither annotations nor a separate self-supervised part-segmentation network. It also handles unaligned point clouds within a certain rotation range. Experiments transferring semantic keypoints and part segmentations compare favorably with state-of-the-art correspondence methods. These results support the shared-surface bottleneck as a useful way to learn cross-shape matching without correspondence annotations.
summary.tldr: A shared canonical surface lets an autoencoder learn dense correspondences between same-category 3D shapes without annotations.

title: Learning 3D Dense Correspondence via Canonical Point Autoencoder

abstract: Recently, there emerges a series of vision Transformers, which show superior performance with a more compact model size than conventional convolutional neural networks, thanks to the strong ability of Transformers to model long-range dependencies. However, the advantages of vision Transformers also come with a price: Self-attention, the core part of Transformer, has a quadratic complexity to the input sequence length. This leads to a dramatic increase of computation and memory cost with the increase of sequence length, thus introducing difficulties when applying Transformers to the vision tasks that require dense predictions based on high-resolution feature maps.In this paper, we propose a new vision Transformer, named Glance-and-Gaze Transformer (GG-Transformer), to address the aforementioned issues. It is motivated by the Glance and Gaze behavior of human beings when recognizing objects in natural scenes, with the ability to efficiently model both long-range dependencies and local context. In GG-Transformer, the Glance and Gaze behavior is realized by two parallel branches: The Glance branch is achieved by performing self-attention on the adaptively-dilated partitions of the input, which leads to a linear complexity while still enjoying a global receptive field; The Gaze branch is implemented by a simple depth-wise convolutional layer, which compensates local image context to the features obtained by the Glance mechanism. We empirically demonstrate our method achieves consistently superior performance over previous state-of-the-art Transformers on various vision tasks and benchmarks.

paragraphs: Vision transformers can connect distant image regions, but standard self-attention has computation that grows quadratically with sequence length. This becomes especially expensive when high-resolution feature maps are needed for dense predictions. The Glance-and-Gaze Transformer addresses that cost while retaining mechanisms for both broad image relationships and nearby visual detail.

The architecture has two parallel branches. The Glance branch applies self-attention within adaptively dilated partitions of the input. This arrangement achieves linear complexity while maintaining a global receptive field, allowing information from widely separated locations to influence the representation. The Gaze branch uses depth-wise convolution to contribute local image context that complements the Glance features.

The human-inspired naming therefore corresponds to a concrete division of computation: attention handles broad relationships through a cheaper partitioned structure, and convolution supplies local context. The authors report consistently better performance than previous state-of-the-art transformers across several vision tasks and benchmarks. The empirical findings support combining these two forms of processing as an efficient way to preserve both global reach and local information.
summary.tldr: Glance-and-Gaze combines linear-complexity global attention with local convolution to improve efficiency and reported vision-task performance.

title: Glance-and-Gaze Vision Transformer

abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) is a task where an agent navigates in an embodied indoor environment under human instructions. Previous works ignore the distribution of sample difficulty and we argue that this potentially degrade their agent performance. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel curriculum- based training paradigm for VLN tasks that can balance human prior knowledge and agent learning progress about training samples. We develop the principle of curriculum design and re-arrange the benchmark Room-to-Room (R2R) dataset to make it suitable for curriculum training. Experiments show that our method is model-agnostic and can significantly improve the performance, the generalizability, and the training efficiency of current state-of-the-art navigation agents without increasing model complexity.

paragraphs: Vision-and-language navigation asks an agent to move through an indoor environment while following human instructions. Training examples differ in difficulty, but earlier approaches often overlook that distribution. The authors argue that ignoring these differences may weaken learning and propose organizing training through a curriculum.

Their training paradigm balances human prior knowledge about examples with the agent's learning progress. This combines an externally informed view of difficulty with information about how training is actually proceeding. The paper develops principles for curriculum design and rearranges the Room-to-Room benchmark dataset so it can support this form of training.

Experiments report significant improvements in navigation performance, generalization, and training efficiency for existing state-of-the-art agents. The approach is described as model-agnostic and achieves these gains without increasing model complexity. Its practical significance is that changes to the organization of training can improve how an existing agent learns. The reported benefits concern both successful navigation and the efficiency and transferability of the learning process, rather than requiring a larger navigation architecture.
summary.tldr: A curriculum balancing human knowledge and agent progress improves navigation learning without increasing model complexity.

title: Curriculum Learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation

abstract: Label noise and class imbalance are two major issues coexisting in real-world datasets. To alleviate the two issues, state-of-the-art methods reweight each instance by leveraging a small amount of clean and unbiased data. Yet, these methods overlook class-level information within each instance, which can be further utilized to improve performance. To this end, in this paper, we propose Generalized Data Weighting (GDW) to simultaneously mitigate label noise and class imbalance by manipulating gradients at the class level. To be specific, GDW unrolls the loss gradient to class-level gradients by the chain rule and reweights the flow of each gradient separately. In this way, GDW achieves remarkable performance improvement on both issues. Aside from the performance gain, GDW efficiently obtains class-level weights without introducing any extra computational cost compared with instance weighting methods. Specifically, GDW performs a gradient descent step on class-level weights, which only relies on intermediate gradients. Extensive experiments in various settings verify the effectiveness of GDW. For example, GDW outperforms state-of-the-art methods by $2.56\%$ under the $60\%$ uniform noise setting in CIFAR10. Our code is available at https://github.com/GGchen1997/GDW-NIPS2021.
