paragraphs: Incorrect labels and uneven class frequencies can occur together in real datasets. Existing weighting approaches address these problems by changing how strongly each training example contributes, using a small clean and unbiased dataset for guidance. This paper argues that assigning one weight to an entire example overlooks useful distinctions among its class-level learning signals.

Generalized Data Weighting, or GDW, applies the chain rule to separate the loss gradient into class-level components. It then weights those components independently. This provides finer control over learning: the influence associated with one class can be adjusted separately from other class contributions within the same example. The method is designed to address label noise and class imbalance simultaneously.

The authors obtain these class-level weights through a gradient-descent step that uses intermediate gradients. They report no extra computational cost compared with instance-weighting methods, making the finer control practical in the evaluated comparison. Experiments across multiple settings support its effectiveness. In one stated example, GDW improves over state-of-the-art methods by 2.56% on CIFAR10 with 60% uniform label noise.
summary.tldr: GDW separately weights class-level gradient contributions to combat label noise and class imbalance without reported extra cost over instance weighting.

title: Generalized DataWeighting via Class-Level Gradient Manipulation

abstract: When a graph neural network (GNN) made a prediction, one raises question about explainability: “Which fraction of the input graph is most inﬂuential to the model’s decision?” Producing an answer requires understanding the model’s inner workings in general and emphasizing the insights on the decision for the instance at hand. Nonetheless, most of current approaches focus only on one aspect: (1) local explainability, which explains each instance independently, thus hardly exhibits the class-wise patterns; and (2) global explainability, which systematizes the globally important patterns, but might be trivial in the local context. This dichotomy limits the ﬂexibility and effectiveness of explainers greatly. A performant paradigm towards multi-grained explainability is until-now lacking and thus a focus of our work. In this work, we exploit the pre-training and ﬁne-tuning idea to develop our explainer and generate multi-grained explanations. Speciﬁcally, the pre-training phase accounts for the contrastivity among different classes, so as to highlight the class-wise characteristics from a global view; afterwards, the ﬁne-tuning phase adapts the explanations in the local context. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show the superiority of our explainer, in terms of AUC on explaining graph classiﬁcation over the leading baselines. Our codes and datasets are available at https://github.com/Wuyxin/ReFine.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network requires identifying which parts of an input graph influence its prediction. Local explanations focus on one example but may miss patterns shared across a class. Global explanations capture broader patterns but may offer little useful detail about a particular example. This paper develops an explainer that connects both levels.

The approach uses pre-training followed by fine-tuning. During pre-training, the explainer accounts for differences between classes to learn class-specific characteristics from a global perspective. Fine-tuning then adapts those explanations to the individual graph. This sequence gives the local explanation access to broader class patterns while allowing it to reflect the example at hand.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show higher AUC for explaining graph classification than the leading baselines considered. The findings support combining global preparation with local adaptation in a single explanation procedure. The contribution is a way to generate explanations at multiple levels of detail, connecting patterns that characterize a class with the graph components relevant to an individual decision.
summary.tldr: A graph explainer learns class-level patterns through pre-training and adapts them through fine-tuning to explain individual predictions.

title: Towards Multi-Grained Explainability for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Despite rapid progress in the recent past, current speech recognition systems still require labeled training data which limits this technology to a small fraction of the languages spoken around the globe. This paper describes wav2vec-U, short for wav2vec Unsupervised, a method to train speech recognition models without any labeled data. We leverage self-supervised speech representations to segment unlabeled audio and learn a mapping from these representations to phonemes via adversarial training. The right representations are key to the success of our method. Compared to the best previous unsupervised work, wav2vec-U reduces the phone error rate on the TIMIT benchmark from 26.1 to 11.3. On the larger English Librispeech benchmark, wav2vec-U achieves a word error rate of 5.9 on test-other, rivaling some of the best published systems trained on 960 hours of labeled data from only two years ago. We also experiment on nine other languages, including low-resource languages such as Kyrgyz, Swahili and Tatar.

paragraphs: Speech recognition usually depends on labeled training examples, restricting its reach to languages with sufficient annotated data. This paper introduces wav2vec-U, a method for training speech recognition models without labeled data. It addresses the supervision requirement by building on representations learned from speech through self-supervision.

The method uses those representations to segment unlabeled audio, then learns a mapping to phonemes through adversarial training. Phonemes provide the speech-sound units targeted by this mapping. The authors emphasize that choosing suitable representations is central to the method's success, connecting the structure learned from audio with the subsequent recognition task.

On TIMIT, wav2vec-U reduces phone error rate from the previous best unsupervised result of 26.1 to 11.3. On LibriSpeech test-other, it achieves a word error rate of 5.9, rivaling some leading published systems from two years earlier that used 960 hours of labeled data. Experiments also cover nine other languages, including Kyrgyz, Swahili, and Tatar. These findings demonstrate substantial progress in recognition without labeled training data across the studied settings.
summary.tldr: wav2vec-U combines self-supervised speech representations and adversarial training to achieve strong speech recognition without labeled training data.

title: Unsupervised Speech Recognition

abstract: Logistic regression remains one of the most widely used tools in applied statistics, machine learning and data science. However, in moderately high-dimensional problems, where the number of features $d$ is a non-negligible fraction of the sample size $n$, the logistic regression maximum likelihood estimator (MLE), and statistical procedures based the large-sample approximation of its distribution, behave poorly. Recently, Sur and Candès (2019) showed that these issues can be corrected by applying a new approximation of the MLE's sampling distribution in this high-dimensional regime. Unfortunately, these corrections are difficult to implement in practice, because they require an estimate of the \emph{signal strength}, which is a function of the underlying parameters $\beta$ of the logistic regression. To address this issue, we propose SLOE, a fast and straightforward approach to estimate the signal strength in logistic regression. The key insight of SLOE is that the Sur and Candès (2019) correction can be reparameterized in terms of the corrupted signal strength, which is only a function of the estimated parameters $\widehat \beta$. We propose an estimator for this quantity, prove that it is consistent in the relevant high-dimensional regime, and show that dimensionality correction using SLOE is accurate in finite samples. Compared to the existing ProbeFrontier heuristic, SLOE is conceptually simpler and orders of magnitude faster, making it suitable for routine use. We demonstrate the importance of routine dimensionality correction in the Heart Disease dataset from the UCI repository, and a genomics application using data from the UK Biobank.

Recently, Sur and Candès (2019) showed that these issues can be corrected by applying a new approximation of the MLE's sampling distribution in this high-dimensional regime. Unfortunately, these corrections are difficult to implement in practice, because they require an estimate of the \emph{signal strength}, which is a function of the underlying parameters $\beta$ of the logistic regression. To address this issue, we propose SLOE, a fast and straightforward approach to estimate the signal strength in logistic regression. The key insight of SLOE is that the Sur and Candès (2019) correction can be reparameterized in terms of the corrupted signal strength, which is only a function of the estimated parameters $\widehat \beta$. We propose an estimator for this quantity, prove that it is consistent in the relevant high-dimensional regime, and show that dimensionality correction using SLOE is accurate in finite samples. Compared to the existing ProbeFrontier heuristic, SLOE is conceptually simpler and orders of magnitude faster, making it suitable for routine use. We demonstrate the importance of routine dimensionality correction in the Heart Disease dataset from the UCI repository, and a genomics application using data from the UK Biobank.

paragraphs: Logistic regression can support unreliable statistical inference when the number of features is a substantial fraction of the number of observations. In this regime, conventional large-sample approximations for the maximum likelihood estimator behave poorly. Existing high-dimensional corrections address this problem, but implementing them requires estimating a signal strength that depends on unknown model parameters.

SLOE makes the correction more practical by expressing it in terms of corrupted signal strength, a quantity depending only on estimated parameters. The authors propose an estimator for this quantity and prove its consistency in the relevant high-dimensional regime. This reparameterization replaces the difficult unknown-parameter input with a quantity that can be estimated from the fitted model.

The paper reports accurate dimensionality correction in finite samples and computation that is orders of magnitude faster than the ProbeFrontier heuristic. Applications use the UCI Heart Disease dataset and UK Biobank genomics data to illustrate why routine correction matters. The contribution is a faster route to established high-dimensional inference corrections, supported by an asymptotic guarantee and empirical finite-sample results.
summary.tldr: SLOE efficiently estimates the quantity needed to correct high-dimensional logistic-regression inference, with consistency and finite-sample accuracy results.

title: SLOE: A Faster Method for Statistical Inference in High-Dimensional Logistic Regression

abstract: The last decade has witnessed a technological arms race to encode the molecular states of cells into DNA libraries, turning DNA sequencers into scalable single-cell microscopes. Single-cell measurement of chromatin accessibility (DNA), gene expression (RNA), and proteins has revealed rich cellular diversity across tissues, organisms, and disease states. However, single-cell data poses a unique set of challenges. A dataset may comprise millions of cells with tens of thousands of sparse features. Identifying biologically relevant signals from the background sources of technical noise requires innovation in predictive and representational learning. Furthermore, unlike in machine vision or natural language processing, biological ground truth is limited. Here we leverage recent advances in multi-modal single-cell technologies which, by simultaneously measuring two layers of cellular processing in each cell, provide ground truth analogous to language translation. We define three key tasks to predict one modality from another and learn integrated representations of cellular state. We also generate a novel dataset of the human bone marrow specifically designed for benchmarking studies. The dataset and tasks are accessible through an open-source framework that facilitates centralized evaluation of community-submitted methods.

paragraphs: Measurements of individual cells can reveal their molecular state through chromatin accessibility, RNA expression, and proteins. These datasets can contain millions of cells and tens of thousands of features, many of them sparse. The paper addresses the challenge of learning biologically meaningful patterns from such measurements while separating those patterns from technical noise.

A central difficulty is the limited availability of biological ground truth. The authors use technologies that measure two molecular layers in the same cell to obtain paired observations. They compare this arrangement to language translation: a measurement in one modality has a corresponding measurement in another, providing a concrete basis for evaluating prediction across modalities.

The contribution combines three tasks for cross-modality prediction and integrated representations with a new human bone marrow dataset designed for benchmarking. An open-source framework supports centralized evaluation of submitted methods. Together, these resources provide a shared setting for comparing how algorithms predict complementary measurements and combine them into representations of cellular state.
summary.tldr: Paired molecular measurements, a bone marrow dataset, and shared tasks support benchmarking prediction and integration across single-cell modalities.

title: A sandbox for prediction and integration of DNA, RNA, and proteins in single cells

abstract: Visual Counterfactual Explanations (VCEs) are an important tool to understand the decisions of an image classifier. They are “small” but “realistic” semantic changes of the image changing the classifier decision. Current approaches for the generation of VCEs are restricted to adversarially robust models and often contain non-realistic artefacts, or are limited to image classification problems with few classes. In this paper, we overcome this by generating Diffusion Visual Counterfactual Explanations (DVCEs) for arbitrary ImageNet classifiers via a diffusion process. Two modifications to the diffusion process are key for our DVCEs: first, an adaptive parameterization, whose hyperparameters generalize across images and models, together with distance regularization and late start of the diffusion process, allow us to generate images with minimal semantic changes to the original ones but different classification. Second, our cone regularization via an adversarially robust model ensures that the diffusion process does not converge to trivial non-semantic changes, but instead produces realistic images of the target class which achieve high confidence by the classifier.

paragraphs: A visual counterfactual explanation changes an image enough to change a classifier's decision while keeping the edit small and realistic. The aim is to make the decision change understandable through image content. This paper develops diffusion-based counterfactuals for arbitrary ImageNet classifiers, addressing restrictions and unrealistic artifacts in earlier approaches.

One part of the method controls how much the image changes. An adaptive parameterization uses hyperparameters that transfer across images and models, while distance regularization and a late start to diffusion keep the generated image close to the original. Together, these components seek a different classification with minimal semantic alteration.

A second component, cone regularization, uses an adversarially robust model to guide the diffusion process away from trivial changes that lack semantic meaning. Thus, the classifier being explained need not itself be robust, although a robust model still contributes to generation. The resulting explanations are described as realistic images of the target class that receive high confidence from the classifier, linking the changed decision to visible content.
summary.tldr: Diffusion-based counterfactuals use controlled image changes and robust-model guidance to explain decisions of arbitrary ImageNet classifiers.

title: Diffusion Visual Counterfactual Explanations

abstract: Avoiding overfitting is a central challenge in machine learning, yet many large neural networks readily achieve zero training loss. This puzzling contradiction necessitates new approaches to the study of overfitting. Here we quantify overfitting via residual information, defined as the bits in fitted models that encode noise in training data. Information efficient learning algorithms minimize residual information while maximizing the relevant bits, which are predictive of the unknown generative models. We solve this optimization to obtain the information content of optimal algorithms for a linear regression problem and compare it to that of randomized ridge regression. Our results demonstrate the fundamental trade-off between residual and relevant information and characterize the relative information efficiency of randomized regression with respect to optimal algorithms. Finally, using results from random matrix theory, we reveal the information complexity of learning a linear map in high dimensions and unveil information-theoretic analogs of double and multiple descent phenomena.

paragraphs: A model can fit its training data perfectly while capturing both meaningful structure and accidental noise. This paper studies that distinction through information: relevant bits help characterize the unknown process generating the data, while residual bits encode training noise. It uses residual information to quantify overfitting rather than relying solely on training loss.

The authors formulate an information-efficiency objective that favors relevant information while limiting residual information. They solve this optimization for a linear-regression problem, obtaining the information content of optimal algorithms. They then compare randomized ridge regression against that reference, assessing how efficiently it preserves useful information relative to the optimum.

The results characterize a fundamental trade-off between retaining signal and encoding noise. Using random matrix theory, the paper also studies the information complexity of learning a linear map in high dimensions and identifies information-theoretic counterparts of double and multiple descent. The work provides a precise analysis within linear regression, using that setting to clarify how fitting data and learning useful structure can differ.
summary.tldr: An information-theoretic analysis of linear regression quantifies the trade-off between learning useful structure and retaining training noise.

title: Information bottleneck theory of high-dimensional regression: relevancy, efficiency and optimality

abstract: Learning generalizable policies that can adapt to unseen environments remains challenging in visual Reinforcement Learning (RL). Existing approaches try to acquire a robust representation via diversifying the appearances of in-domain observations for better generalization. Limited by the specific observations of the environment, these methods ignore the possibility of exploring diverse real-world image datasets. In this paper, we investigate how a visual RL agent would benefit from the off-the-shelf visual representations. Surprisingly, we find that the early layers in an ImageNet pre-trained ResNet model could provide rather generalizable representations for visual RL. Hence, we propose Pre-trained Image Encoder for Generalizable visual reinforcement learning (PIE-G), a simple yet effective framework that can generalize to the unseen visual scenarios in a zero-shot manner. Extensive experiments are conducted on DMControl Generalization Benchmark, DMControl Manipulation Tasks, Drawer World, and CARLA to verify the effectiveness of PIE-G. Empirical evidence suggests PIE-G improves sample efficiency and significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods in terms of generalization performance. In particular, PIE-G boasts a 55% generalization performance gain on average in the challenging video background setting. Project Page: https://sites.google.com/view/pie-g/home.

paragraphs: Visual reinforcement learning agents can struggle when their surroundings look different from the training environment. Existing approaches often vary the appearance of observations already available within that environment. This paper investigates a broader source of visual experience: representations learned beforehand from a large collection of real-world images.

The authors find that early layers of an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet provide representations that generalize well for visual reinforcement learning. They use this finding to build PIE-G, a framework designed to transfer to unseen visual scenarios in a zero-shot manner. The central idea is to reuse suitable off-the-shelf visual features as part of the agent’s representation.

Evaluations cover the DMControl Generalization Benchmark, DMControl Manipulation Tasks, Drawer World, and CARLA. The empirical results suggest improved sample efficiency and substantially better generalization than previous leading methods. In the challenging video-background setting, the authors report an average generalization-performance gain of 55%. These findings support the usefulness of early pretrained visual features for the tested control settings and show that image pretraining can benefit policies facing unfamiliar appearances.
summary.tldr: PIE-G reuses early ImageNet-pretrained ResNet features to improve visual reinforcement learning generalization to unseen appearances.

title: Pre-Trained Image Encoder for Generalizable Visual Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Computing the Jacobian of the solution of an optimization problem is a central problem in machine learning, with applications in hyperparameter optimization, meta-learning, optimization as a layer, and dataset distillation, to name a few. Unrolled differentiation is a popular heuristic that approximates the solution using an iterative solver and differentiates it through the computational path. This work provides a non-asymptotic convergence-rate analysis of this approach on quadratic objectives for gradient descent and the Chebyshev method. We show that to ensure convergence of the Jacobian, we can either 1) choose a large learning rate leading to a fast asymptotic convergence but accept that the algorithm may have an arbitrarily long burn-in phase or 2) choose a smaller learning rate leading to an immediate but slower convergence. We refer to this phenomenon as the curse of unrolling.Finally, we discuss open problems relative to this approach, such as deriving a practical update rule for the optimal unrolling strategy and making novel connections with the field of Sobolev orthogonal polynomials.

paragraphs: Many learning procedures need to know how an optimization solution changes when its inputs or parameters change. Unrolled differentiation estimates this sensitivity by running an iterative solver and differentiating through its sequence of computations. The paper studies how quickly the resulting Jacobian estimate converges, focusing on quadratic objectives solved by gradient descent or the Chebyshev method.

The analysis gives finite-iteration convergence rates and exposes a learning-rate tradeoff. A larger learning rate can produce fast asymptotic convergence of the Jacobian, but may come with an arbitrarily long initial burn-in phase. A smaller learning rate can provide immediate convergence, though at a slower rate. The authors call this tension the curse of unrolling.

The result matters because behavior after many iterations can conceal a long period before derivative estimates become useful. It provides a theoretical way to distinguish eventual convergence speed from progress early in the computation. The paper also identifies open questions, including a practical update rule for choosing an optimal unrolling strategy and connections to Sobolev orthogonal polynomials.
summary.tldr: For quadratic optimization, unrolled differentiation faces a tradeoff between fast eventual Jacobian convergence with potentially long burn-in and slower immediate convergence.

title: The Curse of Unrolling: Rate of Differentiating Through Optimization

abstract: The vast majority of work in self-supervised learning have focused on assessing recovered features by a chosen set of downstream tasks. While there are several commonly used benchmark datasets, this lens of feature learning requires assumptions on the downstream tasks which are not inherent to the data distribution itself. In this paper, we present an alternative lens, one of parameter identifiability: assuming data comes from a parametric probabilistic model, we train a self-supervised learning predictor with a suitable parametric form, and ask whether the parameters of the optimal predictor can be used to extract the parameters of the ground truth generative model.Specifically, we focus on latent-variable models capturing sequential structures, namely Hidden Markov Models with both discrete and conditionally Gaussian observations. We focus on masked prediction as the self-supervised learning task and study the optimal masked predictor. We show that parameter identifiability is governed by the task difficulty, which is determined by the choice of data model and the amount of tokens to predict. Technique-wise, we uncover close connections with the uniqueness of tensor rank decompositions, a widely used tool in studying identifiability through the lens of the method of moments.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning is usually assessed by testing learned features on selected downstream tasks. This paper asks a different question: if data arise from a parametric probabilistic model, can an optimal self-supervised predictor reveal the parameters that generated those data? This perspective evaluates what the prediction task identifies about the data distribution itself.

The authors study masked prediction for sequential latent-variable models, specifically Hidden Markov Models with discrete or conditionally Gaussian observations. They assume a suitable parametric form for the predictor and analyze its optimum. The central question is whether the generative model’s parameters can be extracted from the optimal predictor’s parameters.

The results show that identifiability depends on task difficulty, which is shaped by both the data model and the number of tokens being predicted. The analysis connects this question to uniqueness of tensor rank decompositions, a tool used in moment-based identifiability arguments. This provides a theoretical way to examine how masking-task design affects recoverable information, beyond performance on a chosen downstream benchmark.
summary.tldr: For specified Hidden Markov Models, masked-prediction task difficulty determines whether an optimal predictor identifies the underlying generative parameters.

title: Masked Prediction: A Parameter Identifiability View

abstract: Existing convolutional neural networks widely adopt spatial down-/up-sampling for multi-scale modeling. However, spatial up-sampling operators (e.g., interpolation, transposed convolution, and un-pooling) heavily depend on local pixel attention, incapably exploring the global dependency. In contrast, the Fourier domain is in accordance with the nature of global modeling according to the spectral convolution theorem. Unlike the spatial domain that easily performs up-sampling with the property of local similarity, up-sampling in the Fourier domain is more challenging as it does not follow such a local property. In this study, we propose a theoretically feasible Deep Fourier Up-Sampling (FourierUp) to solve these issues. We revisit the relationships between spatial and Fourier domains and reveal the transform rules on the features of different resolutions in the Fourier domain, which provide key insights for FourierUp's designs. FourierUp as a generic operator consists of three key components: 2D discrete Fourier transform, Fourier dimension increase rules, and 2D inverse Fourier transform, which can be directly integrated with existing networks. Extensive experiments across multiple computer vision tasks, including object detection, image segmentation, image de-raining, image dehazing, and guided image super-resolution, demonstrate the consistent performance gains obtained by introducing our FourierUp. Code will be publicly available.

This paper develops an alternative in the Fourier domain, where the representation supports global modeling, so increasing resolution can draw on relationships beyond nearby pixels.

The difficulty is that Fourier features do not follow the same local similarity property that makes spatial interpolation straightforward. The authors study how representations at different resolutions relate across the spatial and Fourier domains. summary.tldr: FourierUp increases feature resolution through Fourier-domain transformations and improves performance across several vision tasks.

title: Deep Fourier Up-Sampling

abstract: Ranking algorithms find extensive usage in diverse areas such as web search, employment, college admission, voting, etc. The related rank aggregation problem deals with combining multiple rankings into a single aggregate ranking. However, algorithms for both these problems might be biased against some individuals or groups due to implicit prejudice or marginalization in the historical data. We study ranking and rank aggregation problems from a fairness or diversity perspective, where the candidates (to be ranked) may belong to different groups and each group should have a fair representation in the final ranking. We allow the designer to set the parameters that define fair representation. These parameters specify the allowed range of the number of candidates from a particular group in the top-$k$ positions of the ranking. Given any ranking, we provide a fast and exact algorithm for finding the closest fair ranking for the Kendall tau metric under {\em strong fairness}, i.e., when the final ranking is fair for all values of $k$. We also provide an exact algorithm for finding the closest fair ranking for the Ulam metric under strong fairness when there are only $O(1)$ number of groups. Our algorithms are simple, fast, and might be extendable to other relevant metrics. We also give a novel meta-algorithm for the general rank aggregation problem under the fairness framework. Surprisingly, this meta-algorithm works for any generalized mean objective (including center and median problems) and any fairness criteria. As a byproduct, we obtain 3-approximation algorithms for both center and median problems, under both Kendall tau and Ulam metrics. Furthermore, using sophisticated techniques we obtain a $(3-\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm, for a constant $\varepsilon>0$, for the Ulam metric under strong fairness.

paragraphs: Combining rankings can preserve biases already present in their inputs. This paper studies ranking and rank aggregation with explicit group-representation requirements. A designer specifies lower and upper bounds on how many members of each group may appear in the first k positions. Strong fairness requires these bounds to hold across every prefix of the final ranking.

For modifying an existing ranking, the authors give a fast, exact algorithm that finds the closest strongly fair result under Kendall tau distance. They also provide an exact result under Ulam distance when the number of groups is constant. These guarantees make the tradeoff precise: enforce the specified representation rules while minimizing ranking changes according to the chosen metric.

For combining multiple rankings, a broader meta-algorithm accommodates generalized mean objectives and arbitrary fairness criteria. It yields 3-approximation algorithms for center and median objectives under both distances. Additional techniques improve the Ulam guarantee to 3−ε under strong fairness for a constant positive ε. The results distinguish exact fairness-preserving repair from approximation guarantees for aggregation.
summary.tldr: The paper develops exact ranking-repair algorithms and approximation algorithms for aggregation under explicit group-representation constraints.

title: Fair Rank Aggregation

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims at learning effective policies from historical data without extra environment interactions. During our experience of applying offline RL, we noticed that previous offline RL benchmarks commonly involve significant reality gaps, which we have identified include rich and overly exploratory datasets, degraded baseline, and missing policy validation. In many real-world situations, to ensure system safety, running an overly exploratory policy to collect various data is prohibited, thus only a narrow data distribution is available. The resulting policy is regarded as effective if it is better than the working behavior policy; the policy model can be deployed only if it has been well validated, rather than accomplished the training. In this paper, we present a Near real-world offline RL benchmark, named NeoRL, to reflect these properties. NeoRL datasets are collected with a more conservative strategy. Moreover, NeoRL contains the offline training and offline validation pipeline before the online test, corresponding to real-world situations. We then evaluate recent state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms in NeoRL. The empirical results demonstrate that some offline RL algorithms are less competitive to the behavior cloning and the deterministic behavior policy, implying that they could be less effective in real-world tasks than in the previous benchmarks. We also disclose that current offline policy evaluation methods could hardly select the best policy. We hope this work will shed some light on future research and deploying RL in real-world systems.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns policies from historical data without collecting additional interactions during training. The authors argue that common benchmarks can make this task unlike deployment: their data may be overly exploratory, their reference policies weak, and their procedures missing policy validation. Real systems may supply only narrowly distributed data collected conservatively for safety.

NeoRL is designed around those concerns. Its datasets use more conservative collection strategies, and its evaluation process includes offline training and offline validation before an online test. The benchmark also emphasizes whether a learned policy improves on the behavior policy already operating the system. This connects algorithm evaluation to the practical question of whether replacing an existing policy is worthwhile.

Experiments find that some recent offline reinforcement-learning algorithms are less competitive than behavior cloning and the deterministic behavior policy. The authors also find that current offline policy evaluation methods struggle to select the best policy. These results suggest that success on earlier benchmarks may overstate effectiveness in realistic settings, and they highlight policy selection as a substantive part of the deployment problem.
summary.tldr: NeoRL tests offline reinforcement learning with conservative data and explicit validation, exposing weaknesses in some algorithms and policy-selection methods.

title: NeoRL: A Near Real-World Benchmark for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Machine Learning models are often susceptible to poor performance on instances sampled from bad environments. For example, an image classifier could provide low accuracy on images captured under low lighting conditions. In high stake ML applications, such as AI-driven medical diagnostics, a better option could be to provide recourse in the form of alternative environment settings in which to recapture the instance for more reliable diagnostics. In this paper, we propose a model called {\em RecourseNet} that learns to apply recourse on the space of environments so that the recoursed instances are amenable to better predictions by the classifier. Learning to output optimal recourse is challenging because we do not assume access to the underlying physical process that generates the recoursed instances. Also, the optimal setting could be instance-dependent --- for example the best camera angle for object recognition could be a function of the object's shape. We propose a novel three-level training method that (a) Learns a classifier that is optimized for high performance under recourse, (b) Learns a recourse predictor when the training data may contain only limited instances under good environment settings, and (c) Triggers recourse selectively only when recourse is likely to improve classifier confidence.

For example, an image classifier could provide low accuracy on images captured under low lighting conditions. In high stake ML applications, such as AI-driven medical diagnostics, a better option could be to provide recourse in the form of alternative environment settings in which to recapture the instance for more reliable diagnostics. In this paper, we propose a model called {\em RecourseNet} that learns to apply recourse on the space of environments so that the recoursed instances are amenable to better predictions by the classifier. paragraphs: A classifier can struggle because of the conditions under which an example was captured, such as poor lighting in an image. This paper studies recourse that changes those environmental conditions so the instance can be captured again. RecourseNet learns to recommend settings intended to make the resulting instance easier for a classifier to predict accurately.

The recommendation problem is difficult because the physical process that generates a recaptured instance is not assumed to be available. The best environment can also depend on the particular instance: an object's shape may affect which camera angle is useful. A single fixed recommendation therefore cannot express all the instance-dependent choices the method seeks to learn.

That trigger depends on whether classifier confidence is likely to improve. The contribution is a coordinated learning framework for classification and environment recommendations; the abstract does not equate increased confidence with guaranteed correctness.

title: Learning Recourse on Instance Environment to Enhance Prediction Accuracy

abstract: The momentum acceleration technique is widely adopted in many optimization algorithms. However, there is no theoretical answer on how the momentum affects the generalization performance of the optimization algorithms. This paper studies this problem by analyzing the implicit regularization of momentum-based optimization. We prove that on the linear classification problem with separable data and exponential-tailed loss, gradient descent with momentum (GDM) converges to the $L^2$ max-margin solution, which is the same as vanilla gradient descent. That means gradient descent with momentum acceleration still converges to a low-complexity model, which guarantees their generalization. We then analyze the stochastic and adaptive variants of GDM (i.e., SGDM and deterministic Adam) and show they also converge to the $L^2$ max-margin solution. Technically, the implicit regularization of SGDM is established based on a novel convergence analysis of SGDM under a general noise condition called affine noise variance condition. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to derive SGDM’s convergence under such an assumption. Numerical experiments are conducted to support our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms can favor particular solutions even without an explicit penalty specifying that preference. This implicit regularization helps explain the models that training produces. The paper asks whether adding momentum changes that preference, focusing on linear classification where the data are separable and the loss has an exponential tail.

For this setting, the authors prove that gradient descent with momentum converges to the same L2 maximum-margin solution as ordinary gradient descent. This solution separates the classes with the largest margin measured using Euclidean geometry. The finding connects momentum-based optimization to the low-complexity solution preference associated with ordinary gradient descent.

The analysis also covers stochastic gradient descent with momentum and deterministic Adam, showing convergence to the L2 maximum-margin solution in the studied setting. The stochastic result relies on a new convergence analysis under an affine noise variance condition. Numerical experiments support the theory. The significance is a shared implicit bias across these optimizers under the stated classification assumptions, rather than a claim about momentum in arbitrary neural-network training.
summary.tldr: On separable linear classification with exponential-tailed loss, the analyzed momentum methods retain the L2 maximum-margin bias of gradient descent.

title: Does Momentum Change the Implicit Regularization on Separable Data?

abstract: Learned representations are a central component in modern ML systems, serving a multitude of downstream tasks. When training such representations, it is often the case that computational and statistical constraints for each downstream task are unknown. In this context rigid, fixed capacity representations can be either over or under-accommodating to the task at hand. This leads us to ask: can we design a flexible representation that can adapt to multiple downstream tasks with varying computational resources? Our main contribution is Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) which encodes information at different granularities and allows a single embedding to adapt to the computational constraints of downstream tasks. MRL minimally modifies existing representation learning pipelines and imposes no additional cost during inference and deployment. MRL learns coarse-to-fine representations that are at least as accurate and rich as independently trained low-dimensional representations. The flexibility within the learned Matryoshka Representations offer: (a) up to $\mathbf{14}\times$ smaller embedding size for ImageNet-1K classification at the same level of accuracy; (b) up to $\mathbf{14}\times$ real-world speed-ups for large-scale retrieval on ImageNet-1K and 4K; and (c) up to $\mathbf{2}\%$ accuracy improvements for long-tail few-shot classification, all while being as robust as the original representations. Finally, we show that MRL extends seamlessly to web-scale datasets (ImageNet, JFT) across various modalities -- vision (ViT, ResNet), vision + language (ALIGN) and language (BERT). MRL code and pretrained models are open-sourced at https://github.com/RAIVNLab/MRL.

These results retain the robustness of the original representations. Demonstrations span vision, language, and combined vision-language models, as well as web-scale datasets, supporting the method's applicability across several representation-learning settings.
summary.tldr: Matryoshka Representation Learning creates one flexible embedding that supports multiple representation sizes and downstream resource budgets.

title: Matryoshka Representation Learning

abstract: A canonical noise distribution (CND) is an additive mechanism designed to satisfy $f$-differential privacy ($f$-DP), without any wasted privacy budget. $f$-DP is a hypothesis testing-based formulation of privacy phrased in terms of tradeoff functions, which captures the difficulty of a hypothesis test. In this paper, we consider the existence and construction of both log-concave CNDs and multivariate CNDs. Log-concave distributions are important to ensure that higher outputs of the mechanism correspond to higher input values, whereas multivariate noise distributions are important to ensure that a joint release of multiple outputs has a tight privacy characterization. We show that the existence and construction of CNDs for both types of problems is related to whether the tradeoff function can be decomposed by functional composition (related to group privacy) or mechanism composition. In particular, we show that pure $\epsilon$-DP cannot be decomposed in either way and that there is neither a log-concave CND nor any multivariate CND for $\epsilon$-DP. On the other hand, we show that Gaussian-DP, $(0,\delta)$-DP, and Laplace-DP each have both log-concave and multivariate CNDs.

paragraphs: Differential privacy can be expressed through the difficulty of distinguishing datasets in a hypothesis test. In this formulation, a canonical noise distribution provides additive noise that meets a specified privacy tradeoff without wasting privacy budget. The paper studies when such distributions can have two additional useful properties.

Log-concave noise supports an ordered relationship between inputs and outputs, so higher released values correspond to higher input values. Multivariate canonical noise supports a tight privacy description when several outputs are released jointly. The authors connect the existence and construction of these distributions to whether the privacy tradeoff can be decomposed through functional composition or mechanism composition.

They prove that pure epsilon differential privacy admits neither decomposition and has neither a log-concave canonical noise distribution nor a multivariate one. Gaussian differential privacy, zero-epsilon approximate privacy, and Laplace differential privacy admit both kinds. These results distinguish privacy formulations by which tightly matched additive mechanisms they permit; the negative result specifically concerns canonical noise with the stated properties.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes when privacy tradeoffs permit log-concave or multivariate canonical noise, proving contrasting results for different privacy formulations.

title: Log-Concave and Multivariate Canonical Noise Distributions for Differential Privacy

abstract: The two key characteristics of a normalizing flow is that it is invertible (in particular, dimension preserving) and that it monitors the amount by which it changes the likelihood of data points as samples are propagated along the network. Recently, multiple generalizations of normalizing flows have been introduced that relax these two conditions \citep{nielsen2020survae,huang2020augmented}. On the other hand, neural networks only perform a forward pass on the input, there is neither a notion of an inverse of a neural network nor is there one of its likelihood contribution. In this paper we argue that certain neural network architectures can be enriched with a stochastic inverse pass and that their likelihood contribution can be monitored in a way that they fall under the generalized notion of a normalizing flow mentioned above. We term this enrichment \emph{flowification}. We prove that neural networks only containing linear and convolutional layers and invertible activations such as LeakyReLU can be flowified and evaluate them in the generative setting on image datasets.

paragraphs: A conventional normalizing flow is invertible, preserves dimensionality, and tracks how its transformations change data likelihoods. Ordinary neural networks generally provide only a forward computation, without a corresponding inverse or likelihood accounting. This paper studies how certain networks can be enriched so that they fit a generalized definition of normalizing flows.

The enrichment, called flowification, adds a stochastic inverse pass and a way to monitor likelihood contributions. A stochastic inverse introduces randomness into the reverse computation, fitting the relaxed flow framework considered by the authors. This connects familiar neural-network components with a framework designed to account for probabilities as data moves through a model.

The paper proves that networks composed only of linear layers, convolutional layers, and invertible activations such as LeakyReLU can be flowified. It also evaluates the resulting models for image generation. Despite the title’s broad phrasing, the stated theorem concerns this specified family of architectures. The contribution is a constructive bridge between those networks and generalized flows, supported by generative evaluations.
summary.tldr: Flowification adds stochastic inverse computation and likelihood accounting to a specified family of neural networks, making them generalized normalizing flows.

title: Flowification: Everything is a normalizing flow

abstract: We propose a Gaussian manifold variational auto-encoder (GM-VAE) whose latent space consists of a set of Gaussian distributions. It is known that the set of the univariate Gaussian distributions with the Fisher information metric form a hyperbolic space, which we call a Gaussian manifold. To learn the VAE endowed with the Gaussian manifolds, we propose a pseudo-Gaussian manifold normal distribution based on the Kullback-Leibler divergence, a local approximation of the squared Fisher-Rao distance, to define a density over the latent space. We demonstrate the efficacy of GM-VAE on two different tasks: density estimation of image datasets and state representation learning for model-based reinforcement learning. GM-VAE outperforms the other variants of hyperbolic- and Euclidean-VAEs on density estimation tasks and shows competitive performance in model-based reinforcement learning. We observe that our model provides strong numerical stability, addressing a common limitation reported in previous hyperbolic-VAEs. The implementation is available at https://github.com/ml-postech/GM-VAE.

paragraphs: The Gaussian manifold variational autoencoder, or GM-VAE, uses a latent space whose elements are Gaussian distributions. Its geometry comes from a known relationship: univariate Gaussian distributions equipped with the Fisher information metric form a hyperbolic space. The paper uses that relationship to construct a VAE with a geometrically structured latent representation.

Learning in this space requires a way to define a probability density over its elements. The authors introduce a pseudo-Gaussian manifold normal distribution based on Kullback–Leibler divergence. This divergence provides a local approximation to squared Fisher–Rao distance, connecting a tractable distributional comparison with the geometry of the Gaussian manifold.

The authors test GM-VAE on image density estimation and state representation learning for model-based reinforcement learning. It outperforms the compared hyperbolic and Euclidean VAE variants on density estimation and achieves competitive reinforcement learning performance. The evidence therefore supports both the usefulness of the latent geometry and the practical stability of its proposed implementation.
summary.tldr: GM-VAE builds a hyperbolic latent space from Gaussian distributions, improving reported image density estimation while showing strong numerical stability.

title: Hyperbolic VAE via Latent Gaussian Distributions

abstract: A series of recent publications by Awasthi et al. have introduced the key notion of *$H$-consistency bounds* for surrogate loss functions. These are upper bounds on the zero-one estimation error of any predictor in a hypothesis set, expressed in terms of its surrogate loss estimation error. They are both non-asymptotic and hypothesis set-specific and thus stronger and more informative than Bayes-consistency. However, determining if they hold and deriving these bounds have required a specific proof and analysis for each surrogate loss. Can we derive more general tools and characterizations? This paper provides both a general characterization and an extension of $H$-consistency bounds for multi-class classification. We present new and tight $H$-consistency bounds for both the family of constrained losses and that of comp-sum losses, which covers the familiar cross-entropy, or logistic loss applied to the outputs of a neural network. We further extend our analysis beyond the completeness assumptions adopted in previous studies and cover more realistic bounded hypothesis sets. Our characterizations are based on error transformations, which are explicitly defined for each formulation. We illustrate the application of our general results through several special examples. A by-product of our analysis is the observation that a recently derived multi-class $H$-consistency bound for cross-entropy reduces to an excess bound and is not significant. Instead, we prove a much stronger and more significant guarantee.

Their analysis identifies a previously derived multiclass cross-entropy guarantee as an uninformative excess bound and replaces it with a stronger one, improving what the theory says about the connection between training objectives and classification performance.
summary.tldr: The paper develops general, tighter guarantees connecting surrogate-loss error to classification error within specified hypothesis classes.

title: $H$-Consistency Bounds: Characterization and Extensions

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown great promise for developing agents for dialogue management (DM) that are non-myopic, conduct rich conversations, and maximize overall user satisfaction. Despite the advancements in RL and language models (LMs), employing RL to drive conversational chatbots still poses significant challenges. A primary issue stems from RL’s dependency on online exploration for effective learning, a process that can be costly. Moreover, engaging in online interactions with humans during the training phase can raise safety concerns, as the LM can potentially generate unwanted outputs. This issue is exacerbated by the combinatorial action spaces facing these algorithms, as most LM agents generate responses at the word level. We develop various RL algorithms, specialized in dialogue planning, that leverage recent Mixture-of-Expert Language Models (MoE-LMs)---models that capture diverse semantics, generate utterances reflecting different intents, and are amenable for multi-turn DM. By exploiting the MoE-LM structure, our methods significantly reduce the size of the action space and improve the efficacy of RL-based DM. We evaluate our methods in open-domain dialogue to demonstrate their effectiveness with respect to the diversity of intent in generated utterances and overall DM performance.

paragraphs: Dialogue management requires choosing responses with the longer conversation in mind. Reinforcement learning is attractive for this purpose, but learning through online human interactions can be expensive and expose users to unwanted outputs. Planning is also difficult when the agent’s actions are word-level choices, which create a huge space of possible responses.

This paper develops reinforcement-learning algorithms for dialogue planning around mixture-of-expert language models. These models capture varied semantics and produce utterances with different intents. The algorithms exploit that structure to substantially reduce the action space, making reinforcement learning more effective for managing conversations across multiple turns.

The authors evaluate their methods in open-domain dialogue, examining both the diversity of intents expressed in generated utterances and overall dialogue-management performance. The reported results support the effectiveness of organizing dialogue planning around the mixture-of-expert structure. The contribution links the language model’s ability to express distinct intents with a more manageable decision problem for the dialogue policy.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement-learning dialogue planners exploit mixture-of-expert language models to reduce the action space and support diverse, effective conversations.

title: Offline Reinforcement Learning for Mixture-of-Expert Dialogue Management

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is vulnerable to backdoor attacks due to its distributed computing nature. Existing defense solution usually requires larger amount of computation in either the training or testing phase, which limits their practicality in the resource-constrain scenarios. A more practical defense, i.e., neural network (NN) pruning based defense has been proposed in centralized backdoor setting. However, our empirical study shows that traditional pruning-based solution suffers \textit{poison-coupling} effect in FL, which significantly degrades the defense performance.This paper presents Lockdown, an isolated subspace training method to mitigate the poison-coupling effect. Lockdown follows three key procedures. First, it modifies the training protocol by isolating the training subspaces for different clients. Second, it utilizes randomness in initializing isolated subspacess, and performs subspace pruning and subspace recovery to segregate the subspaces between malicious and benign clients. Third, it introduces quorum consensus to cure the global model by purging malicious/dummy parameters. Empirical results show that Lockdown achieves \textit{superior} and \textit{consistent} defense performance compared to existing representative approaches against backdoor attacks. Another value-added property of Lockdown is the communication-efficiency and model complexity reduction, which are both critical for resource-constrain FL scenario. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/git-disl/Lockdown}.

paragraphs: Federated learning distributes training across clients, creating opportunities for backdoor attacks. Defenses can impose substantial computation, which is a problem in resource-constrained settings. The authors investigate pruning as a practical defense but find that traditional pruning suffers from a poison-coupling effect in federated learning that substantially weakens its effectiveness.

The paper also reports communication efficiency and reduced model complexity, properties relevant when clients have limited resources. The contribution therefore includes both a defense mechanism and changes to the training structure that support a less demanding federated learning process in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Lockdown isolates client training subspaces and uses pruning, recovery, and consensus to improve federated backdoor defense while reducing resource demands.

title: Lockdown: Backdoor Defense for Federated Learning with Isolated Subspace Training

abstract: Intrusion detection is a form of anomalous activity detection in communication network traffic. Continual learning (CL) approaches to the intrusion detection task accumulate old knowledge while adapting to the latest threat knowledge. Previous works have shown the effectiveness of memory replay-based CL approaches for this task. In this work, we present two novel contributions to improve the performance of CL-based network intrusion detection in the context of class imbalance and scalability. First, we extend class balancing reservoir sampling (CBRS), a memory-based CL method, to address the problems of severe class imbalance for large datasets. Second, we propose a novel approach titled perturbation assistance for parameter approximation (PAPA) based on the Gaussian mixture model to reduce the number of \textit{virtual stochastic gradient descent (SGD) parameter} computations needed to discover maximally interfering samples for CL. We demonstrate that the proposed approaches perform remarkably better than the baselines on standard intrusion detection benchmarks created over shorter periods (KDDCUP'99, NSL-KDD, CICIDS-2017/2018, UNSW-NB15, and CTU-13) and a longer period with distribution shift (AnoShift). We also validated proposed approaches on standard continual learning benchmarks (SVHN, CIFAR-10/100, and CLEAR-10/100) and anomaly detection benchmarks (SMAP, SMD, and MSL). Further, the proposed PAPA approach significantly lowers the number of virtual SGD update operations, thus resulting in training time savings in the range of 12 to 40\% compared to the maximally interfered samples retrieval algorithm.

The paper targets two difficulties in making replay effective at scale: severe imbalance between classes and the computational expense of choosing examples whose knowledge is most threatened by new updates.

The first contribution extends class balancing reservoir sampling to handle severe class imbalance in large datasets. The second, PAPA, uses a Gaussian mixture model to approximate parameter behavior when identifying maximally interfering samples. Its purpose is to reduce the virtual stochastic gradient updates required during sample selection, lowering the cost of deciding what to replay.

The authors report substantial improvements over baselines on intrusion detection benchmarks spanning shorter collection periods and a longer period with distribution shift. They also validate the approaches on continual learning and anomaly detection benchmarks. PAPA reduces training time by 12–40% relative to the maximally interfered samples retrieval algorithm. These results address both detection performance and the overhead of maintaining useful replay.
summary.tldr: Improved replay balancing and cheaper interference estimation strengthen continual intrusion detection while reducing replay-related training costs.

title: Augmented Memory Replay-based Continual Learning Approaches for Network Intrusion Detection

abstract: A single panel of a comic book can say a lot: it can depict not only where the characters currently are, but also their motions, their motivations, their emotions, and what they might do next. More generally, humans routinely infer complex sequences of past and future events from a *static snapshot* of a *dynamic scene*, even in situations they have never seen before.In this paper, we model how humans make such rapid and flexible inferences. Building on a long line of work in cognitive science, we offer a Monte Carlo algorithm whose inferences correlate well with human intuitions in a wide variety of domains, while only using a small, cognitively-plausible number of samples. Our key technical insight is a surprising connection between our inference problem and Monte Carlo path tracing, which allows us to apply decades of ideas from the computer graphics community to this seemingly-unrelated theory of mind task.

paragraphs: People can look at a static scene and infer a sequence of events: what may have happened, what someone is trying to do, and what might happen next. This paper develops a computational account of that ability. The challenge is explaining rapid, flexible inference even for situations a person has not encountered before.

The authors propose a Monte Carlo algorithm, which forms inferences through sampling. Its key technical insight connects this reasoning problem to Monte Carlo path tracing, a method from computer graphics. That connection makes techniques developed for tracing paths in graphics applicable to reasoning about events and the people involved in them.

The algorithm’s inferences correlate well with human intuitions across a variety of domains while using a small number of samples described as cognitively plausible. This supports the model as an account of how limited computation could produce rich interpretations of a snapshot. The stated result concerns agreement with human judgments, connecting an efficient sampling method to the flexibility of everyday social and temporal reasoning.
summary.tldr: A sampling algorithm inspired by graphics path tracing models human inferences about past and future events from static scenes.

title: Inferring the Future by Imagining the Past

abstract: We propose Neural 3D Articulated object Prior (NAP), the first 3D deep generative model to synthesize 3D articulated object models. Despite the extensive research on generating 3D static objects, compositions, or scenes, there are hardly any approaches on capturing the distribution of articulated objects, a common object category for human and robot interaction. To generate articulated objects, we first design a novel articulation tree/graph parameterization and then apply a diffusion-denoising probabilistic model over this representation where articulated objects can be generated via denoising from random complete graphs. In order to capture both the geometry and the motion structure whose distribution will affect each other, we design a graph denoising network for learning the reverse diffusion process. We propose a novel distance that adapts widely used 3D generation metrics to our novel task to evaluate generation quality. Experiments demonstrate our high performance in articulated object generation as well as its applications on conditioned generation, including Part2Motion, PartNet-Imagination, Motion2Part, and GAPart2Object.

The method introduces a tree or graph representation of articulation and applies a diffusion-denoising model to it. Generation begins from a random complete graph and progressively denoises that representation. A graph denoising network learns geometry and motion structure together, accounting for the way their distributions influence one another.

The paper also proposes a distance measure that adapts established 3D generation metrics to articulated-object generation. Experiments report strong generation performance and demonstrate conditional applications named Part2Motion, PartNet-Imagination, Motion2Part, and GAPart2Object. The contribution combines a representation, a generation process, and an evaluation approach for objects whose movable structure is an essential part of what must be generated.
summary.tldr: NAP generates articulated 3D objects by jointly denoising graph representations of their geometry and motion structure.

title: NAP: Neural 3D Articulated Object Prior

abstract: We show how to "compile" human-readable programs into standard decoder-only transformer models. Our compiler, Tracr, generates models with known structure. This structure can be used to design experiments. For example, we use it to study "superposition" in transformers that execute multi-step algorithms. Additionally, the known structure of Tracr-compiled models can serve as _ground-truth_ for evaluating interpretability methods. Commonly, because the "programs" learned by transformers are unknown it is unclear whether an interpretation succeeded. We demonstrate our approach by implementing and examining programs including computing token frequencies, sorting, and parenthesis checking. We provide an open-source implementation of Tracr at https://github.com/google-deepmind/tracr.

Tracr addresses this problem by compiling human-readable programs into standard decoder-only transformers. Because the model is produced from a specified program, researchers have known structure against which to compare an interpretation.

This creates a controlled setting for experiments about internal computation. The authors use compiled models to study superposition in transformers executing multi-step algorithms. They also demonstrate programs for token-frequency calculation, sorting, and parenthesis checking. These examples provide concrete computations whose intended structure is available before researchers attempt to explain the resulting network.

The main contribution is a source of ground truth for developing and evaluating interpretability methods. An explanation can be checked against known model structure, making success easier to assess than when the learned program is unknown. The authors provide an open-source implementation of the compiler. Tracr therefore supplies both a way to construct experimental transformer models and a practical foundation for investigating how interpretability methods describe their computations.
summary.tldr: Tracr compiles readable programs into transformers with known structure, providing ground truth for interpretability experiments.

title: Tracr: Compiled Transformers as a Laboratory for Interpretability

abstract: Historically applied exclusively to perfect information games, depth-limited search with value functions has been key to recent advances in AI for imperfect information games. Most prominent approaches with strong theoretical guarantees require *subgame decomposition* - a process in which a subgame is computed from public information and player beliefs. However, subgame decomposition can itself require non-trivial computations, and its tractability depends on the existence of efficient algorithms for either full enumeration or generation of the histories that form the root of the subgame. Despite this, no formal analysis of the tractability of such computations has been established in prior work, and application domains have often consisted of games, such as poker, for which enumeration is trivial on modern hardware.Applying these ideas to more complex domains requires understanding their cost. In this work, we introduce and analyze the computational aspects and tractability of filtering histories for subgame decomposition. We show that constructing a single history from the root of the subgame is generally intractable, and then provide a necessary and sufficient condition for efficient enumeration. We also introduce a novel Markov Chain Monte Carlo-based generation algorithm for trick-taking card games - a domain where enumeration is often prohibitively expensive. Our experiments demonstrate its improved scalability in the trick-taking card game *Oh Hell*.These contributions clarify when and how depth-limited search via subgame decomposition can be an effective tool for sequential decision-making in imperfect information settings.

paragraphs: Depth-limited search in imperfect-information games often depends on constructing a subgame from public information and players’ beliefs. This requires enumerating or generating the possible histories at the subgame’s root. Although such computations can be straightforward in games such as poker, they may become a substantial obstacle in more complex settings.

The paper formalizes and analyzes this history-filtering problem. It shows that constructing even a single root history is generally intractable, then establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for efficient enumeration. This identifies a computational requirement behind search methods whose effectiveness depends on subgame decomposition.

The authors also propose a Markov Chain Monte Carlo algorithm for generating histories in trick-taking card games, where full enumeration is often too expensive. Experiments in Oh Hell demonstrate improved scalability. Together, the theoretical analysis and generation method clarify when histories can be obtained efficiently and provide a practical approach for a domain in which listing all possibilities can obstruct otherwise useful search.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes the difficulty of constructing subgame histories and introduces scalable sampling for trick-taking card games.

title: History Filtering in Imperfect Information Games: Algorithms and Complexity

abstract: While language-guided image manipulation has made remarkable progress, the challenge of how to instruct the manipulation process faithfully reflecting human intentions persists. An accurate and comprehensive description of a manipulation task using natural language is laborious and sometimes even impossible, primarily due to the inherent uncertainty and ambiguity present in linguistic expressions. Is it feasible to accomplish image manipulation without resorting to external cross-modal language information? If this possibility exists, the inherent modality gap would be effortlessly eliminated. In this paper, we propose a novel manipulation methodology, dubbed ImageBrush, that learns visual instructions for more accurate image editing.Our key idea is to employ a pair of transformation images as visual instructions, which not only precisely captures human intention but also facilitates accessibility in real-world scenarios. Capturing visual instructions is particularly challenging because it involves extracting the underlying intentions solely from visual demonstrations and then applying this operation to a new image. To address this challenge, we formulate visual instruction learning as a diffusion-based inpainting problem, where the contextual information is fully exploited through an iterative process of generation. A visual prompting encoder is carefully devised to enhance the model's capacity in uncovering human intent behind the visual instructions. Extensive experiments show that our method generates engaging manipulation results conforming to the transformations entailed in demonstrations. Moreover, our model exhibits robust generalization capabilities on various downstream tasks such as pose transfer, image translation and video inpainting.

paragraphs: Describing an image edit precisely in words can be difficult, especially when the intended transformation is visually specific. ImageBrush instead takes a pair of images demonstrating a transformation and uses that pair as an instruction for editing another image. The task is to infer the operation from the example and transfer it to new content.

The method formulates this instruction-learning problem as diffusion-based inpainting. Its iterative generation process uses visual context to construct the edited result. A dedicated visual prompting encoder strengthens the model’s ability to extract the intended transformation from the demonstration, giving visual examples a direct role in controlling the edit.

Experiments show outputs that follow the transformations demonstrated by the example pairs. The model also generalizes across tasks including pose transfer, image translation, and video inpainting. These findings support visual demonstrations as a useful interface for image manipulation, particularly when expressing the desired operation comprehensively through language would be burdensome.
summary.tldr: ImageBrush learns edits from visual transformation pairs and applies those instructions to new images through diffusion-based inpainting.

title: ImageBrush: Learning Visual In-Context Instructions for Exemplar-Based Image Manipulation

abstract: Categorical encoders transform categorical features into numerical representations that are indispensable for a wide range of machine learning models.Existing encoder benchmark studies lack generalizability because of their limited choice of (1) encoders, (2) experimental factors, and (3) datasets. Additionally, inconsistencies arise from the adoption of varying aggregation strategies.This paper is the most comprehensive benchmark of categorical encoders to date, including an extensive evaluation of 32 configurations of encoders from diverse families, with 36 combinations of experimental factors, and on 50 datasets.The study shows the profound influence of dataset selection, experimental factors, and aggregation strategies on the benchmark's conclusions~---~aspects disregarded in previous encoder benchmarks.Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/DrCohomology/EncoderBenchmarking}.

paragraphs: Categorical features describe groups or labels, while many machine learning models require numerical inputs. Encoders provide that translation, and choosing one is an important part of building a classifier. This paper examines how to compare encoders for binary classification, where the prediction has two possible outcomes, through a substantially broader benchmark than earlier studies.

The benchmark evaluates 32 encoder configurations drawn from different families, across 36 combinations of experimental factors and 50 datasets. These dimensions matter together: an encoder comparison depends on which methods enter the comparison, the conditions under which they are evaluated, and the data used to assess them. The study also examines how individual results are combined into overall conclusions.

The central finding is that dataset selection, experimental factors, and aggregation strategies strongly influence the benchmark's conclusions. That makes the evaluation procedure itself a substantive part of the result. The contribution is a broad empirical comparison that shows why encoder recommendations must be interpreted in the context of the choices used to produce them.
summary.tldr: A broad categorical-encoder benchmark shows that datasets, experimental conditions, and result aggregation strongly shape comparison outcomes.

title: A benchmark of categorical encoders for binary classification

abstract: The recent popularity of text-to-image diffusion models (DM) can largely be attributed to the intuitive interface they provide to users. The intended generation can be expressed in natural language, with the model producing faithful interpretations of text prompts. However, expressing complex or nuanced ideas in text alone can be difficult. To ease image generation, we propose MultiFusion that allows one to express complex and nuanced concepts with arbitrarily interleaved inputs of multiple modalities and languages. MultiFusion leverages pre-trained models and aligns them for integration into a cohesive system, thereby avoiding the need for extensive training from scratch. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficient transfer of capabilities from individual modules to the downstream model. Specifically, the fusion of all independent components allows the image generation module to utilize multilingual, interleaved multimodal inputs despite being trained solely on monomodal data in a single language.
