paragraphs: Text-to-image models offer a convenient way to describe a desired picture, but language alone can be awkward for nuanced ideas. MultiFusion broadens the input interface so users can interleave multiple modalities and languages in a single request. The aim is to let different forms of input work together when specifying what an image should express.

The system brings together pretrained models and aligns them into a cohesive whole. This avoids the need for extensive training from scratch and makes existing model capabilities available to the combined system. The technical emphasis is on integration: separately acquired abilities must become usable by the image generation component.

The experiments show efficient transfer of capabilities from the individual modules to the downstream model. In particular, the combined system enables an image generation module to use multilingual, interleaved multimodal inputs even though that module was trained only on monomodal data in one language. The finding demonstrates that the input capabilities of the assembled system can exceed those directly taught to its image generator.
summary.tldr: MultiFusion aligns pretrained models so an image generator can respond to interleaved multilingual and multimodal inputs.

title: MultiFusion: Fusing Pre-Trained Models for Multi-Lingual, Multi-Modal Image Generation

abstract: Procedural activity understanding requires perceiving human actions in terms of a broader task, where multiple keysteps are performed in sequence across a long video to reach a final goal state---such as the steps of a recipe or the steps of a DIY fix-it task. Prior work largely treats keystep recognition in isolation of this broader structure, or else rigidly confines keysteps to align with a particular sequential script. We propose discovering a task graph automatically from how-to videos to represent probabilistically how people tend to execute keysteps, then leverage this graph to regularize keystep recognition in novel videos. On multiple datasets of real-world instructional video, we show the impact: more reliable zero-shot keystep localization and improved video representation learning, exceeding the state of the art.

paragraphs: Recognizing a step in an instructional video requires understanding how it contributes to a larger task. A recipe or repair unfolds through several actions toward a final goal. Earlier approaches often classify steps independently or constrain them to follow a fixed script, leaving limited room for the broader patterns of real execution.

The paper proposes automatically discovering a task graph from how-to videos. This graph represents, probabilistically, how people tend to perform the key steps of a task. The learned structure then regularizes step recognition in new videos. It provides a broader context for interpreting individual actions while representing observed execution patterns through probabilities rather than requiring one rigid sequence.

Experiments across multiple datasets of real instructional videos show more reliable zero-shot localization of key steps and improved video representation learning, exceeding the state of the art. The findings indicate that task structure learned from videos can help both locate actions and improve the representations used to understand them. The graph makes relationships among steps useful during recognition.
summary.tldr: Automatically learned probabilistic task graphs improve key-step localization and representation learning in instructional videos.

title: Video-Mined Task Graphs for Keystep Recognition in Instructional Videos

abstract: We study distributed goodness-of-fit testing for discrete distribution under bandwidth and differential privacy constraints. Information constraint distributed goodness-of-fit testing is a problem that has received considerable attention recently. The important case of discrete distributions is theoretically well understood in the classical case where all data is available in one "central" location. In a federated setting, however, data is distributed across multiple "locations" (e.g. servers) and cannot readily be shared due to e.g. bandwidth or privacy constraints that each server needs to satisfy. We show how recently derived results for goodness-of-fit testing for the mean of a multivariate Gaussian model extend to the discrete distributions, by leveraging Le Cam's theory of statistical equivalence. In doing so, we derive matching minimax upper- and lower-bounds for the goodness-of-fit testing for discrete distributions under bandwidth or privacy constraints in the regime where number of samples held locally are large.

paragraphs: This paper studies goodness-of-fit testing for discrete distributions when observations are spread across multiple servers. The task is to assess whether data agree with a proposed distribution. Unlike a centralized setting, servers cannot freely pool their observations because communication bandwidth or differential privacy requirements restrict the information they can share.

The authors connect this distributed discrete-data problem to existing results for testing the mean of a multivariate Gaussian model. They use Le Cam's theory of statistical equivalence to transfer those results between statistical settings. This provides a route to characterizing the discrete problem through a related problem whose constrained testing behavior has already been analyzed.

The resulting upper and lower minimax bounds match in the regime where each location holds many samples. Upper bounds establish achievable testing performance, while lower bounds establish corresponding worst-case limits. Their agreement identifies optimal performance under the studied bandwidth or privacy constraints. The large local sample regime is central to the scope of this result.
summary.tldr: Matching theoretical bounds characterize distributed discrete goodness-of-fit testing under bandwidth or privacy constraints when local sample sizes are large.

title: Optimal Private and Communication Constraint Distributed Goodness-of-Fit Testing for Discrete Distributions in the Large Sample Regime

abstract: Understanding connections between artificial and biological intelligent systems can reveal fundamental principles of general intelligence. While many artificial intelligence models have a neuroscience counterpart, such connections are largely missing in Transformer models and the self-attention mechanism. Here, we examine the relationship between interacting attention heads and human episodic memory. We focus on induction heads, which contribute to in-context learning in Transformer-based large language models (LLMs). We demonstrate that induction heads are behaviorally, functionally, and mechanistically similar to the contextual maintenance and retrieval (CMR) model of human episodic memory. Our analyses of LLMs pre-trained on extensive text data show that CMR-like heads often emerge in the intermediate and late layers, qualitatively mirroring human memory biases. The ablation of CMR-like heads suggests their causal role in in-context learning. Our findings uncover a parallel between the computational mechanisms of LLMs and human memory, offering valuable insights into both research fields.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether mechanisms supporting in-context learning in transformers resemble mechanisms proposed for human episodic memory. It focuses on induction heads, attention components that contribute to learning from the current context. The comparison uses the contextual maintenance and retrieval model, or CMR, as a specific computational account of human memory.

The authors find similarities between induction heads and CMR at behavioral, functional, and mechanistic levels. In language models pretrained on extensive text collections, heads with CMR-like properties often appear in intermediate and later layers. Their behavior qualitatively resembles human memory biases, connecting internal attention patterns with patterns studied in memory research.

The study also removes CMR-like heads to examine their contribution. Those ablations suggest that the heads play a causal role in in-context learning. Together, the analyses establish a computational parallel between transformer processing and a model of episodic memory. The significance lies in identifying a concrete mechanism that can be investigated across both fields, while the reported correspondence remains a similarity between computational systems.
summary.tldr: Transformer induction heads resemble a computational model of episodic memory, and ablations suggest a causal contribution to in-context learning.

title: Linking In-context Learning in Transformers to Human Episodic Memory

abstract: Current research in adversarial robustness of LLMs focuses on \textit{discrete} input manipulations in the natural language space, which can be directly transferred to \textit{closed-source} models. However, this approach neglects the steady progression of \textit{open-source} models. As open-source models advance in capability, ensuring their safety becomes increasingly imperative. Yet, attacks tailored to open-source LLMs that exploit full model access remain largely unexplored. We address this research gap and propose the \textit{embedding space attack}, which directly attacks the \textit{continuous} embedding representation of input tokens.We find that embedding space attacks circumvent model alignments and trigger harmful behaviors more efficiently than discrete attacks or model fine-tuning. Additionally, we demonstrate that models compromised by embedding attacks can be used to create discrete jailbreaks in natural language. Lastly, we present a novel threat model in the context of unlearning and show that embedding space attacks can extract supposedly deleted information from unlearned LLMs across multiple datasets and models. Our findings highlight embedding space attacks as an important threat model in open-source LLMs.

paragraphs: Many language-model attacks modify ordinary text inputs, an approach that also applies to closed-source systems. This paper examines a different threat enabled by full access to open-source models: modifying the continuous embedding representations associated with input tokens. That access exposes an attack surface that text-only robustness studies do not fully address.

The authors propose embedding-space attacks and find that they bypass alignment and elicit harmful behavior more efficiently than the discrete attacks or model fine-tuning examined in their study. They also show that a model compromised through embeddings can help produce natural-language jailbreaks. This connects a threat involving internal representations with attacks expressed through ordinary text.

The work further tests unlearning, where information is supposed to have been removed from a model. Across multiple datasets and models, embedding attacks extract supposedly deleted information. These findings identify full-model access as an important condition when evaluating safety and unlearning claims: the tested protections can fail when inputs are manipulated in the embedding space rather than only through natural-language prompts.
summary.tldr: Embedding-space attacks expose weaknesses in open-source models' safety alignment and can recover supposedly unlearned information.

title: Soft Prompt Threats: Attacking Safety Alignment and Unlearning in Open-Source LLMs through the Embedding Space

abstract: A prominent family of methods for learning data distributions relies on density ratio estimation (DRE), where a model is trained to *classify* between data samples and samples from some reference distribution. DRE-based models can directly output the likelihood for any given input, a highly desired property that is lacking in most generative techniques. Nevertheless, to date, DRE methods have failed in accurately capturing the distributions of complex high-dimensional data, like images, and have thus been drawing reduced research attention in recent years. In this work we present *classification diffusion models* (CDMs), a DRE-based generative method that adopts the formalism of denoising diffusion models (DDMs) while making use of a classifier that predicts the level of noise added to a clean signal. Our method is based on an analytical connection that we derive between the MSE-optimal denoiser for removing white Gaussian noise and the cross-entropy-optimal classifier for predicting the noise level. Our method is the first DRE-based technique that can successfully generate images beyond the MNIST dataset. Furthermore, it can output the likelihood of any input in a single forward pass, achieving state-of-the-art negative log likelihood (NLL) among methods with this property.
originalAbstract: A prominent family of methods for learning data distributions relies on density ratio estimation (DRE), where a model is trained to *classify* between data samples and samples from some reference distribution. DRE-based models can directly output the likelihood for any given input, a highly desired property that is lacking in most generative techniques. Nevertheless, to date, DRE methods have failed in accurately capturing the distributions of complex high-dimensional data, like images, and have thus been drawing reduced research attention in recent years. In this work we present *classification diffusion models* (CDMs), a DRE-based generative method that adopts the formalism of denoising diffusion models (DDMs) while making use of a classifier that predicts the level of noise added to a clean signal. Our method is based on an analytical connection that we derive between the MSE-optimal denoiser for removing white Gaussian noise and the cross-entropy-optimal classifier for predicting the noise level. Our method is the first DRE-based technique that can successfully generate images beyond the MNIST dataset. Furthermore, it can output the likelihood of any input in a single forward pass, achieving state-of-the-art negative log likelihood (NLL) among methods with this property.

paragraphs: Density ratio estimation learns a data distribution by classifying real samples against samples from a reference distribution. An attractive property is direct likelihood evaluation: the model can assign a likelihood to an input. However, the paper describes a longstanding difficulty in extending this approach to complex, high-dimensional data such as images.

Classification diffusion models connect that classification approach to denoising diffusion. Their classifier predicts how much noise was added to a clean signal. The technical foundation is an analytical relationship between two optimal predictors: a denoiser minimizing mean squared error for white Gaussian noise, and a noise-level classifier minimizing cross-entropy. This connection supplies a basis for building a generative method around classification.

The authors report the first successful image generation beyond MNIST by a density-ratio-based technique. The model also evaluates an input's likelihood in one forward pass. Its reported state-of-the-art negative log likelihood is specifically among methods sharing that single-pass property. The contribution therefore combines a broader demonstrated generation capability with an efficient likelihood-evaluation mechanism.
summary.tldr: Classification diffusion models use noise-level prediction to enable image generation and single-pass likelihood evaluation.

title: Classification Diffusion Models: Revitalizing Density Ratio Estimation

abstract: Most existing theoretical investigations of the accuracy of diffusion models, albeit significant, assume the score function has been approximated to a certain accuracy, and then use this a priori bound to control the error of generation. This article instead provides a first quantitative understanding of the whole generation process, i.e., both training and sampling. More precisely, it conducts a non-asymptotic convergence analysis of denoising score matching under gradient descent. In addition, a refined sampling error analysis for variance exploding models is also provided. The combination of these two results yields a full error analysis, which elucidates (again, but this time theoretically) how to design the training and sampling processes for effective generation. For instance, our theory implies a preference toward noise distribution and loss weighting in training that qualitatively agree with the ones used in [Karras et al., 2022]. It also provides perspectives on the choices of time and variance schedules in sampling: when the score is well trained, the design in [Song et al., 2021] is more preferable, but when it is less trained, the design in [Karras et al., 2022] becomes more preferable.

Much previous theory starts by assuming that the model’s score function has already reached a specified accuracy, then studies how that error affects generation. The authors instead examine how training produces the score estimate and how its quality interacts with the subsequent sampling procedure.

They provide a non-asymptotic convergence analysis of denoising score matching trained with gradient descent. This addresses learning at finite training scales rather than only its limiting behavior. They combine it with a refined sampling-error analysis for variance-exploding diffusion models. Together, these results account for errors arising in both stages and give theoretical guidance for their design.

The implication is conditional guidance, connecting sampling choices to the quality achieved during training.
summary.tldr: A joint analysis of diffusion training and sampling shows how suitable generation choices depend on the accuracy of the learned score.

title: Evaluating the design space of diffusion-based generative models

abstract: Recent advances in Video Large Language Models (Video-LLMs) have demonstrated their great potential in general-purpose video understanding. To verify the significance of these models, a number of benchmarks have been proposed to diagnose their capabilities in different scenarios. However, existing benchmarks merely evaluate models through video-level question-answering, lacking fine-grained event-level assessment and task diversity. To fill this gap, we introduce E.T. Bench (Event-Level & Time-Sensitive Video Understanding Benchmark), a large-scale and high-quality benchmark for open-ended event-level video understanding. Categorized within a 3-level task taxonomy, E.T. Bench encompasses 7.3K samples under 12 tasks with 7K videos (251.4h total length) under 8 domains, providing comprehensive evaluations. We extensively evaluated 8 Image-LLMs and 12 Video-LLMs on our benchmark, and the results reveal that state-of-the-art models for coarse-level (video-level) understanding struggle to solve our fine-grained tasks, e.g., grounding event-of-interests within videos, largely due to the short video context length, improper time representations, and lack of multi-event training data. Focusing on these issues, we further propose a strong baseline model, E.T. Chat, together with an instruction-tuning dataset E.T. Instruct 164K tailored for fine-grained event-level understanding. Our simple but effective solution demonstrates superior performance in multiple scenarios.

summary.tldr: E.T. Bench exposes weaknesses in event-level video understanding and introduces a model and training dataset aimed at those weaknesses.

title: E.T. Bench: Towards Open-Ended Event-Level Video-Language Understanding

abstract: Learning algorithms are often used to make decisions in sequential decision-making environments. In multi-agent settings, the decisions of each agent can affect the utilities/losses of the other agents. Therefore, if an agent is good at anticipating the behavior of the other agents, in particular how they will make decisions in each round as a function of their experience that far, it could try to judiciously make its own decisions over the rounds of the interaction so as to influence the other agents to behave in a way that ultimately benefits its own utility. In this paper, we study repeated two-player games involving two types of agents: a learner, which employs an online learning algorithm to choose its strategy in each round; and an optimizer, which knows the learner's utility function and the learner's online learning algorithm. The optimizer wants to plan ahead to maximize its own utility, while taking into account the learner's behavior. We provide two results: a positive result for repeated zero-sum games and a negative result for repeated general-sum games. Our positive result is an algorithm for the optimizer, which exactly maximizes its utility against a learner that plays the Replicator Dynamics --- the continuous-time analogue of Multiplicative Weights Update (MWU). Additionally, we use this result to provide an algorithm for the optimizer against MWU, i.e.~for the discrete-time setting, which guarantees an average utility for the optimizer that is higher than the value of the one-shot game. Our negative result shows that, unless P=NP, there is no Fully Polynomial Time Approximation Scheme (FPTAS) for maximizing the utility of an optimizer against a learner that best-responds to the history in each round. Yet, this still leaves open the question of whether there exists a polynomial-time algorithm that optimizes the utility up to $o(T)$.

This rules out a particular form of efficient approximation under that complexity assumption. It leaves open whether a polynomial-time algorithm can achieve an optimization error growing sublinearly with the number of rounds.
summary.tldr: Knowing an opponent's learning rule enables utility-maximizing strategies in specified zero-sum settings, while a general-sum setting presents conditional approximation hardness.

title: Maximizing utility in multi-agent environments by anticipating the behavior of other learners

abstract: Diffusion models have become the most popular approach to deep generative modeling of images, largely due to their empirical performance and reliability. From a theoretical standpoint, a number of recent works [CCL+23, CCSW22, BBDD24] have studied the iteration complexity of sampling, assuming access to an accurate diffusion model. In this work, we focus on understanding the *sample complexity* of training such a model; how many samples are needed to learn an accurate diffusion model using a sufficiently expressive neural network? Prior work [BMR20] showed bounds polynomial in the dimension, desired Total Variation error, and Wasserstein error. We show an *exponential improvement* in the dependence on Wasserstein error and depth, along with improved dependencies on other relevant parameters.

paragraphs: Diffusion models work well empirically, but explaining their data requirements remains a theoretical challenge. This paper asks how many training examples are sufficient to learn an accurate diffusion model when the neural network is expressive enough. That question concerns the statistical cost of obtaining the model in the first place.

The analysis focuses on sample complexity, complementing work on how many iterations are needed to generate samples once an accurate model is available. Earlier training bounds depended polynomially on dimension and on accuracy requirements expressed through total variation and Wasserstein error. The new results improve these guarantees, including an exponential improvement in their dependence on Wasserstein error and depth.

The authors also report better dependence on other relevant parameters. These are improvements to mathematical bounds on training data requirements, so their significance lies in a sharper account of what learning can require under the stated expressivity assumption. The result helps distinguish the difficulty of learning a diffusion model from the separate difficulty of sampling with it.
summary.tldr: The paper sharpens diffusion training sample-complexity bounds, exponentially improving their dependence on Wasserstein error and depth.

title: Improved Sample Complexity Bounds for Diffusion Model Training

abstract: We present a novel method for symbolic regression (SR), the task of searching for compact programmatic hypotheses that best explain a dataset. The problem is commonly solved using genetic algorithms; we show that we can enhance such methods by inducing a library of abstract textual concepts. Our algorithm, called LaSR, uses zero-shot queries to a large language model (LLM) to discover and evolve concepts occurring in known high-performing hypotheses. We discover new hypotheses using a mix of standard evolutionary steps and LLM-guided steps (obtained through zero-shot LLM queries) conditioned on discovered concepts. Once discovered, hypotheses are used in a new round of concept abstraction and evolution. We validate LaSR on the Feynman equations, a popular SR benchmark, as well as a set of synthetic tasks. On these benchmarks, LaSR substantially outperforms a variety of state-of-the-art SR approaches based on deep learning and evolutionary algorithms. Moreover, we show that LASR can be used to discover a new and powerful scaling law for LLMs.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for compact programs or mathematical expressions that explain a dataset. Genetic algorithms are a common way to explore possible hypotheses. This paper introduces LaSR, which augments that search with a library of abstract concepts expressed in text and discovered through a large language model.

LaSR asks the language model, through zero-shot queries, to identify and evolve concepts found in already successful hypotheses. It then generates new candidates using a mixture of ordinary evolutionary operations and language-model-guided steps conditioned on those concepts. Successful new hypotheses feed back into another round of concept abstraction, so the library and the search develop together.

On the Feynman equations benchmark and synthetic tasks, LaSR substantially outperforms several state-of-the-art symbolic regression approaches based on deep learning and evolutionary algorithms. The authors also demonstrate discovery of a new scaling law for language models. The contribution is a feedback loop that turns patterns in promising expressions into reusable guidance for further search, rather than treating each candidate only as an isolated program.
summary.tldr: LaSR improves symbolic regression by using an LLM to build and evolve a concept library that guides evolutionary search.

title: Symbolic Regression with a Learned Concept Library

abstract: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) has been shown to improve the generalization of neural networks. However, each SAM update requires _sequentially_ computing two gradients, effectively doubling the per-iteration cost compared to base optimizers like SGD. We propose a simple modification of SAM, termed SAMPa, which allows us to fully parallelize the two gradient computations. SAMPa achieves a twofold speedup of SAM under the assumption that communication costs between devices are negligible. Empirical results show that SAMPa ranks among the most efficient variants of SAM in terms of computational time. Additionally, our method consistently outperforms SAM across both vision and language tasks. Notably, SAMPa theoretically maintains convergence guarantees even for _fixed_ perturbation sizes, which is established through a novel Lyapunov function. We in fact arrive at SAMPa by treating this convergence guarantee as a hard requirement---an approach we believe is promising for developing SAM-based methods in general. Our code is available at https://github.com/LIONS-EPFL/SAMPa.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, can improve how well neural networks generalize, but each update requires two gradient computations performed in sequence. This makes an iteration roughly twice as costly as one using a base optimizer such as stochastic gradient descent. SAMPa modifies SAM so that these two computations can run fully in parallel.

The resulting twofold speedup assumes that communication between devices has negligible cost. That condition matters because the acceleration depends on executing work simultaneously without substantial coordination overhead. Empirically, SAMPa ranks among the most time-efficient SAM variants and consistently outperforms SAM across the vision and language tasks evaluated.

The paper also establishes convergence guarantees when perturbation sizes remain fixed, using a newly developed Lyapunov function. The authors treated that guarantee as a design requirement in deriving the method. SAMPa therefore links an implementation benefit with a theoretical property: its update structure supports parallel computation while retaining the stated convergence behavior, rather than relying only on observed training performance.
summary.tldr: SAMPa parallelizes SAM's two gradient computations, enabling a twofold speedup when communication costs are negligible while retaining convergence guarantees.

title: SAMPa: Sharpness-aware Minimization Parallelized

abstract: ``Distribution shift'' is the primary obstacle to the success of offline reinforcement learning. As a learning policy may take actions beyond the knowledge of the behavior policy (referred to as Out-of-Distribution (OOD) actions), the Q-values of these OOD actions can be easily overestimated. Consequently, the learning policy becomes biasedly optimized using the incorrect recovered Q-value function. One commonly used idea to avoid the overestimation of Q-value is to make a pessimistic adjustment. Our key idea is to penalize the Q-values of OOD actions that correspond to high uncertainty. In this work, we propose Q-Distribution guided Q-learning (QDQ) which pessimistic Q-value on OOD regions based on uncertainty estimation. The uncertainty measure is based on the conditional Q-value distribution, which is learned via a high-fidelity and efficient consistency model. On the other hand, to avoid the overly conservative problem, we introduce an uncertainty-aware optimization objective to update the Q-value function. The proposed QDQ demonstrates solid theoretical guarantees for the accuracy of Q-value distribution learning and uncertainty measurement, as well as the performance of the learning policy. QDQ consistently exhibits strong performance in the D4RL benchmark and shows significant improvements for many tasks. Our code can be found at <code link>.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains from existing data, but the resulting policy may choose actions that are poorly represented in that data. Their estimated Q-values can be overly optimistic, causing the policy to favor actions for which its evidence is weak. Penalizing such estimates helps, but excessive pessimism can also constrain learning.

Q-Distribution guided Q-learning estimates uncertainty from a conditional distribution of Q-values learned with a consistency model. It uses this uncertainty to penalize out-of-distribution actions, making the pessimistic adjustment depend on how uncertain their values are. An uncertainty-aware objective for updating the value function also addresses the risk of becoming overly conservative.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees concerning the learned value distribution, uncertainty measurement, and policy performance. Experiments on D4RL show consistently strong results and significant improvements on many tasks. The contribution is a connection between distributional value learning and targeted pessimism: uncertainty helps determine where unsupported optimism should be reduced, while the optimization objective seeks to preserve useful learning rather than suppressing it indiscriminately.
summary.tldr: QDQ learns distributions of action values to penalize uncertain offline actions while addressing excessive conservatism.

title: Q-Distribution guided Q-learning for offline reinforcement learning: Uncertainty penalized Q-value via consistency model

abstract: Neuromorphic computers open up the potential of energy-efficient computation using spiking neural networks (SNN), which consist of neurons that exchange spike-based information asynchronously. In particular, SNNs have shown promise in solving combinatorial optimization. Underpinning the SNN methods is the concept of energy minimization of an Ising model, which is closely related to quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO). Thus, the starting point for many SNN methods is reformulating the target problem as QUBO, then executing an SNN-based QUBO solver. For many combinatorial problems, the reformulation entails introducing penalty terms, potentially with slack variables, that implement feasibility constraints in the QUBO objective. For more complex problems such as hypergraph minimum vertex cover (HMVC), numerous slack variables are introduced which drastically increase the search domain and reduce the effectiveness of the SNN solver. In this paper, we propose a novel SNN formulation for HMVC. Rather than using penalty terms with slack variables, our SNN architecture introduces additional spiking neurons with a constraint checking and correction mechanism that encourages convergence to feasible solutions. In effect, our method obviates the need for reformulating HMVC as QUBO. Experiments on neuromorphic hardware show that our method consistently yielded high quality solutions for HMVC on real and synthetic instances where the SNN-based QUBO solver often failed, while consuming measurably less energy than global solvers on CPU.

paragraphs: This paper develops a spiking-neural-network approach to hypergraph minimum vertex cover. Many existing spiking optimization methods first translate a problem into quadratic unconstrained binary optimization, or QUBO. Enforcing constraints in that translation can require extra slack variables. For this problem, the resulting increase in the search space can sharply reduce solver effectiveness.

The proposed architecture handles feasibility through additional spiking neurons that check constraints and apply corrections. This removes the need to express the problem through a QUBO formulation with slack-variable penalties. The correction mechanism encourages convergence toward feasible solutions, placing constraint handling directly inside the network's operation rather than expanding the binary optimization formulation.

Experiments on neuromorphic hardware produced consistently high-quality solutions on real and synthetic instances where the spiking QUBO solver often failed. The method also consumed measurably less energy than global solvers running on a CPU. These findings support direct constraint handling as a useful design choice for the evaluated problem, while the stated convergence mechanism encourages feasibility rather than guaranteeing an optimal answer on every instance.
summary.tldr: A spiking network checks and corrects hypergraph-cover constraints directly, avoiding slack-variable expansion and producing strong, energy-efficient experimental results.

title: Slack-Free Spiking Neural Network Formulation for Hypergraph Minimum Vertex Cover

abstract: Digital Twins (DTs) are computational models that simulate the states and temporal dynamics of real-world systems, playing a crucial role in prediction, understanding, and decision-making across diverse domains. However, existing approaches to DTs often struggle to generalize to unseen conditions in data-scarce settings, a crucial requirement for such models. To address these limitations, our work begins by establishing the essential desiderata for effective DTs. Hybrid Digital Twins (**HDTwins**) represent a promising approach to address these requirements, modeling systems using a composition of both mechanistic and neural components. This hybrid architecture simultaneously leverages (partial) domain knowledge and neural network expressiveness to enhance generalization, with its modular design facilitating improved evolvability. While existing hybrid models rely on expert-specified architectures with only parameters optimized on data, *automatically* specifying and optimizing HDTwins remains intractable due to the complex search space and the need for flexible integration of domain priors. To overcome this complexity, we propose an evolutionary algorithm (**HDTwinGen**) that employs Large Language Models (LLMs) to autonomously propose, evaluate, and optimize HDTwins. Specifically, LLMs iteratively generate novel model specifications, while offline tools are employed to optimize emitted parameters. Correspondingly, proposed models are evaluated and evolved based on targeted feedback, enabling the discovery of increasingly effective hybrid models. Our empirical results reveal that HDTwinGen produces generalizable, sample-efficient, and evolvable models, significantly advancing DTs' efficacy in real-world applications.

This paper examines hybrid digital twins, which combine mechanistic components reflecting domain knowledge with neural components that provide flexible modeling capacity. Their modular structure also supports later changes to the model.

HDTwinGen instead uses an evolutionary process in which language models propose model specifications. Offline tools optimize the proposed parameters, and evaluations provide targeted feedback. The system uses that feedback to revise and evolve its candidate hybrid models.

The reported experiments show that HDTwinGen produces models with useful generalization, sample efficiency, and capacity for modification. The approach makes architecture design part of the automated learning process alongside parameter fitting. Its significance is the ability to search for combinations of partial domain knowledge and neural modeling, rather than requiring an expert to choose that combination in advance.
summary.tldr: HDTwinGen uses language models and evolutionary feedback to automatically design hybrid simulations combining domain knowledge with neural components.

title: Automatically Learning Hybrid Digital Twins of Dynamical Systems

abstract: Sparse ridge regression problems play a significant role across various domains. To solve sparse ridge regression, Liu et al. (2023) recently propose an advanced algorithm, Scalable Optimal $K$-Sparse Ridge Regression (OKRidge), which is both faster and more accurate than existing approaches. However, the absence of theoretical analysis on the error of OKRidge impedes its large-scale applications. In this paper, we reframe the estimation error of OKRidge as a Primary Optimization ($\textbf{PO}$) problem and employ the Convex Gaussian min-max theorem (CGMT) to simplify the $\textbf{PO}$ problem into an Auxiliary Optimization ($\textbf{AO}$) problem. Subsequently, we provide a theoretical error analysis for OKRidge based on the $\textbf{AO}$ problem. This error analysis improves the theoretical reliability of OKRidge. We also conduct experiments to verify our theorems and the results are in excellent agreement with our theoretical findings.

That agreement supports the analysis as an account of OKRidge’s estimation error in the studied setting. It strengthens the theoretical basis for using an already effective method by connecting its computational procedure to predictions about estimation accuracy.
summary.tldr: The paper develops an estimation-error analysis for OKRidge using the Convex Gaussian min-max theorem and finds close experimental agreement with its theory.

title: The Reliability of OKRidge Method in Solving Sparse Ridge Regression Problems

abstract: We provide space complexity lower bounds for data structures that approximate logistic loss up to $\epsilon$-relative error on a logistic regression problem with data $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ and labels $\mathbf{y} \in \\{-1,1\\}^d$. The space complexity of existing coreset constructions depend on a natural complexity measure $\mu_\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{X})$. We give an $\tilde{\Omega}(\frac{d}{\epsilon^2})$ space complexity lower bound in the regime $\mu_\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{X}) = \mathcal{O}(1)$ that shows existing coresets are optimal in this regime up to lower order factors. We also prove a general $\tilde{\Omega}(d\cdot \mu_\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{X}))$ space lower bound when $\epsilon$ is constant, showing that the dependency on $\mu_\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{X})$ is not an artifact of mergeable coresets. Finally, we refute a prior conjecture that $\mu_\mathbf{y}(\mathbf{X})$ is hard to compute by providing an efficient linear programming formulation, and we empirically compare our algorithm to prior approximate methods.

paragraphs: Compact data structures can approximate the logistic-regression loss without retaining all the original data. This paper asks how much storage such approximations fundamentally require. It focuses on relative-error guarantees and a data-dependent complexity measure, μ, which already appears in storage bounds for existing coreset constructions.

When μ is bounded by a constant, the authors establish a space lower bound of roughly d/ε², up to lower-order factors. This shows that existing coresets are essentially optimal in that regime. For constant approximation error, they also prove a general lower bound of roughly dμ, up to logarithmic factors. Dependence on μ therefore reflects a broader storage requirement, rather than merely a restriction of mergeable coresets.

The paper additionally shows that μ can be computed efficiently through a linear programming formulation, refuting a previous conjecture of computational difficulty. Empirical comparisons examine this algorithm against earlier approximate methods. Together, these results clarify both the unavoidable memory cost of loss approximation and the tractability of calculating a measure that governs that cost.
summary.tldr: Storage lower bounds establish near-optimality of logistic-loss coresets in a stated regime, while linear programming makes their complexity measure efficiently computable.

title: The Space Complexity of Approximating Logistic Loss

abstract: While the Transformer architecture has achieved remarkable success across various domains, a thorough theoretical foundation explaining its optimization dynamics is yet to be fully developed. In this study, we aim to bridge this understanding gap by answering the following two core questions: (1) Which types of Transformer architectures allow Gradient Descent (GD) to achieve guaranteed convergence? and (2) Under what initial conditions and architectural specifics does the Transformer achieve rapid convergence during training? By analyzing the loss landscape of a single Transformer layer using Softmax and Gaussian attention kernels, our work provides concrete answers to these questions. Our findings demonstrate that, with appropriate weight initialization, GD can train a Transformer model (with either kernel type) to achieve a global optimal solution, especially when the input embedding dimension is large. Nonetheless, certain scenarios highlight potential pitfalls: training a Transformer using the Softmax attention kernel may sometimes lead to suboptimal local solutions. In contrast, the Gaussian attention kernel exhibits a much favorable behavior. Our empirical study further validate the theoretical findings.

The authors show that appropriate weight initialization can allow gradient descent to reach a global optimum with either attention kernel, especially when the input embedding dimension is large. It provides a theoretical explanation for circumstances in which training can converge successfully.

Gaussian attention exhibits more favorable behavior in the studied analysis. Empirical experiments support the theoretical findings. Together, the results show why attention design and initialization deserve attention when reasoning about convergence, while keeping the conclusions grounded in the single-layer setting examined by the paper.
summary.tldr: A single-layer analysis identifies initialization and attention-kernel conditions supporting Transformer convergence, while exposing possible suboptimal outcomes with Softmax.

title: Unraveling the Gradient Descent Dynamics of Transformers

abstract: Querying complex models for precise information (e.g. traffic models, database systems, large ML models) often entails intense computations and results in long response times. Thus, weaker models which give imprecise results quickly can be advantageous, provided inaccuracies can be resolved using few queries to a stronger model. In the fundamental problem of computing a maximum-weight basis of a matroid, a well-known generalization of many combinatorial optimization problems, algorithms have access to a clean oracle to query matroid information. We additionally equip algorithms with a fast but dirty oracle. We design and analyze practical algorithms which only use few clean queries w.r.t. the quality of the dirty oracle, while maintaining robustness against arbitrarily poor dirty oracles, approaching the performance of classic algorithms for the given problem. Notably, we prove that our algorithms are, in many respects, best-possible. Further, we outline extensions to other matroid oracle types, non-free dirty oracles and other matroid problems.

paragraphs: Some optimization algorithms spend much of their effort asking another system for exact information. When that system is a complex model or database, each answer can be expensive. This paper studies how a faster, less reliable source of information can reduce that expense when computing a maximum-weight basis of a matroid, a structure that captures many combinatorial optimization problems.

The algorithms can consult both a precise “clean” oracle and an imprecise “dirty” oracle. They use the dirty oracle to help make progress while reserving clean queries for resolving uncertainty. The analysis connects the number of clean queries to the quality of the dirty oracle, so better approximate information can translate into less expensive verification.

The guarantees also address poor advice: even arbitrarily inaccurate dirty oracles do not destroy robustness, with performance approaching that of classical algorithms. The authors prove that their algorithms are best possible in several respects and outline extensions to additional oracle types, dirty queries that have a cost, and other matroid problems.
summary.tldr: Fast, imperfect information can reduce expensive exact queries in matroid optimization while preserving robustness when that information is poor.

title: Accelerating Matroid Optimization through Fast Imprecise Oracles

abstract: Decoding non-invasive brain recordings is pivotal for advancing our understanding of human cognition but faces challenges due to individual differences and complex neural signal representations. Traditional methods often require customized models and extensive trials, lacking interpretability in visual reconstruction tasks. Our framework integrates 3D brain structures with visual semantics using a *Vision Transformer 3D*. This unified feature extractor efficiently aligns fMRI features with multiple levels of visual embeddings, eliminating the need for subject-specific models and allowing extraction from single-trial data. The extractor consolidates multi-level visual features into one network, simplifying integration with Large Language Models (LLMs). Additionally, we have enhanced the fMRI dataset with diverse fMRI-image-related textual data to support multimodal large model development. Integrating with LLMs enhances decoding capabilities, enabling tasks such as brain captioning, complex reasoning, concept localization, and visual reconstruction. Our approach demonstrates superior performance across these tasks, precisely identifying language-based concepts within brain signals, enhancing interpretability, and providing deeper insights into neural processes. These advances significantly broaden the applicability of non-invasive brain decoding in neuroscience and human-computer interaction, setting the stage for advanced brain-computer interfaces and cognitive models.

paragraphs: Decoding visual information from non-invasive brain recordings is difficult because neural signals are complex and vary between people. This paper introduces a framework that combines three-dimensional brain structure with visual meaning. Its unified feature extractor uses a Vision Transformer 3D to align fMRI features with multiple levels of visual embeddings.

The extractor supports single-trial data and removes the need for subject-specific models within the proposed framework. It consolidates multiple levels of visual features into one network, simplifying integration with large language models. The authors also enrich the fMRI dataset with varied text associated with the brain recordings and images to support multimodal model development.

The integrated system supports brain captioning, complex reasoning, concept localization, and visual reconstruction. The authors report superior performance across these tasks, including precise localization of language-based concepts in brain signals. These results connect reconstruction with language-based interpretation, broadening what the framework can extract from recordings. The contribution supports richer analysis of visual brain data and potential applications in neuroscience and human-computer interaction.
summary.tldr: A unified 3D vision-transformer framework connects single-trial fMRI recordings to visual features and language models for reconstruction and interpretation.

title: Neuro-Vision to Language: Enhancing Brain Recording-based Visual Reconstruction and Language Interaction

abstract: Bayesian optimisation for real-world problems is often performed interactively with human experts, and integrating their domain knowledge is key to accelerate the optimisation process. We consider a setup where experts provide advice on the next query point through binary accept/reject recommendations (labels). Experts’ labels are often costly, requiring efficient use of their efforts, and can at the same time be unreliable, requiring careful adjustment of the degree to which any expert is trusted. We introduce the first principled approach that provides two key guarantees. (1) Handover guarantee: similar to a no-regret property, we establish a sublinear bound on the cumulative number of experts’ binary labels. Initially, multiple labels per query are needed, but the number of expert labels required asymptotically converges to zero, saving both expert effort and computation time. (2) No-harm guarantee with data-driven trust level adjustment: our adaptive trust level ensures that the convergence rate will not be worse than the one without using advice, even if the advice from experts is adversarial. Unlike existing methods that employ a user-defined function that hand-tunes the trust level adjustment, our approach enables data-driven adjustments. Real-world applications empirically demonstrate that our method not only outperforms existing baselines, but also maintains robustness despite varying labelling accuracy, in tasks of battery design with human experts.

paragraphs: Human experts can guide Bayesian optimization by accepting or rejecting proposed query points. Their advice costs time and may be unreliable, so an optimizer needs to decide both how often to ask and how much to trust the answer. This paper develops an approach with theoretical guarantees addressing both decisions.

The handover guarantee bounds the cumulative number of expert labels sublinearly. Although early queries may require several labels, the required labeling effort asymptotically approaches zero. The no-harm guarantee adjusts trust using data so that the convergence rate is no worse than optimization without advice, even when advice is adversarial. This guarantee concerns convergence rate rather than every individual query outcome.

The trust adjustment avoids requiring a manually specified function to control confidence in experts. In battery-design applications involving human experts, the method outperforms existing baselines and remains robust across different labeling accuracies. The contribution is a principled way to benefit from expert knowledge while progressively reducing dependence on it and controlling the effect of unreliable recommendations.
summary.tldr: The method incorporates expert accept/reject advice with guarantees on diminishing labeling effort and protection of the optimizer's convergence rate.

title: Principled Bayesian Optimization in Collaboration with Human Experts

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown impressive success across modalities such as image, video, and audio in a variety of understanding and generation tasks. However, current MLLMs are surprisingly poor at understanding webpage screenshots and generating their corresponding HTML code. To address this problem, we propose Web2Code, a benchmark consisting of a new large-scale webpage-to-code dataset for instruction tuning and an evaluation framework for the webpage understanding and HTML code translation abilities of MLLMs. For dataset construction, we leverage pretrained LLMs to enhance existing webpage-to-code datasets as well as generate a diverse pool of new webpages rendered into images. Specifically, the inputs are webpage images and instructions, while the responses are the webpage's HTML code. We further include diverse natural language QA pairs about the webpage content in the responses to enable a more comprehensive understanding of the web content. To evaluate model performance in these tasks, we develop an evaluation framework for testing MLLMs' abilities in webpage understanding and web-to-code generation. Extensive experiments show that our proposed dataset is beneficial not only to our proposed tasks but also in the general visual domain. We hope our work will contribute to the development of general MLLMs suitable for web-based content generation and task automation. Our data and code are available at https://github.com/MBZUAI-LLM/web2code.

Web2Code addresses this gap with both training data and an evaluation framework. Its focus includes interpreting webpage content as well as translating a rendered page image into code.

The dataset is constructed using pretrained language models to enrich existing webpage-to-code data and generate diverse new webpages. The contribution therefore combines specialized instruction-tuning material with a way to assess the resulting capabilities, supporting research toward multimodal systems for web content generation and task automation.
summary.tldr: Web2Code combines webpage screenshots, HTML, and content questions with an evaluation framework to improve and measure multimodal webpage capabilities.

title: Web2Code: A Large-scale Webpage-to-Code Dataset and Evaluation Framework for Multimodal LLMs

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel theoretical framework for multi-task regression, applying random matrix theory to provide precise performance estimations, under high-dimensional, non-Gaussian data distributions. We formulate a multi-task optimization problem as a regularization technique to enable single-task models to leverage multi-task learning information. We derive a closed-form solution for multi-task optimization in the context of linear models. Our analysis provides valuable insights by linking the multi-task learning performance to various model statistics such as raw data covariances, signal-generating hyperplanes, noise levels, as well as the size and number of datasets. We finally propose a consistent estimation of training and testing errors, thereby offering a robust foundation for hyperparameter optimization in multi-task regression scenarios. Experimental validations on both synthetic and real-world datasets in regression and multivariate time series forecasting demonstrate improvements on univariate models, incorporating our method into the training loss and thus leveraging multivariate information.

paragraphs: This paper studies how regression models can benefit from information shared across tasks. It formulates multi-task learning as a regularization problem, allowing a model focused on one task to incorporate information from others. For linear models, the authors derive a closed-form solution, making the relationship between the optimization problem and its resulting predictions explicit.

The theoretical framework uses random matrix theory to estimate performance for high-dimensional data with non-Gaussian distributions. It connects performance to data covariances, the directions that generate the signal, noise levels, and the sizes and number of datasets. These connections help explain how the statistical properties of the tasks relate to the value of sharing information.

The authors also propose consistent estimates of training and testing error to support hyperparameter selection. Experiments cover synthetic and real regression data, including multivariate time series forecasting. Incorporating the method into the training loss improves univariate models in those evaluations, showing how models for individual series can benefit from information across multiple series.
summary.tldr: A random-matrix analysis explains multi-task regression performance and supports using shared information to improve individual forecasting models.

title: Analysing Multi-Task Regression via Random Matrix Theory with Application to Time Series Forecasting

abstract: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) enriches the expressiveness of variationalfamilies by utilizing a kernel and a mixing distribution to hierarchically define thevariational distribution. Existing SIVI methods parameterize the mixing distributionusing implicit distributions, leading to intractable variational densities. As a result,directly maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is not possible, so theyresort to one of the following: optimizing bounds on the ELBO, employing costlyinner-loop Markov chain Monte Carlo runs, or solving minimax objectives. In thispaper, we propose a novel method for SIVI called Particle Variational Inference(PVI) which employs empirical measures to approximate the optimal mixingdistributions characterized as the minimizer of a free energy functional. PVI arisesnaturally as a particle approximation of a Euclidean–Wasserstein gradient flow and,unlike prior works, it directly optimizes the ELBO whilst making no parametricassumption about the mixing distribution. Our empirical results demonstrate thatPVI performs favourably compared to other SIVI methods across various tasks.Moreover, we provide a theoretical analysis of the behaviour of the gradient flowof a related free energy functional: establishing the existence and uniqueness ofsolutions as well as propagation of chaos results.

paragraphs: Semi-implicit variational inference builds flexible probability approximations by combining a kernel with a mixing distribution. Existing approaches often represent the mixing distribution implicitly, making the resulting density intractable. That prevents direct optimization of the evidence lower bound, or ELBO, and motivates alternatives involving additional bounds, costly inner sampling loops, or minimax objectives.

Particle Variational Inference represents the mixing distribution with an empirical collection of particles. The target mixing distribution is characterized through minimization of a free-energy functional, and the particle method arises from a Euclidean–Wasserstein gradient flow. This construction directly optimizes the ELBO without assuming a parametric form for the mixing distribution.

Experiments show favorable performance against other semi-implicit variational inference methods across several tasks. The authors also analyze a related free-energy gradient flow, establishing existence and uniqueness of solutions and propagation-of-chaos results. The theoretical claims concern that related flow, while the empirical comparisons support the particle algorithm. Together, they offer a computational approach and mathematical grounding for flexible variational inference.
summary.tldr: Particle Variational Inference uses particles to directly optimize the ELBO without a parametric assumption on the mixing distribution.

title: Particle Semi-Implicit Variational Inference

abstract: Recent progress in text–video retrieval has been largely driven by contrastive learning. However, existing methods often overlook the effect of the modality gap, which causes anchor representations to undergo in-place optimization (i.e., optimization tension) that limits their alignment capacity. Moreover, noisy hard negatives further distort the semantics of anchors. To address these issues, we propose GARE, a Gap-Aware Retrieval framework that introduces a learnable, pair-specific increment $\Delta_{ij}$ between text $t_i$ and video $v_j$, redistributing gradients to relieve optimization tension and absorb noise. We derive $\Delta_{ij}$ via a multivariate first-order Taylor expansion of the InfoNCE loss under a trust-region constraint, showing that it guides updates along locally consistent descent directions. A lightweight neural module conditioned on the semantic gap couples increments across batches for structure-aware correction. Furthermore, we regularize $\Delta$ through a variational information bottleneck with relaxed compression, enhancing stability and semantic consistency. Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that GARE consistently improves alignment accuracy and robustness, validating the effectiveness of gap-aware tension mitigation.

paragraphs: Text-video retrieval learns representations that bring matching descriptions and videos together. The paper identifies two obstacles in contrastive training: a gap between the modalities creates tension in updates to anchor representations, and noisy hard negatives can distort their semantics. GARE addresses these problems by adding a learned correction specific to each text-video pair.

This increment redistributes gradients to relieve optimization tension and absorb noise. The authors derive it from a first-order Taylor expansion of the InfoNCE loss under a trust-region constraint, showing that it supports locally consistent descent directions. A lightweight neural module conditions corrections on the semantic gap and couples them across batches, allowing the adjustments to reflect shared structure rather than isolated pairs.

A variational information bottleneck with relaxed compression further regularizes the increments to improve stability and semantic consistency. Across four benchmarks, GARE consistently improves alignment accuracy and robustness. These results support modifying how mismatched representations are updated during training, with the theoretical descent claim applying locally under the stated trust-region formulation.
summary.tldr: GARE learns regularized pair-specific corrections that reduce alignment tension and noise in contrastive text-video retrieval.

title: Rebalancing Contrastive Alignment with Bottlenecked Semantic Increments in Text-Video Retrieval

abstract: The high inference demands of transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) pose substantial challenges in their deployment. To this end, we introduce *Neural Block Linearization* (NBL), a novel framework for accelerating transformer model inference by replacing self-attention layers with linear approximations derived from Linear Minimum Mean Squared Error estimators. NBL leverages Canonical Correlation Analysis to compute a theoretical upper bound on the approximation error. Then, we use this bound as a criterion for substitution, selecting the LLM layers with the lowest linearization error. NBL can be efficiently applied to pre-trained LLMs without the need for fine-tuning. In experiments, NBL achieves notable computational speed-ups while preserving competitive accuracy on multiple reasoning benchmarks. For instance, applying NBL to 12 self-attention layers in *DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B* increases the inference speed by 32% with less than 1% accuracy trade-off, making it a flexible and promising solution to improve the inference efficiency of LLMs.

title: Efficient Large Language Model Inference with Neural Block Linearization

abstract: Language model inversion seeks to recover hidden prompts using only language model outputs. This capability has implications for security and accountability in language model deployments, such as leaking private information from an API-protected language model’s system message. We propose a new method – prompt inversion from logprob sequences (PILS) – that recovers hidden prompts by gleaning clues from the model’s next-token probabilities over the course of multiple generation steps. Our method is enabled by a key insight: The vector-valued outputs of a language model occupy a low-dimensional subspace. This enables us to losslessly compress the full next-token probability distribution over multiple generation steps using a linear map, allowing more output information to be used for inversion. Our approach yields massive gains over previous state-of-the-art methods for recovering hidden prompts, achieving 2–3.5 times higher exact recovery rates across test sets, in one case increasing the recovery rate from 17% to 60%. Our method also exhibits surprisingly good generalization behavior; for instance, an inverter trained on 16 generations steps gets 5–27% higher prompt recovery when we increase the number of steps to 32 at test time. Furthermore, we demonstrate strong performance of our method on the more challenging task of recovering hidden system messages. We also analyze the role of verbatim repetition in prompt recovery and propose a new method for cross-family model transfer for logit-based inverters. Our findings suggest that next-token probabilities are a considerably more vulnerable attack surface for inversion attacks than previously known.

title: Better Language Model Inversion by Compactly Representing Next-Token Distributions

abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has shown promising results in solving Job Scheduling Problems (JSPs), automatically deriving powerful dispatching rules from data without relying on expert knowledge. However, most RL-based methods train only a single decision-maker, which limits exploration capability and leaves significant room for performance improvement. Moreover, designing reward functions for different JSP variants remains a challenging and labor-intensive task. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel and generic learning framework that optimizes multiple policies sharing a common objective and a single neural network, while enabling each policy to learn specialized and diverse strategies. The model optimization process is fully guided in a self-supervised manner, eliminating the need for reward functions. In addition, we develop a training scheme that adaptively controls the imitation intensity to reflect the quality of self-labels. Experimental results show that our method effectively addresses the aforementioned challenges and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art RL methods across six JSP variants. Furthermore, our approach also demonstrates strong performance on other combinatorial optimization problems, highlighting its versatility beyond JSPs.

This links the strength of the learning signal to the reliability of the guidance available, while the multiple policies provide diverse approaches to the same scheduling objective.

Experiments show significant improvements over state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning methods across six job-scheduling variants. The approach also performs strongly on other combinatorial optimization problems, providing evidence of usefulness beyond scheduling. The contribution combines policy diversity with self-supervised optimization, addressing both how broadly the model explores solutions and how it obtains training guidance across different problem variants.
summary.tldr: A self-supervised framework trains diverse scheduling policies in one network without reward functions and outperforms RL methods across six scheduling variants.

title: Towards Generalizable Multi-Policy Optimization with Self-Evolution for Job Scheduling

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures achieve impressive performance and efficiency by dynamically routing inputs to specialized subnetworks, known as experts. However, this sparse routing mechanism inherently exhibits task preferences due to expert specialization, introducing a new and underexplored vulnerability to backdoor attacks. In this work, we investigate the feasibility and effectiveness of injecting backdoors into MoE-based LLMs by exploiting their inherent expert routing preferences. We thus propose \textbf{BadSwitch}, a novel backdoor framework that integrates task-coupled dynamic trigger optimization with a sensitivity-guided Top-S expert tracing mechanism. Our approach jointly optimizes trigger embeddings during pretraining while identifying S most sensitive experts, subsequently constraining the Top-K gating mechanism to these targeted experts. Unlike traditional backdoor attacks that rely on superficial data poisoning or model editing, BadSwitch primarily embeds malicious triggers into expert routing paths with strong task affinity, enabling precise and stealthy model manipulation. Through comprehensive evaluations across three prominent MoE architectures (Switch Transformer, QwenMoE, and DeepSeekMoE), we demonstrate that BadSwitch can efficiently hijack pre-trained models with up to 100\% success rate (ASR) while maintaining the highest clean accuracy (ACC) among all baselines. Furthermore, BadSwitch exhibits strong resilience against both text-level and model-level defense mechanisms, achieving 94.07\% ASR and 87.18\% ACC on the AGNews dataset. Our analysis of expert activation patterns reveals fundamental insights into MoE vulnerabilities. We anticipate this work will expose security risks in MoE systems and contribute to advancing AI safety.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts language models route inputs to specialized subnetworks, giving different experts preferences for particular tasks. This paper investigates whether those routing preferences create opportunities for backdoors. Its BadSwitch framework targets the pathways that select experts, connecting malicious trigger behavior to the model's existing task specialization.

At a high level, BadSwitch combines task-dependent trigger optimization with a mechanism that identifies especially sensitive experts. It then focuses routing on those selected experts. The contribution is an attack mechanism embedded in expert selection paths, and the authors analyze expert activations to understand how those paths relate to the resulting vulnerability.

Evaluations span Switch Transformer, QwenMoE, and DeepSeekMoE. The paper reports attack success rates reaching 100% in evaluated settings while retaining the highest clean accuracy among its baselines. It also reports resilience against text-level and model-level defenses, including 94.07% attack success and 87.18% clean accuracy on AGNews. These results identify routing as a consequential security surface in the studied architectures; the peak success rate is an observed maximum, not a universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: BadSwitch exploits task-linked expert routing to implant effective backdoors in evaluated mixture-of-experts language models.

title: Who Speaks for the Trigger? Dynamic Expert Routing in Backdoored Mixture-of-Experts Transformers

abstract: Recent advancements in bionic prosthetic technology offer transformative opportunities to restore mobility and functionality for individuals with missing limbs. Users of bionic limbs, or bionic humans, learn to seamlessly integrate prosthetic extensions into their motor repertoire, regaining critical motor abilities. The remarkable movement generalization and environmental adaptability demonstrated by these individuals highlight motor intelligence capabilities unmatched by current artificial intelligence systems. Addressing these limitations, MyoChallenge '24 at NeurIPS 2024 established a benchmark for human-robot coordination with an emphasis on joint control of both biological and mechanical limbs. The competition featured two distinct tracks: a manipulation task utilizing the myoMPL model, integrating a virtual biological arm and the Modular Prosthetic Limb (MPL) for a passover task; and a locomotion task using the novel myoOSL model, combining a bilateral virtual biological leg with a trans-femoral amputation and the Open Source Leg (OSL) to navigate varied terrains. Marking the third iteration of the MyoChallenge, the event attracted over 50 teams with more than 290 submissions all around the globe, with diverse participants ranging from independent researchers to high school students. The competition facilitated the development of several state-of-the-art control algorithms for bionic musculoskeletal systems, leveraging techniques such as imitation learning, muscle synergy, and model-based reinforcement learning that significantly surpassed our proposed baseline performance by a factor of 10. By providing the open-source simulation framework of MyoSuite, standardized tasks, and physiologically realistic models, MyoChallenge serves as a reproducible testbed and benchmark for bridging ML and biomechanics. The competition website is featured here: https://sites.google.com/view/myosuite/myochallenge/myochallenge-2024.

paragraphs: MyoChallenge 2024 benchmarks coordinated control of biological and prosthetic limbs. title: MyoChallenge 2024: A New Benchmark for Physiological Dexterity and Agility in Bionic Humans

abstract: As Visual Language Models (VLMs) continue to evolve, they have demonstrated increasingly sophisticated logical reasoning capabilities and multimodal thought generation, opening doors to widespread applications. However, this advancement raises serious concerns about content security, particularly when these models process complex multimodal inputs requiring intricate reasoning. When faced with these safety challenges, the critical competition between logical reasoning and safety objectives of VLMs is often overlooked in previous works. In this paper, we introduce Visualization-of-Thought Attack (\textbf{VoTA}), a novel and automated attack framework that strategically constructs chains of images with risky visual thoughts to challenge victim models. Our attack provokes the inherent conflict between the model's logical processing and safety protocols, ultimately leading to the generation of unsafe content. Through comprehensive experiments, VoTA achieves remarkable effectiveness, improving the average attack success rate (ASR) by 26.71\% (from 63.70\% to 90.41\%) on 9 open-source and 6 commercial VLMs, compared to the state-of-the-art methods. These results expose a critical vulnerability: current VLMs struggle to maintain safety guarantees when processing insecure multimodal visualization-of-thought inputs, highlighting the urgency and necessity of enhancing safety alignment. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Hongqiong12/VoTA. Content Warning: This paper contains harmful contents that may be offensive.

paragraphs: As visual language models become better at reasoning across images, their reasoning capabilities can interact with safety objectives in problematic ways. This paper investigates that tension through Visualization-of-Thought Attack, or VoTA. The framework tests whether models maintain safety when asked to process chains of images containing risky visual reasoning.

VoTA automatically constructs these image chains to challenge a victim model's safety behavior. The authors describe the attack as exploiting a conflict between following the visual reasoning and enforcing safety protocols. Its contribution is an evaluation of vulnerability associated with multimodal reasoning sequences, rather than considering image understanding and safety as independent capabilities.

Across nine open-source and six commercial visual language models, the reported average attack success rate increases from 63.70% to 90.41% compared with state-of-the-art methods. That is a difference of 26.71 percentage points. The results show a substantial weakness in the evaluated systems when processing these insecure visual thought sequences. They motivate stronger safety alignment for multimodal reasoning, while remaining evidence about the tested attacks and models rather than every possible visual interaction.
summary.tldr: VoTA exposes safety weaknesses in visual reasoning, raising average attack success from 63.70% to 90.41% across 15 evaluated visual language models.

title: Towards Visualization-of-Thought Jailbreak Attack against Large Visual Language Models

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have achieved remarkable success in various domains but typically rely on centralized, static graphs, which limits their applicability in distributed, evolving environments. To address this limitation, we define the task of Federated Continual Graph Learning (FCGL), a paradigm for incremental learning on dynamic graphs distributed across decentralized clients. Existing methods, however, neither preserve graph topology during task transitions nor mitigate parameter conflicts in server‐side aggregation. To overcome these challenges, we introduce **MOTION**, a generalizable FCGL framework that integrates two complementary modules: the Graph Topology‐preserving Multi‐Sculpt Coarsening (G‐TMSC) module, which maintains the structural integrity of past graphs through a multi‐expert, similarity‐guided fusion process, and the Graph‐Aware Evolving Parameter Adaptive Engine (G‐EPAE) module, which refines global model updates by leveraging a topology‐sensitive compatibility matrix. Extensive experiments on real‐world datasets show that our approach improves average accuracy (AA) by an average of 30\% $\uparrow$ over the FedAvg baseline across five datasets while maintaining a negative $\downarrow$ average forgetting (AF) rate, significantly enhancing generalization and robustness under FCGL settings. The code is available for anonymous access at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MOTION.
