paragraphs: Graph learning becomes more difficult when graphs evolve over time and their data are spread across decentralized clients. The paper formalizes this combination as Federated Continual Graph Learning. It identifies two problems with existing approaches: preserving earlier graph topology as tasks change and avoiding conflicts when a server combines updates from different clients.

MOTION addresses these problems through two complementary modules. Its graph-coarsening module uses multiple experts and similarity-guided fusion to retain structural information from past graphs. Its parameter-update module uses a topology-sensitive compatibility matrix to refine global updates. The first component focuses on what graph structure is retained, while the second focuses on how distributed model changes are combined.

Across five real-world datasets, the authors report an average 30% improvement in average accuracy over FedAvg, together with a negative average-forgetting rate. They also report improved generalization and robustness in the studied setting. These findings support treating structural preservation and update compatibility as connected requirements when learning continually from distributed, changing graphs.
summary.tldr: MOTION preserves past graph structure and coordinates compatible client updates to improve continual learning on decentralized, evolving graphs.

title: MOTION: Multi-Sculpt Evolutionary Coarsening for Federated Continual Graph Learning

abstract: Random splitting of datasets in image segmentation often leads to unrepresentative test sets, resulting in biased evaluations and poor model generalization. While stratified sampling has proven effective for addressing label distribution imbalance in classification tasks, extending these ideas to segmentation remains challenging due to the multi-label structure and class imbalance typically present in such data. Building on existing stratification concepts, we introduce Iterative Pixel Stratification (IPS), a straightforward, label-aware sampling method tailored for segmentation tasks. Additionally, we present Wasserstein-Driven Evolutionary Stratification (WDES), a novel genetic algorithm designed to minimize the Wasserstein distance, thereby optimizing the similarity of label distributions across dataset splits. We prove that WDES is globally optimal given enough generations. Using newly proposed statistical heterogeneity metrics, we evaluate both methods against random sampling and find that WDES consistently produces more representative splits. Applying WDES across diverse segmentation tasks, including street scenes, medical imaging, and satellite imagery, leads to lower performance variance and improved model evaluation. Our results also highlight the particular value of WDES in handling small, imbalanced, and low-diversity datasets, where conventional splitting strategies are most prone to bias.

paragraphs: Random dataset splits can give image-segmentation models unrepresentative test sets, distorting evaluation. Balancing labels is harder here than in ordinary classification because each image contains many labeled pixels and may include several highly imbalanced classes. The paper develops splitting methods that explicitly account for these segmentation label distributions.

Iterative Pixel Stratification is a straightforward label-aware sampling approach. Wasserstein-Driven Evolutionary Stratification, or WDES, uses a genetic algorithm to minimize a distance between label distributions across splits. The authors prove global optimality given enough generations. This qualification matters: the theorem concerns sufficient evolutionary search, rather than asserting that any finite run has already reached the optimum.

Using new statistical heterogeneity measures, the experiments find that WDES consistently produces more representative splits than random sampling. Across street-scene, medical, and satellite segmentation tasks, it lowers performance variance and improves evaluation. Its reported benefits are especially valuable for small, imbalanced, or low-diversity datasets, where split composition can have a particularly strong influence on measured performance.
summary.tldr: Label-aware segmentation splits, especially WDES, yield more representative evaluations and lower performance variance in the reported experiments.

title: Stratify or Die: Rethinking Data Splits in Image Segmentation

abstract: Recent methods for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human feedback predominantly rely on a single reference model, which limits diversity, model overfitting, and underutilizes the wide range of available pre-trained models. Incorporating multiple reference models has the potential to address these limitations by broadening perspectives, reducing bias, and leveraging the strengths of diverse open-source LLMs. However, integrating multiple reference models into reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) frameworks poses significant theoretical challenges, where achieving exact solutions has remained an open problem. This paper presents the first \emph{exact solution} to the multiple reference model problem in reverse KL-regularized RLHF. We introduce a comprehensive theoretical framework that includes rigorous statistical analysis and provides sample complexity guarantees. Additionally, we extend our analysis to forward KL-regularized RLHF, offering new insights into sample complexity requirements in multiple reference scenarios. Our contributions lay the foundation for more advanced and adaptable LLM alignment techniques, enabling the effective use of multiple reference models. This work paves the way for developing alignment frameworks that are both theoretically sound and better suited to the challenges of modern AI ecosystems.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback commonly uses one reference model to constrain how far an aligned model moves during training. The paper studies the use of several reference models instead. This could draw on a wider range of pretrained capabilities and perspectives, but integrating those references creates a theoretical problem that a single-reference formulation does not resolve.

The main contribution is an exact solution for the multiple-reference problem with reverse KL regularization. Alongside that solution, the authors develop a statistical framework with sample-complexity guarantees, addressing how much data the learning problem requires. They also extend the analysis to forward KL regularization and examine its sample requirements when several references are present.

The value of the work is a mathematical foundation for alignment that can incorporate multiple pretrained models. The stated possibilities of broader perspectives and reduced bias motivate the framework; the concrete contributions are the exact solution and statistical guarantees. These results provide a basis for developing more adaptable alignment methods without treating the anticipated benefits of model diversity as established empirical outcomes.
summary.tldr: The paper gives an exact multiple-reference solution for reverse-KL RLHF and analyzes sample complexity for both KL directions.

title: KL-Regularized RLHF with Multiple Reference Models: Exact Solutions and Sample Complexity

abstract: Integrating the understanding and reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLM) with the self-learning capabilities of Reinforcement Learning (RL) enables more reliable driving performance under complex driving conditions. There has been a lot of work exploring LLM-Dominated RL methods in the field of autonomous driving motion planning. These methods, which utilize LLM to directly generate policies or provide decisive instructions during policy learning of RL agent, are centrally characterized by an over-reliance on LLM outputs. However, LLM outputs are susceptible to hallucinations. Evaluations show that state-of-the-art LLM indicates a non-hallucination rate of only approximately 57.95\% when assessed on essential driving-related tasks. Thus, in these methods, hallucinations from the LLM can directly jeopardize the performance of driving policies. This paper argues that maintaining relative independence between the LLM and the RL is vital for solving the hallucinations problem. Consequently, this paper is devoted to propose a novel LLM-Hinted RL paradigm. The LLM is used to generate semantic hints for state augmentation and policy optimization to assist RL agent in motion planning, while the RL agent counteracts potential erroneous semantic indications through policy learning to achieve excellent driving performance. Based on this paradigm, we propose the HCRMP (LLM-Hinted Contextual Reinforcement Learning Motion Planner) architecture, which is designed that includes ①Augmented Semantic Representation Module to extend state space. ②Contextual Stability Anchor Module enhances the reliability of multi-critic weight hints by utilizing information from the knowledge base. ③Semantic Cache Module is employed to seamlessly integrate LLM low-frequency guidance with RL high-frequency control. Extensive experiments in CARLA validate HCRMP's strong overall driving performance. HCRMP achieves a task success rate of up to 80.3\% under diverse driving conditions with different traffic densities. Under safety-critical driving conditions, HCRMP significantly reduces the collision rate by 11.4\%, which effectively improves the driving performance in complex scenarios.
originalAbstract: Integrating the understanding and reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLM) with the self-learning capabilities of Reinforcement Learning (RL) enables more reliable driving performance under complex driving conditions. There has been a lot of work exploring LLM-Dominated RL methods in the field of autonomous driving motion planning. These methods, which utilize LLM to directly generate policies or provide decisive instructions during policy learning of RL agent, are centrally characterized by an over-reliance on LLM outputs. However, LLM outputs are susceptible to hallucinations. Evaluations show that state-of-the-art LLM indicates a non-hallucination rate of only approximately 57.95\% when assessed on essential driving-related tasks. Thus, in these methods, hallucinations from the LLM can directly jeopardize the performance of driving policies. This paper argues that maintaining relative independence between the LLM and the RL is vital for solving the hallucinations problem. Consequently, this paper is devoted to propose a novel LLM-Hinted RL paradigm. The LLM is used to generate semantic hints for state augmentation and policy optimization to assist RL agent in motion planning, while the RL agent counteracts potential erroneous semantic indications through policy learning to achieve excellent driving performance. Based on this paradigm, we propose the HCRMP (LLM-Hinted Contextual Reinforcement Learning Motion Planner) architecture, which is designed that includes ①Augmented Semantic Representation Module to extend state space. ②Contextual Stability Anchor Module enhances the reliability of multi-critic weight hints by utilizing information from the knowledge base. ③Semantic Cache Module is employed to seamlessly integrate LLM low-frequency guidance with RL high-frequency control. Extensive experiments in CARLA validate HCRMP's strong overall driving performance. HCRMP achieves a task success rate of up to 80.3\% under diverse driving conditions with different traffic densities. Under safety-critical driving conditions, HCRMP significantly reduces the collision rate by 11.4\%, which effectively improves the driving performance in complex scenarios.

paragraphs: HCRMP investigates how language-model reasoning can assist reinforcement learning for driving without making control overly dependent on language-model outputs. The motivation is that erroneous semantic guidance can undermine a driving policy when the language model directly determines actions or gives decisive training instructions. The proposed framework instead treats its outputs as hints.

Those hints augment the agent’s state representation and assist policy optimization, while reinforcement learning can counteract incorrect guidance through learning. An augmented semantic representation module expands the available state information. A contextual stability anchor uses a knowledge base to improve the reliability of multi-critic weighting hints. A semantic cache connects infrequent language-model guidance with frequent control decisions.

In CARLA experiments, the authors report task success rates reaching 80.3% across driving conditions with different traffic densities. They also report an 11.4% collision-rate reduction in safety-critical conditions. These are simulation findings supporting the proposed division of responsibilities: semantic guidance provides context, while the reinforcement learning agent retains relative independence in learning its driving policy.
summary.tldr: HCRMP uses language-model hints to support an independently learning driving policy, reporting improved success and fewer collisions in CARLA.

title: HCRMP: An LLM-Hinted Contextual Reinforcement Learning Framework for Autonomous Driving

abstract: Neural networks generally prefer simple and easy-to-learn features. When these features are spuriously correlated with the labels, the network's performance can suffer, particularly for underrepresented classes or concepts. Self-supervised representation learning methods, such as contrastive learning, are especially prone to this issue, often resulting in worse performance on downstream tasks. We identify a key spectral signature of this failure: early reliance on dominant singular modes of the learned feature matrix. To mitigate this, we propose a novel framework that promotes a uniform eigenspectrum of the feature covariance matrix, encouraging diverse and semantically rich representations. Our method operates in a fully self-supervised setting, without relying on ground-truth labels or any additional information. Empirical results on SimCLR and SimSiam demonstrate consistent gains in robustness and transfer performance, suggesting broad applicability across self-supervised learning paradigms. Code: https://github.com/NaghmehGh/SpuriousCorrelation_SSRL

paragraphs: Neural networks often learn easy features first, even when those features have only a misleading association with the concepts a task requires. This can undermine later performance, especially for underrepresented classes or concepts. The paper examines this problem in self-supervised representation learning, where useful representations must be learned without ground-truth labels.

The authors identify a spectral signature of the failure: the learned feature matrix relies early on a small set of dominant singular modes. In plain terms, a few directions in the representation carry disproportionate weight. Their regularization framework encourages a more uniform spectrum of the feature covariance matrix, aiming to spread information across more directions and promote richer representations.

The method uses neither ground-truth labels nor additional information. Experiments with SimCLR and SimSiam show consistent improvements in robustness and transfer performance. Those results support spectral regularization as a way to reduce reliance on spurious features in the tested systems, and suggest applicability across self-supervised learning approaches without establishing that the benefit holds universally.
summary.tldr: Encouraging a more uniform feature spectrum improves robustness and transfer in tested self-supervised models without requiring labels.

title: Mitigating Spurious Features in Contrastive Learning with Spectral Regularization

abstract: Text-to-image generation models have made significant progress in producing high-quality images from textual descriptions, yet they continue to struggle with maintaining subject consistency across multiple images, a fundamental requirement for visual storytelling. Existing methods attempt to address this by either fine-tuning models on large-scale story visualization datasets, which is resource-intensive, or by using training-free techniques that share information across generations, which still yield limited success. In this paper, we introduce a novel training-free sampling strategy called Zigzag Sampling with Asymmetric Prompts and Visual Sharing to enhance subject consistency in visual story generation. Our approach proposes a zigzag sampling mechanism that alternates between asymmetric prompting to retain subject characteristics, while a visual sharing module transfers visual cues across generated images to enforce consistency. Experimental results, based on both quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluations, demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previous approaches in generating coherent and consistent visual stories. The code is available at https://github.com/Mingxiao-Li/Asymmetry-Zigzag-StoryDiffusion.

paragraphs: Visual storytelling requires a subject to remain recognizable across several generated images. A text-to-image model may produce convincing individual pictures while changing the subject's appearance from one scene to the next. This paper addresses that cross-image consistency problem through the generation procedure, without training the model on a story visualization dataset.

The proposed strategy combines zigzag sampling, asymmetric prompts, and visual sharing. The sampling mechanism alternates asymmetric prompting to help retain subject characteristics. Alongside this, a visual sharing module carries visual cues between generated images. These components address consistency through both the textual guidance used during sampling and information transferred across the images in the story.

Quantitative measurements and qualitative evaluations show that the method significantly outperforms previous approaches in the reported experiments. Its contribution is a training-free way to make a sequence of generated pictures more coherent, especially in how subjects are depicted. This matters because story quality depends on relationships between images as well as the quality of each image considered separately.
summary.tldr: A training-free sampling strategy combines asymmetric prompts and shared visual cues to improve subject consistency across generated story images.

title: Consistent Story Generation: Unlocking the Potential of Zigzag Sampling

abstract: Artificial intelligence is poised to augment dermatological care by enabling scalable image-based diagnostics. Yet, the development of robust and equitable models remains hindered by datasets that fail to capture the clinical and demographic complexity of real-world practice. This complexity stems from region-specific disease distributions, wide variation in skin tones, and the underrepresentation of outpatient scenarios from non-Western populations. We introduce DermaCon-IN, a prospectively curated dermatology dataset comprising 5,450 clinical images from 2,993 patients across outpatient clinics in South India. Each image is annotated by board-certified dermatologists with 245 distinct diagnoses, structured under a hierarchical, etiology-based taxonomy adapted from Rook’s classification. The dataset captures a wide spectrum of dermatologic conditions and tonal variation commonly seen in Indian outpatient care. We benchmark a range of architectures, including convolutional models (ResNet, DenseNet, EfficientNet), transformer-based models (ViT, MaxViT, Swin), and Concept Bottleneck Models to establish baseline performance and explore how anatomical and concept-level cues may be integrated. These results are intended to guide future efforts toward interpretable and clinically realistic models. DermaCon-IN provides a scalable and representative foundation for advancing dermatology AI in real-world settings.

paragraphs: Dermatology image datasets can miss important differences in disease prevalence, skin tone, and everyday clinical settings. DermaCon-IN addresses this representation problem with images collected prospectively in outpatient clinics in South India. It contains 5,450 clinical images from 2,993 patients, grounding the resource in the conditions encountered in Indian outpatient care.

Board-certified dermatologists provide annotations spanning 245 diagnoses. These diagnoses are organized in a hierarchy based on disease causes, using a taxonomy adapted from Rook’s classification. This structure gives the dataset a clinically organized set of labels while capturing a broad range of conditions and skin tones present in the sampled setting.

The authors benchmark convolutional networks, vision transformers, and Concept Bottleneck Models. These evaluations establish starting points for later research and explore incorporating anatomical and concept-level information into predictions. The contribution is both a dataset and an initial experimental foundation for more interpretable, clinically realistic dermatology AI. Its relevance comes from representing outpatient cases and populations that existing resources may inadequately cover.
summary.tldr: DermaCon-IN provides dermatologist-annotated images from South Indian outpatient clinics and benchmarks models for more clinically representative dermatology AI.

title: DermaCon-IN: A Multiconcept-Annotated Dermatological Image Dataset of Indian Skin Disorders for Clinical AI Research

abstract: Structure-based drug design (SBDD), aiming to generate 3D molecules with high binding affinity toward target proteins, is a vital approach in novel drug discovery. Although recent generative models have shown great potential, they suffer from unstable probability dynamics and mismatch between generated molecule size and the protein pockets geometry, resulting in inconsistent quality and off-target effects. We propose PAFlow, a novel target-aware molecular generation model featuring prior interaction guidance and a learnable atom number predictor. PAFlow adopts the efficient flow matching framework to model the generation process and constructs a new form of conditional flow matching for discrete atom types. A protein–ligand interaction predictor is incorporated to guide the vector field toward higher-affinity regions during generation, while an atom number predictor based on protein pocket information is designed to better align generated molecule size with target geometry. Extensive experiments on the CrossDocked2020 benchmark show that PAFlow achieves a new state-of-the-art in binding affinity (up to -8.31 Avg. Vina Score), simultaneously maintains favorable molecular properties.

paragraphs: PAFlow generates three-dimensional molecules conditioned on a target protein. The paper identifies two problems in existing generative approaches: unstable probability dynamics and generated molecules whose size does not fit the target pocket’s geometry. These can undermine consistent molecular quality and target compatibility, motivating a generation process that uses more explicit protein information.

The model uses flow matching and introduces a conditional formulation for discrete atom types. A protein–ligand interaction predictor guides the generation vector field toward regions associated with stronger affinity. Separately, an atom-number predictor uses information about the protein pocket to choose a molecule size better suited to that geometry.

On CrossDocked2020, the authors report state-of-the-art binding-affinity results, with an average Vina score reaching −8.31, while maintaining favorable molecular properties. This supports the combination of interaction guidance and learned molecule size in the benchmark setting. The reported affinity result is expressed through Vina scoring; the abstract’s evidence concerns generated molecular candidates and their evaluated properties, rather than demonstrated therapeutic effectiveness.
summary.tldr: PAFlow guides molecule generation with protein-interaction predictions and a learned atom count, reporting improved affinity scores on CrossDocked2020.

title: Prior-Guided Flow Matching for Target-Aware Molecule Design with Learnable Atom Number

abstract: Recent advances in enhancing the reasoning ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been remarkably successful. LLMs trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) for reasoning demonstrate strong performance in challenging tasks such as mathematics and coding, even with relatively small model sizes. However, despite these impressive improvements in task accuracy, the assessment of creativity in LLM generations has been largely overlooked in reasoning tasks, in contrast to writing tasks. The lack of research on creativity assessment in reasoning primarily stems from two challenges: (1) the difficulty of defining the range of creativity, and (2) the necessity of human evaluation in the assessment process. To address these challenges, we propose CLAWS, a novel method that defines and classifies mathematical solutions into Typical, Creative, and Hallucinated categories without human evaluation, by leveraging attention weights across prompt sections and output. CLAWS outperforms five existing white-box detection methods—Perplexity, Logit Entropy, Window Entropy, Hidden Score, and Attention Score—on five 7–8B math RL models (DeepSeek, Qwen, Mathstral, OpenMath2, and Oreal). We validate CLAWS on 4,545 math problems collected from 181 math contests (A(J)HSME, AMC, AIME). Our code is available at https://github.com/kkt94/CLAWS.

paragraphs: Strong mathematical accuracy does not by itself establish whether a language model produces creative solutions. This paper addresses the separate problem of assessing creativity in mathematical reasoning. The authors identify two obstacles: defining what counts as creativity and avoiding dependence on human evaluation whenever a generated solution needs to be assessed.

CLAWS defines and classifies solutions into three categories: Typical, Creative, and Hallucinated. It uses attention weights linking sections of the prompt and the generated output as evidence for that classification. Because these signals come from inside the model, the method assesses generation through internal behavior. The distinction between creative and hallucinated solutions is central to the proposed classification.

The evaluation covers 4,545 problems from 181 mathematics contests and five mathematical reasoning models with seven to eight billion parameters. CLAWS outperforms five existing methods that use internal signals, including perplexity, entropy, hidden representations, and attention scores. The findings support attention organized around prompt sections as a useful basis for automated creativity assessment within the mathematical settings studied.
summary.tldr: CLAWS uses attention patterns to classify mathematical solutions as typical, creative, or hallucinated without human evaluation.

title: CLAWS:Creativity detection for LLM-generated solutions using Attention Window of Sections

abstract: Recent advancements in video generation have enabled the creation of high-quality, visually compelling videos. However, generating videos that adhere to the laws of physics remains a critical challenge for applications requiring realism and accuracy. In this work, we propose **PhysHPO**, a novel framework for Hierarchical Cross-Modal Direct Preference Optimization, to tackle this challenge by enabling fine-grained preference alignment for physically plausible video generation. PhysHPO optimizes video alignment across four hierarchical granularities: a) ***Instance Level***, aligning the overall video content with the input prompt; b) ***State Level***, ensuring temporal consistency using boundary frames as anchors; c) ***Motion Level***, modeling motion trajectories for realistic dynamics; and d) ***Semantic Level***, maintaining logical consistency between narrative and visuals. Recognizing that real-world videos are the best reflections of physical phenomena, we further introduce an automated data selection pipeline to efficiently identify and utilize *"good data"* from existing large-scale text-video datasets, thereby eliminating the need for costly and time-intensive dataset construction. Extensive experiments on both physics-focused and general capability benchmarks demonstrate that PhysHPO significantly improves physical plausibility and overall video generation quality of advanced models. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to explore fine-grained preference alignment and data selection for video generation, paving the way for more realistic and human-preferred video generation paradigms.

paragraphs: A generated video can look convincing while depicting motion or events that do not make physical sense. PhysHPO addresses this gap through preference optimization that evaluates several aspects of a video separately. Its goal is to improve physical plausibility alongside the broader quality of generated content.

The framework organizes alignment into four levels. At the instance level, it matches the overall video to the prompt. At the state level, it uses boundary frames as anchors for temporal consistency. At the motion level, it models trajectories for realistic dynamics. At the semantic level, it seeks agreement between the narrative and what appears on screen. Together, these levels provide more detailed training guidance than a single overall preference.

The authors also introduce an automated pipeline that selects useful examples from existing large-scale text-video datasets, drawing on real videos as evidence of physical behavior. Experiments on physics-focused and general benchmarks report significant improvements in physical plausibility and overall generation quality. The results support combining finer preference signals with targeted data selection to improve advanced video models.
summary.tldr: PhysHPO improves video plausibility through preference training across content, temporal states, motion, and semantics, supported by automated data selection.

title: Hierarchical Fine-grained Preference Optimization for Physically Plausible Video Generation

abstract: Modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reason over hour-long video, yet their key–value (KV) cache grows linearly with time—quickly exceeding the fixed memory of phones, AR glasses, and edge robots. Prior compression schemes either assume the whole video and user query are available offline or must first build the full cache, so memory still scales with stream length. InfiniPot-V is the first training-free, query-agnostic framework that enforces a hard, length-independent memory cap for \textit{streaming} video understanding. During video encoding it monitors the cache and, once a user-set threshold is reached, runs a lightweight compression pass that (i) removes temporally redundant tokens via Temporal-axis Redundancy (TaR) metric and (ii) keeps semantically significant tokens via Value-Norm (VaN) ranking. Across four open-source MLLMs and four long-video and streaming-video benchmarks, InfiniPot-V cuts peak GPU memory by up to 94\%, sustains real-time generation, and matches or surpasses full-cache accuracy—even in multi-turn dialogues. By dissolving the KV cache bottleneck without retraining or query knowledge, InfiniPot-V closes the gap for on-device streaming video assistants.

paragraphs: A multimodal model's key–value cache grows as it processes more video, creating a problem for devices with fixed memory. Existing compression approaches may require the complete video, the user's question, or an already constructed full cache. InfiniPot-V instead compresses during streaming, enforcing a user-set cache memory cap that does not grow with video length.

The framework monitors the cache during video encoding and compresses it when the threshold is reached. Its Temporal-axis Redundancy metric removes tokens that repeat information across time. Value-Norm ranking helps retain semantically significant tokens. Together, these mechanisms select information to preserve without retraining the model or knowing the eventual query.

The authors report peak GPU memory reductions of up to 94%, real-time generation, and accuracy matching or exceeding full-cache processing, including in multi-turn dialogue. The findings support managing memory continuously as video arrives, making the approach relevant to assistants operating under fixed device-memory constraints.
summary.tldr: InfiniPot-V compresses streaming video caches under a fixed memory cap without retraining or advance knowledge of user queries.

title: InfiniPot-V: Memory-Constrained KV Cache Compression for Streaming Video Understanding

abstract: Learning semantically meaningful representations from unstructured 3D point clouds remains a central challenge in computer vision, especially in the absence of large-scale labeled datasets. While masked point modeling (MPM) is widely used in self-supervised 3D learning, its reconstruction-based objective can limit its ability to capture high-level semantics. We propose AsymDSD, an Asymmetric Dual Self-Distillation framework that unifies masked modeling and invariance learning through prediction in the latent space rather than the input space. AsymDSD builds on a joint embedding architecture and introduces several key design choices: an efficient asymmetric setup, disabling attention between masked queries to prevent shape leakage, multi-mask sampling, and a point cloud adaptation of multi-crop. AsymDSD achieves state-of-the-art results on ScanObjectNN (90.53\%) and further improves to 93.72\% when pretrained on 930k shapes, surpassing prior methods.

paragraphs: AsymDSD learns representations of 3D objects from point clouds without requiring labels during representation learning. The paper addresses a weakness of masked point modeling: reconstructing missing input points can emphasize geometric detail without adequately capturing higher-level meaning. Its central change is to make predictions in a learned representation space, where the objective concerns features rather than the original points.

The framework combines masked modeling with invariance learning in a joint embedding architecture. Its asymmetric design supports efficiency, while disabling attention between masked queries prevents shape information from leaking through those interactions. Multiple masks and an adaptation of multiple cropped views provide complementary ways to train on the same underlying point cloud.

The authors report state-of-the-art results of 90.53% on ScanObjectNN, rising to 93.72% after pretraining on 930,000 shapes. These findings support the proposed combination of latent prediction and architectural choices for 3D representation learning. The larger-pretraining result also shows that the reported performance improves when the method learns from a substantially larger collection of shapes.
summary.tldr: AsymDSD combines masked latent prediction and invariance learning to improve self-supervised representations of 3D point clouds.

title: Asymmetric Dual Self-Distillation for 3D Self-Supervised Representation Learning

abstract: This work analyzes singular-value spectra of weight matrices in pretrained transformer models to understand how information is stored at both ends of the spectrum. Using Random Matrix Theory (RMT) as a zero information hypothesis, we associate agreement with RMT as evidence of randomness and deviations as evidence for learning. Surprisingly, we observe pronounced departures from RMT not only among the largest singular values - the usual outliers - but also among the smallest ones. A comparison of the associated singular vectors with the eigenvectors of the activation covariance matrices shows that there is considerable overlap wherever RMT is violated. Thus, significant directions in the data are captured by small singular values and their vectors as well as by the large ones. We confirm this empirically: zeroing out the singular values that deviate from RMT raises language-model perplexity far more than removing values from the bulk, and after fine-tuning the smallest decile can be the third most influential part of the spectrum. To explain how vectors linked to small singular values can carry more information than those linked to larger values, we propose a linear random-matrix model. Our findings highlight the overlooked importance of the low end of the spectrum and provide theoretical and practical guidance for SVD-based pruning and compression of large language models.

paragraphs: This paper asks where learned information appears in transformer weight matrices when they are decomposed into singular values and associated directions. Large singular values usually receive attention, but the authors also examine the smallest ones. Random matrix theory supplies a zero-information reference, with deviations treated as evidence of learned structure.

Both ends of the spectrum show pronounced departures from that reference. The associated directions overlap substantially with directions in activation covariance wherever those departures occur. This suggests that small singular values can accompany meaningful data directions, so their small magnitude alone does not establish that they are unimportant.

Removing singular values that depart from the random reference increases perplexity much more than removing values from the bulk. After fine-tuning, the smallest tenth can be the spectrum's third most influential portion. A linear random-matrix model helps explain how this can happen. The findings inform compression and pruning by showing why decisions based only on singular-value magnitude may discard learned information.
summary.tldr: Small singular values can encode important learned information in transformers, making magnitude alone an unreliable guide for compression.

title: Small Singular Values Matter: A Random Matrix Analysis of Transformer Models

abstract: With the significant progress of large reasoning models in complex coding and reasoning tasks, existing benchmarks, like LiveCodeBench and CodeElo, are insufficient to evaluate the coding capabilities of large language models (LLMs) in real competition environments. Moreover, current evaluation metrics such as Pass@K fail to capture the reflective abilities of reasoning models. To address these challenges, we propose ICPC-Eval, a top-level competitive coding benchmark designed to probing the frontiers of LLM reasoning. ICPC-Eval includes 118 carefully curated problems from 11 recent ICPC contests held in various regions of the world, offering three key contributions: 1) A challenging realistic ICPC competition scenario, featuring a problem type and difficulty distribution consistent with actual contests. 2) A robust test case generation method and a corresponding local evaluation toolkit, enabling efficient and accurate local evaluation. 3) An effective test-time scaling evaluation metric, Refine@K, which allows iterative repair of solutions based on execution feedback. Furthermore, despite recent advancements in code generation, these models still lag behind top-performing human teams. We release the benchmark at: https://github.com/RUCAIBox/ICPC-Eval

title: ICPC-Eval: Probing the Frontiers of LLM Reasoning with Competitive Programming Contests

abstract: Autoregressive models have driven remarkable progress in language modeling. Their foundational reliance on discrete tokens, unidirectional context, and single-pass decoding, while central to their success, also inspires the exploration of a design space that could offer new axes of modeling flexibility. In this work, we explore an alternative paradigm, shifting language modeling from a discrete token space to a continuous latent space. We propose a novel framework that employs transformer-based autoregressive normalizing flows to model these continuous representations. This approach unlocks substantial flexibility, enabling the construction of models that can capture global bi-directional context through stacked, alternating-direction autoregressive transformations, support block-wise generation with flexible token patch sizes, and facilitate a hierarchical multi-pass generation process. We further propose new mixture-based coupling transformations designed to capture complex dependencies within the latent space shaped by discrete data, and demonstrate theoretical connections to conventional discrete autoregressive models. Extensive experiments on language modeling benchmarks demonstrate strong likelihood performance and highlight the flexible modeling capabilities inherent in our framework.

This paper explores a different design space by modeling continuous latent representations of language. Its framework uses transformer-based autoregressive normalizing flows to build a probability model over those representations.

Stacking autoregressive transformations that alternate direction allows the model to capture global context from both directions. The same framework supports generating blocks with flexible token patch sizes and constructing text through a hierarchy of multiple passes. These capabilities provide several ways to organize language generation within the proposed continuous representation.

They establish theoretical connections to conventional discrete autoregressive models, linking the alternative framework to familiar language modeling. Experiments on language benchmarks show strong likelihood performance and demonstrate its modeling flexibility. The main result is a concrete framework in which bidirectional context, block size, and multiple generation passes become available design choices.
summary.tldr: Transformer-based autoregressive flows model language in continuous space, supporting bidirectional context, flexible generation blocks, and hierarchical decoding passes.

title: Flexible Language Modeling in Continuous Space with Transformer-based Autoregressive Flows

abstract: Predicting protein secondary structure is a fundamental problem in protein structure prediction. Here we present a new supervised generative stochastic network (GSN) based method to predict local secondary structure with deep hierarchical representations. GSN is a recently proposed deep learning technique (Bengio & Thibodeau-Laufer, 2013) to globally train deep generative model. We present the supervised extension of GSN, which learns a Markov chain to sample from a conditional distribution, and applied it to protein structure prediction. To scale the model to full-sized, high-dimensional data, like protein sequences with hundreds of amino-acids, we introduce a convolutional architecture, which allows efficient learning across multiple layers of hierarchical representations. Our architecture uniquely focuses on predicting structured low-level labels informed with both low and high-level representations learned by the model. In our application this corresponds to labeling the secondary structure state of each amino-acid residue. We trained and tested the model on separate sets of non-homologous proteins sharing less than 30% sequence identity. Our model achieves 66.4% Q8 accuracy on the CB513 dataset, better than the previously reported best performance 64.9% (Wang et al., 2011) for this challenging secondary structure prediction problem.

This provides empirical support for the supervised convolutional GSN on the stated prediction task, while the sequence separation is an important feature of the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: A supervised convolutional generative stochastic network improves reported protein secondary-structure prediction by combining multiple levels of learned representation.

title: Deep Supervised and Convolutional Generative Stochastic Network for Protein Secondary Structure Prediction

abstract: Logarithms of determinants of large positive definite matrices appear ubiquitously in machine learning applications including Gaussian graphical and Gaussian process models, partition functions of discrete graphical models, minimum-volume ellipsoids and metric and kernel learning. Log-determinant computation involves the Cholesky decomposition at the cost cubic in the number of variables (i.e., the matrix dimension), which makes it prohibitive for large-scale applications. We propose a linear-time randomized algorithm to approximate log-determinants for very large-scale positive definite and general non-singular matrices using a stochastic trace approximation, called the Hutchinson method, coupled with Chebyshev polynomial expansions that both rely on efficient matrix-vector multiplications. We establish rigorous additive and multiplicative approximation error bounds depending on the condition number of the input matrix. In our experiments, the proposed algorithm can provide very high accuracy solutions at orders of magnitude faster time than the Cholesky decomposition and Shur completion, and enables us to compute log-determinants of matrices involving tens of millions of variables.

A standard Cholesky-based calculation has cubic cost in matrix dimension, which becomes prohibitive for very large matrices. This paper develops a randomized approximation approach for large positive definite and general nonsingular matrices.

The algorithm combines Hutchinson stochastic trace estimation with Chebyshev polynomial expansions. Both components rely on efficient matrix-vector multiplication, replacing the need for the expensive decomposition used by the standard calculation. The proposed linear-time approach therefore centers on operations that can be practical even when a full matrix factorization is too costly.

The authors prove additive and multiplicative error bounds that depend on the input matrix's condition number. Their experiments show that very accurate approximations can be obtained orders of magnitude faster than the compared decomposition methods, and demonstrate computations involving tens of millions of variables. The contribution couples large-scale computational savings with explicit approximation guarantees whose strength depends on matrix conditioning.
summary.tldr: Randomized trace estimation and Chebyshev expansions approximate large-matrix log-determinants efficiently with conditioning-dependent error bounds.

title: Large-scale log-determinant computation through stochastic Chebyshev expansions

abstract: We pose causal inference as the problem of learning to classify probability distributions. In particular, we assume access to a collection {(S_i,l_i)}_i=1^n, where each S_i is a sample drawn from the probability distribution of X_i \times Y_i, and l_i is a binary label indicating whether “X_i \to Y_i” or “X_i ←Y_i”. Given these data, we build a causal inference rule in two steps. First, we featurize each S_i using the kernel mean embedding associated with some characteristic kernel. Second, we train a binary classifier on such embeddings to distinguish between causal directions. We present generalization bounds showing the statistical consistency and learning rates of the proposed approach, and provide a simple implementation that achieves state-of-the-art cause-effect inference. Furthermore, we extend our ideas to infer causal relationships between more than two variables.

paragraphs: This paper treats cause-effect inference as a supervised classification problem over probability distributions. It assumes access to several datasets of paired variables, each labeled with its causal direction. The learning task is to use those examples to build a rule that distinguishes which variable causes the other.

The method has two stages. First, it represents each dataset using a kernel mean embedding associated with a characteristic kernel. This creates features describing the sampled distribution. Second, it trains a binary classifier on those representations to predict causal direction. The unit being classified is thus a distribution represented by observations, rather than an individual paired observation.

The authors provide generalization bounds establishing statistical consistency and learning rates for the approach. A simple implementation achieves reported state-of-the-art cause-effect inference performance, and the ideas are extended to relationships involving more than two variables. The availability of labeled causal examples is central to the setup. The contribution shows how that supervision can support both an inference procedure and a learning-theoretic analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper learns causal direction by classifying kernel representations of distributions, with generalization guarantees and strong reported empirical performance.

title: Towards a Learning Theory of Cause-Effect Inference

abstract: As a widely used non-linear activation, Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) separates noise and signal in a feature map by learning a threshold or bias. However, we argue that the classification of noise and signal not only depends on the magnitude of responses, but also the context of how the feature responses would be used to detect more abstract patterns in higher layers. In order to output multiple response maps with magnitude in different ranges for a particular visual pattern, existing networks employing ReLU and its variants have to learn a large number of redundant filters. In this paper, we propose a multi-bias non-linear activation (MBA) layer to explore the information hidden in the magnitudes of responses. It is placed after the convolution layer to decouple the responses to a convolution kernel into multiple maps by multi-thresholding magnitudes, thus generating more patterns in the feature space at a low computational cost. It provides great flexibility of selecting responses to different visual patterns in different magnitude ranges to form rich representations in higher layers. Such a simple and yet effective scheme achieves the state-of-the-art performance on several benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper argues that the usefulness of a convolutional response depends on more than whether its magnitude clears a single threshold. A response that is useful for one higher-level pattern may be unhelpful for another. Capturing several magnitude ranges with existing ReLU-based networks can therefore require learning many redundant filters.

The proposed multi-bias activation layer follows a convolutional layer and applies multiple thresholds to each kernel’s responses. It converts those responses into several maps, exposing information from different magnitude ranges. Higher layers can then select and combine these maps to construct richer patterns without needing a separate convolutional filter for every range.

The authors describe this expansion of the feature representation as computationally inexpensive and report state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. The significance is that response magnitude becomes a more flexible source of information for later layers. The reported results support this simple architectural change as an effective way to increase representational variety while reusing the responses of existing convolution kernels.
summary.tldr: Multi-bias activation applies several thresholds to convolutional responses, creating richer feature maps at low computational cost.

title: Multi-Bias Non-linear Activation in Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Data aggregation is becoming an increasingly common technique for sharing sensitive information, and for reducing data size when storage and/or communication costs are high. Aggregate quantities such as group-average are a form of semi-supervision as they do not directly provide information of individual values, but despite their wide-spread use, prior literature on learning individual-level models from aggregated data is extremely limited. This paper investigates the effect of data aggregation on parameter recovery for a sparse linear model, when known results are no longer applicable. In particular, we consider a scenario where the data are collected into groups e.g. aggregated patient records, and first-order empirical moments are available only at the group level. Despite this obfuscation of individual data values, we can show that the true parameter is recoverable with high probability using these aggregates when the collection of true group moments is an incoherent matrix, and the empirical moment estimates have been computed from a sufficiently large number of samples. To the best of our knowledge, ours are the first results on structured parameter recovery using only aggregated data. Experimental results on synthetic data are provided in support of these theoretical claims. We also show that parameter estimation from aggregated data approaches the accuracy of parameter estimation obtainable from non-aggregated or “individual" samples, when applied to two real world healthcare applications- predictive modeling of CMS Medicare reimbursement claims, and modeling of Texas State healthcare charges.

paragraphs: Aggregating records can reduce storage and communication costs or support sharing sensitive information, but group summaries hide individual values. This paper asks whether those summaries can still support recovery of an individual-level sparse linear model. It considers grouped data for which only first-order empirical moments are available at the group level.

The authors prove high-probability recovery under two substantive conditions: the matrix of true group moments must be incoherent, and each empirical moment estimate must draw on sufficiently many samples. Thus, aggregation need not erase the information required for parameter recovery when the group structure and estimation accuracy satisfy the stated assumptions.

Synthetic experiments support the theoretical claims. In two healthcare applications involving Medicare reimbursement claims and Texas healthcare charges, estimation from aggregates approaches the accuracy obtained from individual samples. The findings establish a conditional route from group-level information to sparse model parameters, with practical evidence that the loss from aggregation can be small in the evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: Sparse linear-model parameters can be recovered from group aggregates under incoherence and sufficient-sampling conditions.

title: Sparse Parameter Recovery from Aggregated Data

abstract: Black-box alpha (BB-α) is a new approximate inference method based on the minimization of α-divergences. BB-αscales to large datasets because it can be implemented using stochastic gradient descent. BB-αcan be applied to complex probabilistic models with little effort since it only requires as input the likelihood function and its gradients. These gradients can be easily obtained using automatic differentiation. By changing the divergence parameter α, the method is able to interpolate between variational Bayes (VB) (α→0) and an algorithm similar to expectation propagation (EP) (α= 1). Experiments on probit regression and neural network regression and classification problems show that BB-αwith non-standard settings of α, such as α= 0.5, usually produces better predictions than with α→0 (VB) or α= 1 (EP).

paragraphs: The paper introduces black-box alpha, an approximate inference method that minimizes a family of discrepancies called alpha divergences. The parameter alpha changes the criterion used to construct the approximation. This gives a single method a way to explore different inference behaviors instead of committing to one fixed divergence.

The procedure can use stochastic gradient descent, allowing it to scale to large datasets. Applying it requires the model’s likelihood function and its gradients, which can be obtained through automatic differentiation. As alpha approaches zero, the method approaches variational Bayes. At alpha equal to one, it yields an algorithm similar to expectation propagation, connecting two familiar approaches within one adjustable framework.

Experiments cover probit regression and neural-network regression and classification. In these experiments, intermediate or otherwise non-standard alpha settings, including one-half, usually yield better predictions than the variational-Bayes and expectation-propagation-like endpoints. The results suggest that choosing the divergence parameter can matter for predictive performance; they do not establish one alpha value as universally best.
summary.tldr: Black-box alpha provides scalable approximate inference with a tunable divergence whose intermediate settings often improve predictions in the reported experiments.

title: Black-Box Alpha Divergence Minimization

abstract: Robust estimation is much more challenging in high-dimensions than it is in one-dimension: Most techniques either lead to intractable optimization problems or estimators that can tolerate only a tiny fraction of errors. Recent work in theoretical computer science has shown that, in appropriate distributional models, it is possible to robustly estimate the mean and covariance with polynomial time algorithms that can tolerate a constant fraction of corruptions, independent of the dimension. However, the sample and time complexity of these algorithms is prohibitively large for high-dimensional applications. In this work, we address both of these issues by establishing sample complexity bounds that are optimal, up to logarithmic factors, as well as giving various refinements that allow the algorithms to tolerate a much larger fraction of corruptions. Finally, we show on both synthetic and real data that our algorithms have state-of-the-art performance and suddenly make high-dimensional robust estimation a realistic possibility.

paragraphs: Estimating a mean or covariance becomes difficult when data have many dimensions and some observations are corrupted. Earlier approaches often required impractical optimization or could withstand only a very small amount of corruption. Polynomial-time methods had established that stronger robustness was possible under appropriate distributional models, but their data and computational requirements remained too large for practical use.

This paper works on closing that gap between theoretical feasibility and usable algorithms. It establishes bounds on the number of observations required that are optimal apart from logarithmic factors. It also develops refinements that let the algorithms handle a substantially larger fraction of corrupted observations, addressing a central concern in robust estimation.

The authors evaluate their methods on synthetic and real datasets and report state-of-the-art performance. Together, the statistical bounds and empirical results support the claim that high-dimensional robust estimation can become practical. The distributional setting remains important: the result builds on model-based robustness, rather than establishing reliable estimation for every possible data distribution or corruption level.
summary.tldr: Improved sample bounds and algorithmic refinements make robust high-dimensional estimation more practical under appropriate distributional models.

title: Being Robust (in High Dimensions) Can Be Practical

abstract: Block-coordinate descent algorithms and alternating minimization methods are fundamental optimization algorithms and an important primitive in large-scale optimization and machine learning. While various block-coordinate-descent-type methods have been studied extensively, only alternating minimization – which applies to the setting of only two blocks – is known to have convergence time that scales independently of the least smooth block. A natural question is then: is the setting of two blocks special? We show that the answer is “no” as long as the least smooth block can be optimized exactly – an assumption that is also needed in the setting of alternating minimization. We do so by introducing a novel algorithm AR-BCD, whose convergence time scales independently of the least smooth (possibly non-smooth) block. The basic algorithm generalizes both alternating minimization and randomized block coordinate (gradient) descent, and we also provide its accelerated version – AAR-BCD.

A natural question is then: is the setting of two blocks special? paragraphs: Block-coordinate optimization divides the variables into groups and updates selected groups during training. A central question is whether one particularly difficult block must control the convergence time of the entire method. Previously, alternating minimization with two blocks was known to avoid dependence on the least smooth block.

The paper shows that this favorable property can extend beyond two blocks. Its algorithm, Alternating Randomized Block Coordinate Descent, has convergence time that does not scale with the smoothness of the least smooth block. That block can even be nonsmooth, provided it can be optimized exactly. Exact optimization is also an assumption behind the corresponding two-block result.

The basic method brings alternating minimization and randomized block coordinate gradient descent into one framework, and the authors also introduce an accelerated version. The result identifies exact optimization of the difficult block as a sufficient condition for this convergence property beyond the two-block setting. It does not remove the requirement to solve that block accurately.
summary.tldr: AR-BCD extends convergence independent of the least smooth block beyond two blocks, provided that block can be optimized exactly.

title: Alternating Randomized Block Coordinate Descent

abstract: The problem of Knowledge Base Completion can be framed as a 3rd-order binary tensor completion problem. In this light, the Canonical Tensor Decomposition (CP) seems like a natural solution; however, current implementations of CP on standard Knowledge Base Completion benchmarks are lagging behind their competitors. In this work, we attempt to understand the limits of CP for knowledge base completion. First, we motivate and test a novel regularizer, based on tensor nuclear p-norms. Then, we present a reformulation of the problem that makes it invariant to arbitrary choices in the inclusion of predicates or their reciprocals in the dataset. These two methods combined allow us to beat the current state of the art on several datasets with a CP decomposition, and obtain even better results using the more advanced ComplEx model.

In this light, the Canonical Tensor Decomposition (CP) seems like a natural solution; however, current implementations of CP on standard Knowledge Base Completion benchmarks are lagging behind their competitors. In this work, we attempt to understand the limits of CP for knowledge base completion. First, we motivate and test a novel regularizer, based on tensor nuclear p-norms. Then, we present a reformulation of the problem that makes it invariant to arbitrary choices in the inclusion of predicates or their reciprocals in the dataset. These two methods combined allow us to beat the current state of the art on several datasets with a CP decomposition, and obtain even better results using the more advanced ComplEx model.

paragraphs: A knowledge base can be represented as a three-way binary tensor whose entries describe whether relational facts hold. Canonical Tensor Decomposition, or CP, is a natural model for completing missing entries, yet existing implementations had performed poorly against competing knowledge-base completion methods. This paper examines whether the problem lies in CP itself or in how it is trained and formulated.

The authors propose a regularizer based on tensor nuclear p-norms. They also reformulate the completion problem so that results are invariant to arbitrary choices about including a predicate or its reciprocal in the dataset. These changes address both the preference imposed on learned factors and the representation of relational direction.

Together, the two changes allow CP to surpass the then-current state of the art on several datasets. Applying the same ideas to ComplEx produces further improvements. The findings suggest that regularization and dataset formulation can materially change the apparent capabilities of a tensor model, although the abstract does not separate the numerical contribution of each modification.
summary.tldr: Better regularization and reciprocal-relation handling make CP competitive for knowledge-base completion and also improve ComplEx.

title: Canonical Tensor Decomposition for Knowledge Base Completion

abstract: On the way to the robust learner for real-world applications, there are still great challenges, including considering unknown environments with limited data. Learnware (Zhou; 2016) describes a novel perspective, and claims that learning models should have reusable and evolvable properties. We propose to Encode Meta InformaTion of features (EMIT), as the model specification for characterizing the changes, which grants the model evolvability to bridge heterogeneous feature spaces. Then, pre-trained models from related tasks can be Reused by our REctiFy via heterOgeneous pRedictor Mapping (REFORM}) framework. In summary, the pre-trained model is adapted to a new environment with different features, through model refining on only a small amount of training data in the current task. Experimental results over both synthetic and real-world tasks with diverse feature configurations validate the effectiveness and practical utility of the proposed framework.
originalAbstract: On the way to the robust learner for real-world applications, there are still great challenges, including considering unknown environments with limited data. Learnware (Zhou; 2016) describes a novel perspective, and claims that learning models should have reusable and evolvable properties. We propose to Encode Meta InformaTion of features (EMIT), as the model specification for characterizing the changes, which grants the model evolvability to bridge heterogeneous feature spaces. Then, pre-trained models from related tasks can be Reused by our REctiFy via heterOgeneous pRedictor Mapping (REFORM}) framework. In summary, the pre-trained model is adapted to a new environment with different features, through model refining on only a small amount of training data in the current task. Experimental results over both synthetic and real-world tasks with diverse feature configurations validate the effectiveness and practical utility of the proposed framework.

paragraphs: Reusing a trained model becomes difficult when a new environment supplies different features and only a small amount of training data. This paper addresses that mismatch through the learnware perspective, in which models should support reuse and adaptation as their operating conditions change.

The authors introduce EMIT, which encodes feature meta-information as a model specification. That specification characterizes changes and supports bridging heterogeneous feature spaces. Their REFORM framework then reuses pretrained models from related tasks through heterogeneous predictor mapping. The existing model is refined using a small training set from the current task so that it can operate with the new features.

Experiments cover synthetic and real-world tasks with varied feature configurations and support the framework’s effectiveness and practical usefulness. The important shift is to make feature information part of how a model can be reused. Adaptation then has an explicit description of the changing feature space to work with, alongside the limited examples available in the new task, rather than relying solely on retraining from those examples.
summary.tldr: EMIT and REFORM use feature meta-information to adapt related pretrained models to new feature spaces with little training data.

title: Rectify Heterogeneous Models with Semantic Mapping

abstract: The goal of this paper is to provide a unifying view of a wide range of problems of interest in machine learning by framing them as the minimization of functionals defined on the space of probability measures. In particular, we show that generative adversarial networks, variational inference, and actor-critic methods in reinforcement learning can all be seen through the lens of our framework. We then discuss a generic optimization algorithm for our formulation, called probability functional descent (PFD), and show how this algorithm recovers existing methods developed independently in the settings mentioned earlier.

We then discuss a generic optimization algorithm for our formulation, called probability functional descent (PFD), and show how this algorithm recovers existing methods developed independently in the settings mentioned earlier.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common mathematical view of several machine-learning problems by treating probability distributions as the objects being optimized. The objective is a functional: a quantity that assigns a value to an entire probability measure. Learning is then framed as reducing that value over the space of possible measures.

The authors show that generative adversarial networks, variational inference, and actor-critic reinforcement learning can all be expressed within this framework. These areas are usually presented through their own objectives and algorithms. Bringing them into one formulation makes their shared optimization structure explicit and provides a common language for examining how their methods operate.

The paper introduces a generic optimization algorithm called probability functional descent and shows that it recovers existing methods developed independently in those settings. Its stated contribution is therefore a unifying interpretation together with an algorithmic framework. Recovering those methods demonstrates that the formulation connects to established procedures, beyond merely grouping several applications under a broad conceptual description.
summary.tldr: Probability functional descent unifies GANs, variational inference, and actor-critic methods as optimization over probability measures.

title: Probability Functional Descent: A Unifying Perspective on GANs, Variational Inference, and Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Graphs are a fundamental abstraction for modeling relational data. However, graphs are discrete and combinatorial in nature, and learning representations suitable for machine learning tasks poses statistical and computational challenges. In this work, we propose Graphite, an algorithmic framework for unsupervised learning of representations over nodes in large graphs using deep latent variable generative models. Our model parameterizes variational autoencoders (VAE) with graph neural networks, and uses a novel iterative graph refinement strategy inspired by low-rank approximations for decoding. On a wide variety of synthetic and benchmark datasets, Graphite outperforms competing approaches for the tasks of density estimation, link prediction, and node classification. Finally, we derive a theoretical connection between message passing in graph neural networks and mean-field variational inference.

The aim is to connect useful representations of individual nodes with a model of the surrounding graph structure.

The framework uses graph neural networks to parameterize a variational autoencoder. Its decoding procedure repeatedly refines the graph, following a strategy inspired by low-rank approximations. This iterative reconstruction is a central architectural contribution: generating graph structure is treated as a refinement process within the latent-variable model.

These tasks examine both modeling graph data and using the learned representations for predictions. The paper also establishes a theoretical connection between graph-neural-network message passing and mean-field variational inference, linking a neural computation used on graphs to a probabilistic inference procedure.
summary.tldr: Graphite combines graph neural networks with iterative generative decoding to learn node representations and improve several graph tasks.

title: Graphite: Iterative Generative Modeling of Graphs

abstract: We present a general and modular method for privacy-preserving Bayesian inference for Poisson factorization, a broad class of models that includes some of the most widely used models in the social sciences. Our method satisfies limited-precision local privacy, a generalization of local differential privacy that we introduce to formulate appropriate privacy guarantees for sparse count data. We present an MCMC algorithm that approximates the posterior distribution over the latent variables conditioned on data that has been locally privatized by the geometric mechanism. Our method is based on two insights: 1) a novel reinterpretation of the geometric mechanism in terms of the Skellam distribution and 2) a general theorem that relates the Skellam and Bessel distributions. We demonstrate our method’s utility using two case studies that involve real-world email data. We show that our method consistently outperforms the commonly used naive approach, wherein inference proceeds as usual, treating the locally privatized data as if it were not privatized.

This paper develops a modular Bayesian approach for Poisson factorization, a broad family of count-data models used in the social sciences. Its central idea is to account explicitly for the process that privatized the observations when inferring the hidden variables.

Their MCMC algorithm approximates the posterior distribution conditioned on counts privatized through the geometric mechanism. Its construction uses a new interpretation of that mechanism through the Skellam distribution and a theorem connecting the Skellam and Bessel distributions.

These mathematical connections make the privacy mechanism part of the inference procedure rather than something ignored after data collection. In two case studies using real email data, the method consistently outperforms the common naive approach of analyzing privatized counts as though they were untouched. The findings demonstrate the practical value of modeling privacy-induced changes in the evaluated count-data applications.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian count-model inference method explicitly accounts for local privacy noise and outperforms naive inference in two email-data case studies.

title: Locally Private Bayesian Inference for Count Models

abstract: Current saliency map interpretations for neural networks generally rely on two key assumptions. First, they use first-order approximations of the loss function, neglecting higher-order terms such as the loss curvature. Second, they evaluate each feature’s importance in isolation, ignoring feature interdependencies. This work studies the effect of relaxing these two assumptions. First, we characterize a closed-form formula for the input Hessian matrix of a deep ReLU network. Using this formula, we show that, for classification problems with many classes, if a prediction has high probability then including the Hessian term has a small impact on the interpretation. We prove this result by demonstrating that these conditions cause the Hessian matrix to be approximately rank one and its leading eigenvector to be almost parallel to the gradient of the loss. We empirically validate this theory by interpreting ImageNet classifiers. Second, we incorporate feature interdependencies by calculating the importance of group-features using a sparsity regularization term. We use an L0 - L1 relaxation technique along with proximal gradient descent to efficiently compute group-feature importance values. Our empirical results show that our method significantly improves deep learning interpretations.

paragraphs: Saliency maps often explain a neural network using a first-order approximation of its loss and by scoring input features separately. This paper investigates both simplifications. It asks how much curvature changes an explanation and whether accounting for relationships among features produces more useful interpretations.

For deep ReLU networks, the authors derive a closed-form expression for the input Hessian, which describes loss curvature. They show that in classification problems with many classes and a high-probability prediction, adding the Hessian term has little effect on the interpretation. Under these conditions, the Hessian is approximately rank one and its leading direction nearly aligns with the loss gradient. They use an L0-to-L1 relaxation and proximal gradient descent to make the computation efficient, and report significant empirical improvements in interpretation. The two findings distinguish a setting where curvature adds little from an approach where explicitly incorporating feature relationships improves the resulting explanations.
summary.tldr: Curvature adds little to certain confident, many-class predictions, while sparsity-based group-feature importance empirically improves neural-network interpretations.

title: Understanding Impacts of High-Order Loss Approximations and Features in Deep Learning Interpretation

abstract: Convolutional Neural Networks (ConvNets) are commonly developed at a fixed resource budget, and then scaled up for better accuracy if more resources are given. In this paper, we systematically study model scaling and identify that carefully balancing network depth, width, and resolution can lead to better performance. Based on this observation, we propose a new scaling method that uniformly scales all dimensions of depth/width/resolution using a simple yet highly effective compound coefficient. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on MobileNets and ResNet. To go even further, we use neural architecture search to design a new baseline network and scale it up to obtain a family of models, called EfficientNets, which achieve much better accuracy and efficiency than previous ConvNets. In particular, our EfficientNet-B7 achieves stateof-the-art 84.4% top-1 / 97.1% top-5 accuracy on ImageNet, while being 8.4x smaller and 6.1x faster on inference than the best existing ConvNet (Huang et al., 2018). Our EfficientNets also transfer well and achieve state-of-the-art accuracy on CIFAR-100 (91.7%), Flower (98.8%), and 3 other transfer learning datasets, with an order of magnitude fewer parameters.

This paper studies how those choices interact and finds that carefully balancing them can improve performance. Its compound scaling method uses a single coefficient to coordinate growth across all three dimensions.

The authors demonstrate the scaling approach on MobileNets and ResNet. They then use neural architecture search to create a baseline network and scale it into the EfficientNet family. This combines a chosen starting architecture with a systematic rule for increasing capacity, making scaling itself a central part of the model design.
