The family also transfers well, achieving reported state-of-the-art accuracy on five transfer datasets with an order of magnitude fewer parameters. These results support balanced scaling as a route to improved accuracy and efficiency together.
summary.tldr: EfficientNet improves convolutional-network accuracy and efficiency by coordinating the scaling of depth, width, and input resolution.

title: EfficientNet: Rethinking Model Scaling for Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: In the transfer learning problem, the target and the source data domains are typically known. In this article, we study a new paradigm called mutual transfer learning where among many heterogeneous data domains, every data domain could potentially be the target of interest, and it could also be a useful source to help the learning in other data domains. However, it is important to note that given a target not every data domain can be a successful source; only data sets that are similar enough to be thought as from the same population can be useful sources for each other. Under this mutual learnability assumption, a confidence distribution fusion approach is proposed to recover the mutual learnability relation in the transfer learning regime. Our proposed method achieves the same oracle statistical inferential accuracy as if the true learnability structure were known. It can be implemented in an efficient parallel fashion to deal with large-scale data. Simulated and real examples are analyzed to illustrate the usefulness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Transfer learning commonly starts with designated source and target domains. This paper instead considers many heterogeneous domains, each of which might be a target of interest or provide useful information to another domain. The problem becomes identifying which domains can help one another, rather than assuming their transfer roles are already known.

The method relies on mutual learnability: datasets must be similar enough to be regarded as coming from the same population to serve as useful sources for one another. Under this assumption, the authors propose confidence distribution fusion to recover the relationships that determine where information can be shared. The aim is selective transfer across the collection of domains.

The proposed method achieves the same oracle statistical inference accuracy as if the true learnability structure were known. It also supports efficient parallel implementation for large-scale data. Simulated and real examples illustrate its usefulness. The result links discovering suitable transfer partners with preserving inference quality, while grounding that guarantee in the stated mutual learnability assumption.
summary.tldr: Mutual transfer learning identifies compatible domains for sharing information and achieves oracle inference accuracy under a mutual learnability assumption.

title: Mutual Transfer Learning for Massive Data

abstract: In pursuit of resource-economical machine learning, attempts have been made to dynamically adjust computation workloads in different training stages, i.e., starting with a shallow network and gradually increasing the model depth (and computation workloads) during training. However, there is neither guarantee nor guidance on designing such network grow, due to the lack of its theoretical underpinnings. In this work, to explore the theory behind, we conduct theoretical analyses from an ordinary differential equation perspective. Specifically, we illustrate the dynamics of network growth and propose a novel performance measure specific to the depth increase. Illuminated by our analyses, we move towards theoretically sound growing operations and schedulers, giving rise to an adaptive training algorithm for residual networks, LipGrow, which automatically increases network depth thus accelerates training. In our experiments, it achieves comparable performance while reducing ∼ 50% of training time.

paragraphs: Training can be made less expensive by starting with a shallow network and increasing its depth as learning proceeds. The challenge is deciding how and when to grow it. The paper argues that such decisions have lacked sufficient theoretical guidance and studies network growth through an ordinary differential equation perspective.

The authors analyze the dynamics of increasing depth and propose a performance measure specifically for that change. These results guide both the operations used to grow the network and the schedule governing when growth occurs. They lead to LipGrow, an adaptive residual-network training algorithm that automatically increases depth during training.

In the reported experiments, LipGrow achieves comparable performance while reducing training time by approximately half. That finding supports the potential of allocating less computation to earlier training stages and increasing capacity as training progresses. The contribution connects this resource-saving strategy to an analysis of growth itself, providing a basis for the algorithm's design rather than only a manually chosen depth schedule.
summary.tldr: LipGrow uses an ODE-based analysis to grow residual networks during training, roughly halving training time in reported experiments.

title: Towards Adaptive Residual Network Training: A Neural-ODE Perspective

abstract: Graph representation learning is a ubiquitous task in machine learning where the goal is to embed each vertex into a low-dimensional vector space. We consider the bipartite graph and formalize its representation learning problem as a statistical estimation problem of parameters in a semiparametric exponential family distribution: the bipartite graph is assumed to be generated by a semiparametric exponential family distribution, whose parametric component is given by the proximity of outputs of two one-layer neural networks that take high-dimensional features as inputs, while nonparametric (nuisance) component is the base measure. In this setting, the representation learning problem is equivalent to recovering the weight matrices, and the main challenges of estimation arise from the nonlinearity of activation functions and the nonparametric nuisance component of the distribution. To overcome these challenges, we propose a pseudo-likelihood objective based on the rank-order decomposition technique and show that the proposed objective is strongly convex in a neighborhood around the ground truth, so that a gradient descent-based method achieves linear convergence rate. Moreover, we prove that the sample complexity of the problem is linear in dimensions (up to logarithmic factors), which is consistent with parametric Gaussian models. However, our estimator is robust to any model misspecification within the exponential family, which is validated in extensive experiments.

summary.tldr: A semiparametric bipartite-graph estimator combines local convergence guarantees, favorable sample scaling, and robustness within the exponential family.

title: Semiparametric Nonlinear Bipartite Graph Representation Learning with Provable Guarantees

abstract: Initialization, normalization, and skip connections are believed to be three indispensable techniques for training very deep convolutional neural networks and obtaining state-of-the-art performance. This paper shows that deep vanilla ConvNets without normalization nor skip connections can also be trained to achieve surprisingly good performance on standard image recognition benchmarks. This is achieved by enforcing the convolution kernels to be near isometric during initialization and training, as well as by using a variant of ReLU that is shifted towards being isometric. Further experiments show that if combined with skip connections, such near isometric networks can achieve performances on par with (for ImageNet) and better than (for COCO) the standard ResNet, even without normalization at all. Our code is available at https://github.com/HaozhiQi/ISONet.

paragraphs: Very deep convolutional networks commonly use normalization and skip connections alongside careful initialization. This paper investigates whether deep networks can still train effectively without the first two techniques. It reports strong image-recognition performance from plain convolutional networks when their layers are encouraged to behave nearly isometrically.

An isometric transformation preserves geometric size and distance. The method keeps convolution kernels close to this behavior both at initialization and throughout training. It also modifies the ReLU activation by shifting it toward being isometric. The approach therefore coordinates the behavior of the convolutional transformations and the nonlinear activation, rather than relying on initialization alone.

The experiments show that deep networks without normalization or skip connections can perform well on standard recognition benchmarks. When skip connections are added, the near-isometric networks match standard ResNet performance on ImageNet and exceed it on COCO, while still using no normalization. These findings establish a successful alternative in the evaluated settings and challenge the belief that normalization and skip connections are indispensable for training deep convolutional networks.
summary.tldr: Keeping convolutional layers near isometric enables strong visual recognition with deep networks that omit normalization and, in some experiments, skip connections.

title: Deep Isometric Learning for Visual Recognition

abstract: Gaussian processes are the gold standard for many real-world modeling problems, especially in cases where a model’s success hinges upon its ability to faithfully represent predictive uncertainty. These problems typically exist as parts of larger frameworks, wherein quantities of interest are ultimately defined by integrating over posterior distributions. These quantities are frequently intractable, motivating the use of Monte Carlo methods. Despite substantial progress in scaling up Gaussian processes to large training sets, methods for accurately generating draws from their posterior distributions still scale cubically in the number of test locations. We identify a decomposition of Gaussian processes that naturally lends itself to scalable sampling by separating out the prior from the data. Building off of this factorization, we propose an easy-to-use and general-purpose approach for fast posterior sampling, which seamlessly pairs with sparse approximations to afford scalability both during training and at test time. In a series of experiments designed to test competing sampling schemes’ statistical properties and practical ramifications, we demonstrate how decoupled sample paths accurately represent Gaussian process posteriors at a fraction of the usual cost.

paragraphs: Gaussian process models are useful when predictive uncertainty matters, but using that uncertainty can require sampling from a posterior distribution. Those samples support Monte Carlo calculations of quantities that are otherwise intractable. This paper targets the sampling cost: existing accurate approaches can scale cubically with the number of locations where a function is evaluated.

summary.tldr: Separating prior and data contributions enables accurate Gaussian process posterior function sampling at substantially reduced empirical cost.

title: Efficiently sampling functions from Gaussian process posteriors

abstract: In many applications, it is desirable that a classifier not only makes accurate predictions, but also outputs calibrated posterior probabilities. However, many existing classifiers, especially deep neural network classifiers, tend to be uncalibrated. Post-hoc calibration is a technique to recalibrate a model by learning a calibration map. Existing approaches mostly focus on constructing calibration maps with low calibration errors, however, this quality is inadequate for a calibrator being useful. In this paper, we introduce two constraints that are worth consideration in designing a calibration map for post-hoc calibration. Then we present Meta-Cal, which is built from a base calibrator and a ranking model. Under some mild assumptions, two high-probability bounds are given with respect to these constraints. Empirical results on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet and a range of popular network architectures show our proposed method significantly outperforms the current state of the art for post-hoc multi-class classification calibration.

paragraphs: A classifier's probability estimates should communicate how reliable its predictions are, alongside the predictions themselves. Many classifiers, especially deep neural networks, produce probabilities that are poorly calibrated. Post-hoc calibration addresses this by learning a mapping that adjusts a trained model's probability outputs, but the paper argues that low calibration error alone is an inadequate design goal.

The authors introduce two additional constraints for constructing a useful calibration map. Meta-Cal combines a base calibrator with a ranking model to address this broader formulation. Under assumptions described as mild, they establish two high-probability bounds concerning the constraints, giving theoretical control beyond simply minimizing an observed calibration error.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet with a range of popular network architectures. The authors report that Meta-Cal significantly outperforms the compared state-of-the-art methods for post-hoc multiclass calibration. The work pairs empirical improvement with conditional guarantees, emphasizing that the usefulness of adjusted probabilities depends on more than one calibration quality criterion.
summary.tldr: Meta-Cal combines calibration and ranking to improve multiclass probability estimates while providing conditional bounds for two additional calibration constraints.

title: Meta-Cal: Well-controlled Post-hoc Calibration by Ranking

abstract: For machine agents to successfully interact with humans in real-world settings, they will need to develop an understanding of human mental life. Intuitive psychology, the ability to reason about hidden mental variables that drive observable actions, comes naturally to people: even pre-verbal infants can tell agents from objects, expecting agents to act efficiently to achieve goals given constraints. Despite recent interest in machine agents that reason about other agents, it is not clear if such agents learn or hold the core psychology principles that drive human reasoning. Inspired by cognitive development studies on intuitive psychology, we present a benchmark consisting of a large dataset of procedurally generated 3D animations, AGENT (Action, Goal, Efficiency, coNstraint, uTility), structured around four scenarios (goal preferences, action efficiency, unobserved constraints, and cost-reward trade-offs) that probe key concepts of core intuitive psychology. We validate AGENT with human-ratings, propose an evaluation protocol emphasizing generalization, and compare two strong baselines built on Bayesian inverse planning and a Theory of Mind neural network. Our results suggest that to pass the designed tests of core intuitive psychology at human levels, a model must acquire or have built-in representations of how agents plan, combining utility computations and core knowledge of objects and physics.

summary.tldr: AGENT uses animated scenarios to test whether models understand actions through goals, constraints, efficiency, and rewards.

title: AGENT: A Benchmark for Core Psychological Reasoning

abstract: Sparse regression has recently been applied to enable transfer learning from very limited data. We study an extension of this approach to unsupervised learning—in particular, learning word embeddings from unstructured text corpora using low-rank matrix factorization. Intuitively, when transferring word embeddings to a new domain, we expect that the embeddings change for only a small number of words—e.g., the ones with novel meanings in that domain. We propose a novel group-sparse penalty that exploits this sparsity to perform transfer learning when there is very little text data available in the target domain—e.g., a single article of text. We prove generalization bounds for our algorithm. Furthermore, we empirically evaluate its effectiveness, both in terms of prediction accuracy in downstream tasks as well as in terms of interpretability of the results.

Its guiding intuition is that only a small subset of words may need substantially different embeddings, such as words that acquire a new meaning in that domain. This creates an opportunity to transfer existing representations while concentrating adaptation on selected words.

The authors develop a group-sparse penalty for low-rank matrix factorization, the framework they use to learn embeddings from unstructured text. The penalty exploits sparsity in which words change during transfer. This extends ideas from sparse regression into unsupervised representation learning and targets settings with as little target-domain text as a single article.

The paper proves generalization bounds for the algorithm and evaluates it empirically through downstream prediction accuracy and interpretability. Those two evaluation perspectives address both the usefulness of the adapted embeddings and the understandability of the changes. The approach matters when limited target data make selective adaptation appealing, with the expectation of sparse word-level changes providing its central structural motivation.
summary.tldr: A group-sparse matrix-factorization method adapts word embeddings from very little target text by exploiting selective word-level changes.

title: Group-Sparse Matrix Factorization for Transfer Learning of Word Embeddings

abstract: The recent success of supervised learning methods on ever larger offline datasets has spurred interest in the reinforcement learning (RL) field to investigate whether the same paradigms can be translated to RL algorithms. This research area, known as offline RL, has largely focused on offline policy optimization, aiming to find a return-maximizing policy exclusively from offline data. In this paper, we consider a slightly different approach to incorporating offline data into sequential decision-making. We aim to answer the question, what unsupervised objectives applied to offline datasets are able to learn state representations which elevate performance on downstream tasks, whether those downstream tasks be online RL, imitation learning from expert demonstrations, or even offline policy optimization based on the same offline dataset? Through a variety of experiments utilizing standard offline RL datasets, we find that the use of pretraining with unsupervised learning objectives can dramatically improve the performance of policy learning algorithms that otherwise yield mediocre performance on their own. Extensive ablations further provide insights into what components of these unsupervised objectives {–} e.g., reward prediction, continuous or discrete representations, pretraining or finetuning {–} are most important and in which settings.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning commonly tries to learn a reward-maximizing policy directly from a fixed dataset. This paper studies another use for the same kind of data: pretraining representations of states before learning the policy. It asks which unsupervised objectives produce representations that help subsequent sequential decision-making tasks.

The downstream settings include online reinforcement learning, imitation from expert demonstrations, and offline policy optimization using the same dataset. This makes representation learning a component that can support several kinds of policy learning. The question is whether extracting useful state information in advance improves what those algorithms can achieve.

Experiments on standard offline reinforcement learning datasets show that unsupervised pretraining can substantially improve policy-learning methods whose standalone performance is mediocre. Ablations examine components including reward prediction, continuous versus discrete representations, and pretraining versus finetuning. These studies provide evidence about which choices matter in different settings. The findings establish that the value of offline data can lie in the representation it teaches, as well as in direct policy optimization.
summary.tldr: Unsupervised representation pretraining on offline data can substantially improve subsequent reinforcement learning and imitation learning.

title: Representation Matters: Offline Pretraining for Sequential Decision Making

abstract: Bayesian approaches developed to solve the optimal design of sequential experiments are mathematically elegant but computationally challenging. Recently, techniques using amortization have been proposed to make these Bayesian approaches practical, by training a parameterized policy that proposes designs efficiently at deployment time. However, these methods may not sufficiently explore the design space, require access to a differentiable probabilistic model and can only optimize over continuous design spaces. Here, we address these limitations by showing that the problem of optimizing policies can be reduced to solving a Markov decision process (MDP). We solve the equivalent MDP with modern deep reinforcement learning techniques. Our experiments show that our approach is also computationally efficient at deployment time and exhibits state-of-the-art performance on both continuous and discrete design spaces, even when the probabilistic model is a black box.

paragraphs: Sequential experimental design chooses experiments over a sequence of decisions. Bayesian approaches provide a principled formulation but can be computationally demanding. Earlier amortized methods address deployment cost by training a policy in advance, yet may explore inadequately and require both differentiable probabilistic models and continuous design choices.

This paper shows that optimizing the design policy can be reduced to solving a Markov decision process. The authors then apply modern deep reinforcement learning to that equivalent problem. The reformulation makes sequential experimental design accessible to policy-learning techniques that can accommodate discrete as well as continuous choices.

Experiments show efficient deployment and state-of-the-art performance in both types of design space, including cases where the probabilistic model is a black box. The result broadens the settings in which a pretrained design policy can be useful. In particular, the reported approach combines low deployment cost with the ability to work without the differentiable-model requirement of the earlier methods discussed.
summary.tldr: Recasting sequential experimental design as an MDP enables efficient learned policies for continuous or discrete choices, including black-box models.

title: Optimizing Sequential Experimental Design with Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Self-training for unsupervised domain adaptive object detection is a challenging task, of which the performance depends heavily on the quality of pseudo boxes. Despite the promising results, prior works have largely overlooked the uncertainty of pseudo boxes during self-training. In this paper, we present a simple yet effective framework, termed as Probabilistic Teacher (PT), which aims to capture the uncertainty of unlabeled target data from a gradually evolving teacher and guides the learning of a student in a mutually beneficial manner. Specifically, we propose to leverage the uncertainty-guided consistency training to promote classification adaptation and localization adaptation, rather than filtering pseudo boxes via an elaborate confidence threshold. In addition, we conduct anchor adaptation in parallel with localization adaptation, since anchor can be regarded as a learnable parameter. Together with this framework, we also present a novel Entropy Focal Loss (EFL) to further facilitate the uncertainty-guided self-training. Equipped with EFL, PT outperforms all previous baselines by a large margin and achieve new state-of-the-arts.

paragraphs: Adapting an object detector to an unlabeled target domain often relies on pseudo boxes: predicted object locations and categories used as training targets. Their quality strongly influences self-training. This paper focuses on uncertainty in those predictions, which previous approaches had largely overlooked.

Probabilistic Teacher uses a gradually evolving teacher to capture uncertainty in target-domain examples and guide a student detector. Uncertainty informs consistency training for both category prediction and object localization. The framework therefore uses uncertainty throughout adaptation instead of relying on an elaborate confidence threshold to filter boxes. It also adapts anchors alongside localization, treating anchors as learnable parameters.

The authors introduce Entropy Focal Loss to further support this uncertainty-guided training. With that loss, they report that Probabilistic Teacher substantially outperforms the previous baselines considered and achieves new state-of-the-art results. The central idea is to make the reliability of generated supervision part of the learning process. Classification, localization, and anchor adaptation are brought together within a framework designed to learn from unlabeled target data whose predicted annotations are uncertain.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic Teacher uses uncertainty in pseudo boxes to guide object-detector adaptation to unlabeled target data.

title: Learning Domain Adaptive Object Detection with Probabilistic Teacher

abstract: Causal discovery in the form of a directed acyclic graph (DAG) for time series data has been widely studied in various domains. The resulting DAG typically represents a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN), capturing both the instantaneous and time-delayed relationships among variables of interest. We propose a new algorithm, IDYNO, to learn the DAG structure from potentially nonlinear times series data by using a continuous optimization framework that includes a recent formulation for continuous acyclicity constraint. The proposed algorithm is designed to handle both observational and interventional time series data. We demonstrate the promising performance of our method on synthetic benchmark datasets against state-of-the-art baselines. In addition, we show that the proposed method can more accurately learn the underlying structure of a sequential decision model, such as a Markov decision process, with a fixed policy in typical continuous control tasks.

paragraphs: Causal models of time series must represent relationships within a time step as well as delayed effects across steps. Those relationships can be nonlinear, and experimental interventions may provide information unavailable in passive observations. IDYNO is designed to learn a directed acyclic graph for this combined dynamic setting.

The method uses continuous optimization with a continuous acyclicity constraint, allowing graph structure to be learned within an optimization framework. It handles both observational and interventional time-series data and permits nonlinear relationships. The resulting structure is a dynamic Bayesian network that distinguishes instantaneous from time-delayed dependencies.

On synthetic benchmarks, IDYNO shows promising performance against state-of-the-art baselines. It also more accurately learns underlying structure for fixed-policy sequential decision models in typical continuous-control tasks. The contribution is a graph-learning procedure for dynamic data with interventions; the abstract does not assert that every causal relationship is identifiable from arbitrary observational sequences or intervention designs.
summary.tldr: IDYNO uses continuous constrained optimization to learn nonlinear dynamic causal graphs from observational and interventional time series.

title: IDYNO: Learning Nonparametric DAGs from Interventional Dynamic Data

abstract: We consider the setting where the members of a society (voters) have preferences over candidates, and the candidates can be ordered on an axis so that the voters’ preferences are single-peaked on this axis. We ask whether this axis can be identified by sampling the voters’ preferences. For several natural distributions, we obtain tight bounds on the number of samples required and show that, surprisingly, the bounds are independent of the number of candidates. We extend our results to the case where voters’ preferences are sampled from two different axes over the same candidate set (one of which may be known). We also consider two alternative models of learning: (1) sampling pairwise comparisons rather than entire votes, and (2) learning from equivalence queries.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover an underlying ordering of candidates from voters’ preferences. It assumes the preferences are single-peaked along an axis: each voter has a preferred point, with less preferred candidates farther away along either side. The learning problem is to identify that axis by sampling votes.

For several natural distributions of preferences, the authors establish tight bounds on the required number of samples. A striking feature is that these bounds do not depend on the number of candidates. Under the distributions studied, adding candidates therefore does not force the number of sampled votes to grow. The distributional qualification is central to the scope of this result.

The analysis also considers preferences generated from two axes over the same candidates, including cases where one axis is known. Finally, the authors study learning from pairwise comparisons and from equivalence queries rather than only complete votes. These extensions examine how recovering preference structure changes when the population’s structure or the available form of feedback changes.
summary.tldr: For several preference distributions, the axis underlying single-peaked votes can be learned with sample bounds independent of candidate count.

title: Exact Learning of Preference Structure: Single-peaked Preferences and Beyond

abstract: We study cooperative online learning in stochastic and adversarial Markov decision process (MDP). That is, in each episode, $m$ agents interact with an MDP simultaneously and share information in order to minimize their individual regret. We consider environments with two types of randomness: fresh – where each agent’s trajectory is sampled i.i.d, and non-fresh – where the realization is shared by all agents (but each agent’s trajectory is also affected by its own actions). More precisely, with non-fresh randomness the realization of every cost and transition is fixed at the start of each episode, and agents that take the same action in the same state at the same time observe the same cost and next state. We thoroughly analyze all relevant settings, highlight the challenges and differences between the models, and prove nearly-matching regret lower and upper bounds. To our knowledge, we are the first to consider cooperative reinforcement learning (RL) with either non-fresh randomness or in adversarial MDPs.

paragraphs: This paper studies multiple agents learning simultaneously in a Markov decision process and sharing information to reduce their individual regret. The setting covers both stochastic and adversarial environments. A central question is how the benefit of cooperation changes depending on the way randomness is shared across agents.

With fresh randomness, each agent receives an independently sampled trajectory. With non-fresh randomness, the episode’s costs and transitions are fixed in a shared realization before interaction begins. Consequently, agents taking the same action in the same state at the same time observe the same cost and next state. Their own actions still influence which trajectories they experience.

The authors analyze the relevant combinations of these settings and prove upper and lower regret bounds that nearly match. The distinction matters because collecting experiences from several agents need not produce independent observations. By explicitly modeling this difference, the paper characterizes the challenges and attainable performance of cooperation, including non-fresh randomness and adversarial MDPs as new settings in its stated research context.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes nearly matching regret bounds for cooperative learning under independent or shared randomness in stochastic and adversarial MDPs.

title: Cooperative Online Learning in Stochastic and Adversarial MDPs

abstract: We present the Local Self-Balancing sampler (LSB), a local Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method for sampling in purely discrete domains, which is able to autonomously adapt to the target distribution and to reduce the number of target evaluations required to converge. LSB is based on (i) a parametrization of locally balanced proposals, (ii) an objective function based on mutual information and (iii) a self-balancing learning procedure, which minimises the proposed objective to update the proposal parameters. Experiments on energy-based models and Markov networks show that LSB converges using a smaller number of queries to the oracle distribution compared to recent local MCMC samplers.

paragraphs: Sampling from a distribution over discrete possibilities can require many evaluations of that distribution before a sampler converges. The Local Self-Balancing sampler, or LSB, addresses this cost with a local Markov Chain Monte Carlo method that adapts automatically to its target. The focus is on purely discrete domains, where the sampler’s proposed moves determine how it explores possible states.

LSB combines three components. It parameterizes locally balanced proposals, defines an objective based on mutual information, and learns the proposal parameters by minimizing that objective. This makes the proposal mechanism adjustable during the self-balancing learning procedure. The method therefore connects the design of sampling moves to an explicit learning objective, rather than leaving the proposals unchanged.

Experiments on energy-based models and Markov networks show convergence with fewer queries to the target distribution than recent local MCMC samplers. The reported efficiency benefit is specifically a reduction in target evaluations. These findings support learning the proposal mechanism as a way to improve sampling efficiency on the evaluated discrete models.
summary.tldr: LSB learns locally balanced MCMC proposals and converges with fewer target-distribution queries in the reported discrete-model experiments.

title: LSB: Local Self-Balancing MCMC in Discrete Spaces

abstract: We study Stochastic Gradient Descent with AdaGrad stepsizes: a popular adaptive (self-tuning) method for first-order stochastic optimization. Despite being well studied, existing analyses of this method suffer from various shortcomings: they either assume some knowledge of the problem parameters, impose strong global Lipschitz conditions, or fail to give bounds that hold with high probability. We provide a comprehensive analysis of this basic method without any of these limitations, in both the convex and non-convex (smooth) cases, that additionally supports a general “affine variance” noise model and provides sharp rates of convergence in both the low-noise and high-noise regimes.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent with AdaGrad step sizes adapts its updates during optimization, reducing the need to choose them using problem-specific information. This paper analyzes that basic method with stronger guarantees than several previous analyses. Its focus is on understanding when the self-tuning behavior can be justified without assuming knowledge that the method is supposed to avoid requiring.

The analysis covers convex objectives and smooth non-convex objectives. It does not require advance knowledge of problem parameters or impose the strong global Lipschitz conditions identified as limitations of earlier work. It also provides bounds that hold with high probability, giving control over the likelihood of the optimization guarantee rather than relying only on an average outcome.

The results accommodate a general affine-variance noise model and establish sharp convergence rates in both low-noise and high-noise regimes. Together, these properties extend the theoretical coverage of a widely used adaptive method. The contribution is a comprehensive analysis of AdaGrad step sizes under broader conditions, connecting automatic adaptation with probabilistic convergence guarantees across different noise levels.
summary.tldr: A new AdaGrad analysis gives high-probability adaptive convergence guarantees without known problem parameters or strong global Lipschitz assumptions.

title: SGD with AdaGrad Stepsizes: Full Adaptivity with High Probability to Unknown Parameters, Unbounded Gradients and Affine Variance

abstract: Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is an emerging neural network training approach that enables multiple agents to train a model collaboratively and simultaneously. Rather than using a central parameter server to collect gradients from all the agents, each agent keeps a copy of the model parameters and communicates with a small number of other agents to exchange model updates. Their communication, governed by the communication topology and gossip weight matrices, facilitates the exchange of model updates. The state-of-the-art approach uses the dynamic one-peer exponential-2 topology, achieving faster training times and improved scalability than the ring, grid, torus, and hypercube topologies. However, this approach requires a power-of-2 number of agents, which is impractical at scale. In this paper, we remove this restriction and propose Decentralized SGD with Communication-optimal Exact Consensus Algorithm (DSGD-CECA), which works for any number of agents while still achieving state-of-the-art properties. In particular, DSGD-CECA incurs a unit per-iteration communication overhead and an $\tilde{O}(n^3)$ transient iteration complexity. Our proof is based on newly discovered properties of gossip weight matrices and a novel approach to combine them with DSGD’s convergence analysis. Numerical experiments show the efficiency of DSGD-CECA.

paragraphs: Decentralized stochastic gradient descent lets multiple agents train together without a central parameter server. Each agent maintains model parameters and exchanges updates with a small set of peers. The communication pattern and the weights used to combine messages affect how efficiently information spreads, making communication design part of the optimization problem.

A strong existing approach uses a changing one-peer exponential-2 topology, but requires the number of agents to be a power of two. DSGD-CECA removes that restriction by incorporating a communication-optimal exact consensus algorithm. It supports any number of agents while retaining the stated favorable communication and convergence properties, making the method applicable beyond specially sized groups.

The paper proves unit communication overhead per iteration and a transient iteration complexity of order n cubed, up to logarithmic factors. Its analysis uses newly identified properties of gossip weight matrices and integrates them into decentralized SGD convergence arguments. Numerical experiments support the method’s efficiency. The contribution combines flexible agent counts with theoretical control of communication and training behavior.
summary.tldr: DSGD-CECA enables efficient decentralized training for any number of agents while preserving strong communication and convergence properties.

title: DSGD-CECA: Decentralized SGD with Communication-Optimal Exact Consensus Algorithm

abstract: Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) synthesizes weighted samples from an intractable distribution given its unnormalized density function. This algorithm relies on a sequence of interpolating distributions bridging the target to an initial tractable distribution such as the well-known geometric mean path of unnormalized distributions which is assumed to be suboptimal in general. In this paper, we prove that the geometric annealing corresponds to the distribution path that minimizes the KL divergence between the current particle distribution and the desired target when the feasible change in the particle distribution is constrained. Following this observation, we derive the constant rate discretization schedule for this annealing sequence, which adjusts the schedule to the difficulty of moving samples between the initial and the target distributions. We further extend our results to $f$-divergences and present the respective dynamics of annealing sequences based on which we propose the Constant Rate AIS (CR-AIS) algorithm and its efficient implementation for $\alpha$-divergences. We empirically show that CR-AIS performs well on multiple benchmark distributions while avoiding the computationally expensive tuning loop in existing Adaptive AIS.

This algorithm relies on a sequence of interpolating distributions bridging the target to an initial tractable distribution such as the well-known geometric mean path of unnormalized distributions which is assumed to be suboptimal in general. In this paper, we prove that the geometric annealing corresponds to the distribution path that minimizes the KL divergence between the current particle distribution and the desired target when the feasible change in the particle distribution is constrained. Following this observation, we derive the constant rate discretization schedule for this annealing sequence, which adjusts the schedule to the difficulty of moving samples between the initial and the target distributions. paragraphs: Annealed Importance Sampling generates weighted samples from a difficult distribution by passing through intermediate distributions that connect it to an easier starting point. Its effectiveness depends on both the path through these distributions and the spacing of steps along that path. This paper investigates how to choose these elements more systematically.

The authors give a conditional justification for the commonly used geometric path: it minimizes KL divergence from the current particle distribution to the target when the allowable change in the particle distribution is constrained. This does not establish that geometric annealing is universally optimal. It explains its role under a particular restriction on movement.

Using this interpretation, the authors derive a schedule intended to maintain a constant rate of progress, adapting steps to how difficult it is to move samples toward the target. They extend the analysis to other divergence measures and develop CR-AIS, including an efficient implementation for alpha-divergences. Experiments on several benchmark distributions show good performance while avoiding the expensive tuning loop used by existing adaptive AIS.
summary.tldr: CR-AIS adapts annealing steps to maintain constant progress toward a target distribution while avoiding an expensive tuning loop.

title: Adaptive Annealed Importance Sampling with Constant Rate Progress

abstract: Multi-View Reinforcement Learning (MVRL) seeks to find an optimal control for an agent given multi-view observations from various sources. Despite recent advances in multi-view learning that aim to extract the latent representation from multi-view data, it is not straightforward to apply them to control tasks, especially when the observations are temporally dependent on one another. The problem can be even more challenging if the observations are intermittently missing for a subset of views. In this paper, we introduce Fuse2Control (F2C), an information-theoretic approach to capturing the underlying state space model from the sequences of multi-view observations. We conduct an extensive set of experiments in various control tasks showing that our method is highly effective in aggregating task-relevant information across many views, that scales linearly with the number of views while retaining robustness to arbitrary missing view scenarios.

Multi-view reinforcement learning aims to combine these observations to choose effective actions. The challenge goes beyond summarizing several inputs: observations depend on one another over time, and some sources may intermittently disappear.

Fuse2Control, or F2C, uses an information-theoretic approach to learn an underlying state space model from sequences of these observations. Its focus is the information relevant to control. Learning from sequences addresses the temporal structure that makes direct application of ordinary multi-view representation methods difficult.

Across experiments on several control tasks, the authors report that F2C effectively combines task-relevant information from many views. They also report linear scaling with the number of views and robustness to arbitrary missing-view scenarios. These findings support the approach as a way to combine multiple observation streams without requiring every stream to remain continuously available. The contribution connects representation learning to the needs of an acting agent, with empirical evidence covering both aggregation and missing observations.
summary.tldr: Fuse2Control learns control-relevant state models from multiple observation streams, with reported linear scaling and robustness to missing views.

title: Information-Theoretic State Space Model for Multi-View Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Anytime neural networks (AnytimeNNs) are a promising solution to adaptively adjust the model complexity at runtime under various hardware resource constraints. However, the manually-designed AnytimeNNs are biased by designers’ prior experience and thus provide sub-optimal solutions. To address the limitations of existing hand-crafted approaches, we first model the training process of AnytimeNNs as a discrete-time Markov chain (DTMC) and use it to identify the paths that contribute the most to the training of AnytimeNNs. Based on this new DTMC-based analysis, we further propose TIPS, a framework to automatically design AnytimeNNs under various hardware constraints. Our experimental results show that TIPS can improve the convergence rate and test accuracy of AnytimeNNs. Compared to the existing AnytimeNNs approaches, TIPS improves the accuracy by 2%-6.6% on multiple datasets and achieves SOTA accuracy-FLOPs tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Anytime neural networks adjust their computational complexity during execution to fit available hardware resources. Their design therefore has to support useful predictions at different computational budgets. The paper argues that manually designed networks are constrained by designers' experience and can leave better solutions unexplored.

The authors model the training process as a discrete-time Markov chain. They use that analysis to identify network paths that contribute most to training, then build TIPS, a framework for automatically designing anytime networks under different hardware constraints. The key idea is to use the structure of training paths as evidence for design decisions.

Experiments show improvements in convergence rate and test accuracy. Compared with existing anytime-network approaches, the paper reports accuracy gains of 2%–6.6% across multiple datasets and state-of-the-art tradeoffs between accuracy and floating-point operation counts. These results support the use of training-path analysis to guide automatic architecture design, with benefits measured both in prediction quality and computational tradeoffs.
summary.tldr: TIPS uses a Markov-chain analysis of training paths to automatically design anytime networks with improved accuracy and computational tradeoffs.

title: TIPS: Topologically Important Path Sampling for Anytime Neural Networks

abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) trains a constraint satisfaction policy by interacting with the environment. We aim to tackle a more challenging problem: learning a safe policy from an offline dataset. We study the offline safe RL problem from a novel multi-objective optimization perspective and propose the $\epsilon$-reducible concept to characterize problem difficulties. The inherent trade-offs between safety and task performance inspire us to propose the constrained decision transformer (CDT) approach, which can dynamically adjust the trade-offs during deployment. Extensive experiments show the advantages of the proposed method in learning an adaptive, safe, robust, and high-reward policy. CDT outperforms its variants and strong offline safe RL baselines by a large margin with the same hyperparameters across all tasks, while keeping the zero-shot adaptation capability to different constraint thresholds, making our approach more suitable for real-world RL under constraints.

paragraphs: Offline safe reinforcement learning asks an agent to learn useful behavior that respects constraints using an existing dataset. The challenge includes balancing task performance against safety without collecting new training experience through interaction. This paper studies that balance through a multi-objective optimization perspective and introduces epsilon-reducibility as a concept for characterizing problem difficulty.

The resulting method, the constrained decision transformer, is designed to adjust the balance between reward and constraints during deployment. This matters when the acceptable constraint threshold changes after training. Instead of being tied to one fixed operating point, the learned policy retains the ability to adapt to different thresholds without additional training.

The reported experiments find that CDT learns policies combining high reward with safety, robustness, and adaptability. It substantially outperforms its variants and strong offline safe reinforcement learning baselines while using the same hyperparameters across tasks. These findings support flexible deployment under different constraints, with the demonstrated zero-shot threshold adaptation being a central benefit.
summary.tldr: CDT learns constrained policies from offline data and can adjust the reward–safety trade-off to new constraint thresholds during deployment.

title: Constrained Decision Transformer for Offline Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The training process of generative adversarial networks (GANs) is unstable and does not converge globally. In this paper, we examine the stability of GANs from the perspective of control theory and propose a universal higher-order noise-based controller called Brownian Motion Controller (BMC). Starting with the prototypical case of Dirac-GANs, we design a BMC to retrieve precisely the same but reachable optimal equilibrium. We theoretically prove that the training process of DiracGANs-BMC is globally exponential stable and derive bounds on the rate of convergence. Then we extend our BMC to normal GANs and provide implementation instructions on GANs-BMC. Our experiments show that our GANs-BMC effectively stabilizes GANs’ training under StyleGANv2-ada frameworks with a faster rate of convergence, a smaller range of oscillation, and better performance in terms of FID score.

paragraphs: Training generative adversarial networks can be unstable, motivating this paper's use of control theory to study the learning dynamics. The authors propose a higher-order, noise-based mechanism called the Brownian Motion Controller. Its purpose is to stabilize training while preserving the desired optimal equilibrium.

The theoretical development begins with the simplified Dirac-GAN setting. There, the controller makes the same optimal equilibrium reachable, and the authors prove global exponential stability of the controlled training process. They also derive bounds on its convergence rate. This provides a precise theoretical result for the prototypical system used in the analysis.

The authors then extend the controller to ordinary GANs and provide implementation guidance. Experiments within the StyleGANv2-ada framework show faster convergence, reduced oscillation, and improved FID scores. The theoretical and empirical claims apply at different levels: the global exponential stability proof concerns DiracGANs-BMC, while the broader GAN results demonstrate stabilization experimentally. Together, they support noise-based control as a practical way to improve the behavior of adversarial training.
summary.tldr: A Brownian Motion Controller provides proven stability for Dirac-GANs and experimentally improves training stability in a broader GAN framework.

title: Stabilizing GANs’ Training with Brownian Motion Controller

abstract: Graph generative models become increasingly effective for data distribution approximation and data augmentation. While they have aroused public concerns about their malicious misuses or misinformation broadcasts, just as what Deepfake visual and auditory media has been delivering to society. Hence it is essential to regulate the prevalence of generated graphs. To tackle this problem, we pioneer the formulation of the generated graph detection problem to distinguish generated graphs from real ones. We propose the first framework to systematically investigate a set of sophisticated models and their performance in four classification scenarios. Each scenario switches between seen and unseen datasets/generators during testing to get closer to real-world settings and progressively challenge the classifiers. Extensive experiments evidence that all the models are qualified for generated graph detection, with specific models having advantages in specific scenarios. Resulting from the validated generality and oblivion of the classifiers to unseen datasets/generators, we draw a safe conclusion that our solution can sustain for a decent while to curb generated graph misuses.

paragraphs: As graph generators improve, distinguishing synthetic graphs from observed ones becomes a separate research problem. This paper formalizes generated-graph detection and develops a framework for evaluating classifiers on it. The motivation includes identifying misleading uses of synthetic relational data, rather than evaluating graph-generation quality alone.

The evaluation covers four classification scenarios that vary whether datasets and generators seen at test time were available during training. These scenarios progressively challenge a detector’s ability to generalize beyond familiar sources. Several models are assessed systematically, allowing the study to separate ordinary detection performance from transfer to unseen datasets or generation methods.

The experiments show that the evaluated models can detect generated graphs, with different models performing best in different scenarios. The results provide evidence that detection can generalize beyond some training conditions. They do not establish permanent detectability of future generators, so the lasting contribution is the task formulation, evaluation framework, and measured generalization behavior rather than a guarantee against all synthetic-graph misuse.
summary.tldr: A generated-graph detection benchmark tests whether classifiers can distinguish synthetic graphs across familiar and unseen datasets and generators.

title: Generated Graph Detection

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the best possible policy from a fixed dataset, known as offline Reinforcement Learning (RL). A common taxonomy of existing offline RL works is policy regularization, which typically constrains the learned policy by distribution or support of the behavior policy. However, distribution and support constraints are overly conservative since they both force the policy to choose similar actions as the behavior policy when considering particular states. It will limit the learned policy’s performance, especially when the behavior policy is sub-optimal. In this paper, we find that regularizing the policy towards the nearest state-action pair can be more effective and thus propose Policy Regularization with Dataset Constraint (PRDC). When updating the policy in a given state, PRDC searches the entire dataset for the nearest state-action sample and then restricts the policy with the action of this sample. Unlike previous works, PRDC can guide the policy with proper behaviors from the dataset, allowing it to choose actions that do not appear in the dataset along with the given state. It is a softer constraint but still keeps enough conservatism from out-of-distribution actions. Empirical evidence and theoretical analysis show that PRDC can alleviate offline RL’s fundamentally challenging value overestimation issue with a bounded performance gap. Moreover, on a set of locomotion and navigation tasks, PRDC achieves state-of-the-art performance compared with existing methods. Code is available at https://github.com/LAMDA-RL/PRDC

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must improve a policy using a fixed dataset. A common safeguard keeps its actions close to those of the policy that collected the data. The paper argues that constraints based on that policy's distribution or support can be overly restrictive at individual states, especially when the original behavior was suboptimal.

Policy Regularization with Dataset Constraint, or PRDC, instead searches the entire dataset for the nearest state-action sample during a policy update. It uses that sample's action to constrain the learned policy. This allows guidance to come from a suitable example elsewhere in the dataset, including an action that was not recorded together with the particular state being updated.

The softer constraint aims to permit improvement while retaining protection against unsupported actions. The authors provide theoretical analysis and empirical evidence that PRDC can reduce value overestimation, with a bounded performance gap. They also report state-of-the-art results on the locomotion and navigation tasks evaluated. These findings support using proximity to dataset examples as a more flexible source of conservatism in offline learning.
summary.tldr: PRDC constrains offline policies using nearby state-action examples from the full dataset, enabling more flexible actions while reducing value overestimation.

title: Policy Regularization with Dataset Constraint for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Model fairness is an essential element for Trustworthy AI. While many techniques for model fairness have been proposed, most of them assume that the training and deployment data distributions are identical, which is often not true in practice. In particular, when the bias between labels and sensitive groups changes, the fairness of the trained model is directly influenced and can worsen. We make two contributions for solving this problem. First, we analytically show that existing in-processing fair algorithms have fundamental limits in accuracy and group fairness. We utilize the notion of correlation shifts between labels and groups, which can explicitly capture the change of the above bias. Second, we propose a novel pre-processing step that samples the input data to reduce correlation shifts and thus enables the in-processing approaches to overcome their limitations. We formulate an optimization problem for adjusting the data ratio among labels and sensitive groups to reflect the shifted correlation. A key benefit of our approach lies in decoupling the roles of pre- and in-processing approaches: correlation adjustment via pre-processing and unfairness mitigation on the processed data via in-processing. Experiments show that our framework effectively improves existing in-processing fair algorithms w.r.t. accuracy and fairness, both on synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: A model trained to satisfy fairness goals can behave differently when deployed on data with changed relationships between labels and sensitive groups. This paper studies such changes as correlation shifts. The issue is more specific than a general change in the data distribution: the label-group association that shaped training may no longer match the association encountered in deployment.

The authors analytically identify limits on accuracy and group fairness for existing methods that enforce fairness during training. They then add a preprocessing step that samples the input data to address the correlation shift. An optimization problem determines how to adjust the proportions of examples across labels and sensitive groups so that the processed data reflects the shifted correlation.

The approach assigns different jobs to the two stages: preprocessing adjusts correlations, while the existing training procedure mitigates unfairness on the adjusted data. This makes the proposal a way to improve those training methods. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report gains in both accuracy and fairness, supporting the value of explicitly addressing label-group shifts before applying fairness-aware training.
summary.tldr: Optimizing label-group sampling proportions before fairness-aware training improves accuracy and fairness under the correlation shifts studied.

title: Improving Fair Training under Correlation Shifts

abstract: Two central paradigms have emerged in the reinforcement learning (RL) community: online RL and offline RL. In the online RL setting, the agent has no prior knowledge of the environment, and must interact with it in order to find an $\epsilon$-optimal policy. In the offline RL setting, the learner instead has access to a fixed dataset to learn from, but is unable to otherwise interact with the environment, and must obtain the best policy it can from this offline data. Practical scenarios often motivate an intermediate setting: if we have some set of offline data and may also interact with the environment, how can we best use the offline data to minimize the number of online interactions necessary to learn an $\epsilon$-optimal policy. In this work, we consider this setting, which we call the FineTuneRL setting, for MDPs with linear structure. We characterize the necessary number of online samples needed in this setting given access to some offline dataset, and develop an algorithm, FTPedel, which is provably optimal, up to $H$ factors. We show through an explicit example that combining offline data with online interactions can lead to a provable improvement over either purely offline or purely online RL. Finally, our results illustrate the distinction between verifiable learning, the typical setting considered in online RL, and unverifiable learning, the setting often considered in offline RL, and show that there is a formal separation between these regimes.

paragraphs: An agent may already have a dataset of past experience while still being allowed to interact with its environment. This paper asks how that dataset can reduce the additional interactions needed to learn a policy within epsilon of optimal. It names this combined setting FineTuneRL and studies Markov decision processes with linear structure.

The authors characterize the number of online samples necessary given an offline dataset and introduce FTPedel, an algorithm that is provably optimal up to factors involving H. This provides a theoretical account of how existing data change the remaining learning requirement. An explicit example shows that combining stored experience with new interactions can provably improve on either purely offline or purely online learning.

The analysis also distinguishes verifiable learning, typically considered in online reinforcement learning, from the unverifiable learning often considered offline. It proves a formal separation between these regimes. That distinction matters when interpreting what it means to succeed with existing data: the learning requirement includes whether success must be verifiable, alongside the quality of the policy obtained.
summary.tldr: For linearly structured MDPs, FTPedel nearly optimally combines offline data with online interaction, with a provable example of gains over either alone.

title: Leveraging Offline Data in Online Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent work on mini-batch consistency (MBC) for set functions has brought attention to the need for sequentially processing and aggregating chunks of a partitioned set while guaranteeing the same output for all partitions. However, existing constraints on MBC architectures lead to models with limited expressive power. Additionally, prior work has not addressed how to deal with large sets during training when the full set gradient is required. To address these issues, we propose a Universally MBC (UMBC) class of set functions which can be used in conjunction with arbitrary non-MBC components while still satisfying MBC, enabling a wider range of function classes to be used in MBC settings. Furthermore, we propose an efficient MBC training algorithm which gives an unbiased approximation of the full set gradient and has a constant memory overhead for any set size for both train- and test-time. We conduct extensive experiments including image completion, text classification, unsupervised clustering, and cancer detection on high-resolution images to verify the efficiency and efficacy of our scalable set encoding framework. Our code is available at github.com/jeffwillette/umbc

paragraphs: Large sets may need to be processed in chunks, but their representation should not depend on how those chunks are chosen. Mini-batch consistency formalizes that requirement: partitioning and aggregating the same set must give the same output. Existing architectures enforcing it can restrict expressive power, and training creates a separate challenge when full-set gradients are needed.

The paper introduces Universally Mini-Batch Consistent set functions that can be combined with arbitrary non-consistent components while preserving the framework’s consistency property. This expands the function classes available for set encoding. It also proposes a training algorithm that gives an unbiased approximation of the full-set gradient.

The algorithm has constant memory overhead with respect to set size during training and testing. Experiments cover image completion, text classification, unsupervised clustering, and cancer detection in high-resolution images, supporting the framework’s efficiency and effectiveness. The contribution addresses both representation design and training scalability, so processing a set in chunks need not force the same architectural restrictions or require storing a full-set gradient computation.
summary.tldr: UMBC expands expressive set encoding while preserving partition consistency and supplies unbiased full-set gradient approximation with constant memory overhead.

title: Scalable Set Encoding with Universal Mini-Batch Consistency and Unbiased Full Set Gradient Approximation

abstract: A promising approach to preserving model performance in linearized transformers is to employ position-based re-weighting functions. However, state-of-the-art re-weighting functions rely heavily on target sequence lengths, making it difficult or impossible to apply them to autoregressive and simultaneous tasks, where the target and sometimes even the input sequence length are unknown. To address this issue, we propose Learned Proportions (LeaP) and LeaPformers. Our contribution is built on two major components. First, we generalize the dependence on explicit positional representations and sequence lengths into dependence on sequence proportions for re-weighting. Second, we replace static positional representations with dynamic proportions derived via a compact module, enabling more flexible attention concentration patterns. We evaluate LeaPformer against eight representative efficient transformers on the Long-Range Arena benchmark, where we show that LeaPformer achieves the best quality-throughput trade-off, as well as apply LeaPformer to Wikitext-103b autoregressive language modeling and simultaneous speech-to-text translation for two language pairs, achieving competitive results in both tasks.

paragraphs: Position-based reweighting can help linearized Transformers retain model quality, but leading approaches rely on knowing sequence lengths. That creates a problem when output is generated incrementally or input arrives while output is being produced. In those settings, the final target length, and sometimes the input length, is unavailable.

LeaPformer addresses this dependency through Learned Proportions. First, it reformulates reweighting in terms of sequence proportions instead of explicit positions and lengths. Second, a compact module produces dynamic proportions in place of static position representations. This gives the model more flexible ways to concentrate attention while making the approach usable for autoregressive and simultaneous tasks.

These findings support the practicality of replacing length-dependent reweighting with learned proportions across the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: LeaPformer learns dynamic sequence proportions to support efficient attention when final sequence lengths are unknown.

title: LeaPformer: Enabling Linear Transformers for Autoregressive and Simultaneous Tasks via Learned Proportions

abstract: Non-linear mixed-effects models are a powerful tool for studying heterogeneous populations in various fields, including biology, medicine, economics, and engineering. Here, the aim is to find a distribution over the parameters that describe the whole population using a model that can generate simulations for an individual of that population. However, fitting these distributions to data is computationally challenging if the description of individuals is complex and the population is large. To address this issue, we propose a novel machine learning-based approach: We exploit neural density estimation based on conditional normalizing flows to approximate individual-specific posterior distributions in an amortized fashion, thereby allowing for efficient inference of population parameters. Applying this approach to problems from cell biology and pharmacology, we demonstrate its unseen flexibility and scalability to large data sets compared to established methods.

paragraphs: Non-linear mixed-effects models describe populations whose members differ from one another. An individual-level model generates simulations, while a distribution over its parameters describes variation across the population. Fitting that population distribution becomes computationally demanding when individual simulations are complex or the dataset contains many individuals.

The paper addresses this bottleneck by learning approximate posterior distributions for individual-specific parameters. It uses conditional normalizing flows, a neural density-estimation approach, to represent these distributions. The inference is amortized: the learned inference mechanism is reused across individuals, rather than treating each individual’s posterior estimation as an entirely separate computational problem.

These individual-level approximations then support efficient inference of population parameters. Applications in cell biology and pharmacology demonstrate flexibility and scalability to large datasets compared with established methods. The contribution connects two levels of modeling: learning uncertainty about individual parameters helps make population-level estimation more manageable. The posterior distributions remain approximations, but the reported applications show how that approach can address the computational burden of fitting heterogeneous populations.
summary.tldr: Reusable neural posterior estimates make population-level inference more scalable in non-linear mixed-effects models.

title: An amortized approach to non-linear mixed-effects modeling based on neural posterior estimation

abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is a young but very promising field of research. Unfortunately, the progress in this field is currently slowed down by divergent and incompatible goals. We separate various threads tangled within the area of XAI into two complementary cultures of human/value-oriented explanations (BLUE XAI) and model/validation-oriented explanations (RED XAI). This position paper argues that the area of RED XAI is currently under-explored, i.e., more methods for explainability are desperately needed to question models (e.g., extract knowledge from well-performing models as well as spotting and fixing bugs in faulty models), and the area of RED XAI hides great opportunities and potential for important research necessary to ensure the safety of AI systems. We conclude this paper by presenting promising challenges in this area.

paragraphs: Explainable AI includes several goals that can pull research in different directions. This position paper argues that divergent and incompatible objectives are slowing progress. To clarify the discussion, it separates two complementary cultures: BLUE XAI, centered on people and values, and RED XAI, centered on models and validation.

The authors argue that RED XAI is underexplored. In this view, an explanation should help investigators question a model: they might use it to extract knowledge from a successful system or identify and repair faults in an unsuccessful one. The purpose of explaining a model therefore includes testing and investigating its behavior.

The paper presents this investigative role as an important research opportunity for AI safety and concludes with promising challenges. Its contribution is a position on how the field should organize and prioritize its goals. By distinguishing complementary purposes for explanations, it makes a case for more methods that support model scrutiny and improvement, alongside methods designed around human understanding and values.
summary.tldr: This position paper calls for more explainability methods that investigate, validate, and repair models, alongside human- and value-oriented explanations.

title: Position: Explain to Question not to Justify

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a building block in graph data processing, with wide applications in critical domains. The growing needs to deploy GNNs in high-stakes applications necessitate explainability for users in the decision-making processes. A popular paradigm for the explainability of GNNs is to identify explainable subgraphs by comparing their labels with the ones of original graphs. This task is challenging due to the substantial distributional shift from the original graphs in the training set to the set of explainable subgraphs, which prevents accurate prediction of labels with the subgraphs. To address it, in this paper, we propose a novel method that generates proxy graphs for explainable subgraphs that are in the distribution of training data. We introduce a parametric method that employs graph generators to produce proxy graphs. A new training objective based on information theory is designed to ensure that proxy graphs not only adhere to the distribution of training data but also preserve explanatory factors. Such generated proxy graphs can be reliably used to approximate the predictions of the labels of explainable subgraphs. Empirical evaluations across various datasets demonstrate our method achieves more accurate explanations for GNNs.

paragraphs: A common way to explain a graph neural network is to find a smaller subgraph that preserves the original graph’s predicted label. However, removing graph structure can produce inputs very different from the graphs used in training. The model’s prediction on such a subgraph may then be unreliable, undermining the comparison used to judge the explanation.

This paper proposes generating proxy graphs for candidate explanatory subgraphs. The proxies are designed to resemble the training distribution while retaining the factors relevant to the explanation. A parametric method uses graph generators to construct them, and an information-theoretic training objective balances distributional compatibility with preservation of explanatory content.

Predictions on these generated proxies provide approximations to the labels associated with the explanatory subgraphs. Evaluations across multiple datasets show more accurate explanations. The approach matters because it addresses the reliability of the model queries underlying explanation, rather than treating every extracted subgraph as an equally valid input. It seeks to preserve the explanatory signal while avoiding the distribution shift caused by extraction.
summary.tldr: Generated proxy graphs improve GNN explanations by preserving explanatory factors while staying close to the training-data distribution.

title: Generating In-Distribution Proxy Graphs for Explaining Graph Neural Networks

abstract: We leverage convex and bilevel optimization techniques to develop a general gradient-based parameter learning framework for neural-symbolic (NeSy) systems. We demonstrate our framework with NeuPSL, a state-of-the-art NeSy architecture. To achieve this, we propose a smooth primal and dual formulation of NeuPSL inference and show learning gradients are functions of the optimal dual variables. Additionally, we develop a dual block coordinate descent algorithm for the new formulation that naturally exploits warm-starts. This leads to over $100 \times$ learning runtime improvements over the current best NeuPSL inference method. Finally, we provide extensive empirical evaluations across $8$ datasets covering a range of tasks and demonstrate our learning framework achieves up to a $16$% point prediction performance improvement over alternative learning methods.

paragraphs: Neural-symbolic systems combine neural components with symbolic structure, making parameter learning depend on how inference is performed. This paper develops a general gradient-based learning framework using convex and bilevel optimization. It demonstrates the framework with NeuPSL, connecting the optimization used to produce predictions with the gradients needed to learn model parameters.

The authors introduce smooth primal and dual formulations of NeuPSL inference and show that learning gradients can be expressed using optimal dual variables. They then design a dual block coordinate descent algorithm that naturally uses warm starts. Reusing a previous solution gives the optimization procedure a useful starting point when solving subsequent inference problems during learning.
