Across eight datasets spanning different tasks, the learning framework also achieves prediction improvements of up to 16 percentage points over alternative learning methods. Together, these results show that reformulating inference can improve both the efficiency of parameter learning and the predictions obtained in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A convex and bilevel optimization framework makes NeuPSL learning substantially faster and yields prediction gains of up to 16 percentage points.

title: Convex and Bilevel Optimization for Neural-Symbolic Inference and Learning

abstract: Overfitting in RL has become one of the main obstacles to applications in reinforcement learning(RL). Existing methods do not provide explicit semantic constrain for the feature extractor, hindering the agent from learning a unified cross-domain representation and resulting in performance degradation on unseen domains. Besides, abundant data from multiple domains are needed. To address these issues, in this work, we propose prompt-based visual alignment (PVA), a robust framework to mitigate the detrimental domain bias in the image for zero-shot policy transfer. Inspired that Visual-Language Model (VLM) can serve as a bridge to connect both text space and image space, we leverage the semantic information contained in a text sequence as an explicit constraint to train a visual aligner. Thus, the visual aligner can map images from multiple domains to a unified domain and achieve good generalization performance. To better depict semantic information, prompt tuning is applied to learn a sequence of learnable tokens. With explicit constraints of semantic information, PVA can learn unified cross-domain representation under limited access to cross-domain data and achieves great zero-shot generalization ability in unseen domains. We verify PVA on a vision-based autonomous driving task with CARLA simulator. Experiments show that the agent generalizes well on unseen domains under limited access to multi-domain data.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can learn visual features that work in its training domain but transfer poorly to unfamiliar appearances. This paper attributes part of that problem to the lack of explicit semantic constraints on the feature extractor. Prompt-based Visual Alignment, or PVA, introduces such constraints to support zero-shot policy transfer with limited cross-domain data.

PVA uses a vision-language model to connect images with semantic information expressed through text. That information supervises a visual aligner, which maps images from different domains into a unified domain. Prompt tuning learns a sequence of tokens to better express the semantic information used for alignment.

The aim is to give the agent a representation that remains useful across domains despite differences in visual appearance. The authors evaluate PVA on a vision-based autonomous driving task in the CARLA simulator. Their experiments show good generalization to unseen domains under limited access to data from multiple domains. This supports semantic alignment as a practical mechanism for transfer in the evaluated driving setting.
summary.tldr: PVA uses learned text prompts and a vision-language model to align visual domains and improve zero-shot policy transfer with limited cross-domain data.

title: Prompt-based Visual Alignment for Zero-shot Policy Transfer

abstract: Schrödinger Bridges (SB) have recently gained the attention of the ML community as a promising extension of classic diffusion models which is also interconnected to the Entropic Optimal Transport (EOT). Recent solvers for SB exploit the pervasive bridge matching procedures. Such procedures aim to recover a stochastic process transporting the mass between distributions given only a transport plan between them. In particular, given the EOT plan, these procedures can be adapted to solve SB. This fact is heavily exploited by recent works giving rives to matching-based SB solvers. The cornerstone here is recovering the EOT plan: recent works either use heuristical approximations (e.g., the minibatch OT) or establish iterative matching procedures which by the design accumulate the error during the training. We address these limitations and propose a novel procedure to learn SB which we call the optimal Schrödinger bridge matching. It exploits the optimal parameterization of the diffusion process and provably recovers the SB process (a) with a single bridge matching step and (b) with arbitrary transport plan as the input. Furthermore, we show that the optimal bridge matching objective coincides with the recently discovered energy-based modeling (EBM) objectives to learn EOT/SB. Inspired by this observation, we develop a light solver (which we call LightSB-M) to implement optimal matching in practice using the Gaussian mixture parameterization of the adjusted Schrödinger potential. We experimentally showcase the performance of our solver in a range of practical tasks.

paragraphs: A Schrödinger bridge describes a stochastic process that transports probability mass between distributions and connects diffusion modeling with entropic optimal transport. Existing matching-based approaches face a key difficulty: obtaining the appropriate entropic optimal transport plan, often through approximations or iterative procedures that accumulate training error.

The paper proposes optimal Schrödinger bridge matching, using an optimal parameterization of the diffusion process. Its theoretical result establishes recovery of the bridge in a single matching step with an arbitrary input transport plan. Within this formulation, the starting plan therefore need not already be the entropic optimal transport solution that earlier approaches seek.

The authors also show that their matching objective coincides with recently developed energy-based modeling objectives for learning these transport processes. This connection motivates LightSB-M, a practical solver that represents an adjusted Schrödinger potential with a Gaussian mixture. Experiments demonstrate the solver on several practical tasks, connecting the theoretical matching result to an implementable learning method.
summary.tldr: Optimal Schrödinger bridge matching theoretically recovers the bridge in one matching step from an arbitrary transport plan and motivates the LightSB-M solver.

title: Light and Optimal Schrödinger Bridge Matching

abstract: Self-attention has been widely used in various machine learning models, such as vision transformers. The standard dot-product self-attention is arguably the most popular structure, and there is a growing interest in understanding the mathematical properties of such attention mechanisms. This paper presents a fine-grained local sensitivity analysis of the standard dot-product self-attention, leading to new non-vacuous certified robustness results for vision transformers. Despite the well-known fact that dot-product self-attention is not (globally) Lipschitz, we develop new theoretical analysis of Local Fine-grained Attention Sensitivity (LoFAST) quantifying the effect of input feature perturbations on the attention output. Our analysis reveals that the local sensitivity of dot-product self-attention to $\ell_2$ perturbations can actually be controlled by several key quantities associated with the attention weight matrices and the unperturbed input. We empirically validate our theoretical findings by computing non-vacuous certified $\ell_2$-robustness for vision transformers on CIFAR-10 and SVHN datasets. The code for LoFAST is available at https://github.com/AaronHavens/LoFAST.

paragraphs: Standard dot-product self-attention is widely used, but understanding how input changes affect its output presents a mathematical challenge. It is not globally Lipschitz, so a single global bound cannot control its sensitivity in the usual way. This complicates attempts to certify the robustness of models that contain it.

The paper develops Local Fine-grained Attention Sensitivity, or LoFAST, to analyze behavior around an unperturbed input. It quantifies how changes measured in the l2 norm affect attention outputs. The analysis shows that local sensitivity can be controlled through quantities associated with the attention weight matrices and the original input, allowing the bound to reflect the particular setting being examined.

The authors use this analysis to compute non-vacuous certified l2 robustness results for vision transformers on CIFAR-10 and SVHN. These certificates provide meaningful guarantees in the evaluated settings. The central insight is that the absence of global Lipschitz control still leaves room for useful, mathematically grounded local robustness analysis.
summary.tldr: LoFAST bounds the local sensitivity of dot-product attention and enables meaningful certified robustness results for vision transformers.

title: Fine-grained Local Sensitivity Analysis of Standard Dot-Product Self-Attention

abstract: Causal dynamics learning has recently emerged as a promising approach to enhancing robustness in reinforcement learning (RL). Typically, the goal is to build a dynamics model that makes predictions based on the causal relationships among the entities. Despite the fact that causal connections often manifest only under certain contexts, existing approaches overlook such fine-grained relationships and lack a detailed understanding of the dynamics. In this work, we propose a novel dynamics model that infers fine-grained causal structures and employs them for prediction, leading to improved robustness in RL. The key idea is to jointly learn the dynamics model with a discrete latent variable that quantizes the state-action space into subgroups. This leads to recognizing meaningful context that displays sparse dependencies, where causal structures are learned for each subgroup throughout the training. Experimental results demonstrate the robustness of our method to unseen states and locally spurious correlations in downstream tasks where fine-grained causal reasoning is crucial. We further illustrate the effectiveness of our subgroup-based approach with quantization in discovering fine-grained causal relationships compared to prior methods.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning dynamics model predicts how an environment changes after an action. Causal dynamics models make those predictions using relationships among entities, but the relevant relationships can depend on the current situation. This paper addresses the loss of detail that occurs when a model overlooks these context-dependent connections.

The proposed model jointly learns its predictions and a discrete latent variable that partitions the state-action space into subgroups. Each subgroup represents a context in which a relatively sparse set of dependencies can be learned. The model therefore uses different fine-grained causal structures for different parts of the space, learning those structures throughout training.

Experiments show robustness to previously unseen states and locally spurious correlations in downstream tasks that require fine-grained causal reasoning. The authors also report more effective discovery of these relationships than prior methods. The result supports learning context and dynamics together: identifying which situation applies helps determine which dependencies should guide prediction, rather than treating causal connections as equally relevant everywhere.
summary.tldr: The method learns context-specific causal dynamics by quantizing state-action space, improving robustness in the evaluated reinforcement-learning tasks.

title: Fine-Grained Causal Dynamics Learning with Quantization for Improving Robustness in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Automation is one of the cornerstones of contemporary material discovery. Bayesian optimization (BO) is an essential part of such workflows, enabling scientists to leverage prior domain knowledge into efficient exploration of a large molecular space. While such prior knowledge can take many forms, there has been significant fanfare around the ancillary scientific knowledge encapsulated in large language models (LLMs). However, existing work thus far has only explored LLMs for heuristic materials searches. Indeed, recent work obtains the uncertainty estimate—an integral part of BO—from point-estimated, non-Bayesian LLMs. In this work, we study the question of whether LLMs are actually useful to accelerate principled Bayesian optimization in the molecular space. We take a sober, dispassionate stance in answering this question. This is done by carefully (i) viewing LLMs as fixed feature extractors for standard but principled BO surrogate models and by (ii) leveraging parameter-efficient finetuning methods and Bayesian neural networks to obtain the posterior of the LLM surrogate. Our extensive experiments with real-world chemistry problems show that LLMs can be useful for BO over molecules, but only if they have been pretrained or finetuned with domain-specific data.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization helps scientists choose which molecules to investigate by combining predictions with uncertainty about those predictions. Language models might contribute useful scientific knowledge, but the paper questions whether that knowledge actually improves a principled Bayesian search. In particular, it distinguishes Bayesian uncertainty from estimates obtained using language models that provide point estimates without a Bayesian treatment.

The authors investigate two routes for incorporating language models. One uses a model as a fixed feature extractor, passing its representations into established Bayesian optimization surrogate models. The other combines parameter-efficient fine-tuning with Bayesian neural networks to obtain a posterior for the language-model surrogate. Both approaches connect language-model representations to an explicitly Bayesian prediction framework.

Experiments on real-world chemistry problems find that language models can help molecular Bayesian optimization, but only when pretrained or fine-tuned with domain-specific data in the settings studied. The result makes domain preparation central to the reported benefit. General language-model capability alone does not establish the usefulness of a surrogate for this scientific search task.
summary.tldr: Experiments find that language models help Bayesian optimization over molecules only when they receive domain-specific pretraining or fine-tuning.

title: A Sober Look at LLMs for Material Discovery: Are They Actually Good for Bayesian Optimization Over Molecules?

abstract: Code generation, symbolic math reasoning, and other tasks require LLMs to produce outputs that are both syntactically and semantically correct. Constrained LLM generation is a promising direction to enforce adherence to formal grammar, but prior works have empirically observed that strict enforcement of formal constraints often diminishes the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. In this work, we first provide a theoretical explanation for why constraining LLM outputs to very restrictive grammars that only allow syntactically valid final answers reduces the reasoning capabilities of the model. Second, we demonstrate that by augmenting the output grammar with carefully designed additional rules, it is always possible to preserve the reasoning capabilities of the LLM while ensuring syntactic and semantic correctness in its outputs. Building on these theoretical insights, we propose a reasoning-augmented constrained decoding algorithm, CRANE, which effectively balances the correctness of constrained generation with the flexibility of unconstrained generation. Experiments on multiple open-source LLMs and benchmarks show that CRANE significantly outperforms both state-of-the-art constrained decoding strategies and standard unconstrained decoding, showing up to 10% points accuracy improvement over baselines on challenging symbolic reasoning benchmarks GSM-symbolic and FOLIO.

paragraphs: Tasks such as code generation and symbolic mathematics require answers that follow formal rules and have the right meaning. Constrained decoding can enforce a grammar, but restrictive grammars may interfere with a language model's reasoning. The paper explains theoretically why allowing only syntactically valid final answers can reduce reasoning capability.

Its central theoretical result concerns expanding the grammar with carefully designed additional rules. The authors show that such an expansion can always preserve the model's reasoning capabilities while ensuring syntactic and semantic correctness within their theoretical treatment. This motivates CRANE, a decoding algorithm that augments constrained generation with room for reasoning.

Experiments across multiple open-source models and benchmarks report improvements over both existing constrained decoding strategies and ordinary unconstrained decoding. On GSM-symbolic and FOLIO, gains reach up to 10 percentage points in accuracy. These findings support the practical importance of grammar design: constraints should accommodate the reasoning process as well as specify the form of the eventual answer.
summary.tldr: CRANE adds reasoning-supporting grammar rules to constrained decoding, improving symbolic reasoning accuracy while retaining formal output constraints.

title: CRANE: Reasoning with constrained LLM generation

abstract: Transformer models encounter inefficiency when scaling hidden dimensions due to the uniform expansion of parameters. When delving into the sparsity of hidden dimensions, we observe that only a small subset of dimensions are highly activated, where some dimensions are commonly activated across tokens, and some others uniquely activated for individual tokens. To leverage this, we propose MoHD (Mixture of Hidden Dimensions), a sparse architecture that combines shared sub-dimensions for common features and dynamically routes specialized sub-dimensions per token. To address the potential information loss from sparsity, we introduce activation scaling and group fusion mechanisms. MoHD efficiently expands hidden dimensions with minimal computational increases, outperforming vanilla Transformers in both parameter efficiency and task performance across 10 NLP tasks. MoHD achieves 1.7% higher performance with 50% fewer activatied parameters and 3.7% higher performance with 3$\times$ total parameters expansion at constant activated parameters cost. MoHD offers a new perspective for scaling the model, showcasing the potential of hidden dimension sparsity.

paragraphs: Increasing a Transformer's hidden dimensions usually expands parameters uniformly. This paper investigates whether all those dimensions need to participate equally. The authors observe that only a small subset is highly activated: some dimensions are active across many tokens, while others are distinctive to individual tokens.

Mixture of Hidden Dimensions, or MoHD, turns that observation into a sparse architecture. Shared sub-dimensions represent common features, while specialized sub-dimensions are routed dynamically for each token. Activation scaling and group fusion address potential information loss from this sparsity. The design aims to increase representational capacity with only small increases in computation.

Across 10 natural language processing tasks, MoHD outperforms vanilla Transformers in parameter efficiency and task performance. The authors report 1.7% higher performance with 50% fewer activated parameters, and 3.7% higher performance with three times the total parameters at a constant activated-parameter cost. These results distinguish total model capacity from the parameters activated during computation, supporting hidden-dimension sparsity as a promising approach to model scaling.
summary.tldr: MoHD combines shared and token-specific hidden dimensions to improve Transformer capacity and performance with fewer activated parameters.

title: Mixture of Hidden-Dimensions: Not All Hidden-States’ Dimensions are Needed in Transformer

abstract: This paper proposes SHARP-Distill (Speedy Hypergraph And Review-based Personalised Distillation), a novel knowledge distillation approach based on the teacher-student framework that combines Hypergraph Neural Networks (HGNNs) with language models to enhance recommendation quality while significantly improving inference time. The teacher model leverages HGNNs to generate user and item embeddings from interaction data, capturing high-order and group relationships, and employing a pre-trained language model to extract rich semantic features from textual reviews. We utilize a contrastive learning mechanism to ensure structural consistency between various representations. The student includes a shallow and lightweight GCN called CompactGCN designed to inherit high-order relationships while reducing computational complexity. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that SHARP-Distill achieves up to 68$\times$ faster inference time compared to HGNN and 40$\times$ faster than LightGCN while maintaining competitive recommendation accuracy.

Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that SHARP-Distill achieves up to 68$\times$ faster inference time compared to HGNN and 40$\times$ faster than LightGCN while maintaining competitive recommendation accuracy.

paragraphs: Recommendation models can draw on both interaction structure and the meaning of written reviews, but rich representations can be expensive to use at inference time. SHARP-Distill addresses this tradeoff through a teacher-student framework. A more elaborate teacher learns from these complementary sources, and a lightweight student inherits useful information for faster recommendation.

The teacher uses hypergraph neural networks to build user and item embeddings that capture group and higher-order relationships in interaction data. A pretrained language model extracts semantic features from reviews. Contrastive learning encourages structural consistency across representations. The student contains CompactGCN, a shallow graph convolutional network designed to retain higher-order relationship information with lower computational complexity.

Experiments on real-world datasets report inference speedups of up to 68 times relative to HGNN and 40 times relative to LightGCN, while maintaining competitive recommendation accuracy. These are reported upper-end gains in the evaluated settings. The findings support distilling a richer combination of graph and language representations into a compact model for efficient recommendation.
summary.tldr: SHARP-Distill transfers hypergraph and review-based knowledge into a compact recommender, reporting up to 68-fold faster inference with competitive accuracy.

title: SHARP-Distill: A 68$\times$ Faster Recommender System with Hypergraph Neural Networks and Language Models

abstract: Diffusion models have emerged as a dominant approach for text-to-image generation. Key components such as the human preference alignment and classifier-free guidance play a crucial role in ensuring generation quality. However, their independent application in current text-to-image models continues to face significant challenges in achieving strong text-image alignment, high generation quality, and consistency with human aesthetic standards. In this work, we for the first time, explore facilitating the collaboration of human performance alignment and test-time sampling to unlock the potential of text-to-image models. Consequently, we introduce CHATS (Combining Human-Aligned optimization and Test-time Sampling), a novel generative framework that separately models the preferred and dispreferred distributions and employs a proxy-prompt-based sampling strategy to utilize the useful information contained in both distributions. We observe that CHATS exhibits exceptional data efficiency, achieving strong performance with only a small, high-quality funetuning dataset. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CHATS surpasses traditional preference alignment methods, setting new state-of-the-art across various standard benchmarks. The code is publicly available at github.com/AIDC-AI/CHATS.

paragraphs: Text-to-image diffusion models need to satisfy several goals together: follow the prompt, produce high-quality images, and match human aesthetic preferences. Preference alignment and guidance during generation both contribute to these goals. This paper argues that treating training-time alignment and generation-time sampling independently leaves useful opportunities for cooperation unexplored.

CHATS connects these stages by separately modeling distributions of preferred and dispreferred outputs. It then uses a sampling strategy based on proxy prompts to draw useful information from both distributions. The distinctive idea is that dispreferred outputs also provide information for generation, rather than serving only as examples to discourage during alignment. The framework makes this information part of the sampling process.

The authors report strong performance from a small, high-quality fine-tuning dataset, suggesting substantial data efficiency in their experiments. Across standard benchmarks, CHATS surpasses traditional preference-alignment methods and achieves reported state-of-the-art results. These findings support coordinating how a model learns human preferences with how it generates images, rather than evaluating either component only in isolation.
summary.tldr: CHATS coordinates preference learning and sampling, using preferred and dispreferred distributions to improve text-to-image generation with little fine-tuning data.

title: CHATS: Combining Human-Aligned Optimization and Test-Time Sampling for Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: Knowledge distillation typically minimizes the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between teacher and student logits. However, optimizing the KL divergence can be challenging for the student and often leads to sub-optimal solutions. We further show that gradients induced by KL divergence scale with the magnitude of the teacher logits, thereby diminishing updates on low-probability channels. This imbalance weakens the transfer of inter-class information and in turn limits the performance improvements achievable by the student. To mitigate this issue, we propose a plug-and-play auxiliary ranking loss based on Kendall’s $\tau$ coefficient that can be seamlessly integrated into any logit-based distillation framework. It supplies inter-class relational information while rebalancing gradients toward low-probability channels. We demonstrate that the proposed ranking loss is largely invariant to channel scaling and optimizes an objective aligned with that of KL divergence, making it a natural complement rather than a replacement. Extensive experiments on CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and COCO datasets, as well as various CNN and ViT teacher-student architecture combinations, demonstrate that our plug-and-play ranking loss consistently boosts the performance of multiple distillation baselines.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers behavior from a teacher model to a student by matching their output scores. This paper examines a weakness of the commonly used KL-divergence objective: its gradients depend on the magnitude of teacher logits, leaving low-probability channels with weaker updates. That imbalance can reduce the transfer of relationships between classes.

The authors add an auxiliary loss based on Kendall's τ, a ranking coefficient. It supplies information about inter-class ordering and rebalances learning toward low-probability channels. They show that the loss is largely invariant to channel scaling and has an objective aligned with KL divergence. It is therefore designed to supplement the existing distillation objective.

Experiments on CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and COCO include teacher-student combinations built from convolutional networks and vision transformers. The added ranking loss consistently improves multiple distillation baselines in these evaluations. The contribution is a broadly integrable way to preserve relational information that uneven gradients can otherwise underemphasize, strengthening the information passed from teacher to student.
summary.tldr: An auxiliary Kendall's τ ranking loss improves distillation by strengthening inter-class information and updates to low-probability channels.

title: Enhancing Logits Distillation with Plug&Play Kendall’s $τ$ Ranking Loss

abstract: The design of target-specific molecules such as small molecules, peptides, and antibodies is vital for biological research and drug discovery. Existing generative methods are restricted to single-domain molecules, failing to address versatile therapeutic needs or utilize cross-domain transferability to enhance model performance. In this paper, we introduce Unified generative Modeling of 3D Molecules (UniMoMo), the first framework capable of designing binders of multiple molecular domains using a single model. In particular, UniMoMo unifies the representations of different molecules as graphs of blocks, where each block corresponds to either a standard amino acid or a molecular fragment. Based on these unified representations, UniMoMo utilizes a geometric latent diffusion model for 3D molecular generation, featuring an iterative full-atom autoencoder to compress blocks into latent space points, followed by an E(3)-equivariant diffusion process. Extensive benchmarks across peptides, antibodies, and small molecules demonstrate the superiority of our unified framework over existing domain-specific models, highlighting the benefits of multi-domain training.

paragraphs: Designing molecules that bind a chosen target spans several molecular domains, including small molecules, peptides, and antibodies. Existing generative methods typically specialize in one domain. UniMoMo brings these domains into a single model, allowing training across molecular types to contribute to target-specific binder generation.

The framework represents molecules as graphs of blocks, with each block corresponding to an amino acid or a molecular fragment. An iterative full-atom autoencoder compresses those blocks into points in a latent space. A geometric diffusion process then generates representations in that space, using E(3) equivariance to maintain consistent behavior under spatial transformations.

This shared representation provides the connection between otherwise different molecular domains, while the latent diffusion model supplies a common generation mechanism. Benchmarks spanning peptides, antibodies, and small molecules show better performance than the evaluated domain-specific models. The findings support the benefit of multi-domain training for binder design and demonstrate that one generative framework can cover several classes of molecules through a unified structural representation.
summary.tldr: UniMoMo uses shared molecular block representations and geometric latent diffusion to design small-molecule, peptide, and antibody binders within one model.

title: UniMoMo: Unified Generative Modeling of 3D Molecules for De Novo Binder Design

abstract: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) can be utilized to recover a clean signal from its degraded observation(s) by conditioning the model on the degraded signal. The degraded signals are themselves contaminated versions of the clean signals; due to this correlation, they may encompass certain useful information about the target clean data distribution. However, existing adoption of the standard Gaussian as the prior distribution in turn discards such information when shaping the prior, resulting in sub-optimal performance. In this paper, we propose to improve conditional DDPMs for signal restoration by leveraging a more informative prior that is jointly learned with the diffusion model. The proposed framework, called RestoreGrad, seamlessly integrates DDPMs into the variational autoencoder (VAE) framework, taking advantage of the correlation between the degraded and clean signals to encode a better diffusion prior. On speech and image restoration tasks, we show that RestoreGrad demonstrates faster convergence (5-10 times fewer training steps) to achieve better quality of restored signals over existing DDPM baselines and improved robustness to using fewer sampling steps in inference time (2-2.5 times fewer), advocating the advantages of leveraging jointly learned prior for efficiency improvements in the diffusion process.

paragraphs: A degraded image or speech signal still contains information about the clean signal that produced it. Conditional diffusion models use the degraded observation during restoration, but a standard Gaussian starting distribution does not incorporate that information into the prior itself. RestoreGrad asks whether learning a more informative prior can make restoration better and more efficient.

The framework integrates a denoising diffusion model with a variational autoencoder and learns the prior jointly with the diffusion model. Correlations between degraded and clean signals help shape this starting distribution. The design therefore uses the observation both as conditioning information and as a source of information for the diffusion prior.

On speech and image restoration tasks, the authors report better restored-signal quality than existing diffusion baselines while requiring five to ten times fewer training steps to converge. They also report greater robustness when reducing inference sampling steps, with two to two-and-a-half times fewer steps. These findings connect a more informative learned prior to efficiency in both training and restoration, alongside improvements in output quality in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: RestoreGrad jointly learns an observation-informed diffusion prior, improving restoration quality while reducing training and inference steps.

title: RestoreGrad: Signal Restoration Using Conditional Denoising Diffusion Models with Jointly Learned Prior

abstract: Score-based generative models are essential in various machine learning applications, with strong capabilities in generation quality. In particular, high-order derivatives (scores) of data density offer deep insights into data distributions, building on the proven effectiveness of first-order scores for modeling and generating synthetic data, unlocking new possibilities for applications. However, learning them typically requires complete data, which is often unavailable in domains such as healthcare and finance due to data corruption, acquisition constraints, or incomplete records. To tackle this challenge, we introduce MissScore, a novel framework for estimating high-order scores in the presence of missing data. We derive objective functions for estimating high-order scores under different missing data mechanisms and propose a new algorithm specifically designed to handle missing data effectively. Our empirical results demonstrate that MissScore accurately and efficiently learns the high-order scores from incomplete data and generates high-quality samples, resulting in strong performance across a range of downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Score-based methods learn information about the shape of a data distribution to support generation and other tasks. Higher-order scores describe higher-order derivatives of the data density, offering additional information about that distribution. Learning these quantities typically requires complete observations, creating a problem when records contain missing entries because of corruption, collection constraints, or incomplete documentation.

MissScore is a framework for estimating these higher-order quantities directly in the presence of missing data. The authors derive training objectives for different missing-data mechanisms and introduce an algorithm designed for incomplete observations. Accounting for how data become missing is part of the estimation problem, rather than treating complete records as a prerequisite.

The empirical results show that MissScore learns higher-order scores accurately and efficiently from incomplete data. It also generates high-quality samples and performs strongly across a range of downstream tasks. These findings support the usefulness of higher-order distributional information even when the available dataset is incomplete, extending the practical setting in which score estimation can contribute to learning and generation.
summary.tldr: MissScore estimates higher-order distributional scores from incomplete data using objectives tailored to different missing-data mechanisms.

title: MissScore: High-Order Score Estimation in the Presence of Missing Data

abstract: The training and deployment of large language models (LLMs) create a feedback loop with human users: models learn human beliefs from data, reinforce these beliefs with generated content, reabsorb the reinforced beliefs, and feed them back to users again and again. This dynamic resembles an echo chamber. We hypothesize that this feedback loop entrenches the existing values and beliefs of users, leading to a loss of diversity in human ideas and potentially the lock-in of false beliefs. We formalize this hypothesis and test it empirically with agent-based LLM simulations and real-world GPT usage data. Analysis reveals sudden but sustained drops in diversity after the release of new GPT iterations, consistent with the hypothesized human-AI feedback loop. Website: https://thelockinhypothesis.com

paragraphs: The paper proposes that interactions between people and language models can form a reinforcing feedback loop. Models learn beliefs from human-produced data, generate content that reinforces those beliefs, and later absorb the reinforced beliefs through further data. Repetition could make existing views harder to dislodge and reduce the diversity of ideas.

The authors call this the lock-in hypothesis and formalize it for empirical study. They examine it using both simulations with language-model agents and real-world GPT usage data. Combining these forms of evidence lets them investigate the proposed feedback mechanism alongside patterns observed in actual model use.

Their analysis finds abrupt declines in diversity after releases of new GPT iterations, with those declines persisting afterward. The authors interpret this pattern as consistent with the hypothesized feedback loop. The stated conclusion retains an important distinction: sustained diversity losses support the hypothesis, while entrenchment of false beliefs remains a potential consequence. The paper frames human-model interaction as a process whose repeated cycles may shape the range of ideas people encounter and preserve.
summary.tldr: The paper finds sustained diversity declines consistent with a hypothesis that human–LLM feedback loops can entrench existing beliefs.

title: The Lock-in Hypothesis: Stagnation by Algorithm

abstract: Increasing diversity in language models is a challenging yet essential objective. A common approach is to raise the decoding temperature. In this work, we investigate this approach through a simplistic yet common case to provide insights into why decreasing temperature can improve quality (Precision), while increasing it often fails to boost coverage (Recall). Our analysis reveals that for a model to be effectively tunable through temperature adjustments, it must be trained toward coverage. To address this, we propose rethinking loss functions in language models by leveraging the Precision-Recall framework. Our results demonstrate that this approach achieves a substantially better trade-off between Precision and Recall than merely combining negative log-likelihood training with temperature scaling. These findings offer a pathway toward more versatile and robust language modeling techniques.

paragraphs: Raising a language model's decoding temperature is a common way to seek more varied outputs. This paper examines why that adjustment may fail to increase meaningful coverage, even though lowering temperature can improve output quality. It frames the distinction through precision, representing quality, and recall, representing coverage.

Using a simple but common case, the authors analyze what temperature adjustment can accomplish. Their analysis indicates that effective temperature tuning requires training that already encourages coverage. Changing the sampling setting alone therefore may not provide the desired range of good outputs when the training objective has not supported that range.

The proposed response is to rethink training losses through the precision-recall framework. The reported results show a substantially better quality-coverage trade-off than negative log-likelihood training combined with temperature scaling. The contribution connects a generation-time control to the objective used during learning: improving diversity may require changing what the model learns, as well as how its outputs are sampled.
summary.tldr: Training losses that encourage coverage improve the precision-recall trade-off beyond what temperature scaling alone achieves in the reported results.

title: Improving Diversity in Language Models: When Temperature Fails, Change the Loss

abstract: Molecular machine learning has gained popularity with the advancements of geometric deep learning. In parallel, retrieval-augmented generation has become a principled approach commonly used with language models. However, the optimal integration of retrieval augmentation into molecular machine learning remains unclear. Graph neural networks stand to benefit from clever matching to understand the structural alignment of retrieved molecules to a query molecule. Neural graph matching offers a compelling solution by explicitly modeling node and edge affinities between two structural graphs while employing a noise-robust, end-to-end neural network to learn affinity metrics. We apply this approach to mass spectrum simulation and introduce MARASON, a novel model that incorporates neural graph matching to enhance a fragmentation-based neural network. Experimental results highlight the effectiveness of our design, with MARASON achieving 27% top-1 accuracy, a substantial improvement over the non-retrieval state-of-the-art accuracy of 19%. Moreover, MARASON outperforms both naive retrieval-augmented generation methods and traditional graph matching approaches. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/coleygroup/ms-pred.

paragraphs: Retrieval can give a molecular prediction model useful reference molecules, but the model still needs to understand how each reference relates structurally to its query. This paper studies that integration through neural graph matching. The method explicitly models affinities between the nodes and edges of two molecular graphs.

MARASON applies this matching approach to mass-spectrum simulation by enhancing a fragmentation-based neural network. An end-to-end neural matching system learns affinity measures while being robust to noise. The structural alignment provides a way to connect retrieved molecular information with the query, making the relationship between their graphs part of the prediction process.

Experiments report 27% top-1 accuracy, compared with 19% for the non-retrieval state of the art. MARASON also outperforms naive retrieval-augmented methods and traditional graph-matching approaches. These results support the importance of learned structural matching in this application: retrieving molecules becomes more useful when the model explicitly represents their correspondence to the molecule being studied. The evidence concerns the reported mass-spectrum task and evaluated comparisons.
summary.tldr: MARASON uses neural graph matching to connect retrieved molecules to a query, improving reported top-1 accuracy from 19% to 27%.

title: Neural Graph Matching Improves Retrieval Augmented Generation in Molecular Machine Learning

abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent capabilities in LLMs. Interestingly, we observe that both CoT reasoning and self-training share the core objective: iteratively leveraging model-generated information to progressively reduce prediction uncertainty. Building on this insight, we propose a novel CoT framework to improve reasoning performance. Our framework integrates two key components: (i) a task-specific prompt module that optimizes the initial reasoning process, and (ii) an adaptive reasoning iteration module that dynamically refines the reasoning process and addresses the limitations of previous CoT approaches, i.e., over-reasoning and high similarity between consecutive reasoning iterations. Extensive experiments show that the proposed method achieves significant advantages in both performance and computational efficiency. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zongqianwu/ST-COT.

paragraphs: Chain-of-thought reasoning and self-training both reuse information produced by a model to reduce uncertainty over successive steps. This paper takes that shared objective as a starting point for a new reasoning framework. The aim is to make iterative reasoning more productive, rather than assuming that additional reasoning automatically improves an answer.

The framework has two components. A task-specific prompt module improves the initial reasoning process, while an adaptive iteration module refines what follows. The latter addresses two identified problems in prior chain-of-thought approaches: continuing to reason excessively and generating successive iterations that are highly similar. These problems matter because repeated model output can consume computation without providing much new information.

Extensive experiments show significant advantages in both reasoning performance and computational efficiency. The reported combination supports the idea that better use of model-generated information can improve answers while reducing unproductive reasoning. The contribution is a framework that treats the initial prompt and subsequent refinement as connected design choices, with iteration adapted to address redundancy and over-reasoning.
summary.tldr: A self-training-inspired chain-of-thought framework improves reasoning and efficiency through task-specific prompting and adaptive refinement.

title: Rethinking Chain-of-Thought from the Perspective of Self-Training

abstract: Causal inference seeks to estimate the effect given a treatment such as a medicine or the dosage of a medication. To reduce the confounding bias caused by the non-randomized treatment assignment, most existing methods reduce the shift between subpopulations receiving different treatments. However, these methods split limited training samples into smaller groups, which cuts down the number of samples in each group, while precise distribution estimation and alignment highly rely on a sufficient number of training samples. In this paper, we propose a distribution alignment paradigm without data splitting, which can be naturally applied in the settings of binary and continuous treatments. To this end, we characterize the confounding bias by considering different probability measures of the same set including all the training samples, and exploit the optimal transport theory to analyze the confounding bias and outcome estimation error. Based on this, we propose to learn balanced representations by reducing the bias between the marginal distribution and the conditional distribution of a treatment. As a result, data reduction caused by splitting is avoided, and the outcome prediction model trained on one treatment group can be generalized to the entire population. The experiments on both binary and continuous treatment settings demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Estimating treatment effects from nonrandomized data requires addressing differences between people receiving different treatments. Many methods align treatment subpopulations after splitting the data into groups. The paper points out that this reduces the samples available within each group, making distribution estimation and alignment harder when training data is limited.

The proposed approach compares different probability measures over the same complete set of training samples. Optimal transport theory provides an analysis of confounding bias and outcome estimation error in this formulation. The method learns balanced representations by reducing the discrepancy between the marginal distribution and the distribution conditional on a treatment.

Keeping the full sample set in the alignment formulation avoids the data reduction caused by splitting. The authors state that the resulting representations allow an outcome model trained on one treatment group to generalize to the broader population. Experiments with both binary and continuous treatments demonstrate effectiveness, supporting a common alignment framework for these two treatment settings.
summary.tldr: The method uses optimal transport to reduce confounding through distribution alignment over all training samples, avoiding treatment-based data splitting.

title: Reducing Confounding Bias without Data Splitting for Causal Inference via Optimal Transport

abstract: Referring MLLMs extend conventional multimodal large language models by allowing them to receive referring visual prompts and generate responses tailored to the indicated regions. However, these models often suffer from suboptimal performance due to incorrect responses tailored to misleading areas adjacent to or similar to the target region. This work introduces CPCF, a novel framework to address this issue and achieve superior results. CPCF contrasts outputs generated from the indicated visual prompt with those from contrastive prompts sampled from misleading regions, effectively suppressing the influence of erroneous information outside the target region on response generation. To further enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of our framework, several novel designs are proposed, including a prompt extraction network to automatically identify suitable contrastive prompts, a self-training method that leverages unlabeled data to improve training quality, and a distillation approach to reduce the additional computational overhead associated with contrastive decoding. Incorporating these novel designs, CPCF achieves state-of-the-art performance, as demonstrated by extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks. Project page: https://lanyunzhu.site/CPCF/

paragraphs: Referring multimodal language models answer questions about an indicated image region. Their responses can go wrong when a nearby or visually similar region draws attention away from the intended target. CPCF addresses this specific source of error by comparing responses associated with the target against responses associated with potentially misleading regions.

The framework generates outputs using both the supplied visual prompt and contrastive prompts drawn from distracting areas. Comparing those outputs helps suppress information that comes from outside the target. A prompt extraction network automatically identifies useful contrastive prompts, making the choice of distracting regions part of the method itself.

CPCF also includes self-training with unlabeled data to improve training quality and a distillation approach to reduce the extra computation required by contrastive decoding. Experiments across multiple benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance. The findings support using explicit comparisons between image regions to improve response specificity, while the additional training and distillation components address the quality and efficiency of that comparison process.
summary.tldr: CPCF compares responses to target and distracting image regions to make multimodal models answer more accurately about the intended region.

title: CPCF: A Cross-Prompt Contrastive Framework for Referring Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Recent advances in diffusion bridge models leverage Doob’s $h$-transform to establish fixed endpoints between distributions, demonstrating promising results in image translation and restoration tasks. However, these approaches frequently produce blurred or excessively smoothed image details and lack a comprehensive theoretical foundation to explain these shortcomings. To address these limitations, we propose UniDB, a unified framework for diffusion bridges based on Stochastic Optimal Control (SOC). UniDB formulates the problem through an SOC-based optimization and derives a closed-form solution for the optimal controller, thereby unifying and generalizing existing diffusion bridge models. We demonstrate that existing diffusion bridges employing Doob’s $h$-transform constitute a special case of our framework, emerging when the terminal penalty coefficient in the SOC cost function tends to infinity. By incorporating a tunable terminal penalty coefficient, UniDB achieves an optimal balance between control costs and terminal penalties, substantially improving detail preservation and output quality. Notably, UniDB seamlessly integrates with existing diffusion bridge models, requiring only minimal code modifications. Extensive experiments across diverse image restoration tasks validate the superiority and adaptability of the proposed framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/UniDB-SOC/UniDB/.

title: UniDB: A Unified Diffusion Bridge Framework via Stochastic Optimal Control

abstract: Progress in AI has relied on human-generated data, from annotator marketplaces to the wider Internet. However, the widespread use of large language models now threatens the quality and integrity of human-generated data on these very platforms. We argue that this issue goes beyond the immediate challenge of filtering AI-generated content -- it reveals deeper flaws in how data collection systems are designed. Existing systems often prioritize speed, scale, and efficiency at the cost of intrinsic human motivation, leading to declining engagement and data quality. We propose that rethinking data collection systems to align with contributors' intrinsic motivations -- rather than relying solely on external incentives -- can help sustain high-quality data sourcing at scale while maintaining contributor trust and long-term participation.

paragraphs: AI development depends on human-generated contributions from sources such as annotation marketplaces and the wider internet. This position paper argues that widespread language model use threatens the quality and integrity of those sources. It treats the problem as a challenge to the design of data collection systems, extending beyond identifying and filtering generated material.

The authors argue that existing systems often emphasize speed, scale, and efficiency while neglecting contributors’ intrinsic motivations. In their account, this imbalance weakens engagement and data quality. The way a platform encourages participation therefore becomes part of the explanation for why its supply of useful human contributions may deteriorate.

The proposed response is to design collection systems around the motivations that make people want to contribute, without relying solely on external incentives. The authors suggest that this could support high-quality data at scale while preserving trust and continued participation. The contribution is a shift in the data sourcing agenda: sustaining human involvement requires attention to the conditions of contribution as well as to the content collected.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that supporting contributors’ intrinsic motivations could help preserve high-quality human data, trust, and long-term participation.

title: Position: When Incentives Backfire, Data Stops Being Human

abstract: We consider problems of parameter estimation where design variables can be actively optimized to maximize information gain. To this end, we introduce JADAI, a framework that jointly amortizes Bayesian adaptive design and inference by training a policy, a history network, and an inference network end-to-end. The networks minimize a generic loss that aggregates incremental reductions in posterior error along experimental sequences without density evaluations. Inference networks are instantiated with diffusion models that can approximate high-dimensional and multimodal posteriors at every experimental step. JADAI achieves superior or competitive performance across adaptive design benchmarks.

paragraphs: When estimating unknown parameters, an experimenter can often choose what measurement or experiment to perform next. A useful choice depends on what previous observations have already revealed. JADAI addresses this coupled problem: selecting informative experiments while updating a Bayesian estimate of the parameters throughout the experimental sequence.

The framework trains three components together: a policy, a history network, and an inference network. Its objective combines incremental reductions in posterior error across the sequence, and does not require density evaluations. Joint amortization moves the learning of both design and inference into this end-to-end training process, tying experiment selection to improvements in the evolving parameter estimate.

The inference component uses diffusion models to approximate posterior distributions at every experimental step. This supports high-dimensional posteriors and distributions with multiple distinct plausible explanations, rather than requiring uncertainty to collapse to a single estimate. JADAI achieves superior or competitive results across adaptive-design benchmarks. Its contribution is a unified training framework that coordinates decisions about what to observe with inference about what those observations mean.
summary.tldr: JADAI jointly trains experiment selection and diffusion-based Bayesian inference to improve parameter estimation over adaptive experimental sequences.

title: JADAI: Jointly Amortizing Adaptive Design and Bayesian Inference

abstract: Modern federated and streaming learning systems often release intermediate models, so privacy must hold for the full trajectory under adaptive interaction. Motivated by participation privacy, we study single-edit neighboring user streams, where one insertion/deletion shifts all subsequent updates and defeats standard Hamming-neighbor continual-release analyses. We give an auditable modular recipe. A randomized buffering wrapper emits bins of size $[U,2U]$, reducing single-edit streams to a Hamming-style per-bin update stream with explicit backlog/delay guarantees, where $U$ is calibrated by the privacy parameters $(\varepsilon,\delta)$. We then prove a certification theorem for independently decomposable (prefix-causal, fresh-noise) continual mechanisms: any non-adaptive Hamming-neighbor DP proof lifts to adaptive inputs. Together, these ingredients yield trajectory-level $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP for single-edit streams using standard primitives (e.g., tree prefix sums), with an explicit privacy–latency link via $U$. Streaming DP-SGD experiments validate the privacy-utility-latency tradeoffs and the induced delay distributions.

paragraphs: A learning system that releases models throughout training must protect privacy across the entire sequence of releases. This paper studies participation privacy when neighboring user streams differ by one insertion or deletion. Such an edit shifts subsequent updates, making standard analyses based on changing a fixed stream position insufficient for this setting.

The proposed recipe first places incoming updates into randomized buffers containing between U and twice U items. This converts the stream comparison into a form that standard per-bin privacy mechanisms can handle, with explicit guarantees on backlog and delay. The buffer scale U is chosen using the desired privacy parameters, directly connecting privacy protection with waiting time.

A second result lifts non-adaptive privacy proofs to adaptive inputs for mechanisms satisfying the stated decomposition, prefix-causality, and fresh-noise conditions. Together, these components give differential privacy for the full release trajectory under single-edit stream changes using standard primitives such as tree prefix sums. Streaming DP-SGD experiments examine the resulting utility, privacy, latency, and delay distributions.
summary.tldr: Randomized buffering and a conditional certification theorem provide participation privacy across adaptively released learning trajectories.

title: Continual Learning With Participation Privacy: An Auditable Buffering-Aggregation Recipe

abstract: Simulation-based data synthesis has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing real-world robotic manipulation. However, existing synthetic datasets remain insufficient for robust bimanual manipulation due to two key challenges: (1) the lack of an autonomous self-correcting mechanism to resolve execution failures in complex coordination tasks, and (2) the scarcity of diverse visual and spatial variations required to bridge the sim-to-real gap. To this end, we present RoboTwin 2.0, a scalable simulation framework that enables closed-loop, automated, large-scale generation of diverse and realistic data, along with unified evaluation protocols for dual-arm manipulation. Built upon RoboTwin-OD, a foundational library of 731 instances across 147 categories with rich semantic annotations, our framework integrates Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) with simulation-in-the-loop verification. This integration forms an automated feedback mechanism that significantly boosts the success rate of expert task program generation. To enhance robust sim-to-real transfer, RoboTwin 2.0 incorporates structured domain randomization along five axes: clutter, lighting, background, tabletop height and language instructions, thereby maximizing data diversity. We instantiate this framework across 50 dual-arm tasks spanning five robot embodiments. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models pre-trained on our synthetic data achieve a 3.6x improvement in few-shot real-world transfer (over a 10-demo baseline) and a 2.2x gain in zero-shot generalization. We release the data generator, benchmark, pre-collected dataset, and code to support scalable research in robust bimanual manipulation.

title: RoboTwin 2.0: A Scalable Data Generator and Benchmark with Strong Domain Randomization for Robust Bimanual Robotic Manipulation

abstract: Predicting street-level socioeconomic indicators from street view imagery is fundamental to urban planning. Existing methods typically extract visual features via pretrained encoders and propagate information through graph-based learning, but they fail to fully exploit the structured, task-relevant, and label-efficient learning signals inherent in urban scenes. We propose MetaStreet, a semi-supervised multimodal framework with three components: (1) a semantic-spatial visual encoder that jointly models object co-occurrence and spatial adjacency at the semantic category level, (2) a task-aware textual encoder that steers LLMs toward prediction-relevant features via task-specific prompts, and (3) a geography-aware graph contrastive learning module that leverages spatial autocorrelation to extend contrastive supervision to unlabeled streets, enabling them to actively participate in representation learning. Experiments on two cities across three socioeconomic prediction tasks demonstrate that MetaStreet consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: MetaStreet predicts street-level socioeconomic indicators using urban imagery and additional structured learning signals. The paper argues that extracting generic visual features and propagating them through a graph leaves useful information underused. Urban scenes contain relationships between objects, task-relevant descriptions, and geographic structure that can help learning when labeled streets are limited.

The framework combines three components. A visual encoder models which object categories occur together and which are spatially adjacent. A textual encoder uses task-specific prompts to steer a language model toward features relevant to the prediction. A geography-aware graph contrastive module uses spatial autocorrelation to extend learning signals to streets without labels.

This last component lets unlabeled streets actively shape the learned representations, giving the framework its semi-supervised character. Experiments spanning two cities and three socioeconomic prediction tasks report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining semantic relationships, task-directed text, and geographic structure to obtain more useful street representations for these prediction tasks.
summary.tldr: MetaStreet combines visual structure, task-focused text, and geographic learning signals to improve socioeconomic prediction from street scenes.

title: MetaStreet: Semi-Supervised Multimodal Learning for Street-Level Socioeconomic Prediction

abstract: Code-writing large language models (CodeLLMs) generate executable code policies for embodied agents by translating natural language goals and environmental constraints into structured control programs. However, policy generation in open-domain embodied environments suffers from two fundamental limitations: (i) delayed decoding caused by repetitive prefill computation over long prompts, and (ii) limited robustness due to fully generative decoding, which often produces API mismatches, missing safety guards, and unstable control logic. To address these limitations, we present FCGraft, a Functional Cache Grafting framework. FCGraft maintains a library of function-level validated code skeletons and their associated prompt-level Transformer key–value (KV) caches, and synthesizes new policies by retrieving relevant functions and grafting their KV caches when a new task is provided. Given retrieved function caches, FCGraft performs cache grafting via stitching, which composes cached function segments into a composite policy, and patching, which locally adapts only the necessary code regions to satisfy task-specific parameters and constraints with minimal additional decoding. By eliminating redundant prefill computation, this approach reduces generation latency, while reusing validated control structures improves robustness over prompt-level caching methods RAGCache, achieving $18.31$% higher task success rate and $2.3$\times$$ faster policy synthesis.

The findings support function-level reuse as a way to improve both generation speed and the reliability of embodied code policies.
summary.tldr: FCGraft combines validated function skeletons and cached Transformer computations to synthesize embodied control code faster and more reliably.

title: Functional Cache Grafting: Robust and Rapid Code-Policy Synthesis for Embodied Agents

abstract: The minimal norm weight perturbations of DNNs required to achieve a specified change in output are derived and the factors determining its size are discussed. These single-layer exact formulae are contrasted with more generic multi-layer Lipschitz constant based robustness guarantees; both are observed to be of the same order which indicates similar efficacy in their guarantees. These results are applied to precision-modification-activated backdoor attacks, establishing provable compression thresholds below which such attacks cannot succeed, and show empirically that low-rank compression can reliably activate latent backdoors while preserving full-precision accuracy. These expressions reveal how back-propagated margins govern layer-wise sensitivity and provide certifiable guarantees on the smallest parameter updates consistent with a desired output shift.

paragraphs: How much must a neural network's weights change to produce a specified change in its output? This paper derives exact minimum-norm perturbation formulas for changes within a single layer and studies what determines their size. The formulas expose layer-specific sensitivity through margins propagated backward through the network.

The authors compare these exact expressions with more general robustness guarantees based on multi-layer Lipschitz constants. They observe that the two approaches give guarantees of the same order, indicating similar efficacy at that level of comparison. The exact formulas additionally provide certificates for the smallest parameter update consistent with a desired output shift.

It establishes provable compression thresholds below which such attacks cannot succeed, and empirically shows that low-rank compression can reliably activate latent backdoors while preserving full-precision accuracy. Together, the theoretical and empirical results connect parameter sensitivity to a concrete transformation risk: behavior associated with a backdoor can emerge when compression changes the weights, even when full-precision accuracy is preserved.
summary.tldr: Exact single-layer weight-perturbation formulas yield sensitivity certificates and compression thresholds for precision-activated backdoors.

title: Theory of Minimal Weight Perturbations in Deep Networks and its Applications for Low-Rank Activated Backdoor Attacks

abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (RL) is a key paradigm for aligning policies with human judgments, yet its theoretical behavior in distributed settings where preference data are fragmented across heterogeneous users remains poorly understood. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) avoids explicit reward modeling but lacks convergence guarantees under federated and decentralized training, where communication constraints and non-IID preferences fundamentally alter optimization dynamics. We provide the first convergence and time-complexity analysis of DPO in distributed environments. Modeling personalized offline RL with user-specific preference distributions, we characterize the induced global optimization landscape. For federated DPO, we derive convergence rates that quantify the impact of client drift, communication frequency, and preference heterogeneity; for decentralized DPO, we establish convergence over general communication graphs and show how spectral connectivity governs optimization speed and consensus. Empirically, we corroborate our theoretical insights on standard alignment benchmarks, demonstrating that our proposed methods not only enjoy strong theoretical guarantees but also deliver robust and scalable performance in practice. The code base is available here.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization aligns policies using preference comparisons without explicitly fitting a reward model. This paper studies what happens when those comparisons are distributed across users whose preferences differ. Such fragmentation changes optimization because local updates can pull in different directions, while communication limits how frequently participants can reconcile those differences.

The authors formulate personalized offline reinforcement learning with user-specific preference distributions and characterize the resulting global optimization problem. For federated training, they derive convergence rates that account for client drift, communication frequency, and preference heterogeneity. The contribution connects distributed DPO's behavior to concrete features of the training system. In particular, it provides a framework for understanding how differing preferences and communication structure influence progress toward a shared optimization objective.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes distributed DPO, showing how preference differences, communication frequency, and network connectivity affect convergence.

title: Distributed Direct Preference Optimization

abstract: Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are expected to enhance decision-making by pooling distributed information, yet systematically evaluating this capability has remained challenging. We introduce HiddenBench, a 65-task benchmark grounded in the Hidden Profile paradigm, which isolates collective reasoning under distributed information from individual reasoning ability. Evaluating 15 frontier LLMs, we find that multi-agent LLMs achieve only 30.1% accuracy under distributed information, compared to 80.7% accuracy for single agents given complete information. We trace this gap to a systematic failure mode: agents cannot recognize or act under latent information asymmetry—they fail to reason about what others might know but have not yet expressed, leading to premature convergence on shared evidence while critical distributed facts remain unexplored. These failures persist across prompting strategies, communication depths, and group sizes—and worsen as groups scale. While some models (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Flash/Pro) outperform others, neither model scale nor individual reasoning accuracy reliably predicts collective performance. We further show that this bottleneck is actionable: a lightweight structured communication protocol substantially improves collective reasoning across model families. Our results identify failures in collective information exploration in decision-making as a key limitation of multi-agent LLMs, and provide a theory-grounded, reproducible framework for diagnosing collective reasoning failures.

paragraphs: A group of language-model agents can only benefit from distributed information if it discovers and combines what different members know. HiddenBench isolates this collective challenge from individual reasoning ability using 65 tasks grounded in the Hidden Profile paradigm. The benchmark tests whether groups can explore information that is not initially shared.

Across 15 frontier models, multi-agent systems achieve 30.1% accuracy with distributed information, compared with 80.7% for single agents given all information. The authors attribute the gap to failures to consider what others may know but have not expressed. Groups settle prematurely on common evidence while leaving important distributed facts unexplored.

These failures persist across tested prompts, communication depths, and group sizes, and worsen with larger groups. Neither model scale nor individual reasoning accuracy reliably predicts collective performance. However, a lightweight structured communication protocol substantially improves results across model families. The findings locate an actionable bottleneck in information exploration: strong individual reasoning does not by itself ensure that a group will uncover the evidence needed for a good decision.
summary.tldr: HiddenBench shows that agent groups often fail to uncover distributed evidence, although structured communication substantially improves collective reasoning.

title: Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information in Multi-Agent LLMs

abstract: As a multimodal extension of Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Thinking with Images (TWI) has emerged as a promising avenue to enhance the reasoning capability of Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), which generates interleaved CoT by incorporating visual cues into the textual reasoning process. However, the success of existing TWI methods heavily relies on the assumption that interleaved CoTs are faultless, which is easily violated due to the complexity of multimodal understanding. In this paper, we reveal and study a highly-practical yet under-explored problem in TWI, termed Noisy Thinking (NT). Specifically, NT refers to the imperfect visual cues mining and answer reasoning process. As the saying goes, “One mistake leads to another”, erroneous interleaved CoT would cause error accumulation, thus significantly degrading the performance. To solve NT, we propose a novel method dubbed Reliable Thinking with Images (RTWI). In brief, RTWI estimates the reliability of visual cues and textual CoT in a unified text-centric manner and then employs robust filtering and voting modules to prevent NT from contaminating final answer. Extensive experiments on seven benchmarks verify the effectiveness of RTWI against NT.

paragraphs: Thinking with Images mixes visual cues into a model’s textual reasoning process. The paper identifies a vulnerability in approaches that depend on those intermediate steps being correct: a mistaken visual interpretation or reasoning step can contaminate later steps. The authors call this problem Noisy Thinking and study how accumulated errors damage final-answer performance.

Reliable Thinking with Images, or RTWI, evaluates the reliability of both visual cues and textual reasoning using a unified text-centered approach. It then applies filtering and voting modules to reduce the influence of unreliable intermediate information. The method therefore makes the trustworthiness of the reasoning process itself part of how the final answer is produced.

Experiments on seven benchmarks support RTWI’s effectiveness against Noisy Thinking. The significance is that adding visual material to a chain of reasoning also introduces information whose reliability needs assessment. The reported findings support checking and aggregating intermediate evidence as a way to keep mistakes in visual cue extraction or textual reasoning from propagating unchecked into the answer.
summary.tldr: RTWI assesses, filters, and votes over intermediate visual and textual reasoning to reduce error accumulation in image-based thinking.

title: Reliable Thinking with Images

abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), agents benefit from exploration only because they repeatedly encounter similar states: trying different actions can improve performance or reduce uncertainty; without such retries, a greedy policy is optimal. We formalize this intuition with ReMax, an objective that evaluates a policy by the expected maximum return over a retry set of size $M$ ($M \in \mathbb{N}$), while accounting for return uncertainty. Optimizing this objective induces stochastic exploration as an emergent property, without explicit bonus terms. For efficient policy optimization, we derive a new policy-gradient formulation for ReMax and introduce ReMax PPO (RePPO), a PPO variant that optimizes ReMax while generalizing the discrete retry count $M$ to a continuous parameter $m > 0$, enabling fine-grained control of exploration. Empirically, RePPO promotes exploration—without any explicit exploration bonuses—on the MinAtar and Craftax benchmarks. The official code is available at https://github.com/nissymori/remax-rl.
