paragraphs: The paper frames exploration around opportunities to retry similar situations. Trying a different action can be valuable when later encounters allow an agent to benefit from what it discovers. The authors formalize this intuition through an objective that evaluates the best return across a set of retries while accounting for uncertainty in returns.

Called ReMax, this objective uses the expected maximum return from a retry set of size M. Optimizing it induces stochastic exploration without adding an explicit exploration bonus. Exploration therefore arises from the criterion used to judge the policy: the objective values what a policy can achieve across repeated opportunities.

The authors derive a policy-gradient formulation and build RePPO, a variant of PPO that optimizes ReMax. They extend the integer retry count to a continuous positive parameter, allowing finer control over exploration. Experiments on MinAtar and Craftax show that RePPO promotes exploration without explicit bonuses. The stated empirical finding supports retry-based objective design as a way to influence exploratory behavior, rather than establishing universal performance gains across reinforcement learning tasks.
summary.tldr: ReMax evaluates the best outcome across retries, making exploration emerge from policy optimization without explicit exploration bonuses.

title: Emergence of Exploration in Policy Gradient Reinforcement Learning via Retrying

abstract: Multiple-choice question (MCQ) benchmarks have been a standard evaluation practice for measuring LLMs’ ability to reason and answer knowledge-based questions. Through a synthetic NonsenseQA benchmark, we observe that different LLMs exhibit varying degrees of label-position-few-shot-prompt bias, where the model either uses the answer position, the label in front of the answer, the distributions of correct answers present in the few-shot prompt, or a combination of all to answer each MCQ question. We propose a simple bias-reduced evaluation protocol that replaces the labels of each question with uniform, unordered labels and prompts the LLM to use the whole answer presented. With a simple sentence similarity model, we demonstrate improved robustness and lower standard deviation between different permutations of answers with a minimal drop in the LLM’s performance, exposing the LLM’s capabilities under reduced evaluation artifacts, without any help from the prompt examples or the option labels. Across multiple benchmarks and models, this protocol substantially improves the robustness to answer permutations, reducing mean accuracy variance $3\times$ with only a minimal decrease in the model’s mean performance. Through ablation studies on various embedding models and similarity functions, we show that the method is more robust than the standard ones.

paragraphs: Multiple-choice tests can reward habits that have little to do with understanding the question. Using a synthetic benchmark called NonsenseQA, this paper finds that language models differ in how strongly they rely on option positions, answer labels, and patterns in the correct answers shown in prompt examples. These influences can also act together.

The proposed evaluation protocol changes how answers are presented and returned. It uses uniform, unordered labels and asks the model to provide the complete answer text. A sentence-similarity model then supports matching the response to the available answers. This reduces the opportunity for arbitrary labels and ordering to drive the result.

Across multiple models and benchmarks, the protocol makes scores more stable when answer options are rearranged. The authors report a threefold reduction in mean accuracy variance, with only a small decrease in average performance. Ablations involving different embedding models and similarity functions support the method's robustness. The resulting scores better expose capabilities under reduced evaluation artifacts.
summary.tldr: Changing multiple-choice labels and requesting full answer text reduces evaluation bias and makes scores more stable across answer orderings.

title: ABCD: All Biases Come Disguised

abstract: Imitation Learning (IL) learns high-quality policies from expert demonstrations but degrades in low-expert-data regimes. To address this, recent work studies “offline IL with supplementary data", augmenting expert data with trajectories from suboptimal policies. A prominent framework is Distribution Correction Estimation (DICE), which estimates density ratios via the dual of a divergence minimization problem between learned and expert visitation distributions. However, existing DICE-based methods either rely on a strict coverage assumption or introduce additional dataset regularization, limiting performance. We propose ReDICE, a new DICE-based method that addresses these issues through an objective-level reformulation. Our approach constructs a mixture-distribution objective that preserves the original expert-imitation objective while removing the coverage assumption, and its dual reduces to a stable Gumbel regression objective for efficient optimization. We further introduce a novel policy extraction mechanism that improves performance. Experiments on standard and real-world offline IL benchmarks show that ReDICE consistently outperforms prior methods and achieves state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: Imitation learning becomes harder when expert demonstrations are scarce. Supplementing them with trajectories from weaker policies provides more data, but introduces the problem of learning expert-like behavior from a mixed-quality dataset. This paper revisits Distribution Correction Estimation, which uses density ratios to reconcile the visitation distributions of a learned policy and an expert.

Earlier DICE-based methods either impose a strict coverage assumption or add dataset regularization, which the authors identify as performance limitations. ReDICE changes the objective itself. It constructs a mixture-distribution objective that retains the original expert-imitation objective while removing the coverage assumption. Its dual becomes a stable Gumbel regression problem, providing a route to efficient optimization.

The framework also introduces a new mechanism for extracting a policy from the learned solution. Experiments on standard and real-world offline imitation benchmarks report consistent improvements over prior methods and state-of-the-art results. The key contribution is an objective reformulation that changes how supplementary data can be used while preserving the expert-imitation goal, together with an optimization form and policy extraction procedure that make the reformulation practical.
summary.tldr: ReDICE reformulates offline imitation learning to remove a strict coverage assumption while preserving the expert-imitation objective.

title: Revisiting Distribution Correction Estimation for Offline Imitation Learning with Suboptimal Dataset

abstract: Graph neural networks have been widely used in Boolean satisfiability (SAT) tasks to learn structural information from SAT formulas. The goal of these studies is to solve SAT instances or to enhance SAT solvers, including tasks such as unsat-core prediction. However, most existing approaches model a SAT formula as a bipartite graph or a directed acyclic graph, which are less direct in capturing clause-level and higher-order interactions among literals and clauses. Moreover, these approaches are limited in modeling intrinsic polarity-related properties of SAT, such as the complementary relationship between the positive and negative literals of a variable. To address these limitations, we propose a polarity-aware representation learning framework over clause-literal hypergraphs. We model SAT formulas as clause-literal hypergraphs augmented with a clause incidence graph to capture higher-order structural interactions. We then introduce a polarity-aware decomposition mechanism that separates variable representations into polarity invariant and equivariant components, explicitly modeling the relationship between positive and negative literals, with the resulting literal representations propagated along the hypergraph structure. We further incorporate a polarity-inversion consistency regularization to reinforce polarity-consistent representations during training. Experimental results on multiple SAT datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Boolean satisfiability problems involve clauses built from positive and negative literals. Learning useful representations requires capturing both interactions among clauses and the complementary relationship between the two forms of a variable. This paper targets unsat-core prediction, arguing that common graph representations capture these higher-order and polarity-related properties less directly.

The proposed framework represents formulas as clause-literal hypergraphs, supplemented by a clause incidence graph. This structure models interactions involving groups of literals and clauses. A polarity-aware decomposition separates each variable’s representation into an invariant component and an equivariant component, allowing the model to represent both shared information and information that changes with polarity.

The resulting literal representations propagate through the hypergraph. During training, polarity-inversion consistency regularization further encourages representations to behave consistently when polarity is inverted. Experiments on multiple SAT datasets demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness. The contribution combines a representation of clause-level structure with an explicit treatment of positive-negative relationships, giving the learning system access to two important aspects of SAT formulas.
summary.tldr: A polarity-aware hypergraph framework improves SAT representation learning by explicitly modeling clause interactions and positive-negative literal relationships.

title: Unsat Core Prediction through Polarity-Aware Representation Learning over Clause-Literal Hypergraphs

abstract: Negative sampling is an important yet challenging component in self-supervised graph representation learning, particularly for recommendation systems where user-item interactions are modeled as bipartite graphs. Existing methods often rely on heuristics or human-specified principles to design negative sampling distributions. This potentially overlooks the usage of an underlying “true” negative distribution, which we might be able to access as an oracle despite not knowing its exact form. In this work, we shift the focus from manually designing negative sampling distributions to a more principled method that approximates and leverages the underlying true distribution from the ground up. We expand this idea in the analysis of two scenarios: (1) when the observed graph is an unbiased sample from the true distribution, and (2) when the observed graph is biased with partially observable positive edges. The analysis result is the derivation of a sampling strategy as the numerical approximation of a well-established learning objective. Our theoretical findings are also empirically validated, and our new sampling methods achieve state-of-the-art performance on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems can represent users and items as two sets of nodes connected by observed interactions. Learning useful representations from this graph depends partly on how negative examples are sampled. The paper questions the usual practice of choosing a sampling distribution through heuristics or manually specified principles.

The authors instead investigate whether an underlying true negative distribution can be approximated and used, even when its exact mathematical form is unknown. Their starting point is the possibility of accessing that distribution through an oracle. They analyze two observation settings: one in which the graph is an unbiased sample, and another in which observations are biased and positive edges are only partially visible.

From this analysis, they derive a sampling strategy as a numerical approximation to an established learning objective. This ties the sampling rule to the objective and observation assumptions rather than treating it as a separate design choice. Empirical results validate the theoretical findings and report state-of-the-art performance on real-world datasets. The work offers a principled route from assumptions about observed interactions to the construction of negative samples.
summary.tldr: The paper derives recommendation negative-sampling strategies from an underlying distribution and learning objective, analyzing both unbiased and partially observed biased graphs.

title: Negative Sampling From the Ground Up: A Redesign for Recommendations

abstract: 4-bit quantization reduces the memory footprint and latency of large language model inference, but its aggressive precision reduction can severely degrade accuracy. Prior methods address this by decomposing each weight matrix into two components (e.g., via singular value decomposition) and quantizing them separately, assigning the bulk of values to a low-precision residual component while handling outliers with a high-precision low-rank component. However, such decompositions are designed to minimize the real-valued energy of the residual, rather than the post-quantization error of the residual and low-rank components. We propose TwinQuant, a 4-bit quantization framework that learns quantization-friendly decomposed subspaces and jointly reshapes both the low-rank and residual components. TwinQuant learns component-specific transformations via a joint optimization over the Stiefel and general linear manifolds, flattening their distributions and reducing dynamic-range imbalance. To enable efficient end-to-end execution, we further design a fused dual-component kernel that pipelines the two-stage low-rank computation on-chip and merges both components with a single epilogue, avoiding intermediate global-memory traffic. Across LLaMA3 and Qwen3 models, TwinQuant preserves near-FP16 accuracy and delivers up to $1.8\times$ end-to-end speedup over an FP16 baseline.

paragraphs: Four-bit quantization can reduce language-model memory use and inference latency, but accuracy can suffer. Existing decomposition methods separate weights into a residual and a low-rank component, often handling outliers in the latter. TwinQuant identifies a mismatch: a decomposition that reduces real-valued residual energy need not minimize error after both components are quantized.

TwinQuant learns subspaces suited to quantization and jointly reshapes the residual and low-rank components. Across LLaMA3 and Qwen3 models, TwinQuant retains accuracy close to FP16 and achieves up to 1.8 times end-to-end speedup over an FP16 baseline. The results connect quantization-aware representation design with an execution strategy that makes the decomposition efficient.
summary.tldr: TwinQuant learns quantization-friendly weight decompositions and uses a fused kernel to retain near-FP16 accuracy with up to 1.8× speedup.

title: TwinQuant: Learnable Subspace Decomposition for 4-Bit LLM Quantization

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) perform well on commonsense reasoning tasks but struggle with visual spatial reasoning. Most existing solutions introduce extra 3D prior inputs or external spatial encoders, which increase complexity and degrade the underlying VLMs’ general-purpose capabilities after spatial fine-tuning. To this end, we propose a parameter-efficient Spatio-vision Language Models (SpatioLM), that enhances spatial intelligence without extra 3D prior inputs or third-party spatial encoders. Concretely, we design a plug-and-play and non-invasive spatio-vision module that elicits the spatial knowledge inherent in VLMs. Furthermore, we innovatively leverage pseudo depth and camera information as supervision to guide the model in learning physically coherent representations. Extensive experiments show that SpatioLM achieves significant improvements in diverse tasks, including spatial perception and understanding while effectively limiting the degradation of general capabilities. Notably, the model achieves an impressive score of 71.6 on the VSI-Bench (the first model to surpass 70). In addition, it attains competitive performance when transferred to embodied manipulation tasks.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can handle commonsense questions while still struggling to reason about spatial relationships in images. SpatioLM aims to improve this ability with a parameter-efficient addition to an existing model. It avoids requiring extra 3D prior inputs or a separate third-party spatial encoder, both of which can add complexity to spatial adaptation.

The approach introduces a plug-and-play spatio-vision module designed to elicit spatial knowledge already present in the underlying model. Training uses pseudo depth and camera information as supervision to encourage physically coherent representations. This distinction matters: depth-related information guides learning without being introduced as an extra 3D prior input requirement.

Experiments show significant improvements across spatial perception and understanding tasks while limiting degradation of general-purpose capabilities. SpatioLM reaches 71.6 on VSI-Bench, which the authors report as the first result above 70, and transfers competitively to embodied manipulation tasks. These findings support a focused adaptation strategy that strengthens spatial reasoning while reducing the disruption to broader model abilities that can accompany spatial fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: SpatioLM improves visual spatial reasoning with a compact module and pseudo-depth supervision while limiting losses in general capabilities.

title: SpatioLM: Towards General Physical Spatial Intelligence in Vision-Language Models

abstract: Effective time series forecasting enables various real-world applications, benefiting from the proliferation of mobile devices. However, the volume of time series data may vary significantly across domains due to high data acquisition costs and data regulations. To maximally create value from sparse data, this study focuses on a new problem of source-free time series forecasting, aiming to adapt a pretrained model from sufficient source time series to the sparse target time series without access to the source data, enabling data protection. To achieve this, we propose TimeID, a novel source-free time series forecasting framework with a large language model (LLM) centric proxy denoising inspired by the powerful generalization capabilities of LLMs. Specifically, TimeID consists of three key components: (1) dual-branch invariant disentangled feature learning that enforces representation- and gradient-wise invariance by means of season-trend decomposition; (2) lightweight, parameter-free proxy denoising that dynamically calibrates systematic biases of LLMs; and (3) knowledge distillation that bidirectionally aligns the denoised prediction and the original target prediction. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that TimeID outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving MSE and MAE by 10.7% and 9.3% on average. The code is available at https://github.com/decisionintelligence/TimeID.

paragraphs: TimeID studies adapting a pretrained forecasting model to a target domain with little time-series data, without accessing the source data used for pretraining. This source-free setting matters when acquisition costs or data regulations prevent pooling observations across domains. The available model must carry useful source knowledge into adaptation while learning from sparse target observations.

The framework combines three components. A dual-branch feature learner separates seasonal and trend information and enforces invariance at both the representation and gradient levels. A lightweight, parameter-free proxy denoising mechanism dynamically corrects systematic biases associated with the language model. Finally, bidirectional knowledge distillation aligns the denoised prediction with the original target prediction, linking the corrected guidance to the target forecasting process.

Across real-world datasets, the authors report average improvements of 10.7% in mean squared error and 9.3% in mean absolute error over state-of-the-art baselines. The results support using invariant features together with calibrated language-model guidance for source-free adaptation. The practical contribution is improved forecasting in a setting where target observations are limited and source observations are unavailable during adaptation.
summary.tldr: TimeID combines invariant features, language-model proxy denoising, and distillation to adapt forecasting models using sparse target data without source-data access.

title: Invariant Representation Learning for Source-Free Time Series Forecasting with LLM-Centric Proxy Denoising

abstract: D-peptide binders targeting L-proteins have promising therapeutic potential. Despite rapid advances in machine learning-based target-conditioned peptide design, generating D-peptide binders remains largely unexplored. In this work, we show that by injecting axial features to E(3)-equivariant (polar) vector features, it is feasible to achieve cross-chirality generalization from homo-chiral (L-L) training data to hetero-chiral (D-L) design tasks. By implementing this method within a latent diffusion model, we achieved D-peptide binder design that not only outperforms existing tools in in silico benchmarks, but also demonstrates efficacy in wet-lab validation. To our knowledge, our approach represents the first experimentally validated AI generative model for the de novo design of D-peptide binders, offering new perspectives on handling chirality in protein design. Codes are available at https://github.com/YZY010418/PepMirror

paragraphs: Designing D-peptides that bind L-proteins requires a model to handle interactions between molecules with different handedness. The paper studies whether training on L-peptide–L-protein interactions can support this different design task. This matters because D-peptide binders have therapeutic potential, while their generation has received relatively little attention in machine-learning peptide design.

The proposed method adds axial features to the polar vector features of an E(3)-equivariant model. The authors show that this representation change makes generalization from same-handed training interactions to differently handed design interactions feasible. They implement the approach within a latent diffusion model to generate new D-peptide binders conditioned on protein targets.

The resulting designs outperform existing tools in computational benchmarks and demonstrate efficacy in laboratory validation. The authors describe the model, to their knowledge, as the first experimentally validated AI generative approach for designing D-peptide binders from scratch. The findings support the value of explicitly representing chirality when transferring learned interaction patterns across molecular handedness.
summary.tldr: Adding axial features enables a peptide diffusion model trained on L-L interactions to design D-peptide binders with computational and laboratory validation.

title: Cross-Chirality Generalization by Axial Vectors for Hetero-Chiral Protein-Peptide Interaction Design

abstract: LLM workflows, which coordinate structured calls to individual LLMs/agents to achieve a particular goal, offer a promising path towards building powerful AI systems that can tackle diverse tasks. However, existing approaches for building such workflows generally rely on human-crafted pipelines and prompts, which presents a substantial bottleneck in real world deployment. How can we automatically induce LLM-based agents and workflows in a data-driven way? This paper describes a simple data-driven approach for automatically inducing agents and LLM workflows. We formulate workflow induction as a bilevel optimization problem: an outer loop which optimizes a high-level sketch of the workflow (in particular how the LLM calls should be structured), and an inner loop which optimizes each individual LLM call one-by one. Both loops are optimized with "textual gradients" where for the inner loop we optimize each component in a modular way through "backpropagating" textual gradients layer-by-layer. We find that LLM workflows discovered through our FlowBot (workflow induction through bilevel optimization and textual gradients) approach performs competitively against strong baselines that make use of human-crafted or generated workflows.

Both loops are optimized with "textual gradients" where for the inner loop we optimize each component in a modular way through "backpropagating" textual gradients layer-by-layer. paragraphs: An LLM workflow coordinates several model or agent calls to complete a task. Designing both the arrangement of those calls and their individual prompts often requires substantial human effort. FlowBot studies how to learn these workflows from data, treating their construction as an optimization problem with two connected levels.

The outer optimization loop changes a high-level sketch describing how the calls should be organized. The inner loop improves the individual calls one at a time. Both use textual gradients: feedback expressed in language to guide revisions. Within the inner loop, that feedback is passed backward through the workflow layer by layer so components can be improved modularly.

The discovered workflows perform competitively against strong baselines using human-crafted or generated workflows. That finding supports automated workflow induction as a viable approach, without claiming that it consistently beats those alternatives. The distinctive idea is to optimize the overall arrangement and its local components together, giving data-driven feedback a role at both levels of system design.
summary.tldr: FlowBot learns LLM workflow structures and individual calls through nested optimization with textual feedback, achieving competitive performance against strong baselines.

title: FlowBot: Inducing LLM Workflows with Bilevel Optimization and Textual Gradients

abstract: Human gameplay is a visually grounded interaction loop in which players act, reflect on failures, and watch tutorials to refine strategies. Can Vision-Language Models (VLMs) also learn from video-based reflection? We present GameVerse, a comprehensive video game benchmark that enables a reflective visual interaction loop. Moving beyond traditional fire-and-forget evaluations, it uses a novel reflect-and-retry paradigm to assess how VLMs internalize visual experience and improve policies. To facilitate systematic and scalable evaluation, we also introduce a cognitive hierarchical taxonomy spanning 15 globally popular games, dual action space for both semantic and GUI control, and milestone evaluation using advanced VLMs to quantify progress. Our experiments show that VLMs benefit from video-based reflection in varied settings, and perform best by combining failure trajectories and expert tutorials—a training-free analogue to reinforcement learning (RL) plus supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

paragraphs: GameVerse asks whether vision-language models can improve gameplay by reviewing visual experience. A single attempt measures what a model can do immediately, but does not capture whether watching a failed attempt or an expert demonstration helps it choose better actions. The benchmark therefore centers evaluation on reflection followed by another attempt.

It covers 15 globally popular games, organized through a hierarchical taxonomy of cognitive demands. Models can act through either semantic controls or graphical-interface controls. Progress is measured through milestones evaluated with advanced vision-language models. These elements provide a systematic setting for studying how visual experience affects later behavior across different games and interaction modes.

The experiments find benefits from video-based reflection in varied settings. Models perform best when they combine recordings of their own failures with expert tutorials. The authors describe this as a training-free analogue of combining reinforcement learning with supervised fine-tuning: failures and demonstrations both inform improvement, without training the model through those procedures. The result supports evaluating adaptation across attempts as a distinct capability.
summary.tldr: GameVerse finds that vision-language models improve gameplay through video reflection, especially when combining their failures with expert tutorials.

title: GameVerse: Can Vision-Language Models Learn from Video-based Reflection?

abstract: We address the challenging task of 3D object segmentation in complex scene point clouds without relying on any scene-level human annotations during training. Existing methods are typically constrained to identifying simple objects, primarily due to insufficient object priors in the learning process. In this paper, we present FoundObj, a novel framework featuring a superpoint-based object discovery agent that incrementally merges suitable neighboring superpoints, guided by our innovative semantic and geometric reward modules. These modules synergistically leverage semantic and geometric priors from self-supervised 2D/3D foundation models, providing complementary feedback to the object discovery agent and enabling robust identification of multi-class objects through reinforcement learning. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines. Notably, our method exhibits strong generalization in zero-shot and long-tail scenarios, underscoring its potential for scalable, label-free 3D object segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/vLAR-group/FoundObj

paragraphs: FoundObj tackles the task of separating objects within complex 3D point clouds without scene-level human annotations during training. The authors argue that existing approaches struggle beyond simple objects because their learning process lacks sufficient prior knowledge about objects. Their approach obtains that guidance from self-supervised foundation models operating on 2D and 3D information.

The framework uses an object-discovery agent that starts from superpoints, which are groups of points, and progressively merges suitable neighboring groups. Reinforcement learning guides these decisions through two reward modules. One supplies semantic feedback about object meaning, while the other supplies geometric feedback about shape and structure. These complementary signals provide a way to learn object groupings without the scene annotations the task excludes.

Across diverse benchmarks, FoundObj consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines. The authors also report strong generalization in zero-shot and long-tail settings. These findings support the potential of foundation-model rewards to extend label-free segmentation to multiple object classes and to settings where examples or familiar categories are limited.
summary.tldr: FoundObj learns to merge 3D point groups into objects using semantic and geometric rewards from self-supervised foundation models.

title: FoundObj: Self-supervised Foundation Models as Rewards for Label-free 3D Object Segmentation

abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance by explicitly generating chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, but this reasoning process can be manipulated by adversarial prompts. Inference-time CoT interventions offer a simple and lightweight approach to improving safety, yet existing methods typically apply static heuristics that ignore the dynamic nature of reasoning, leading to an inherent trade-off between robustness and over-refusal. This paper introduces SafeCompass, a plug-and-play framework for dynamically steering chain-of-thought reasoning using inference-time safety signals extracted from internal states. At different reasoning positions, SafeCompass derives a latent safety direction through contrastive analysis of internal representations and uses this direction to quantify the model’s current safety state. These signals enable selective intervention, allowing the model’s reasoning trajectory to be modified only when and where it becomes unsafe. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SafeCompass significantly improves robustness, reducing the average attack success rate up to $10\times$ compared to the best baseline, while preserving general reasoning performance and minimizing over-refusal rates.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can be manipulated through adversarial prompts, including attacks that influence their generated reasoning. Static interventions apply fixed rules despite changes in the reasoning process, creating tension between resisting attacks and refusing legitimate requests. SafeCompass addresses this by using the model’s evolving internal state to decide when intervention is needed.

At different positions in reasoning, the framework compares internal representations to derive a latent safety direction. It uses that direction to measure the current safety state and selectively steer the reasoning trajectory when it becomes unsafe. The framework operates at inference time and is presented as a plug-and-play method.

Experiments report reductions in average attack success rate of up to tenfold relative to the best baseline, while preserving general reasoning performance and minimizing over-refusal. The result supports the value of making intervention responsive to the model’s state during generation. The reported improvement is an experimental outcome, with the largest reduction describing an achieved result rather than a uniform effect across every setting.
summary.tldr: SafeCompass uses internal safety signals to selectively steer reasoning during inference, reducing attack success while preserving general reasoning performance.

title: SafeCompass: Dynamic Chain-of-Thought Steering via Inference-Time Safety Signals

abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding answers free-form text queries over reconstructed scenes. However, lifting dense 2D foundation-model embeddings into 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is still challenging. Existing 3DGS-based methods often average normalized embeddings in Euclidean space. This ignores their hyperspherical geometry and can cause feature collapse. They also distill supervision from all views equally, which amplifies occlusion noise and mixed-depth artifacts. We propose Rh-3DGS, a robust semantic 3DGS framework that uses reliability-aware distillation and manifold-consistent aggregation. Visibility-Calibrated Distillation (VCD) computes per-pixel reliability weights from rasterization statistics and down-weights ambiguous pixels. Visibility-Weighted Fréchet Mean (VFM) aggregates embeddings on the unit hypersphere with a Riemannian Huber objective for robust distillation. Lightweight Consistency Contrast (LIC) regularizes the 3D semantic field with neighborhood-based multi-positive contrast to improve local consistency and sharper boundaries. Experiments on three benchmarks show that Rh-3DGS is best on open-vocabulary segmentation, boundary quality, and view-consistent rendering.

This ignores their hyperspherical geometry and can cause feature collapse. They also distill supervision from all views equally, which amplifies occlusion noise and mixed-depth artifacts. Lightweight Consistency Contrast (LIC) regularizes the 3D semantic field with neighborhood-based multi-positive contrast to improve local consistency and sharper boundaries. paragraphs: Open-vocabulary scene understanding connects free-form text queries to reconstructed 3D scenes. Transferring image-model embeddings into 3D Gaussian Splatting is difficult because observations can be occluded or mix depths. The paper also identifies a geometric problem: averaging normalized embeddings in ordinary Euclidean space ignores their location on a unit hypersphere and can cause feature collapse.

Rh-3DGS addresses reliability and geometry together. Visibility-Calibrated Distillation derives per-pixel weights from rasterization statistics to reduce the influence of ambiguous observations. Visibility-Weighted Fréchet Mean aggregates embeddings on the hypersphere using a Riemannian Huber objective, providing robust distillation that respects their geometry. A Lightweight Consistency Contrast component further organizes the semantic field through neighborhood-based, multi-positive contrast.

These components aim to preserve local consistency and produce sharper semantic boundaries across views. On three benchmarks, the authors report the best performance in open-vocabulary segmentation, boundary quality, and view-consistent rendering. The results support treating observation reliability and embedding geometry as complementary considerations when transferring two-dimensional semantic information into a shared three-dimensional scene.
summary.tldr: Rh-3DGS combines visibility-aware supervision with hyperspherical feature aggregation to improve text-queryable 3D scene understanding.

title: Rh-3DGS: Robust Open-Vocabulary Scene Understanding via Riemannian Huber Distillation and Manifold-Aware Sampling

abstract: Model collapse, the degradation in performance that arises when generative models are trained on the outputs of prior models, is an increasing concern as artificially generated content proliferates. Related critiques of large language models have highlighted their tendency to reproduce frequent patterns in training data, their reliance on vast datasets, and their substantial environmental cost. Together, these factors contribute to data degradation, the reinforcement of cultural biases, and inefficient resource use. In this position paper we aim to combine these views and argue that model collapse threatens current efforts to democratise AI. By reducing training efficiency and skewing data distributions away from the tails of their support, model collapse disproportionately impacts low-resource and marginalized communities. We examine both the environmental and cultural implications of this phenomenon, situate our position within recent position papers on model collapse, and conclude with a call to action. Finally, we outline initial directions for mitigating these effects.

paragraphs: This position paper connects model collapse to concerns about who benefits from AI. Model collapse is performance degradation associated with training generative models on outputs from earlier models. The authors argue that growing amounts of generated content can make this phenomenon a threat to efforts to democratize AI.

Their argument brings together critiques of language models’ tendency to reproduce common patterns, dependence on large datasets, and environmental costs. Model collapse can shift data distributions away from less common content while reducing training efficiency. The paper argues that these effects disproportionately burden low-resource and marginalized communities, linking a technical degradation process to cultural exclusion and unequal access.

The authors examine environmental and cultural implications, place their position alongside recent discussions of collapse, and outline initial mitigation directions. Their central contribution is to frame data degradation as a distributional concern: the loss of less frequent patterns matters for communities already poorly represented in training material. Inefficient resource use adds another pressure to the same democratization goals.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that model collapse disproportionately threatens low-resource communities through loss of uncommon data patterns and reduced training efficiency.

abstract: We propose a formulation of the Decision Tree learning algorithm in the Compression settings and derive tight generalization error bounds. In particular, we propose Sample Compression and Occam’s Razor bounds. We show how such bounds, unlike the VC dimension or Rademacher complexities based bounds, are more general and can also perform a margin-sparsity trade-off to obtain better classifiers. Potentially, these risk bounds can also guide the model selection process and replace traditional pruning strategies.
originalAbstract: We propose a formulation of the Decision Tree learning algorithm in the Compression settings and derive tight generalization error bounds. In particular, we propose Sample Compression and Occam’s Razor bounds. We show how such bounds, unlike the VC dimension or Rademacher complexities based bounds, are more general and can also perform a margin-sparsity trade-off to obtain better classifiers. Potentially, these risk bounds can also guide the model selection process and replace traditional pruning strategies.

paragraphs: This paper recasts decision-tree learning in a compression setting and derives tight bounds on generalization error. Generalization error concerns how a learned classifier performs beyond its training examples. The compression perspective provides a way to analyze that risk through the information used to specify the learned classifier.

The authors develop both sample-compression bounds and Occam's Razor bounds. They describe these bounds as more general than bounds based on VC dimension or Rademacher complexities. A further feature is their ability to support a tradeoff between margin and sparsity, allowing these aspects of a classifier to be balanced in obtaining better classifiers.

The proposed bounds therefore have a potential role beyond assessing a completed tree. They could guide model selection by comparing candidate models through their risk bounds. The authors also suggest that this could replace traditional pruning strategies, which simplify decision trees. That replacement is presented as a possibility, not as an established outcome. The core contribution is the compression-based analysis and the decision-making possibilities it opens for tree learning.
summary.tldr: Compression-based generalization bounds for decision trees support margin–sparsity tradeoffs and could guide model selection instead of pruning.

title: Sample compression bounds for decision trees

abstract: Rich representations in reinforcement learning have been studied for the purpose of enabling generalization and making learning feasible in large state spaces. We introduce Object-Oriented MDPs (OO-MDPs), a representation based on objects and their interactions, which is a natural way of modeling environments and offers important generalization opportunities. We introduce a learning algorithm for deterministic OO-MDPs, and prove a polynomial bound in its sample complexity. We illustrate the performance gains of our representation and algorithm in the well-known Taxi domain, plus a real-life videogame.
originalAbstract: Rich representations in reinforcement learning have been studied for the purpose of enabling generalization and making learning feasible in large state spaces. We introduce Object-Oriented MDPs (OO-MDPs), a representation based on objects and their interactions, which is a natural way of modeling environments and offers important generalization opportunities. We introduce a learning algorithm for deterministic OO-MDPs, and prove a polynomial bound in its sample complexity. We illustrate the performance gains of our representation and algorithm in the well-known Taxi domain, plus a real-life videogame.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when an environment has a large number of possible states. The representation of those states matters because it determines what structure a learner can reuse across experiences. This paper introduces Object-Oriented Markov Decision Processes, which describe environments through objects and their interactions.

The representation creates opportunities to generalize by expressing the environment in terms of its constituent entities and their relationships. The authors pair it with a learning algorithm for deterministic object-oriented environments. They prove a polynomial bound on the algorithm's sample complexity, giving a theoretical account of how much experience learning requires within that setting.

The paper illustrates performance gains in the Taxi domain and a real-life video game. These demonstrations connect the representational proposal to concrete learning tasks. The contribution includes both a way to describe structured environments and an algorithm with a learning-efficiency guarantee. The deterministic setting is an explicit part of the algorithm and bound, so that guarantee should be understood within that scope.
summary.tldr: Object-Oriented MDPs represent objects and interactions, enabling a deterministic learning algorithm with polynomial sample complexity.

title: An object-oriented representation for efficient reinforcement learning

abstract: We consider feature extraction (dimensionality reduction) for compositional data, where the data vectors are constrained to be positive and constant-sum. In real-world problems, the data components (variables) usually have complicated "correlations" while their total number is huge. Such scenario demands feature extraction. That is, we shall de-correlate the components and reduce their dimensionality. Traditional techniques such as the Principle Component Analysis (PCA) are not suitable for these problems due to unique statistical properties and the need to satisfy the constraints in compositional data. This paper presents a novel approach to feature extraction for compositional data. Our method first identifies a family of dimensionality reduction projections that preserve all relevant constraints, and then finds the optimal projection that maximizes the estimated Dirichlet precision on projected data. It reduces the compositional data to a given lower dimensionality while the components in the lower-dimensional space are de-correlated as much as possible. We develop theoretical foundation of our approach, and validate its effectiveness on some synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Compositional data consists of positive components whose sum is fixed. When there are many components and complicated relationships among them, dimensionality reduction is attractive. The difficulty is that the smaller representation must respect the data's constraints and statistical properties. The paper identifies these requirements as a reason traditional techniques such as PCA are unsuitable for the problems considered.

The proposed method first identifies a family of projections that preserve the relevant compositional constraints. It then chooses the projection that maximizes estimated Dirichlet precision in the projected data. Thus, the optimization takes place within a family of representations already designed to remain valid for compositional data.

The result has a specified lower dimensionality, with its components decorrelated as much as possible under the approach. The authors develop a theoretical foundation and validate effectiveness on synthetic and real-world datasets. The central contribution is to treat constraint preservation and reduction of component dependence as connected parts of feature extraction, rather than handling dimensionality alone.
summary.tldr: Dirichlet component analysis reduces compositional data while preserving its constraints and seeking components that are as decorrelated as possible.

title: Dirichlet component analysis: feature extraction for compositional data

abstract: Online sequence prediction is the problem of predicting the next element of a sequence given previous elements. This problem has been extensively studied in the context of individual sequence prediction, where no prior assumptions are made on the origin of the sequence. Individual sequence prediction algorithms work quite well for long sequences, where the algorithm has enough time to learn the temporal structure of the sequence. However, they might give poor predictions for short sequences. A possible remedy is to rely on the general model of prediction with expert advice, where the learner has access to a set of r experts, each of which makes its own predictions on the sequence. It is well known that it is possible to predict almost as well as the best expert if the sequence length is order of log (r) . But, without firm prior knowledge on the problem, it is not clear how to choose a small set of good experts. In this paper we describe and analyze a new algorithm that learns a good set of experts using a training set of previously observed sequences. We demonstrate the merits of our approach by experimenting with the task of click prediction on the web.

paragraphs: Online sequence prediction uses the elements already observed to predict the next one. Methods that make no assumptions about a sequence's origin can learn useful temporal structure when sequences are long. For short sequences, however, there may be too little time to learn that structure before predictions are needed.

Prediction with expert advice offers a possible remedy by combining a set of predictors. With r experts, established results allow performance close to the best expert when sequence length is on the order of log(r). The practical difficulty is obtaining a small set that contains useful experts when prior knowledge of the task is limited.

The paper introduces and analyzes an algorithm that learns the expert set from previously observed training sequences. This transfers information from earlier sequences into the collection available for predicting new ones. Experiments on web click prediction demonstrate the approach's merits. The contribution addresses the construction of the expert pool itself, a necessary practical choice behind applying expert-advice methods to short sequences.
summary.tldr: Learning a compact set of prediction experts from past sequences helps address the difficulty of predicting short new sequences.

title: Learning the Experts for Online Sequence Prediction
